ANAT-1 Embryology of the respiratory system

133 questions · 31 high-yield
Learning questions 95

Where the airway comes from: lung bud and germ layers

L1Learning
What is the first sign of the developing respiratory system?
  1. A. The tracheo-oesophageal septum
  2. B. The laryngotracheal diverticulum
  3. C. The hypopharyngeal eminence
AnswerB. The laryngotracheal diverticulum
The laryngotracheal diverticulum (respiratory diverticulum, lung bud) is the first sign of the respiratory system: a pouch growing out of the foregut around day 28.
Explanation

The laryngotracheal diverticulum is a pouch of foregut endoderm, with its coat of splanchnic mesoderm, that grows out of the floor of the primordial pharynx in week 4. It is also called the respiratory diverticulum or lung bud. The larynx, trachea, bronchi and lungs all grow from it.

  • The tracheo-oesophageal septum comes afterwards: folds on either side of the diverticulum fuse to wall it off from the oesophagus.
  • The hypopharyngeal eminence is a swelling in the pharyngeal floor that forms the back of the tongue. It is a landmark beside the laryngotracheal groove, not the start of the airway.
Slide (1)
L2Learning
From which part of the gut tube does the lung bud arise?
  1. A. The ventral wall of the foregut
  2. B. The dorsal wall of the foregut
  3. C. The ventral wall of the hindgut
AnswerA. The ventral wall of the foregut
The respiratory diverticulum buds from the ventral wall of the foregut, which is why the trachea lies in front of (ventral to) the oesophagus.
Explanation

The foregut is the cranial part of the gut tube formed by embryonic folding; its first part is the primordial pharynx. The respiratory diverticulum pushes out of its ventral (front) wall into the surrounding splanchnic mesoderm. Its distal end swells into the lung bud, and its proximal part becomes the trachea.

  • Dorsal wall of the foregut: the dorsal part of the partitioned foregut becomes the oesophagus, not the airway.
  • Hindgut: the caudal end of the gut tube (distal colon, rectum) has nothing to do with the lungs.

Hook: airway in front, food tube behind, in the embryo as in the adult.

Slide (1)
L3Learning
Around when does the laryngotracheal diverticulum appear?
  1. A. Day 35 (week 5)
  2. B. Day 21 (week 3)
  3. C. Day 28 (week 4)
AnswerC. Day 28 (week 4)
The laryngotracheal diverticulum appears in week 4, around day 28; the two bronchial buds follow in week 5.
Explanation

The lecture calls this stage the 28-day embryo. By about day 28 (the 4th week) the diverticulum has budded from the foregut, and the tracheo-oesophageal septum forms over weeks 4–5.

  • Day 21 (end of week 3): the embryo is only starting to fold and the heart tube has not yet begun to beat (that starts around day 22); there is no airway bud yet.
  • Day 35 (end of week 5) is too late: by then the respiratory bud has already divided into the bronchial buds (week 5), and they are starting to branch.
Slides (2)
L4Learning
What is the laryngotracheal groove, and what does it become?
  1. A. The opening of the diverticulum into the pharynx → the laryngeal inlet
  2. B. The furrow between the tracheo-oesophageal folds → the tracheo-oesophageal septum
  3. C. The opening of the diverticulum into the pharynx → the foramen caecum
AnswerA. The opening of the diverticulum into the pharynx → the laryngeal inlet
The laryngotracheal groove is the diverticulum's opening in the floor of the pharynx; it persists as the (primordial) laryngeal inlet.
Explanation

As the diverticulum grows down from the floor of the primordial pharynx, its mouth stays open to the pharynx. That opening is the laryngotracheal groove. It becomes the primordial laryngeal inlet, framed by swellings of pharyngeal-arch mesenchyme: the epiglottal swelling in front and the two arytenoid swellings at the sides.

  • The foramen caecum is a pit higher up in the pharyngeal floor, on the tongue (where the thyroid starts); it is not the airway opening.
  • The tracheo-oesophageal septum forms from folds that fuse in the midline below the inlet; it separates the two tubes rather than opening the airway.
Slides (3)
L5Learning
In the developing larynx, which swelling becomes the epiglottis?
  1. A. The arytenoid swellings on either side of the laryngotracheal groove
  2. B. The lateral lingual swellings of the first pharyngeal arch
  3. C. The epiglottal swelling at the caudal end of the hypopharyngeal eminence
AnswerC. The epiglottal swelling at the caudal end of the hypopharyngeal eminence
The epiglottis grows from the epiglottal swelling, the caudal part of the hypopharyngeal eminence, which sits just in front of the laryngeal inlet.
Explanation

The hypopharyngeal eminence is a midline bulge in the floor of the pharynx, made by mesenchyme of the 3rd and 4th pharyngeal arches. Its caudal part becomes a separate epiglottal swelling, which lies directly in front of the laryngeal inlet and develops into the epiglottis. Meanwhile the two arytenoid swellings grow up beside the opening and turn the slit-like laryngotracheal groove into a T-shaped laryngeal inlet.

  • Arytenoid swellings form the sides of the inlet, not the flap in front of it.
  • Lateral lingual swellings (arch 1) form the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, well in front of the larynx.

Hook: front to back in the pharyngeal floor: tongue, then epiglottis, then the inlet framed by the arytenoid swellings.

Slide (1)
L6Learning
Which germ layer forms the epithelial lining and the glands of the larynx, trachea and bronchi?
  1. A. Surface ectoderm
  2. B. Endoderm
  3. C. Splanchnic mesoderm
AnswerB. Endoderm
The lining comes from the endoderm of the foregut diverticulum, so airway epithelium and glands are endodermal, like the gut lining.
Explanation

The respiratory diverticulum is an outgrowth of foregut endoderm. Everything that grows from that endodermal tube is endodermal: the pseudostratified ciliated epithelium with goblet cells of the trachea and bronchi, the submucosal glands (which bud from the epithelium) and, further down, the alveolar epithelium.

  • Splanchnic mesoderm wraps around the tube and forms the wall: cartilage, smooth muscle and connective tissue.
  • Surface ectoderm lines the mouth and nasal cavity, not the lower airway.

Hook: lining = endoderm; everything around it = mesoderm.

Slides (2)
L7Learning
What forms the cartilage, smooth muscle and connective tissue of the trachea and bronchi?
  1. A. Mesoderm of pharyngeal arches 4 and 6
  2. B. Somatic mesoderm of the body wall
  3. C. Splanchnic (visceral) mesoderm around the foregut
AnswerC. Splanchnic (visceral) mesoderm around the foregut
Splanchnic mesoderm around the foregut forms the airway wall: cartilage, smooth muscle and connective tissue, plus vessels and visceral pleura.
Explanation

Splanchnic (visceral) mesoderm is the layer of lateral plate mesoderm that clings to the endoderm of the gut tube. As the diverticulum grows into it, this mesenchyme forms the C-shaped tracheal cartilages, the trachealis and bronchial smooth muscle, the connective tissue and the vessels. It also coats the lung bud as the visceral pleura.

  • Somatic mesoderm lines the body wall; for the lungs it gives only the parietal pleura.
  • Pharyngeal arches 4 and 6 form the muscles and cartilages of the larynx, not of the trachea and bronchi.
Slides (2)
L8Learning
Which of these lung components develops from endoderm?
  1. A. The endothelium of the alveolar capillaries
  2. B. The epithelial cells lining the alveoli (pneumocytes)
  3. C. The smooth muscle wrapped around the bronchi
AnswerB. The epithelial cells lining the alveoli (pneumocytes)
Lung-bud endoderm lines the whole tree down to the alveoli; muscle, cartilage and capillaries come from splanchnic mesoderm.
Explanation

As the lung buds branch, their endoderm keeps lining every new tube. It becomes the mucosal epithelium of the bronchi and, at the far end, the type I and type II pneumocytes of the alveoli.

  • Bronchial smooth muscle, like cartilage and connective tissue, comes from the surrounding splanchnic mesoderm.
  • Capillary endothelium also comes from splanchnic mesoderm. The blood–air barrier therefore has a double origin: endodermal type I cell plus mesodermal endothelium.
Slides (2)
L9Learning
What do the laryngeal muscles and cartilages develop from, and which nerve supplies the larynx as a result?
  1. A. Mesoderm of pharyngeal arches 1 and 2 → trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V)
  2. B. Mesoderm of pharyngeal arch 3 → glossopharyngeal nerve (cranial nerve IX)
  3. C. Mesoderm of pharyngeal arches 4 and 6 → vagus nerve (cranial nerve X)
AnswerC. Mesoderm of pharyngeal arches 4 and 6 → vagus nerve (cranial nerve X)
Laryngeal muscles and cartilages come from arches 4 and 6, whose nerve is the vagus (CN X): superior laryngeal (arch 4) and recurrent laryngeal (arch 6).
Explanation

Unlike the trachea, whose wall comes from splanchnic mesoderm, the larynx is built from pharyngeal arch mesoderm. Each arch brings its own nerve, so muscles from arches 4 and 6 are supplied by branches of the vagus: the superior laryngeal nerve (arch 4, cricothyroid) and the recurrent laryngeal nerve (arch 6, the other intrinsic laryngeal muscles).

  • Arch 3 forms the stylopharyngeus, supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX).
  • Arches 1 and 2 give the muscles of mastication (trigeminal, CN V) and of facial expression (facial, CN VII).
Slides (2)

Splitting the airway from the oesophagus

L10Learning
Before it is walled off, the lumen of the respiratory diverticulum is continuous with which space?
  1. A. The lumen of the foregut (primordial pharynx)
  2. B. The pericardial cavity
  3. C. The pericardioperitoneal canals
AnswerA. The lumen of the foregut (primordial pharynx)
The diverticulum is an outgrowth of the foregut, so at first its lumen opens freely into the gut; a septum has to separate the two.
Explanation

Because the airway starts as a pouch of the gut, the future air passage and food passage first share one lumen. The tracheo-oesophageal septum then grows in and divides them, leaving only the upper opening (the laryngeal inlet) shared with the pharynx.

  • The pericardioperitoneal canals are coelomic spaces outside the gut. The lung buds grow into them later, pushing their wall ahead of them, but the airway lumen never opens into them.
  • The pericardial cavity is another coelomic space, around the heart; it is never connected to the gut lumen.
Slides (2)
L11Learning
Which structure partitions the foregut into the trachea and the oesophagus?
  1. A. The tracheo-oesophageal septum
  2. B. The pleuropericardial folds
  3. C. The septum transversum
AnswerA. The tracheo-oesophageal septum
The tracheo-oesophageal septum, made by the fused tracheo-oesophageal folds, partitions the foregut into the laryngotracheal tube and the oesophagus.
Explanation

The tracheo-oesophageal septum is the midline partition that separates the airway from the food tube. When it forms incompletely or deviates, the result is tracheo-oesophageal fistula and/or oesophageal atresia.

  • The septum transversum is a plate of mesoderm below the heart that becomes the central tendon of the diaphragm. It separates body cavities, not gut lumens. The names are a classic mix-up.
  • The pleuropericardial folds separate the pericardial cavity from the pleural cavities.
Slides (2)
L12Learning
How does the tracheo-oesophageal septum form?
  1. A. The foregut lumen fills with an epithelial plug that later recanalises
  2. B. Tracheo-oesophageal folds grow in from each side and fuse in the midline
  3. C. A single fold grows down from the roof of the pharynx and fuses with its floor
AnswerB. Tracheo-oesophageal folds grow in from each side and fuse in the midline
Longitudinal tracheo-oesophageal folds (ridges) appear on both sides of the diverticulum and fuse into the septum.
Explanation

The tracheo-oesophageal folds are ridges that bulge into the foregut lumen from its two sides. As they grow toward each other and fuse, they form the tracheo-oesophageal septum. The tube in front becomes the laryngotracheal tube; the one behind becomes the oesophagus.

  • Epithelial plug and recanalisation is how the oesophagus later restores its own lumen; incomplete recanalisation gives oesophageal stenosis, not a septum.
  • The folds come from the sides, not from the roof. That is why the slides show them in cross-section as two indentations meeting in the middle.
Slides (2)
L13Learning
What does the tracheo-oesophageal septum divide the foregut into?
  1. A. A ventral laryngotracheal tube and a dorsal oesophagus
  2. B. A right laryngotracheal tube and a left oesophagus
  3. C. A dorsal laryngotracheal tube and a ventral oesophagus
AnswerA. A ventral laryngotracheal tube and a dorsal oesophagus
The septum leaves the laryngotracheal tube ventrally (in front) and the oesophagus dorsally (behind), as in the adult neck.
Explanation

The laryngotracheal tube is the primordium of the larynx, trachea, bronchi and lungs; its distal end is the respiratory bud. The dorsal part of the foregut becomes the oesophagus.

  • Dorsal trachea, ventral oesophagus swaps the pair: the diverticulum budded from the ventral wall, so the airway stays in front.
  • The partition runs in the coronal plane, separating front from back, not right from left.
Slides (2)

Tracheo-oesophageal fistula and oesophageal atresia

L14Learning
What developmental error causes tracheo-oesophageal fistula with oesophageal atresia?
  1. A. Failure of the pleuroperitoneal membranes to fuse
  2. B. Incomplete fusion of the tracheo-oesophageal folds (faulty septum)
  3. C. Incomplete recanalisation of the oesophagus after its plug
AnswerB. Incomplete fusion of the tracheo-oesophageal folds (faulty septum)
TEF and oesophageal atresia come from faulty partitioning: the tracheo-oesophageal folds fail to fuse fully, so the septum leaves trachea and oesophagus connected.
Explanation

A fistula is an abnormal passage between two organs. In TEF the trachea and oesophagus stay connected because the tracheo-oesophageal septum is incomplete (standard texts describe it deviating posteriorly). The same faulty partition usually leaves the oesophagus interrupted (oesophageal atresia), which is why the two so often occur together.

  • Incomplete recanalisation of the oesophagus gives oesophageal stenosis: a narrowed lumen with no connection to the airway.
  • Pleuroperitoneal membrane failure gives a congenital diaphragmatic hernia.
Slide (1)
L15Learning
What is oesophageal atresia?
  1. A. An interrupted lumen: the upper oesophagus ends in a blind pouch
  2. B. An abnormal passage connecting the trachea to the oesophagus
  3. C. A narrowed but continuous oesophageal lumen
AnswerA. An interrupted lumen: the upper oesophagus ends in a blind pouch
Atresia means an obstructed lumen: the oesophagus is not continuous, and its upper segment ends in a blind pouch.
Explanation

In oesophageal atresia the oesophagus does not form one continuous tube. The upper (proximal) segment ends blindly in the neck or upper chest, so nothing swallowed can reach the stomach that way. It is usually combined with a fistula to the trachea.

  • An abnormal passage between trachea and oesophagus is the fistula, the other half of the TEF/EA pair.
  • A narrowed but continuous lumen is stenosis, which allows some passage.

Hook: atresia = a-tresis, "no opening".

Slides (2)
L16Learning
How common is tracheo-oesophageal fistula, and which sex is more often affected?
  1. A. About 1 in 3000–4500 live births; girls more often
  2. B. About 1 in 3000–4500 live births; boys more often
  3. C. About 1 in 300–450 live births; girls more often
AnswerB. About 1 in 3000–4500 live births; boys more often
TEF affects about 1 in 3000–4500 live births, and males more often than females.
Explanation

TEF is one of the more common serious congenital anomalies, at roughly 1 in 3000–4500 live births, with a male predominance. Oesophageal atresia accompanies it in most cases.

  • 1 in 300–450 is ten times too common.
  • It is boys, not girls, who are more often affected.
Slide (1)
L17Learning
What is the commonest variety of tracheo-oesophageal fistula (about 85%)?
  1. A. H-type fistula between a continuous trachea and oesophagus, with no atresia
  2. B. Oesophageal atresia with a blind lower pouch + a fistula from the trachea to the upper oesophagus
  3. C. Oesophageal atresia with a blind upper pouch + a fistula from the trachea to the lower oesophagus
AnswerC. Oesophageal atresia with a blind upper pouch + a fistula from the trachea to the lower oesophagus
About 85% of cases are atresia with a distal fistula: blind upper pouch, and the lower oesophagus opening into the trachea.
Explanation

In this commonest variety (type C in the gross classification on the slide, about 82–87%) the upper oesophagus ends blindly, and the lower oesophagus arises from the trachea near the carina. Saliva and milk pool in the pouch and spill into the larynx; air passes from the trachea into the stomach; gastric juice can reflux up into the lungs.

  • A fistula from the upper pouch alone is rare (about 1–4%).
  • H-type (fistula without atresia) is about 4%.

Remaining varieties: isolated atresia (about 8%) and fistulas at both ends (rare).

Slides (2)
L18Learning
A newborn with oesophageal atresia has gas in the stomach on an abdominal X-ray. What does the gas show?
  1. A. A fistula connects the trachea to the lower oesophagus
  2. B. A fistula connects the trachea to the blind upper pouch only
  3. C. Swallowed air passes through the blind upper pouch to the stomach
AnswerA. A fistula connects the trachea to the lower oesophagus
With atresia nothing swallowed reaches the stomach, so stomach gas must come from the airway through a distal fistula (trachea → lower oesophagus).
Explanation

Every breath and every cry pushes air from the trachea through the fistula into the lower oesophagus and stomach, so the stomach and bowel contain gas and may be distended. This is the commonest variety: blind upper pouch + distal fistula.

  • A fistula from the upper pouch only sends swallowed feed into the trachea, but no air can reach the stomach: the abdomen is gasless.
  • A blind pouch passes nothing down; that is what atresia means.

Rule: atresia + gas in the stomach = distal fistula. Atresia + gasless abdomen = isolated atresia or a proximal fistula only.

Slides (2)
L19Learning
A newborn with oesophageal atresia has no gas at all in the stomach or bowel. Which variety fits?
  1. A. Atresia with fistulas at both the upper and the lower ends
  2. B. Atresia with a fistula between the trachea and the lower oesophagus
  3. C. Atresia with a fistula between the upper pouch and the trachea
AnswerC. Atresia with a fistula between the upper pouch and the trachea
No stomach gas means no distal fistula. Of these, only atresia with a proximal (upper-pouch) fistula leaves the stomach airless.
Explanation

In the proximal-fistula variety the blind upper pouch opens into the trachea, so all swallowed contents go into the airway, with choking and aspiration at every feed. The lower oesophagus is sealed off from both air and food. Isolated atresia without any fistula gives the same gasless abdomen.

  • A distal fistula lets air pass from the trachea into the stomach.
  • With fistulas at both ends, the distal one again lets air reach the stomach.
Slides (2)
L20Learning
A newborn chokes as swallowed milk enters the trachea, and also aspirates refluxed gastric contents through the trachea. Which variety explains both findings?
  1. A. Atresia with a fistula at the lower end only
  2. B. Atresia with a fistula at the upper end only
  3. C. Atresia with fistulas at both the upper and the lower ends
AnswerC. Atresia with fistulas at both the upper and the lower ends
Swallowed feed reaching the trachea needs a proximal fistula; gastric reflux reaching it needs a distal one. Both together = double fistula.
Explanation

In the double-fistula variety the oesophagus is interrupted, and both segments open into the trachea. Swallowed milk crosses the proximal fistula into the airway, and acid gastric contents reflux up the lower oesophagus and through the distal fistula into the lungs. The risk of aspiration and pneumonitis is very high.

  • A lower-end fistula only explains reflux into the lungs, but swallowed milk would pool in the blind pouch and be regurgitated rather than enter the trachea directly.
  • An upper-end fistula only explains swallowed milk entering the trachea, but the stomach is sealed off from the airway, so reflux cannot reach it.
Slide (1)
L21Learning
What is an H-type tracheo-oesophageal fistula?
  1. A. A fistula between a continuous trachea and a continuous oesophagus, with no atresia
  2. B. A blind upper oesophageal pouch with no fistula to the trachea
  3. C. A blind upper oesophageal pouch, with the lower oesophagus joined to the trachea
AnswerA. A fistula between a continuous trachea and a continuous oesophagus, with no atresia
H-type = fistula without atresia: both tubes are continuous and joined by a cross-bar, like the letter H.
Explanation

Because the oesophagus is patent, feeds reach the stomach. But some liquid crosses the fistula into the trachea (coughing, choking, recurrent aspiration pneumonia), and air crosses into the oesophagus and stomach. As swallowing works, an H-type fistula can be missed at birth and found later in an infant with repeated chest infections. It makes up about 4% of cases.

  • A blind pouch with no fistula is isolated oesophageal atresia (about 8%).
  • A blind upper pouch with the lower oesophagus joined to the trachea is the commonest variety, atresia with a distal fistula.
Slide (1)
L22Learning
What is seen in the mouth and nose of a newborn with oesophageal atresia and fistula?
  1. A. A dry mouth, because no saliva is produced
  2. B. Clear watery nasal discharge that stops after suctioning
  3. C. Excess saliva: fine white frothy mucus that returns after suctioning
AnswerC. Excess saliva: fine white frothy mucus that returns after suctioning
Saliva cannot pass the blind pouch, so it pools as fine white frothy mucus in the mouth and nose and comes back after suctioning.
Explanation

A newborn swallows saliva continuously. With atresia it fills the blind upper pouch and wells back up, so the baby looks as if it is drooling or blowing bubbles of fine white froth from the mouth and nose. Suctioning clears it only briefly. This is often the first sign, even before the first feed.

  • Saliva production is normal; the problem is that it cannot be swallowed, so the mouth is wet, not dry.
  • The secretions are frothy mucus that recurs after suction, not a clear discharge that stops.
Slides (2)
L23Learning
What happens at feeds in a newborn with oesophageal atresia and fistula?
  1. A. Chokes, gags and turns cyanotic; regurgitates milk (because of the atresia)
  2. B. Feeds well, then develops projectile non-bilious vomiting after a few weeks
  3. C. Chokes and gags but never regurgitates milk (because of the fistula)
AnswerA. Chokes, gags and turns cyanotic; regurgitates milk (because of the atresia)
Milk fills the blind pouch and spills into the larynx: gagging, coughing and cyanosis at feeds, with regurgitation of the milk the atresia blocks.
Explanation

The blind upper pouch holds only a few millilitres. When it fills, milk comes back up (regurgitation) and overflows into the larynx and trachea, so the baby gags, coughs, chokes and turns blue (cyanosis) during or right after the feed.

  • Regurgitation is the hallmark of the atresia: milk that cannot pass must come back up.
  • Feeding well, then projectile non-bilious vomiting at a few weeks is hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, a classic distractor.
Slides (2)
L24Learning
How does a distal tracheo-oesophageal fistula cause aspiration pneumonia or pneumonitis?
  1. A. The septum compresses the main bronchi, so secretions are trapped
  2. B. Gastric contents reflux through the fistula into the lungs
  3. C. Saliva cannot drain into the stomach, so the stomach wall breaks down
AnswerB. Gastric contents reflux through the fistula into the lungs
Acid stomach contents reflux up the lower oesophagus, cross the fistula into the trachea and reach the lungs: chemical pneumonitis and aspiration pneumonia.
Explanation

The distal fistula connects the trachea to the stomach end of the oesophagus. Gastric acid and feed can travel the wrong way, up into the airway, and inflame the lungs (pneumonitis) or seed infection (aspiration pneumonia). Overflow from the blind upper pouch adds further aspiration.

  • Saliva that cannot reach the stomach pools in the pouch and is aspirated from there; the stomach itself is not damaged.
  • The septum does not compress the bronchi; the problem is an abnormal opening, not a narrowing.
Slides (2)
L25Learning
Why does a pregnancy with oesophageal atresia often show polyhydramnios?
  1. A. The fetus inhales amniotic fluid into its lungs instead of swallowing it
  2. B. The fetal kidneys produce excess urine
  3. C. The fetus cannot swallow amniotic fluid into its gut
AnswerC. The fetus cannot swallow amniotic fluid into its gut
Amniotic fluid is normally cleared by fetal swallowing and absorption in the gut. With atresia it cannot pass, while urine keeps adding fluid: polyhydramnios.
Explanation

Polyhydramnios is an excess of amniotic fluid. The fetus keeps passing urine into the amniotic cavity, and normally swallows the fluid, absorbs it in the gut and passes it via the placenta to the mother. A blind oesophagus breaks this loop, so fluid builds up.

  • Fetal breathing movements move fluid in and out of the lungs, but the lungs cannot take over the job of removing it; if anything they add their own secreted fluid to the amniotic cavity.
  • Urine output is normal; it is removal that fails. The opposite problem, no urine (bilateral renal agenesis), gives oligohydramnios.
Slide (1)
L26Learning
Which prenatal ultrasound findings suggest oesophageal atresia with tracheo-oesophageal fistula?
  1. A. Polyhydramnios
    Small or absent stomach bubble
    Low fetal weight
  2. B. Polyhydramnios
    Large, dilated stomach bubble
    High fetal weight
  3. C. Oligohydramnios
    Small or absent stomach bubble
    Low fetal weight
AnswerA. Polyhydramnios
Small or absent stomach bubble
Low fetal weight
Prenatally: polyhydramnios, little or no fluid ("air") in the fetal stomach, and low fetal weight.
Explanation

The stomach bubble is the fluid-filled fetal stomach seen on ultrasound (the slide says "lack of air in fetal stomach"). If swallowed fluid cannot get past the atresia, the stomach stays small or invisible. Low fetal weight is the third prenatal clue.

  • Oligohydramnios is the opposite (too little fluid), seen with renal agenesis or urinary obstruction.
  • A large stomach bubble would mean fluid is getting in; with duodenal atresia a dilated stomach plus duodenum gives a "double bubble".
Slide (1)
L27Learning
How is oesophageal atresia usually diagnosed after birth?
  1. A. A chest X-ray shows a "double bubble" sign
  2. B. A catheter cannot be passed from the mouth into the stomach
  3. C. A catheter cannot be passed from the nose into the trachea
AnswerB. A catheter cannot be passed from the mouth into the stomach
Most cases are found after birth (birth to about 12 days) when a catheter passed from the mouth cannot reach the stomach: it stops or coils in the blind pouch.
Explanation

A soft orogastric or nasogastric tube is advanced from the mouth (or nose) toward the stomach. In atresia it meets resistance at the end of the upper pouch, and an X-ray shows the radiopaque tube curled in the upper chest. Although prenatal clues exist, most cases are diagnosed between birth and about 12 days.

  • The tube is passed into the oesophagus toward the stomach, not into the trachea.
  • The double bubble (stomach + duodenum full of gas) is the sign of duodenal atresia.
Slide (1)
L28Learning
How is tracheo-oesophageal fistula with oesophageal atresia treated?
  1. A. Surgery, always at once regardless of weight or illness
  2. B. Surgery, postponed if the baby is very small or has pneumonia
  3. C. Nasogastric feeding until the fistula closes on its own
AnswerB. Surgery, postponed if the baby is very small or has pneumonia
Treatment is surgical correction, which may be postponed for very low birth weight or complications such as pneumonia.
Explanation

The fistula has to be divided and the oesophagus joined, so surgery is the definitive treatment. If the infant is very small or already has aspiration pneumonia, the operation may be delayed while the baby is stabilised (the upper pouch is kept suctioned and the infant is fed by other routes).

  • A fistula from failed partitioning does not close on its own.
  • Surgery is not "always immediate": the lecture specifically allows postponement.
Slide (1)

Bronchial buds, lobes and pleura

L29Learning
What does the distal end of the laryngotracheal tube swell into?
  1. A. The primordial laryngeal inlet
  2. B. The hypopharyngeal eminence
  3. C. The respiratory (lung) bud
AnswerC. The respiratory (lung) bud
The distal end of the laryngotracheal tube swells into the respiratory bud, which divides into the bronchial buds.
Explanation

The laryngotracheal tube has two ends. Its distal (lower) end expands into a globular respiratory (lung) bud, from which the whole bronchial tree branches. Its proximal end becomes the larynx and trachea.

  • The laryngeal inlet is at the proximal end, where the tube opens into the pharynx.
  • The hypopharyngeal eminence is a swelling in the pharyngeal floor (back of the tongue), not part of the tube.
Slides (2)
L30Learning
What does the respiratory bud divide into in week 5?
  1. A. Two bronchial buds: the future right and left main bronchi
  2. B. Three bronchial buds: the future lobar bronchi
  3. C. Five bronchial buds: one for each future lobe
AnswerA. Two bronchial buds: the future right and left main bronchi
In week 5 the respiratory bud divides into two bronchial buds, the primary buds that become the right and left main bronchi.
Explanation

The first division of the respiratory bud is into two (primary) bronchial buds, one per lung. Each then branches again: 3 secondary buds on the right and 2 on the left (the lobes), then 10 and 8 tertiary buds (the segments).

  • Three buds is the count of secondary buds on the right side only, one division later.
  • Five is the total number of lobes; they come from secondary, not primary, buds.
Slides (2)
L31Learning
Which bronchial buds correspond to the lobes of the lungs?
  1. A. Primary bronchial buds: 3 on the right, 2 on the left
  2. B. Secondary bronchial buds: 3 on the right, 2 on the left
  3. C. Secondary bronchial buds: 2 on the right, 3 on the left
AnswerB. Secondary bronchial buds: 3 on the right, 2 on the left
The secondary (lobar) bronchial buds, 3 right and 2 left, give the right upper/middle/lower and left upper/lower lobes.
Explanation

Branching runs: respiratory bud → 2 primary buds (main bronchi) → secondary buds (lobar bronchi: 3 right, 2 left, hence 3 and 2 lobes) → tertiary buds (segmental bronchi: 10 right, 8 left).

  • 2 right, 3 left swaps the sides: the right lung is the one with the middle lobe.
  • There are only two primary buds, one per lung.

The older slide calls the lobar branches "3 main bronchi on the right, 2 on the left"; anatomically, "main" bronchi are the two primary ones.

Slides (2)
L32Learning
How many tertiary (segmental) bronchial buds form on each side, and what does each become?
  1. A. 8 on the right, 10 on the left; each supplies a bronchopulmonary segment
  2. B. 10 on the right, 8 on the left; each supplies a bronchopulmonary segment
  3. C. 10 on the right, 8 on the left; each supplies a lung lobe
AnswerB. 10 on the right, 8 on the left; each supplies a bronchopulmonary segment
Secondary buds give 10 right and 8 left tertiary buds, the segmental bronchi, each supplying one bronchopulmonary segment.
Explanation

A bronchopulmonary segment is the part of a lobe supplied by one segmental (tertiary) bronchus with its own artery; it is the smallest surgically removable unit of lung. The pattern is set by the tertiary buds around week 7.

  • 8 right, 10 left swaps the sides: the larger right lung has more segments.
  • Lobes correspond to the secondary buds, one level up.
Slides (2)
L33Learning
What drives the repeated branching of the bronchial buds into the bronchial tree?
  1. A. The endoderm of the buds on its own; the surrounding tissue only wraps the finished tubes
  2. B. The surrounding splanchnic mesoderm (connective tissue), which signals the endodermal buds to divide
  3. C. The somatic mesoderm of the body wall, which the buds press against as they grow
AnswerB. The surrounding splanchnic mesoderm (connective tissue), which signals the endodermal buds to divide
Branching is driven by the splanchnic mesoderm (connective tissue) around the buds: its signals make the endodermal buds divide again and again.
Explanation

The bronchial tree is built by an epithelial–mesenchymal interaction. The endodermal bud supplies the tube, but it branches only where the surrounding splanchnic mesoderm (the future connective tissue, cartilage and smooth muscle of the airway wall) signals it to; these signals include members of the fibroblast growth factor (FGF) family. The review slide puts it as “branching occurs via septation from connective tissue in the walls”: the connective tissue around and between the buds splits each tip into new branches. Each segmental bronchus with its own mass of mesenchyme becomes a bronchopulmonary segment.

  • Endoderm on its own does not branch: stripped of its mesoderm, the bud stops dividing.
  • Somatic mesoderm lines the body wall and forms only the parietal pleura; the pleural cavity separates it from the growing buds.
Slides (2)
L34Learning
Into which spaces do the growing lung buds push, and what do those spaces become?
  1. A. The pericardioperitoneal canals → the pleural cavities
  2. B. The pleuroperitoneal canals → the peritoneal cavity
  3. C. The pericardioperitoneal canals → the pericardial cavity
AnswerA. The pericardioperitoneal canals → the pleural cavities
The lung buds grow laterally into the pericardioperitoneal canals, the channels on either side of the foregut that become the pleural cavities.
Explanation

The pericardioperitoneal canals are narrow coelomic channels that link the pericardial and peritoneal cavities on each side of the foregut. As the lungs expand into them, the canals enlarge into the pleural cavities; folds later seal them off from the pericardial cavity (pleuropericardial folds) and from the peritoneal cavity (pleuroperitoneal membranes).

  • The lungs never enter the peritoneal cavity; the openings toward it are closed off by the pleuroperitoneal membranes.
  • The pericardial cavity houses the heart; the lungs grow around it, not into it.
Slides (2)
L35Learning
What does the visceral pleura develop from?
  1. A. Somatic mesoderm lining the body wall
  2. B. Endoderm of the lung buds
  3. C. Splanchnic mesoderm carried on the growing lung buds
AnswerC. Splanchnic mesoderm carried on the growing lung buds
The lung buds push into the canals wearing their coat of splanchnic mesoderm; that coat becomes the visceral pleura.
Explanation

The visceral pleura is the serous membrane stuck to the lung surface. It comes from the splanchnic (visceral) mesoderm that surrounds the foregut and is carried outward on the lung buds as they grow. The pairing helps: splanchnic mesoderm = organ (viscus) side.

  • Somatic mesoderm lines the body wall and forms the parietal pleura.
  • Endoderm forms the airway and alveolar epithelium inside the lung, not its outer covering.
Slide (1)
L36Learning
What does the parietal pleura develop from?
  1. A. Splanchnic mesoderm covering the lung buds
  2. B. Somatic mesoderm lining the body wall
  3. C. Endoderm lining the pericardioperitoneal canals
AnswerB. Somatic mesoderm lining the body wall
The parietal pleura lines the cavity wall, so it comes from the somatic mesoderm of the body wall.
Explanation

Lateral plate mesoderm splits into two layers: somatic (with the body wall) and splanchnic (with the gut). The pleural cavity forms between them. The somatic layer lines the outside of the cavity as the parietal pleura; the splanchnic layer covers the lung as the visceral pleura.

  • Splanchnic mesoderm covering the buds gives the visceral pleura.
  • The canals are coelomic spaces lined by mesoderm, not endoderm.
Slide (1)

Stages of lung maturation: timing and landmarks

L37Learning
What are the four classic stages of lung maturation, in order, with their timing?
  1. A. Pseudoglandular 6–16 wk → canalicular 16–26 wk → terminal sac 26 wk–birth → alveolar 32 wk–8 yr
  2. B. Pseudoglandular 6–16 wk → terminal sac 16–26 wk → canalicular 26 wk–birth → alveolar 32 wk–8 yr
  3. C. Canalicular 6–16 wk → pseudoglandular 16–26 wk → terminal sac 26 wk–birth → alveolar 32 wk–8 yr
AnswerA. Pseudoglandular 6–16 wk → canalicular 16–26 wk → terminal sac 26 wk–birth → alveolar 32 wk–8 yr
Pseudoglandular 6–16 wk, Canalicular 16–26 wk, Terminal sac 26 wk–birth, Alveolar 32 wk–8 yr.
Explanation

The stages follow the airway outward: first the conducting tubes (pseudoglandular), then the respiratory bronchioles and a blood supply (canalicular), then thin-walled terminal sacs (terminal sac), then mature alveoli (alveolar). The alveolar stage overlaps the terminal sac stage from 32 weeks.

  • The current lecture adds an embryonic stage (weeks 4–5) before these four. Newer textbooks give overlapping windows: about 5–17, 16–25, 24 weeks to late fetal life, and late fetal life to 8 years.
  • The wrong orders swap canalicular with its neighbours.

Hook: "Please Call The Alveoli".

Slide (1)
L38Learning
What happens in the embryonic stage of lung development (weeks 4–5 in the lecture)?
  1. A. The conducting airways branch down to the terminal bronchioles
  2. B. The lung bud forms and divides into bronchial buds (main, lobar, segmental)
  3. C. Respiratory bronchioles and alveolar ducts form and capillaries invade
AnswerB. The lung bud forms and divides into bronchial buds (main, lobar, segmental)
The embryonic stage is lung-bud formation and its first divisions into main, lobar and segmental bronchial buds.
Explanation

The current lecture lists the embryonic stage as weeks 4–5 (a review session gives weeks 4–7): the respiratory diverticulum appears, the tracheo-oesophageal septum forms, and the bud divides into the primary, secondary and tertiary bronchial buds.

  • Branching down to the terminal bronchioles is the pseudoglandular stage (6–16 weeks).
  • Respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts and rich capillaries are the canalicular stage (16–26 weeks).
Slide (1)
L39Learning
In which stage is a 12-week fetal lung that has bronchi and terminal bronchioles but no respiratory bronchioles or alveoli?
  1. A. Pseudoglandular stage (6–16 weeks)
  2. B. Terminal sac stage (26 weeks to birth)
  3. C. Canalicular stage (16–26 weeks)
AnswerA. Pseudoglandular stage (6–16 weeks)
At 12–14 weeks the lung is pseudoglandular: every conducting airway down to the terminal bronchioles exists, but nothing that exchanges gas.
Explanation

The pseudoglandular stage builds the whole conducting tree by repeated rounds of branching (the lecture's "15–25" counts these rounds, not individual bronchioles), ending in terminal bronchioles. Respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, sacs and alveoli all come later.

  • Canalicular lungs already have respiratory bronchioles and alveolar ducts.
  • Terminal sac lungs have thin-walled sacs (primitive alveoli) with capillaries bulging into them.

Exam trap: at 14 weeks the only structure in the list that exists is the terminal bronchiole.

Slides (2)
L40Learning
What forms in the pseudoglandular stage (6–16 weeks)?
  1. A. Simple columnar endodermal tubes branch repeatedly down to terminal bronchioles; few capillaries
  2. B. Terminal sacs bud from alveolar ducts; capillaries bulge into them
  3. C. Cuboidal tubes form respiratory bronchioles and alveolar ducts; rich capillaries
AnswerA. Simple columnar endodermal tubes branch repeatedly down to terminal bronchioles; few capillaries
Pseudoglandular: endodermal tubes of simple columnar epithelium branch repeatedly (about 15–25 rounds) down to the terminal bronchioles; only some capillaries. The lung looks like a gland.
Explanation

Under the microscope the lung resembles an exocrine gland: blind-ending epithelial tubes in loose mesenchyme with few capillaries. All the conducting airways form here. The lecture's "15–25 terminal bronchioles" counts rounds (generations) of branching, not individual bronchioles: the finished conducting tree ends in tens of thousands of terminal bronchioles. The current slide adds that the epithelium starts to differentiate (pseudostratified ciliated columnar cells, goblet cells).

  • Respiratory bronchioles and alveolar ducts with rich capillaries describe the canalicular stage.
  • Terminal sacs with bulging capillaries describe the terminal sac stage.
Slides (2)
L41Learning
Why can a fetus born in the pseudoglandular stage not survive?
  1. A. Its alveoli have formed but have no capillaries yet
  2. B. It has conducting airways but no respiratory bronchioles or alveoli
  3. C. Its airways are still solid epithelial cords with no lumen
AnswerB. It has conducting airways but no respiratory bronchioles or alveoli
In the pseudoglandular stage there are no alveoli (no gas-exchanging part at all), so respiration is impossible and the fetus cannot survive.
Explanation

Gas exchange needs thin air spaces next to capillaries. A pseudoglandular lung has only tubes (ducts): the respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts and alveoli have not formed. A fetus born now cannot breathe however much support it gets.

  • The airways are already hollow endodermal tubes, not solid cords.
  • There are no alveoli yet, so they cannot be missing capillaries.
Slide (1)
L42Learning
In the canalicular stage, what does each terminal bronchiole give rise to?
  1. A. Three or more respiratory bronchioles, each dividing into 3–6 alveolar ducts
  2. B. 15–25 alveolar ducts directly, with no respiratory bronchioles
  3. C. Three or more terminal sacs, each dividing into 3–6 alveoli
AnswerA. Three or more respiratory bronchioles, each dividing into 3–6 alveolar ducts
Canalicular branching: terminal bronchiole → ≥3 respiratory bronchioles → 3–6 alveolar ducts, now lined by simple cuboidal epithelium.
Explanation

In the canalicular stage (16–26 weeks) the lumens of the bronchi and bronchioles widen, the tissue becomes much more vascular, and the first respiratory (gas-exchanging) portion appears: each terminal bronchiole gives off respiratory bronchioles, which divide into alveolar ducts lined by simple cuboidal epithelium. The lecture says three or more respiratory bronchioles; standard texts say two or more.

  • Terminal sacs bud from the alveolar ducts later, in the terminal sac stage.
  • 15–25 is the pseudoglandular figure (rounds of branching down to the terminal bronchioles), and alveolar ducts always come off respiratory bronchioles.
Slides (2)
L43Learning
An aborted fetus's lungs show branching tubules with thinning mesenchyme, new vascularisation around the tubules, and respiratory bronchioles. Which stage is this?
  1. A. Canalicular stage
  2. B. Alveolar stage
  3. C. Pseudoglandular stage
AnswerA. Canalicular stage
Respiratory bronchioles plus increasing vascularisation mark the canalicular stage (16–26 weeks).
Explanation

The canalicular stage gets its name from the vascular "canals" that grow into the thinning mesenchyme. Its two landmarks are the first respiratory bronchioles (branching from the terminal bronchioles) and a rich capillary network around the tubules.

  • Pseudoglandular lungs stop at terminal bronchioles, with only some capillaries.
  • Alveolar-stage lungs have mature alveoli formed by septation, long after respiratory bronchioles appeared.
Slides (2)
L44Learning
At what gestational age are alveolar ducts lined by simple cuboidal epithelium first seen?
  1. A. 32 weeks to 8 years
  2. B. 6–16 weeks
  3. C. 16–26 weeks
AnswerC. 16–26 weeks
Alveolar ducts lined by simple cuboidal epithelium appear in the canalicular stage, 16–26 weeks.
Explanation

As the canalicular stage builds the respiratory portion, the new alveolar ducts are lined by simple cuboidal cells. In the next stage this cuboidal lining thins and differentiates into type I and type II pneumocytes.

  • 6–16 weeks (pseudoglandular): the tubes are simple columnar and end in terminal bronchioles; there are no alveolar ducts yet.
  • 32 weeks–8 years (alveolar): alveolar ducts keep increasing in number, but they first appeared much earlier.
Slide (1)
L45Learning
When does respiration first become (just) possible?
  1. A. At the start of the alveolar stage
  2. B. At the end of the pseudoglandular stage
  3. C. At the end of the canalicular stage
AnswerC. At the end of the canalicular stage
By the end of the canalicular stage (about 24–26 weeks) enough respiratory bronchioles, ducts and capillaries exist for respiration to be possible, with intensive care.
Explanation

The canalicular slide says respiration "may be possible by the end of the period". Before about 20 weeks premature infants usually do not survive; survival then rises steeply with each week (in one large cohort, from about 6% at 22 weeks to about 92% at 28 weeks).

  • At the end of the pseudoglandular stage (16 weeks) there is no respiratory tissue at all.
  • The alveolar stage starts at 32 weeks, long after breathing first became possible.
Slide (1)
L46Learning
A baby is born at 24 weeks and cannot make enough surfactant. By the lecture's timings, which stage is its lung in?
  1. A. Alveolar stage
  2. B. Canalicular stage
  3. C. Pseudoglandular stage
AnswerB. Canalicular stage
24 weeks falls in the canalicular stage (16–26 weeks): surfactant production has only just begun, so there is too little.
Explanation

A 24-week lung has respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts and growing capillaries, and its first type II cells have started secreting a little surfactant. That is why such babies can sometimes survive with intensive care but nearly always develop respiratory distress.

  • Pseudoglandular ends at 16 weeks.
  • Alveolar starts at 32 weeks.

Newer textbooks start the saccular stage at 24 weeks, so 24–26 weeks is a boundary zone; with the course timings, 24 weeks is canalicular.

Slides (2)

Late stages: terminal sacs, pneumocytes and alveoli

L47Learning
In which stage do type II pneumocytes start producing surfactant, according to the current lecture?
  1. A. Canalicular stage (16–26 weeks)
  2. B. Alveolar stage (32 weeks–8 years)
  3. C. Pseudoglandular stage (6–16 weeks)
AnswerA. Canalicular stage (16–26 weeks)
The current lecture puts the start of surfactant production by type II pneumocytes in the canalicular stage (from about 20 weeks); amounts then rise.
Explanation

The first type II cells and the first small amounts of surfactant appear late in the canalicular stage (standard texts: by about 20 weeks). A 25-week preterm baby therefore has some surfactant, just not enough. Output rises through the terminal sac stage and especially from about 32–34 weeks.

  • Pseudoglandular lungs have only conducting tubes; there is no respiratory epithelium to make surfactant.
  • In the alveolar stage surfactant becomes plentiful, but production began weeks earlier.

The older lecture places the differentiation of the cuboidal cells into type I and type II pneumocytes in the terminal sac stage; both fit, because differentiation starts at the end of the canalicular stage and most of it happens in the terminal sac stage.

Slide (1)
L48Learning
What happens to the terminal sacs in the terminal sac stage (26 weeks to birth)?
  1. A. They fuse into alveolar ducts and thicken, and capillaries regress from them
  2. B. They bud from the terminal bronchioles and thicken, and capillaries stay separate
  3. C. They bud from the alveolar ducts and thin out, and capillaries bulge into them
AnswerC. They bud from the alveolar ducts and thin out, and capillaries bulge into them
Terminal sacs bud from alveolar ducts, their lining thins, and capillaries bulge into them, so gas exchange can begin.
Explanation

The terminal sacs are the primitive alveoli. As their epithelium thins and the capillary network pushes right up against it, the distance between air and blood falls enough for gas exchange. The current slide adds that vascularisation and rising surfactant reduce the risk of airway collapse, and that infants born after 24 weeks have an increasing chance of survival.

  • Development runs toward thinner walls and closer capillaries, not thicker walls and regression.
  • Sacs come from alveolar ducts; terminal bronchioles give respiratory bronchioles.
Slides (2)
L49Learning
In which stage does the simple cuboidal epithelium of the terminal sacs differentiate into type I and type II pneumocytes?
  1. A. Pseudoglandular stage (6–16 weeks)
  2. B. Alveolar stage (32 weeks–8 years)
  3. C. Terminal sac stage (26 weeks to birth)
AnswerC. Terminal sac stage (26 weeks to birth)
In the terminal sac stage the cuboidal lining differentiates into type I (gas exchange) and type II (surfactant) pneumocytes.
Explanation

Type I pneumocytes are flat (squamous) cells that cover most of the alveolar surface and form the gas-exchange side of the barrier. Type II pneumocytes are cuboidal cells with lamellar bodies that secrete surfactant. Both differentiate from the cuboidal epithelium that lined the alveolar ducts and sacs.

  • The pseudoglandular epithelium is simple columnar, lining conducting tubes only.
  • The alveolar stage adds more alveoli by septation; the cell types already exist.
Slide (1)
L50Learning
What forms the blood–air barrier in the terminal sac stage?
  1. A. Type I pneumocytes together with alveolar macrophages
  2. B. Type I pneumocytes together with the capillary endothelium
  3. C. Type II pneumocytes together with the capillary endothelium
AnswerB. Type I pneumocytes together with the capillary endothelium
In the terminal sac stage the capillaries and type I pneumocytes come into contact and form the blood–air barrier.
Explanation

The blood–air barrier is the thin layer gas must cross: the type I pneumocyte, the fused basal laminae and the capillary endothelium. It is established in the terminal sac stage, which is why survival improves from then on.

  • Type II cells are scattered cuboidal cells that secrete surfactant; they do not form the thin exchange surface.
  • Alveolar macrophages wander over the alveolar surface and clear debris; they are not part of the barrier.
Slides (2)
L51Learning
A baby is born at 27 weeks. By the lecture's timings, which stage is its lung in?
  1. A. Terminal sac stage
  2. B. Alveolar stage
  3. C. Canalicular stage
AnswerA. Terminal sac stage
27 weeks lies in the terminal sac stage (26 weeks to birth): sacs are forming, capillaries bulging in, type I and II cells differentiating.
Explanation

At 27 weeks terminal sacs are budding from the alveolar ducts, capillaries are bulging into them, and the cuboidal cells are becoming type I and type II pneumocytes. Surfactant is still often too scarce, so these infants commonly need intensive respiratory support.

  • The canalicular stage ends at 26 weeks (25 weeks in newer texts); some question stems still describe a 27-week lung as "canalicular", but on the course timings it is past that stage.
  • The alveolar stage starts at 32 weeks.
Slides (2)
L52Learning
According to the lecture, which premature infants can survive with intensive care?
  1. A. Those born at 25–28 weeks
  2. B. Those born at 12–16 weeks
  3. C. Those born at 16–20 weeks
AnswerA. Those born at 25–28 weeks
The terminal-sac slide states that infants born at 25–28 weeks can survive with intensive care; before about 20 weeks they usually do not.
Explanation

Viability tracks lung development. By 25–28 weeks terminal sacs, a blood–air barrier and some surfactant exist, so with ventilation, surfactant and oxygen many infants survive.

  • 12–16 weeks is the pseudoglandular stage: no respiratory tissue, so survival is impossible.
  • 16–20 weeks is the early canalicular stage: infants born before 20 weeks usually do not survive.
Slide (1)
L53Learning
Which two things must both be in place for a premature baby to be viable?
  1. A. A thick enough blood–air barrier
    Enough surfactant to stop alveoli overinflating
  2. B. A thin enough blood–air barrier
    Enough fetal haemoglobin to load oxygen
  3. C. A thin enough blood–air barrier
    Enough surfactant to stop alveoli collapsing
AnswerC. A thin enough blood–air barrier
Enough surfactant to stop alveoli collapsing
Viability needs a thin blood–air barrier for gas exchange and enough surfactant to keep the alveoli from collapsing.
Explanation

Both depend on the terminal sac stage: the type I cells and capillaries must be close enough for diffusion, and the type II cells must make enough surfactant to keep the small air spaces open at the end of each breath. Delivery before surfactant is adequate causes neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.

  • Fetal haemoglobin is present throughout fetal life; it is not the limiting factor.
  • The barrier must be thin, not thick, and surfactant prevents collapse, not overinflation.
Slides (2)
L54Learning
How many alveoli are there at birth and at age 8, and how are the new ones made?
  1. A. 20–70 million → 300–400 million; enlargement of existing alveoli only
  2. B. 2–7 million → 30–40 million; septation and branching of existing alveoli
  3. C. 20–70 million → 300–400 million; septation and branching of existing alveoli
AnswerC. 20–70 million → 300–400 million; septation and branching of existing alveoli
Alveoli rise from 20–70 million at birth to 300–400 million by age 8, by septation and branching of existing alveoli (alveolar stage).
Explanation

In the alveolar stage (32 weeks to 8 years) new connective tissue septa grow into the primitive sacs and subdivide them into smaller, highly vascular mature alveoli. That multiplies the surface area for gas exchange. Respiratory bronchioles, terminal sacs and alveolar ducts also keep increasing in number.

  • Enlargement only would not add alveoli; growth is mainly by adding new ones.
  • 2–7 million → 30–40 million is ten times too small.
Slide (1)
L55Learning
When do the large majority of mature alveoli form?
  1. A. After birth, from late fetal life to about 8 years
  2. B. Between 16 and 24 weeks of gestation
  3. C. Between 26 weeks of gestation and birth
AnswerA. After birth, from late fetal life to about 8 years
Most mature alveoli (about 90%) form after birth, in the alveolar stage that runs from late fetal life to about 8 years.
Explanation

A newborn has only a fraction of the adult number of alveoli. Lung maturation continues well into childhood: septation subdivides the sacs into mature alveoli, and by about age 8 the lungs reach their full alveolar number.

  • 26 weeks to birth is the terminal sac stage, which makes primitive sacs rather than mature alveoli.
  • 16–24 weeks is the canalicular stage: respiratory bronchioles and alveolar ducts.
Slides (2)

Surfactant and neonatal respiratory distress syndrome

L56Learning
Which cells make surfactant, and what does it do?
  1. A. Type II pneumocytes; it raises surface tension in the alveoli
  2. B. Type I pneumocytes; it lowers surface tension in the alveoli
  3. C. Type II pneumocytes; it lowers surface tension in the alveoli
AnswerC. Type II pneumocytes; it lowers surface tension in the alveoli
Type II pneumocytes secrete surfactant into the alveolar space, where it lowers surface tension and prevents collapse at the end of expiration.
Explanation

Surfactant is a phospholipid–protein film (mainly dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine) stored in the lamellar bodies of type II cells and secreted onto the fluid lining the alveoli. By lowering surface tension it keeps the alveoli open during exhalation and makes them easy to inflate.

  • Raising surface tension would favour collapse, the opposite of its job.
  • Type I cells are thin gas-exchange cells and do not secrete surfactant.
Slide (1)
L57Learning
What happens to an alveolus at the end of each breath when surfactant is missing?
  1. A. It overinflates and ruptures at the end of each inspiration
  2. B. It fills with amniotic fluid that cannot be cleared
  3. C. It collapses, and reopening it with each breath takes great effort
AnswerC. It collapses, and reopening it with each breath takes great effort
Without surfactant the alveolus is unstable and collapses at the end of each breath; opening it again with every breath takes tremendous work.
Explanation

The film of fluid lining each alveolus pulls inward through surface tension. Surfactant normally cuts that pull. Without it, alveoli (the small ones first) collapse at the end of expiration, and the baby must generate large pressures to reopen them on every breath. That is why premature infants with RDS tire, grunt and retract.

  • The problem is collapse (atelectasis), not overinflation.
  • Fetal lung fluid is cleared at birth by the normal routes; RDS is a surface-tension problem, not retained fluid.
Slides (2)
L58Learning
Which phospholipid is the main surface-active component of surfactant?
  1. A. Dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC, a lecithin)
  2. B. Sphingomyelin (a sphingophospholipid)
  3. C. Phosphatidylserine (an inner-membrane lipid)
AnswerA. Dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC, a lecithin)
The key surfactant lipid is dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC); phosphatidylcholine is also called lecithin.
Explanation

Surfactant is mostly phospholipid, and its main surface-active component is DPPC, a phosphatidylcholine (lecithin) carrying two saturated palmitate chains, plus surfactant proteins. Type II pneumocytes make it and store it in lamellar bodies.

  • Sphingomyelin is a membrane sphingolipid whose amniotic-fluid level stays fairly constant; it is the reference in the lecithin:sphingomyelin ratio, not the active agent.
  • Phosphatidylserine is an inner-membrane phospholipid with no surfactant role.
Slide (1)
L59Learning
Which amniotic-fluid result indicates that the fetal lungs are mature?
  1. A. A lecithin:sphingomyelin ratio below 2
  2. B. A sphingomyelin:lecithin ratio above 2
  3. C. A lecithin:sphingomyelin ratio above 2
AnswerC. A lecithin:sphingomyelin ratio above 2
Lecithin (surfactant) rises late in gestation while sphingomyelin stays flat; an L:S ratio above 2 means enough surfactant, so the lungs are mature.
Explanation

Fetal lung fluid drains into the amniotic fluid, so amniocentesis samples the surfactant the lungs are making. Sphingomyelin serves as a steady reference. When the lecithin:sphingomyelin (L:S) ratio exceeds 2, the risk of RDS is low.

  • Below 2 means immature lungs and a high risk of RDS: the trigger for giving the mother corticosteroids if delivery cannot be delayed.
  • S:L above 2 is the ratio upside down (L:S below 0.5), a very immature result.
Slides (2)
L60Learning
During which weeks of gestation does the lecithin:sphingomyelin ratio normally rise sharply above 2?
  1. A. Weeks 16–20
  2. B. Weeks 24–26
  3. C. Weeks 31–34
AnswerC. Weeks 31–34
The L:S ratio rises sharply in weeks 31–34, passing 2 as surfactant output surges; delivery before then carries a higher risk of RDS.
Explanation

Type II cells start making surfactant at the end of the canalicular stage, but output stays low until the third trimester. Around weeks 31–34 lecithin production climbs steeply and the ratio passes 2, the usual threshold for lung maturity.

  • Weeks 16–20 is the early canalicular stage, before any surfactant is made.
  • Weeks 24–26: surfactant has just begun and the ratio is well below 2, which is why babies born then usually develop RDS.
Slide (1)
L61Learning
What is given to the mother before an expected preterm delivery to speed up fetal surfactant production?
  1. A. Insulin, to keep fetal blood glucose low
  2. B. A glucocorticoid such as dexamethasone or betamethasone
  3. C. Oestrogen, to speed placental maturation
AnswerB. A glucocorticoid such as dexamethasone or betamethasone
Antenatal glucocorticoids (dexamethasone or betamethasone) given to the mother before preterm delivery boost fetal surfactant synthesis and reduce RDS.
Explanation

Corticosteroids cross the placenta and accelerate fetal lung maturation. They are given when preterm delivery cannot be stopped, for example after preterm labour, rupture of membranes or a low L:S ratio.

  • Insulin does the opposite: fetal hyperinsulinaemia (in infants of diabetic mothers) delays surfactant production.
  • Oestrogen is not used to mature the fetal lungs.
Slides (2)
L62Learning
How do antenatal corticosteroids lower the risk of respiratory distress syndrome?
  1. A. They block catecholamine release so existing surfactant breaks down more slowly
  2. B. They promote maturation of type II pneumocytes, increasing surfactant (DPPC) synthesis
  3. C. They thicken the alveolar–capillary membrane so the alveoli resist collapse
AnswerB. They promote maturation of type II pneumocytes, increasing surfactant (DPPC) synthesis
Corticosteroids mature type II pneumocytes and switch on surfactant (DPPC) synthesis, so more surfactant is present at birth.
Explanation

Glucocorticoids act on the fetal lung to speed differentiation of type II cells and raise production of DPPC and surfactant proteins. More surfactant at birth means lower surface tension, better lung compliance and less RDS.

  • A thicker barrier would hinder gas exchange; maturation thins it.
  • Steroids raise synthesis. They do not act by blocking catecholamines, and catecholamines actually stimulate surfactant secretion.
Slide (1)
L63Learning
What is neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (RDS), what else is it called, and how common is it?
  1. A. Meconium aspiration in a premature baby; hyaline membrane disease; about 2% of live newborns
  2. B. Surfactant deficiency in an immature lung; bronchopulmonary dysplasia; about 0.2% of live newborns
  3. C. Surfactant deficiency in an immature lung; hyaline membrane disease; about 2% of live newborns
AnswerC. Surfactant deficiency in an immature lung; hyaline membrane disease; about 2% of live newborns
RDS is surfactant deficiency from incomplete lung development (prematurity), also called hyaline membrane disease, affecting about 2% of live newborns.
Explanation

RDS results from incomplete lung development; premature babies are at risk because their type II cells have not made enough surfactant. The alveoli collapse, and the damaged lining leaks protein that forms eosinophilic hyaline membranes (fibrin plus cell debris), hence the other name.

  • Bronchopulmonary dysplasia is chronic lung damage that can follow RDS and its treatment; it is not another name for RDS.
  • Meconium aspiration is a different neonatal problem, usually of term or post-term babies.
Slide (1)
L64Learning
A baby born at 28 weeks becomes cyanotic within hours, with rapid shallow breathing, grunting, nasal flaring and retractions. What is the underlying cause?
  1. A. Paralysis of the diaphragm from phrenic nerve injury
  2. B. Too little surfactant from immature type II pneumocytes
  3. C. Too few type I pneumocytes to cover the alveolar surface
AnswerB. Too little surfactant from immature type II pneumocytes
Preterm + grunting, flaring, retractions and cyanosis = RDS, caused by surfactant deficiency from immature type II pneumocytes.
Explanation

Grunting (exhaling against a partly closed glottis to keep the alveoli open), nasal flaring and chest retractions are signs of a stiff lung that keeps collapsing. In a preterm baby this pattern means surfactant deficiency: the type II cells are present but not yet producing enough.

  • Type I pneumocytes form the gas-exchange surface; the defect in RDS is surfactant, not missing type I cells.
  • Phrenic nerve palsy (birth trauma) gives a raised, paralysed hemidiaphragm, not this picture in a premature infant.
Slides (2)
L65Learning
What does the chest X-ray typically show in neonatal respiratory distress syndrome?
  1. A. Diffuse bilateral "ground-glass" lungs with air bronchograms and low volumes
  2. B. Bowel loops in the left hemithorax with the heart pushed to the right
  3. C. One small lung with the mediastinum pulled toward it
AnswerA. Diffuse bilateral "ground-glass" lungs with air bronchograms and low volumes
RDS shows diffuse "ground-glass" opacity from countless collapsed alveoli (microatelectasis), with air-filled bronchi standing out, in small lungs.
Explanation

When millions of alveoli collapse, both lungs look evenly hazy, like frosted glass, while the bronchi, still full of air, show up as dark branching lines (air bronchograms). Lung volumes are low because the lungs cannot stay inflated.

  • Bowel in the left chest with a right-shifted heart is congenital diaphragmatic hernia.
  • One small lung with the mediastinum pulled toward it is unilateral pulmonary hypoplasia.
Slide (1)
L66Learning
What are the signs of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome?
  1. A. Laboured or unusual breathing
    Jaundice
    Seizures
    Decreased urine output
  2. B. Laboured or unusual breathing
    Cyanosis
    Apnoea
    Decreased urine output
  3. C. Laboured or unusual breathing
    Plethora
    Apnoea
    Increased urine output
AnswerB. Laboured or unusual breathing
Cyanosis
Apnoea
Decreased urine output
RDS presents with laboured breathing, cyanosis, apnoea and decreased urine output.
Explanation

Collapsing alveoli make breathing hard work (laboured breathing, grunting, retractions); poor oxygenation gives cyanosis; tired, immature infants have pauses in breathing (apnoea); and the sick newborn's kidneys are under-perfused, so urine output falls.

  • Plethora (a red, congested look) and more urine are the opposite of what hypoxic, sick infants show.
  • Jaundice and seizures are not features of RDS itself.
Slide (1)
L67Learning
How is neonatal respiratory distress syndrome treated?
  1. A. Artificial surfactant, oxygen and routine mechanical ventilation from birth
  2. B. Corticosteroids to the newborn, oxygen and routine mechanical ventilation
  3. C. Artificial surfactant, oxygen and CPAP; mechanical ventilation only if severe
AnswerC. Artificial surfactant, oxygen and CPAP; mechanical ventilation only if severe
Treat RDS with artificial surfactant, O2 and CPAP; mechanical ventilation only in severe cases, avoided when possible.
Explanation

Surfactant given down the trachea replaces what is missing. CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure) keeps a steady pressure in the airways so the alveoli do not collapse at the end of each breath. Oxygen corrects hypoxaemia. Mechanical ventilation can injure immature lungs (contributing to bronchopulmonary dysplasia), so it is kept for severe cases.

  • Steroids are given to the mother before delivery to prevent RDS, not to the newborn as treatment.
  • Routine ventilation is exactly what the lecture says to avoid.
Slide (1)
L68Learning
Why is a premature infant of a diabetic mother at extra risk of respiratory distress syndrome?
  1. A. Maternal ketones stop fetal breathing movements
  2. B. Maternal hyperglycaemia destroys type I pneumocytes
  3. C. Fetal hyperinsulinaemia delays surfactant production
AnswerC. Fetal hyperinsulinaemia delays surfactant production
Maternal hyperglycaemia makes the fetus hyperinsulinaemic, and high fetal insulin delays surfactant production by type II cells.
Explanation

Glucose crosses the placenta, so the fetal pancreas responds to maternal hyperglycaemia by over-secreting insulin. Insulin opposes the maturing effect of cortisol on type II pneumocytes, so surfactant comes later than expected for gestational age. Infants of diabetic mothers can develop RDS even at gestational ages when other babies would not.

  • The problem is delayed surfactant, not destruction of type I cells.
  • Fetal breathing movements are not abolished by maternal ketones; this is not the mechanism.
Slides (2)

Fetal breathing and the switch at birth

L69Learning
What do fetal breathing movements do?
  1. A. Draw amniotic fluid into the lungs → supply nutrients to the developing lung epithelium
  2. B. Draw amniotic fluid into the lungs → condition the breathing muscles and stimulate lung maturation
  3. C. Expel amniotic fluid from the lungs → condition the breathing muscles and stimulate lung maturation
AnswerB. Draw amniotic fluid into the lungs → condition the breathing muscles and stimulate lung maturation
The fetus "practises" breathing: it aspirates amniotic fluid, which conditions the breathing muscles and stimulates lung maturation.
Explanation

Fetal breathing movements happen before birth. Moving fluid in and out keeps the lungs distended and trains the diaphragm and other respiratory muscles. Lungs that cannot be distended by fluid (for example with oligohydramnios) do not grow normally.

  • The key event is drawing fluid in; the lungs are about half full of fluid by birth.
  • The fluid's role is mechanical (distension) and training, not nutrition.
Slide (1)
L70Learning
How full of fluid are the lungs at birth?
  1. A. Completely full
  2. B. About half full
  3. C. About a quarter full
AnswerB. About half full
By birth the lungs are about half filled with fluid (aspirated amniotic fluid plus fluid the lungs secrete).
Explanation

The fluid is normal and helps the lungs grow. At birth it has to be cleared fast so that air can take its place, by three routes: mouth and nose, blood vessels and lymphatics.

  • A quarter underestimates it.
  • Completely full overstates it.
Slide (1)
L71Learning
By which three routes is lung fluid cleared at birth?
  1. A. Out through the mouth and nose (chest squeezed in vaginal delivery)
    Into the pulmonary capillaries, arteries and veins
    Into the pleural cavity
  2. B. Out through the mouth and nose (chest squeezed in caesarean delivery)
    Into the pulmonary capillaries, arteries and veins
    Into the lymphatics
  3. C. Out through the mouth and nose (chest squeezed in vaginal delivery)
    Into the pulmonary capillaries, arteries and veins
    Into the lymphatics
AnswerC. Out through the mouth and nose (chest squeezed in vaginal delivery)
Into the pulmonary capillaries, arteries and veins
Into the lymphatics
Lung fluid leaves by mouth and nose (thorax squeezed during vaginal delivery), into the pulmonary blood vessels, and into the lymphatics.
Explanation

As the chest passes through the birth canal it is compressed, squeezing fluid out of the upper airways. The rest is absorbed across the alveolar wall into the pulmonary capillaries and vessels and into the lymphatics.

  • In caesarean delivery the chest is not squeezed by the birth canal; that is one reason these babies more often have retained lung fluid.
  • Fluid does not drain into the pleural cavity; fluid there would be an effusion.
Slides (2)
L72Learning
Which changes mark the lung's transition from placental dependence to gas exchange at birth, according to the lecture?
  1. A. Surfactant production in the alveolar sacs
    Lungs change from gas-exchanging to secretory organs
    Separate ("parallel") pulmonary and systemic circulations are established
  2. B. Surfactant production stops in the alveolar sacs
    Lungs change from secretory to gas-exchanging organs
    Fetal shunts open to join the two circulations
  3. C. Surfactant production in the alveolar sacs
    Lungs change from secretory to gas-exchanging organs
    Separate ("parallel") pulmonary and systemic circulations are established
AnswerC. Surfactant production in the alveolar sacs
Lungs change from secretory to gas-exchanging organs
Separate ("parallel") pulmonary and systemic circulations are established
At birth: surfactant in the alveolar sacs, lungs switch from secretory to gas-exchanging, and separate pulmonary and systemic circulations are established.
Explanation

Before birth the lungs secrete fluid and the placenta does gas exchange; most blood bypasses the lungs through the fetal shunts. At birth the lungs take over gas exchange, surfactant keeps the new air spaces open, and the shunts close so each circulation becomes a separate circuit carrying the whole cardiac output.

  • The switch is secretory → gas-exchanging, not the reverse.
  • Surfactant production continues, and the shunts close, separating the circulations.

The slide calls the new circulations "parallel" (side-by-side, separate circuits). In haemodynamic terms the two separated circuits are in series, each receiving the full output.

Slide (1)

Pulmonary hypoplasia

L73Learning
What is pulmonary hypoplasia, and is it usually primary or secondary?
  1. A. Incomplete development of lung tissue; usually secondary to another condition
  2. B. Incomplete development of lung tissue; usually primary (genetic)
  3. C. Overgrowth of lung tissue; usually secondary to another condition
AnswerA. Incomplete development of lung tissue; usually secondary to another condition
Pulmonary hypoplasia is incomplete development of lung tissue, and it is usually secondary to something else, such as diaphragmatic hernia or oligohydramnios.
Explanation

Hypoplasia means underdevelopment: fewer airways and alveoli and a smaller lung. It has multiple causes, its severity depends on the cause, and its true incidence is unknown. Most cases are secondary to a condition that takes away the lung's room or its fluid.

  • Primary (genetic) hypoplasia exists but is the exception.
  • Overgrowth would be hyperplasia, the opposite.
Slides (2)
L74Learning
Which two things does normal lung growth need?
  1. A. The right transcription factors
    Enough amniotic fluid
  2. B. Surfactant from type I cells
    Enough amniotic fluid
  3. C. The right transcription factors
    Very little amniotic fluid
AnswerA. The right transcription factors
Enough amniotic fluid
Normal lung development needs various transcription factors (the genetic programme) and an adequate amniotic fluid volume.
Explanation

The genetic programme drives branching, but the lung also needs physical support: amniotic fluid keeps the lungs distended and leaves the thorax room to grow. The review session summed this up as "room + fluid": take away either and the lung stays small.

  • Surfactant comes from type II cells and matters for breathing after birth, not for lung growth.
  • Too little amniotic fluid (oligohydramnios) causes hypoplasia.
Slide (1)
L75Learning
Besides diaphragmatic hernia, what is the classic cause of pulmonary hypoplasia?
  1. A. Tracheo-oesophageal fistula
  2. B. Oesophageal atresia
  3. C. Bilateral renal agenesis
AnswerC. Bilateral renal agenesis
Bilateral renal agenesis: no fetal urine → oligohydramnios → pulmonary hypoplasia.
Explanation

Fetal urine is the main source of amniotic fluid from the second trimester on. With no kidneys there is almost no fluid (oligohydramnios, the Potter sequence), and the lungs fail to grow. The other classic cause is congenital diaphragmatic hernia, where viscera compress the lung.

  • Oesophageal atresia causes polyhydramnios (too much fluid), not hypoplasia.
  • TEF affects feeding and aspiration; it does not stop the lungs growing.
Slide (1)
L76Learning
How does bilateral renal agenesis cause pulmonary hypoplasia?
  1. A. No fetal urine → urea builds up in amniotic fluid → type II cells destroyed
  2. B. No fetal urine → oligohydramnios → lungs not distended and thorax squeezed by the uterus
  3. C. No fetal urine → oligohydramnios → lungs lack growth factors made by the kidneys
AnswerB. No fetal urine → oligohydramnios → lungs not distended and thorax squeezed by the uterus
Oligohydramnios leaves the lungs without fluid to distend them and lets the uterine wall compress the small thorax, so the lungs cannot grow.
Explanation

Without kidneys the fetus makes no urine, so amniotic fluid volume falls (oligohydramnios). Lack of fluid restricts the size of the fetal thorax, the uterine walls press directly on it, and fetal breathing movements cannot fill the lungs. Lung growth stops short; the infant may die of respiratory failure at birth.

  • The lungs do not depend on a kidney-derived growth factor; the mechanism is mechanical.
  • Urea does not destroy type II cells; the problem is lung size, not surfactant.
Slides (2)
L77Learning
What is the clinical range and mortality of pulmonary hypoplasia?
  1. A. From no symptoms to severe respiratory distress; mortality about 71–95%
  2. B. Always severe respiratory distress; mortality about 71–95%
  3. C. From no symptoms to severe respiratory distress; mortality about 11–25%
AnswerA. From no symptoms to severe respiratory distress; mortality about 71–95%
Presentation varies from asymptomatic to severe respiratory distress, depending on how much lung is missing; mortality is about 71–95%.
Explanation

A mildly small lung may cause few symptoms; a severely hypoplastic lung cannot oxygenate the baby. Because severe cases dominate, overall mortality is high, roughly 71–95%.

  • It is not always severe: mild cases can be asymptomatic.
  • 11–25% is far too low for this condition.
Slides (2)
L78Learning
In unilateral pulmonary hypoplasia, which way does the mediastinum shift, and what happens to breath sounds?
  1. A. Away from the affected side; breath sounds decreased on that side
  2. B. Toward the affected side; breath sounds decreased on that side
  3. C. Toward the affected side; breath sounds increased on that side
AnswerB. Toward the affected side; breath sounds decreased on that side
The small lung gives less push, so the mediastinum shifts toward the affected side, and breath sounds are decreased there.
Explanation

Each lung holds the mediastinum in the middle by pushing against it. If one lung is much smaller, that side pushes less, and the heart and mediastinal structures drift toward it. Less aerated lung means quieter breath sounds over that side.

  • Breath sounds are reduced, not increased, over the small lung.
  • A shift away is what a space-occupying lesion does (diaphragmatic hernia, large effusion, tension pneumothorax).

Hook: small lung → smaller side → mediastinum shifts toward it.

Slide (1)
L79Learning
Why can right-sided pulmonary hypoplasia be mistaken for dextrocardia?
  1. A. The mediastinum shifts toward the affected side, moving the heart to the left
  2. B. The mediastinum shifts toward the affected side, moving the heart to the right
  3. C. The mediastinum shifts away from the affected side, moving the heart to the right
AnswerB. The mediastinum shifts toward the affected side, moving the heart to the right
With a small right lung the mediastinum moves toward it, so the heart sits in the right chest and can look like dextrocardia.
Explanation

Dextrocardia is a heart that lies in the right chest with its apex pointing right. A hypoplastic right lung pulls the heart and mediastinum into the right hemithorax, which mimics it on examination and X-ray, although the heart itself is normal.

  • Moving toward the right lung puts the heart on the right, not the left.
  • The shift is toward the affected side, not away from it.
Slides (2)
L80Learning
How is pulmonary hypoplasia managed?
  1. A. Fetal surgery if possible (e.g. relieving urinary obstruction); otherwise ventilation until the lungs cope
