  2. B. Fetal surgery in every case (e.g. closing the diaphragm); otherwise lung transplant at birth
  3. C. Maternal steroids to regrow lung tissue; otherwise antibiotics until the lungs cope
AnswerA. Fetal surgery if possible (e.g. relieving urinary obstruction); otherwise ventilation until the lungs cope
If found in utero, fetal surgery may help (e.g. restoring urine flow); otherwise artificial ventilation and support until the lungs can sustain life. It may be fatal.
Explanation

Because hypoplasia is usually secondary, treatment aims at the cause. If a urinary obstruction is causing oligohydramnios, restoring urine flow in utero can restore the fluid and let the lungs resume growing. After birth, care is supportive: ventilation and support until the lungs can sustain life, though the condition may be fatal.

  • Fetal surgery is used when possible, not in every case, and transplantation is not standard.
  • Steroids mature surfactant production; they cannot create missing lung tissue, and antibiotics treat infection, not hypoplasia.
Slides (2)

Building the diaphragm

L81Learning
Which four components fuse to form the diaphragm?
  1. A. Septum transversum
    Pleuroperitoneal membranes
    Muscular ingrowth from the body wall
    Dorsal mesentery of the oesophagus
  2. B. Septum transversum
    Pleuropericardial membranes
    Muscular ingrowth from the body wall
    Dorsal mesentery of the oesophagus
  3. C. Septum transversum
    Pleuroperitoneal membranes
    Muscular ingrowth from the body wall
    Ventral mesentery of the stomach
AnswerA. Septum transversum
Pleuroperitoneal membranes
Muscular ingrowth from the body wall
Dorsal mesentery of the oesophagus
Diaphragm = septum transversum + pleuroperitoneal membranes + body-wall muscular ingrowth + dorsal mesentery of the oesophagus (weeks 4–10).
Explanation

Each part has a destination: septum transversum → central tendon; pleuroperitoneal membranes → posterolateral parts, closing the pleuroperitoneal canals; body-wall ingrowth (myoblasts from the C3–5 somites) → peripheral muscle; dorsal mesentery of the oesophagus → crura.

  • The pleuropericardial membranes separate the pericardial and pleural cavities and form the fibrous pericardium, not the diaphragm.
  • The ventral mesentery of the stomach forms the lesser omentum and falciform ligament; it is the dorsal mesentery of the oesophagus that contributes.

Hook: "Several Parts Build Diaphragm" (Septum, Pleuroperitoneal, Body wall, Dorsal mesentery).

Slides (2)
L82Learning
Which embryonic component forms the central tendon of the diaphragm?
  1. A. Dorsal mesentery of the oesophagus
  2. B. Septum transversum
  3. C. Pleuroperitoneal membranes
AnswerB. Septum transversum
The septum transversum, a thick plate of mesoderm between the heart and the liver, becomes the central tendon.
Explanation

In week 4, after head folding, the septum transversum lies just caudal to the pericardial cavity and forms the first, incomplete partition between the thoracic and abdominal cavities. It becomes the central tendon, which fuses above with the fibrous pericardium. A defect here (rare) leaves a central or anterior gap.

  • The pleuroperitoneal membranes form the posterolateral parts; their failure gives the common (Bochdalek) hernia.
  • The dorsal mesentery of the oesophagus forms the crura.
Slides (2)
L83Learning
What does the dorsal mesentery of the oesophagus form in the diaphragm?
  1. A. The peripheral muscular rim
  2. B. The crura
  3. C. The central tendon
AnswerB. The crura
The dorsal mesentery of the oesophagus forms the median part of the diaphragm, from which the crura develop.
Explanation

The oesophagus hangs from the posterior body wall by its dorsal mesentery. Myoblasts grow into this mesentery, which becomes the median dorsal part of the diaphragm; the right and left crura develop from it and anchor the diaphragm to the lumbar vertebrae around the aorta and oesophagus.

  • The central tendon is from the septum transversum.
  • The peripheral muscular rim is from the body-wall ingrowth.
Slides (2)
L84Learning
What do the pleuroperitoneal membranes do in diaphragm development?
  1. A. Form the central tendon in front of the oesophagus
  2. B. Separate the pericardial cavity from the pleural cavities and form the fibrous pericardium
  3. C. Close the pleuroperitoneal canals and form the posterolateral parts of the diaphragm
AnswerC. Close the pleuroperitoneal canals and form the posterolateral parts of the diaphragm
The pleuroperitoneal membranes grow in to close the pleuroperitoneal canals, fusing with the septum transversum to form the posterolateral diaphragm.
Explanation

After the septum transversum forms, the pleural and peritoneal cavities still connect through the pleuroperitoneal canals at the back. The pleuroperitoneal membranes close these openings by about weeks 6–7, fusing with the septum transversum and the dorsal mesentery. If one fails to close, the canal persists: a posterolateral (Bochdalek) congenital diaphragmatic hernia.

  • Separating the pericardial from the pleural cavities is the job of the pleuropericardial membranes.
  • The central tendon is from the septum transversum.
Slides (2)
L85Learning
Which diaphragm component forms its peripheral muscular rim?
  1. A. Septum transversum
  2. B. Dorsal mesentery of the oesophagus
  3. C. Muscular ingrowth from the body wall
AnswerC. Muscular ingrowth from the body wall
Muscular ingrowth from the body wall forms the peripheral muscular part of the diaphragm (myoblasts from the C3–5 somites, per the current lecture).
Explanation

As the lungs and pleural cavities expand, they burrow into the lateral body wall, and tissue from the wall is added to the rim of the diaphragm. The current slide describes it as somites of the body-wall perimeter with migrating myoblasts from C3–5, which is also why the phrenic nerve (C3–C5) supplies the muscle.

  • The septum transversum forms the central tendon.
  • The dorsal mesentery of the oesophagus forms the crura.
Slides (2)
L86Learning
As the growing pleural cavities burrow further into the lateral body wall around the rim of the developing diaphragm, what do they form?
  1. A. The costodiaphragmatic recesses, giving the diaphragm its dome shape
  2. B. The costomediastinal recesses, giving the diaphragm its dome shape
  3. C. The pleuroperitoneal canals, linking the pleural and peritoneal cavities
AnswerA. The costodiaphragmatic recesses, giving the diaphragm its dome shape
Pleural cavities extending into the lateral body wall form the costodiaphragmatic recesses, which give the diaphragm its dome shape.
Explanation

The costodiaphragmatic recess is the gutter of pleural cavity between the costal and diaphragmatic pleura, below the lower edge of the lung. In development the expanding lungs and pleural cavities burrow into the lateral body wall and split it in two: the outer layer becomes the thoracic wall, and the inner layer adds muscle to the rim of the diaphragm. As the pleural cavities keep extending downward around that rim, the recesses form and the diaphragm takes on its dome shape.

  • The costomediastinal recesses lie in front, where costal pleura meets mediastinal pleura behind the sternum; they are not at the diaphragm's rim.
  • The pleuroperitoneal canals exist earlier and are closed by the pleuroperitoneal membranes; the burrowing does not create them.

In the adult this is the recess where an upright patient's pleural effusion collects first.

Slides (2)
L87Learning
Which nerve supplies the diaphragm, and why that nerve?
  1. A. Phrenic nerve (C5–C7): the diaphragm starts at thoracic level and its nerve grows up to it
  2. B. Phrenic nerve (C3–C5): the diaphragm starts at cervical level and takes its nerve with it as it descends
  3. C. Vagus nerve (CN X): the diaphragm starts at cervical level and takes its nerve with it as it descends
AnswerB. Phrenic nerve (C3–C5): the diaphragm starts at cervical level and takes its nerve with it as it descends
The diaphragm begins opposite the cervical (C3–C5) somites; their nerve, the phrenic, stays with it as it descends to the lower thorax.
Explanation

In week 4 the septum transversum lies at the level of the upper cervical segments, and myoblasts from the C3–5 somites invade the developing diaphragm. As the body grows, the diaphragm comes to lie much lower, but it keeps its C3–5 innervation, which explains the long course of the phrenic nerves. Memory: "C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive."

  • The vagus supplies the larynx and viscera, not the diaphragm's skeletal muscle.
  • C5–C7 is wrong (that is the long thoracic nerve), and the diaphragm starts in the neck, not the thorax.
Slides (3)

Congenital diaphragmatic hernia

L88Learning
A newborn has severe respiratory distress, a scaphoid abdomen and bowel sounds over the left chest; X-ray shows bowel loops in the left hemithorax. A defect in which structure caused this?
  1. A. Dorsal mesentery of the oesophagus
  2. B. Left pleuroperitoneal membrane
  3. C. Septum transversum
AnswerB. Left pleuroperitoneal membrane
This is a congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH): the left pleuroperitoneal membrane failed to close, leaving a posterolateral opening.
Explanation

If a pleuroperitoneal membrane fails to close its canal, abdominal organs can slide up into the chest when the intestines return to the abdomen. Bowel sounds are then heard in the chest, the abdomen looks sunken (scaphoid) because its contents have moved up, and the compressed lung cannot ventilate.

  • A septum transversum defect would affect the central tendon: a rare central or anterior defect.
  • The dorsal mesentery of the oesophagus forms the crura; it is not the usual site.
Slides (2)
L89Learning
Why does congenital diaphragmatic hernia usually occur on the left?
  1. A. The left pleuroperitoneal membrane lags in development and may never fully fuse
  2. B. The right pleuroperitoneal membrane lags in development and may never fully fuse
  3. C. The left half of the septum transversum is thinner and may never fully fuse
AnswerA. The left pleuroperitoneal membrane lags in development and may never fully fuse
The left pleuroperitoneal membrane closes later than the right; if it lags and never fully fuses, an opening is left.
Explanation

The right pleuroperitoneal canal closes before the left (the large liver on the right may also help seal it). The left canal stays open longer, so it is more likely to remain patent and let abdominal organs herniate into the left chest.

  • It is the left membrane that lags, which is why most hernias are left-sided.
  • The septum transversum forms the central tendon; it is not the lagging component.
Slides (2)
L90Learning
On which side, and in which part of the diaphragm, does congenital diaphragmatic hernia usually occur?
  1. A. Left, posterolateral (Bochdalek type)
  2. B. Right, anteromedial (Morgagni type)
  3. C. Right, posterolateral (Bochdalek type)
AnswerA. Left, posterolateral (Bochdalek type)
Most CDHs are left posterolateral (Bochdalek) hernias, through the part of the diaphragm formed by the pleuroperitoneal membrane.
Explanation

The pleuroperitoneal membranes form the posterolateral diaphragm, so their failure leaves a posterolateral gap: the Bochdalek hernia, about 85% on the left.

  • Right posterolateral hernias occur but are much rarer; the liver plugs the right side.
  • Morgagni hernias are small anterior (retrosternal) defects near the septum transversum; they are rare.
Slides (2)
L91Learning
Why is a congenital diaphragmatic hernia so dangerous for the newborn?
  1. A. Herniated viscera compress the developing heart → heart failure
  2. B. Herniated viscera compress the developing lung → pulmonary hypoplasia
  3. C. Herniated viscera compress the developing lung → tracheo-oesophageal fistula
AnswerB. Herniated viscera compress the developing lung → pulmonary hypoplasia
The herniated viscera compress the developing lung, impeding its growth; the resulting pulmonary hypoplasia is what makes CDH lethal.
Explanation

The hernia is present while the lung is growing. Bowel, stomach and spleen in the left chest take the lung's room, so the ipsilateral lung (and often the contralateral one, from mediastinal shift) stays hypoplastic. Mortality is driven by the small lungs more than by the hole itself; CDH raises the mortality of pulmonary hypoplasia.

  • The heart is pushed aside, but the life-threatening problem is the lung.
  • TEF is a foregut partition defect, unrelated to the diaphragm.
Slide (1)
L92Learning
In a left posterolateral diaphragmatic hernia, which organs typically herniate into the chest?
  1. A. Bladder, sigmoid colon and uterus
  2. B. Small intestine, colon, spleen and stomach
  3. C. Liver, right kidney and right adrenal gland
AnswerB. Small intestine, colon, spleen and stomach
Through a left Bochdalek defect the small intestine, colon, spleen and stomach pass into the left chest; about half of affected babies survive.
Explanation

The organs that sit just below the left posterolateral diaphragm, or are mobile enough to slide up, are the ones that herniate: loops of small intestine and colon, the spleen and the stomach (sometimes part of the left lobe of the liver). Children born with diaphragmatic hernia have about a 50/50 chance of survival.

  • The liver, right kidney and adrenal lie on the right and are retroperitoneal or fixed.
  • The bladder, sigmoid and uterus are pelvic organs, far from the diaphragm.
Slides (2)
L93Learning
In a left congenital diaphragmatic hernia, which way is the heart displaced, compared with a hypoplastic lung of other cause?
  1. A. Toward the hernia (to the left), exactly as with a hypoplastic lung of other cause
  2. B. Toward the hernia (to the left); a simply hypoplastic lung instead pushes it away
  3. C. Away from the hernia (to the right); a simply hypoplastic lung instead pulls it toward itself
AnswerC. Away from the hernia (to the right); a simply hypoplastic lung instead pulls it toward itself
Herniated viscera are a space-occupying mass, so they push the heart away, to the right. A small lung with nothing beside it pulls the mediastinum toward itself.
Explanation

The direction of mediastinal shift tells you whether something is filling a hemithorax or emptying it. In left CDH the bowel and stomach fill the left chest: the heart sounds and apex beat move to the right, and the right lung may be compressed too. In isolated hypoplasia (e.g. a small right lung) there is less volume on that side, so the mediastinum moves toward it.

  • CDH does not pull the heart toward the hernia: the viscera take up space.
  • The two conditions shift the mediastinum in opposite directions; that contrast is the exam point.
Slides (3)
L94Learning
Why does a newborn with congenital diaphragmatic hernia have a scaphoid (sunken) abdomen?
  1. A. Abdominal viscera have moved up into the chest
  2. B. Oligohydramnios compressed the abdomen in utero
  3. C. The abdominal wall muscles failed to develop
AnswerA. Abdominal viscera have moved up into the chest
The abdomen looks scaphoid (boat-shaped, sunken) because much of its contents have herniated into the chest.
Explanation

A normal newborn has a rounded abdomen. In CDH loops of bowel, the stomach and the spleen lie in the thorax, so the abdomen is flat or hollow, while the chest may look barrel-shaped. Scaphoid abdomen + respiratory distress + bowel sounds in the chest is the classic triad.

  • The abdominal wall muscles are normal; a muscle defect would give a bulging (prune-belly type) abdomen.
  • Oligohydramnios compresses the thorax and causes pulmonary hypoplasia; it does not empty the abdomen.
Slide (1)
L95Learning
A newborn with suspected congenital diaphragmatic hernia needs airway support. What should be avoided, and what is done instead?
  1. A. Avoid intubation; give bag-mask ventilation and feed through a nasogastric tube
  2. B. Avoid nasogastric tubes; give bag-mask ventilation until surgery
  3. C. Avoid bag-mask ventilation; intubate and put a nasogastric tube on suction
AnswerC. Avoid bag-mask ventilation; intubate and put a nasogastric tube on suction
No bag-mask ventilation: it blows air into the herniated gut. Intubate at once and place a nasogastric tube on suction to decompress the bowel.
Explanation

Face-mask ventilation pushes air down the oesophagus into the stomach and bowel. In CDH that gut lies in the chest, so inflating it squeezes the remaining lung even more and can cause fatal hypoxia. Endotracheal intubation delivers air only to the lungs, and continuous nasogastric suction keeps the herniated bowel deflated.

  • Bag-mask ventilation is the one thing the lecture calls an absolute contraindication.
  • The nasogastric tube is for decompression, not feeding.

Which of the following is an appropriate treatment for premature babies earlier than 25 weeks?
  1. A. Nasal continuous positive airway pressure
  2. B. Oxygen therapy
  3. C. Treatment with a phospholipid that reduces alveolar surface tension
  4. D. All of the above
AnswerD. All of the above
Explanation from the source
NRDS/ Atelectasis We haven’t quite hit on all of this yet, but you should know from the lecture videos that <25 week old premature babies do not have surfactant production. This has a marked effect on the compliance of the lung and the ability to breathe fresh air. Since we know there is going to be difficulty in breathing (compliance of lung) and gas exchange (collapsed alveoli cannot exchange gas…and amniotic fluid exacerbates things), what would be effective in treatment? Continuous positive airway pressure would help to keep the lungs open at end expiration and help them fill during inspiration. Oxygen therapy may help as well, particularly if there is significant physiological dead space caused by ventilation perfusion mismatch (more on this later). Finally, “a phospholipid that reduces alveolar surface tension” mimics the definition of surfactant. Thus, this would be incredibly helpful.

A 32-year-old woman in her third trimester of pregnancy is undergoing a routine ultrasound examination. The examination of the fetus reveals enlarged and echogenic lungs, an inverted diaphragm, and fetal ascites. Which condition is best characterized by these signs?
  1. A. Laryngeal atresia
  2. B. Tracheal atresia
  3. C. Polyhydramnios
  4. D. Lung hypoplasia
  5. E. Oligohydramnios
AnswerA. Laryngeal atresia
Explanation from the source
A. Laryngeal atresia (congenital high airway obstruction syndrome) is a rare obstruction of the upper fetal airway. Distal to the site of the atresia, the airways dilate, lungs enlarge and become echogenic, the diaphragm flattens or inverts, and fetal ascites and/or hydrops develop. Tracheal atresia is a rare obstruction of the trachea, commonly found with a tracheoesophageal fistula, probably resulting from the unequal division of foregut into esophagus and trachea. Polyhydramnios is an excess of amniotic fluid, often associated with esophageal atresia or tracheoesophageal fistula. Lung hypoplasia is reduced lung volume, often seen in infants with a congenital diaphragmatic hernia. Oligohydramnios, or a decrease in amniotic fluid, is associated with stunted lung development and pulmonary hypoplasia. GAS 172-178; N 230; McM 200, 201, 204

A newborn baby is diagnosed with eventration of the diaphragm. In this condition, half of the diaphragm ascends into the thorax during inspiration, while the other half contracts normally. What is the cause of this condition?
  1. A. Absence of a pleuropericardial fold
  2. B. Absence of musculature in one half of the diaphragm
  3. C. Failure of migration of diaphragm
  4. D. Failure of the septum transversum to develop
  5. E. Absence of a pleuroperitoneal fold
AnswerB. Absence of musculature in one half of the diaphragm
Explanation from the source
B. An absence of musculature in one half of the diaphragm causes it to protrude into the thoracic cavity forming a pouch into which the abdominal viscera protrude. Pleuropericardial folds are responsible for separating the pericardial cavity from the pleural cavity. Typically, the diaphragm migrates to its position with the fibrous pericardium. The septum transversum is the primordial central tendon of the diaphragm that separates the heart from the liver. The pleuroperitoneal folds form the pleuroperitoneal membranes that separate the pleural cavity from the peritoneal cavity. Absence of any of these would not have anything to do with eventration of the diaphragm. GAS 262; N 191; McM 184

After a 2-day-old newborn male swallows milk he becomes cyanotic. After 3 days, he develops aspiration pneumonia. A tracheoesophageal fistula is suspected. Failure of development has occurred most specifically in which of the following structures?

  3. C. Tongue
  4. D. Tracheoesophageal septum
  5. E. Pharynx
AnswerD. Tracheoesophageal septum
Explanation from the source
D. The tracheoesophageal septum is a primordial structure that separates the trachea from the esophagus. If this structure fails to develop, a tracheoesophageal fistula will result, in which event the two structures will not separate completely. When the infant attempts to swallow milk, it spills into the esophageal pouch and is regurgitated. The child becomes cyanotic because an insufficient amount of oxygen is reaching the lungs as a result of the malformed trachea. GAS 218; N 230; McM 197

A 3-day-old newborn has difficulties breathing. A computed tomography (CT) scan of his chest and abdomen reveals the absence of the central tendon of the diaphragm. Which of the following structures failed to develop normally?
  1. A. Pleuroperitoneal folds
  2. B. Pleuropericardial folds
  3. C. Septum transversum
  4. D. Cervical myotomes
  5. E. Dorsal mesentery of the esophagus
AnswerC. Septum transversum
Explanation from the source
C. The septum transversum is a thickened layer of mesoderm that gives origin to the central tendon of the diaphragm. It is situated between the thoracic cavity and the omphaloenteric duct. As the lungs grow into the pericardioperitoneal canal, they give rise to two folds: the pleuroperitoneal and pleuropericardial folds. The pleuroperitoneal folds are responsible for formation of the posterolateral aspect of the diaphragm, and the pleuropericardial folds develop into the fibrous pericardium. The crura provide origin of the dorsal mesentery of the esophagus, whereas the cervical myotomes are responsible for the musculature of the diaphragm. (Note that these are cervical myotomes C3 to C5, the levels of origin of the phrenic nerve.) GAS 262, 203; N 192; McM 192-213

A 4-day-old infant is admitted to the pulmonary unit suffering from dyspnea and cyanosis. Radiologic examination revealed a left hypoplastic lung and herniation of the abdominal intestines into the left thoracic cavity.   1. A. Septum transversum
  2. B. Pleuroperitoneal membrane
  3. C. Tracheoesophageal septum
  4. D. Laryngotracheal groove
  5. E. Foregut

Explanation from the source
B. The pleuroperitoneal membrane forms the posterolateral aspect of the diaphragm. A defect in this membrane would allow for communication between the upper left abdominal cavity and thoracic cavity and could result in a congenital diaphragmatic hernia. The septum transversum provides origin to the central tendon of the diaphragm but is not involved in herniation of the intestines. The tracheoesophageal septum, laryngotracheal groove, and oligohydramnios are not associated with development of the diaphragm. GAS 262; N 191; McM 213

A neonate was born at 34 weeks of gestation and was admitted for pneumonitis. A CT scan examination reveals that the upper segment of the esophagus ends blindly and the presence of an abnormal communication between the trachea and the lower segment of esophagus. Which of the following clinical condition is commonly seen in association with this congenital anomaly?
  1. A. Polyhydramnios
  2. B. Oligodramnios
  3. C. Anhydramnios
  4. D. Hydatidiform mole
  5. E. Choriocarcinomas
AnswerA. Polyhydramnios
Explanation from the source
A. A tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF) is an abnormal communication between the trachea and esophagus. This is a congenital anomaly that results from incomplete fusion of the tracheoesophageal folds that separate the trachea from the esophagus embryologically. In most cases it is accompanied by esophageal atresia. Polyhydramnios is commonly associated with TEF and esophageal atresia, as the amniotic fluid is unable to pass into the stomach and intestines for absorption and collects in the amniotic sac. Oligohydramnios and anhydramnios are associated with genitourinary anomalies. Hydatidiform mole and choriocarcinomas are tumors of the placenta and are not usually associated with polyhydramnios. GAS 262; N 230; McM 196

A 3-day-old newborn is admitted to the surgical unit with severe dyspnea and cyanosis. On physical examination the patient appears to have a flat abdomen. Imaging reveals a left side pneumothorax and pockets of air in the left hemithorax. Which of the following conditions is the most likely diagnosis?
  1. A. Congenital diaphragmatic hernia
  2. B. Laryngeal atresia
  3. C. Emphysema
  4. D. Respiratory distress syndrome
  5. E. Tracheoesophageal fistula
AnswerA. Congenital diaphragmatic hernia
Explanation from the source
A. Congenital diaphragmatic hernia is a relatively common congenital anomaly. It is most often seen as a posterolateral defect in the diaphragm resulting from the defective formation or fusion of the pleuroperitoneal membranes with the other three embryological parts of the diaphragm. If this defect persists when the intestines return to the stomach from the umbilicus during the tenth week, some of the intestines and abdominal viscera may pass into the thorax. This compresses the developing lungs and results in pulmonary hypoplasia. In cases of severe hypoplasia, some primordial alveoli may rupture, causing air to enter into the pleural cavity (pneumothorax). On physical exam, the patient has severe dyspnea and a flat “scaphoid” abdomen. Laryngeal atresia is a rare anomaly that results in obstruction of the upper airways. Emphysema is a condition usually seen in adults where the elasticity of the lung tissue is lost resulting in rupture of the alveoli and the development of large air pockets. Respiratory distress syndrome is usually seen in premature infants due to a surfactant deficiency. Tracheoesophageal fistula is a congenital condition where there is an abnormal connection between the trachea and esophagus and is usually accompanied by esophageal atresia. Patients usually present with dyspnea and choking when attempting to feed. GAS 262; N 192; McM 213

A 4-day-old female infant was admitted to the pulmonary unit suffering from dyspnea and cyanosis. Radiographic examination revealed herniation of bowel into the left thoracic cavity and a hypoplastic left lung. Which embryologic structure probably failed to develop and resulted in the herniation?

  4. D. Laryngotracheal groove
  5. E. Ventral mesogastrium

Explanation from the source
B. Congenital diaphragmatic hernia is usually unilateral and results from defective formation and/ or fusion of the pleuroperitoneal membranes with the other three parts of the diaphragm. This results in a large opening in the posterolateral region of the diaphragm. As a result, the peritoneal and pleural cavities are continuous with one another along the posterior body wall. In septum transversum defect the patient presents with midline diaphragmatic hernia. Tracheoesophageal septum defect can lead to esophageal atresia or tracheoesophageal fistula. The lesser omentum and falciform ligament form from the ventral mesogastrium, which is formed by the septum transversum. GAS 262-263; N 191; McM 213

A newborn baby was diagnosed with eventration of the diaphragm, wherein one half of the diaphragm ascends into the thorax during inspiration, but the other half contracts normally. What is the most likely cause of this condition?
  1. A. Absence of a pleuropericardial fold
  2. B. Absence of musculature in one half of the diaphragm
  3. C. Failure of migration of the diaphragm
  4. D. Failure of development of the septum transversum
  5. E. Absence of a pleuroperitoneal fold
AnswerB. Absence of musculature in one half of the diaphragm
Explanation from the source
B. The diaphragm develops from several components. Initially, the septum transversum (which will become the central tendon) forms in the cervical region, gaining innervation from C3, C4, and C5. Later, myoblasts migrate in from the body wall to form the muscular part of the diaphragm, often considered to be two bilateral hemidiaphragms. These muscles are innervated by the phrenic nerves that are derived from C3, C4, and C5. Eventration of the diaphragm occurs when one muscular hemidiaphragm fails to develop. With positive pressure in the abdominal cavity, and low or negative pressure in the thoracic cavity, abdominal organs are pushed into the thorax. The pleuroperitoneal folds contribute to a portion of the diaphragm posteriorly. GAS 371; N 191, 192; McM 213, 260

A 2-day-old newborn male is cyanotic after attempts to swallow milk result in collection of the milk in his mouth. After 2 days he develops aspiration pneumonia. A tracheoesophageal fistula is suspected. Which of the following structures has most likely failed to develop properly?
  1. A. Esophagus
  2. B. Trachea
  3. C. Tongue
  4. D. Tracheoesophageal septum
  5. E. Pharynx
AnswerD. Tracheoesophageal septum
Explanation from the source
D. The tracheoesophageal septum is the downgrowth that separates the ventral wall of the foregut (esophagus) from the laryngotracheal tube. The presence of a fistula would result in passage of fluid from the esophagus into the trachea and could cause aspiration pneumonia. If the esophagus did not develop correctly, as in esophageal atresia, it would end as a blind tube. This kind of defect, although associated with tracheoesophageal fistula, is not the result of an opening into the trachea, and pneumonia would not result. Abnormal tracheal development can be associated with tracheoesophageal fistula, therefore, but it is not the direct cause of it. Abnormal tongue development does not result in a tracheoesophageal fistula. Abnormal development of the pharynx is not associated with a tracheoesophageal fistula. GAS 172; N 230; McM 196

A 3-day-old newborn male has difficulties in breathing. A computed tomography (CT) scan of his chest and abdomen reveals the absence of the central tendon of the diaphragm. Which of the following structures most likely failed to develop properly?

C. The septum transversum forms the central tendon of the diaphragm. The pleuroperitoneal folds form the posterolateral part of the diaphragm. The pleuropericardial folds separate the pericardial cavity from the pleural cavity and form the fibrous pericardium. The cervical myotomes form the musculature of the diaphragm. The dorsal part of the dorsal mesentery of the esophagus forms the crura of the diaphragm. GAS 161; N 191, 192; McM 213, 260

A 2-day-old male infant is hospitalized in the intensive care unit with acute respiratory distress. The patient is found to have anuria, oligohydramnios, and hypoplastic lungs.   2. B. Polycystic kidney
  3. C. Renal agenesis
  4. D. Wilms tumor
  5. E. Extrophy of the bladder
AnswerC. Renal agenesis
Explanation from the source
C. Potter sequence, or Potter syndrome, is a rare autosomal recessive trait and is associated with renal agenesis or hypoplasia. Altered facial characteristics include flattened nasal bridge, mandibular micrognathia, malformed low-set ears, etc. Absence or lack of proper development of the kidneys causes oligohydramnios, or possibly anhydramnios. Multicystic dysplastic kidney and polycystic kidney are usually secondary to Potter sequence and are therefore not the cause of Potter sequence or oligohydramnios. Wilms tumor is a relatively common renal tumor that presents in children; it is not associated with oligohydramnios and Potter sequence. Extrophy of the bladder is a congenital defect that exposes the posterior surface of the bladder on the exterior of the abdominal wall; there is no indication of this defect in the patient. A 4-month-old female infant is admitted to the hospital with cyanosis. Physical examination reveals decreased breath sounds, abdominal sounds in the thorax, and respiratory distress. A radiographic examination reveals a posterolateral defect of the diaphragm and abdominal contents in the left pleural cavity. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this defect?

  2. B. Absence of musculature in one half of the diaphragm
  3. C. Failure of migration of diaphragm
  4. D. Failure of the septum transversum to develop
  5. E. Failure of pleuroperitoneal fold to close
AnswerE. Failure of pleuroperitoneal fold to close
Explanation from the source
E. Failure of fusion of the pleuroperitoneal folds can cause herniation of abdominal contents into the thorax (congenital diaphragmatic hernia), most commonly on the left side. This defect can impair lung function, causing respiratory distress and cyanosis. The absence of the pleuropericardial fold would cause communication between the pericardial sac and the pleural cavity of the lung and would not lead to the symptoms described. The musculature of the diaphragm is derived from the third to fifth cervical myotomes. Absence of musculature in one half of the diaphragm (eventration of the diaphragm) would cause paradoxical respiration. The downward migration of the diaphragm is due to the elongation of the posterior body wall and is not likely to lead to this patient’s condition. Failure of the septum transversum to develop would cause an absence of the central tendon of the diaphragm and is not normally associated with congenital diaphragmatic hernia. GAS 373; N 191; McM 260

A neonate was born at 34 weeks of gestation and was admitted for pneumonitis. A CT scan reveals that the upper segment of the esophagus ends blindly and the presence of an abnormal communication between trachea and the lower segment of esophagus. A. Polyhydramnios is associated with esophageal atresia, tracheoesophageal fistulas and central nervous system defects due to lack of circulation and absorption of the amniotic fluid, which occurs in the respiratory and digestive tracts. Bilateral renal agenesis or obstructive uropathy is associated with oligohydramnios because little or no urine is excreted into the amniotic cavity. A 25-year-old woman in her 28th week of pregnancy visits her obstetrician for a routine check-up. Her doctor explains that her baby’s lungs are starting to produce surfactant, a necessary component for respiration. Surfactant is produced during which of the following periods of lung development?
  1. A. Pseudoglandular period
  2. B. Canalicular period
  3. C. Terminal sac period
  4. D. Bronchiole period
  5. E. Alveolar period
AnswerC. Terminal sac period
Explanation from the source
C. The development of the lungs occurs in four stages: the pseudoglandular stage (6 to 16 weeks), where the lungs resemble exocrine lungs. The parts of the lung involved in gaseous exchange have not yet formed. The canalicular stage (16 to 26 weeks) involves maturation of the bronchioles and development of a few primordial alveoli. The terminal sac stage (26 weeks to birth) is when the alveoli begin maturing, the blood gas barrier is formed, and surfactant is secreted by type 2 pneumocytes. The final stage is the alveolar stage (32 weeks to 8 years); alveoli continue to develop as the lungs prepare for the transition to autonomous gas exchange (Fig. 8-7). 130-135

A 20 year old woman delivers a stillborn infant with bilateral agenesis of the kidneys. During the later stages of pregnancy, the fetus likely also had which of the following conditions?
  1. A. Polyhydramnios
  2. B. Oligohydramnios
  3. C. Renal hypoplasia
  4. D. Pelvic kidneys
  5. E. Polycystic kidneys
AnswerB. Oligohydramnios
Explanation from the source
The answer is B: Oligohydramnios. Oligohydramnios is a diminution in the volume of amniotic fluid as a result of the fetus’ failure to excrete urine into the amniotic sac, for example, as resulting from renal agenesis or urethral obstruction. Renal agenesis occurs when the ureteric bud fails to develop, thus preventing formation of the kidney. Normally, the fetus pro- duces urine and excretes it into the amniotic cavity, where it mixes with the amniotic fluid. The fetus drinks amniotic fluid, which is absorbed into the bloodstream, filtered at the placenta, and excreted by the fetus. Thus, the prenatal kidneys are not necessary for waste exchange but are important in regulating the volume of amniotic fluid. In renal agenesis (no kidneys), urine is not produced and not secreted, thus reducing the vol- ume of fluid in the amniotic sac (oligohydramnios). Choice A (Polyhydramnios) is incorrect. Polyhydramnios is an increased volume of amniotic fluid in the amniotic sac. In this case, the kidneys are normal, and urine is produced and excreted into the amniotic sac. However, obstruction (atresia) of the gut tube prevents the fetus from drinking and/or absorbing that fluid, resulting in accumula- tion of greater volume of fluid in the amniotic sac.
Renal agenesis -> oligohydramnios is taught in ANAT-1 as the cause of pulmonary hypoplasia; the question itself is framed as renal/amniotic-fluid embryology (Renal/GI) and does not ask about the lung.

A 32-year-old pregnant woman at 30 weeks of gestation comes to her physician due to excess weight gain in a 2-week period. Ultrasonography reveals polyhydramnios. Which fetal abnormality is most likely responsible for the polyhydramnios?
  1. (A) Bilateral kidney agenesis
  2. (B) Urinary tract obstruction
  3. (C) Uteroplacental insufficiency
  4. (D) Hypoplastic lungs
  5. (E) Esophageal atresia
AnswerE. Esophageal atresia
Explanation from the source
Esophageal atresia. Polyhydramnios is associated with the inability of the fetus to swallow because of esophageal atresia or anencephaly. Polyhydramnios can also be due to absorption defects such as duodenal atresia. The inability of the embryo to swallow amniotic fluid means that the fluid will not be absorbed into the fetal blood, removed by the placenta, and passed into the maternal blood. Therefore, the amount of fluid in the amniotic cavity is greater than normal causing polyhydramnios. Choice A (Bilateral kidney agenesis) is incorrect. Bilateral kidney agenesis would lead to reduced amniotic fluid volume (oligohydramnios) because the fetal kidneys, when present, increase the amniotic fluid volume through fetal urine production. Choice B (Urinary tract obstruction) is incorrect. Fetal urinary tract obstruction is defined as partial or complete obstruction of any portion of the urinary tract from the kidney to the urethra. This obstruction would not allow the fetal urine to enter the amniotic cavity, so this condition would lead to decreased amniotic fluid volume (oligohydramnios). Choice C (Uteroplacental insufficiency) is incorrect. Uteroplacental insufficiency is defined as insufficient blood flow to the placenta during pregnancy. This condition can negatively affect the fetus, leading to “fetal distress.” However, uteroplacental insufficiency leads to oligohydramnios, which is not seen in this patient. Choice D (Hypoplastic lungs) is incorrect. Hypoplastic lungs are often caused by inadequate amounts of amniotic fluid (oligohydramnios). Swallowing of the amniotic fluid by the fetus promotes normal lung development, so hypoplastic lungs are associated with oligohydramnios, not polyhydramnios.
Slides (2)
108
A pregnant woman is in a car accident and goes into premature labor. Her fetus is approximately 24 weeks in gestation. Her physicians administer her steroids and try to delay the birth of her baby. The survival rate of a premature baby rises significantly if the baby can reach 28 weeks gestation mainly due to the maturation of the lungs. What stage of lung maturation are the doctors hoping to reach, in which the blood-air barrier is beginning to be established?
  1. (A) Embryonic period
  2. (B) Pseudoglandular period
  3. (C) Canalicular period
  4. (D) Terminal sac period
  5. (E) Alveolar period
AnswerD. Terminal sac period
Explanation from the source
Terminal sac period. The simple cuboidal epithelium within the terminal sacs differentiates into pneumocytes within the terminal sac period. The rapidly proliferating capillary network makes intimate contact with the terminal sacs, and the blood-air barrier is established with Type I pneumocytes (or alveolar epithelial cells). These events take place in the terminal sac period, which runs from embryonic week 24 until birth and are crucial for the survival of an infant born prematurely. Administration of steroids to the infant in utero can promote lung maturation by increasing the proliferation of Type II pneumocytes (or alveolar epithelial cells), which secrete surfactant, a fluid capable of decreasing the surface tension at the air-alveolar interface. Due to the terminal sac period of lung maturation, a premature infant’s survival rate will increase considerably from week 24 to 28 as the bloodair barrier continues to be established. Choice A (Embryonic period) is incorrect. At approximately 4 weeks of gestation, the respiratory diverticulum, or lung bud, begins to arise from the ventral wall of the foregut. Two longitudinal tracheoesophageal ridges fuse in the midline to form the tracheoesophageal septum, which separates the lung bud away from the foregut, specifically the esophagus, forming the trachea. The distal end of the trachea divides into two lateral bronchial buds. At the beginning of week 5, the bronchial buds elongate to form the primary (left and right main stem) bronchi, which further divide into the secondary bronchi. Choice B (Pseudoglandular period) is incorrect. The pseudoglandular period occurs from week 5 to 16 of gestation. During this period of lung maturation, the terminal bronchioles, which were established in the embryonic period of lung development, continue to divide to establish respiratory bronchioles and alveolar ducts. The vascular supply to the lungs also increases; however, respiration is not possible until there are enough capillaries within the lungs to enable sufficient gas exchange. Adequate gas exchange is not possible until the terminal sac period is reached at approximately the seventh month of gestation. Choice C (Canalicular period) is incorrect. The canalicular period of lung maturation occurs from week 16 to 26 of gestation. During this period of lung development, the terminal sacs (primitive alveoli) form, and capillaries within the lung tissue begins to establish close contact with the primitive alveoli. However, respiration is not possible until the terminal sac period when an adequate supply of capillaries exist to enable sufficient gas exchange. Adequate gas exchange is not possible until the seventh month of gestation. Choice E (Alveolar period) is incorrect. The alveolar period of lung maturation continues from month 8 of gestation and/ or birth until well into childhood. During this period of lung development, the number of mature alveoli within the lungs continues to increase in number and the blood-air barrier is now well established. However, it is during the terminal sac period of lung development (week 26–birth) when adequate gas exchange is established, making respiration possible in a premature infant.
Slide (1)
109High-yield
A preterm neonate chokes and coughs throughout her first feeding with her mother with the breast milk regurgitating from the infant’s mouth and nose. Noticing the difficulty feeding, a pediatrician tries to pass a catheter into the baby’s stomach and meets resistance. A chest film is taken of the baby while in an incubator. The given radiograph reveals the location of the radiopaque catheter, shows no air within the stomach of the infant, and verifies normal lungs. What is the most likely diagnosis based upon the results of the X-ray?
Show figure
  1. (A) Pyloric stenosis
  2. (B) Tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF)
  3. (C) Large bowel obstruction
  4. (D) Respiratory distress syndrome (RDS)
  5. (E) Esophageal atresia
AnswerE. Esophageal atresia
Explanation from the source
Esophageal atresia. Esophageal atresia is a congenital disorder in which the esophagus ends in a blind-ending pouch and is not connected to the stomach. In the given chest film, the catheter is resting in the blindending esophagus. The absence of air in the stomach also indicates an esophageal atresia. These malformations are detected during the infant’s first feeding due to choking, coughing, and even sneezing. Excessive salivation may also be noted due to inability to swallow this secretion. In prenatal examinations, esophageal atresia is often associated with polyhydramnios in the third trimester. Also, an esophageal atresia can present with or without a tracheoesophageal fistula. The latter scenario is more probable due to the appearance of normal lungs on X-ray. Choice A (Pyloric stenosis) is incorrect. Due to the location of the catheter on the X-ray, which is located within the esophagus, a pyloric stenosis (narrowing of the pyloric end of the stomach) is not probable. Infants usually do not present with symptoms of pyloric stenosis until approximately 2 to 3 weeks after birth when they feed normally, but follow each feeding with nonbilious, projectile vomiting and a ravenous desire to continue to feed. Pyloric stenosis is usually detected with abdominal ultrasound and is prevalent in first-born Caucasian boys. Choice B (Tracheoesophageal fistula [TEF]) is incorrect. A TEF is an abnormal connection between the trachea and the esophagus due to incomplete development of the tracheoesophageal septum, which normally separates the developing trachea from the esophageal portion of the foregut. TEFs are often seen with esophageal atresia; however, in these cases, the baby would usually aspirate fluids into the lungs. In the given X-ray, there is no evidence of fluid accumulation in the lungs (pneumonia) secondary to the esophageal atresia. Normal lungs rule out the possibility of a TEF. Choice C (Large bowel obstruction) is incorrect. Large bowel obstruction would not explain the location of the catheter, which is stuck in the esophagus. Also, babies with large bowel obstruction would be able to feed; however, they would present with bilious, projectile vomiting a few hours after feeding. This patient exhibited feeding problems immediately, which rules out large bowel obstruction. Choice D (Respiratory distress syndrome [RDS]) is incorrect. RDS is common in babies of diabetic mothers and premature infants (born before 34 weeks of gestation). This patient is not exhibiting symptoms of RDS, which would include rapid breathing and shortness of breath. RDS rarely occurs in full-term infants.
Slide (1)
110
Which of the following components of the respiratory tract would be directly affected by a developmental failure of normal differentiation of the foregut endoderm?
  1. (A) Nasal epithelium
  2. (B) Intrinsic laryngeal muscles
  3. (C) Bronchial cartilages
  4. (D) Trachealis muscle
  5. (E) Alveoli
AnswerE. Alveoli
Explanation from the source
Alveoli. The lower respiratory tract (larynx, trachea, bronchi, lungs) develops from a single ventral outgrowth (respiratory diverticulum; lung bud) off the floor of the foregut. Thus, the epithelial lining of these structures, including the alveoli, is entirely derived from endoderm. The surrounding cartilage, muscle, and connective tissues are derived from the neighboring splanchnic mesoderm. Choice A (Nasal epithelium) is incorrect. The nasal cavities are derived from the nasal placodes, which are thickenings of surface ectoderm. Thus, the nasal epithelium is of ectodermal origin rather than endodermal origin. Choice B (Intrinsic laryngeal muscles) is incorrect. Intrinsic laryngeal muscles are all skeletal muscles derived from the 4th and 6th pharyngeal arches and of mesodermal origin. Due to their pharyngeal arch origins, these muscles are all innervated by the vagus nerve. Choice C (Bronchial cartilages) is incorrect. The bronchial cartilages that support the respiratory tree are derived from splanchnic mesoderm. Choice D (Trachealis muscle) is incorrect. The smooth trachealis muscle is derived from surrounding splanchnic mesoderm.
Slides (2)
111
An infant is born with a large defect in the central tendon of the diaphragm. This condition is most likely the result of malformation of which of the following structures?
  1. (A) Dorsal mesentery of the esophagus
  2. (B) Ventral mesentery of the gut tube
  3. (C) Pleuroperitoneal folds
  4. (D) Septum transversum
  5. (E) Cervical somites
AnswerD. Septum transversum
Explanation from the source
Septum transversum. The central tendon of the diaphragm is the expansive tendinous area into which the diaphragmatic muscle inserts and acts upon to produce respiratory movements. Also, it provides passage of the inferior vena cava, which traverses the diaphragm at the 8th thoracic (T8) vertebral level. The central tendon is formed from the embryonic septum transversum. The initial intraembryonic coelom is a single continuous area spanning the length of the trunk. Formation of the diaphragm separates the thoracic and peritoneal cavities. The diaphragm forms from fusion of tissues that originate from four different sources: septum transversum, paired pleuroperitoneal membranes, dorsal mesentery of the esophagus, and cervical somites. The septum transversum is a mesodermal wall that forms between the primitive heart tube and developing liver. It forms most of the diaphragm. Choice A (Dorsal mesentery of the esophagus) is incorrect. This portion of the dorsal mesentery of the gut tube forms the crura of the diaphragm. These muscular legs attach the diaphragm to the vertebral column and form the margins of the aortic hiatus. Additionally, the right crus forms the esophageal hiatus. Choice B (Ventral mesentery of the gut tube) is incorrect. The ventral mesentery of the gut tube is not related to formation of the diaphragm. It gives rise to the lesser omentum, falciform ligament, and the coronary and triangular ligaments of the liver. Choice C (Pleuroperitoneal folds) is incorrect. The paired pleuroperitoneal folds are extensions from the posterolateral body wall. They form much of the posterolateral aspect of the diaphragm that is not derived from the septum transversum or the dorsal esophageal mesentery. Choice E (Cervical somites) is incorrect. The septum transversum is initially located along cervical somites and spinal cord segments C3-5. Differential rates of body growth between the trunk and internal organs cause shifting and repositioning of the diaphragm to its final thoracolumbar position. However, myoblasts from the cervical somites invade the initial diaphragmatic folds and form the muscular parts of the diaphragm. Further, the cervical spinal cord segments give rise to the phrenic nerves that provide motor innervation to the diaphragm.
Slides (2)
112
A 32-year-old pregnant woman at 30 weeks of gestation comes to her physician because of excess weight gain in a 2-week period. Ultrasonography reveals polyhydramnios. Which fetal abnormality is most likely responsible for the polyhydramnios?
  1. (A) Bilateral kidney agenesis
  2. (B) Umbilical cord knots
  3. (C) Velamentous placenta
  4. (D) Hypoplastic lungs
  5. (E) Esophageal atresia
AnswerE. Esophageal atresia
Explanation from the source
E. Polyhydramnios is associated with the inability of the fetus to swallow because of esophageal atresia or anencephaly. Polyhydramnios can also result from absorption defects such as duodenal atresia. The inability of the embryo to swallow the amniotic fluid means that the fluid cannot be absorbed into the fetal blood and removed by the placenta and passed into the maternal blood.

A young mother brings her recently born infant into your office and complains that the infant gags and chokes after swallowing milk. A physical examination indicates excessive saliva and mucus around the mouth and nose, abdominal distention, pneumonitis, and radiographs indicate air in the infant’s stomach. What is the most likely cause?
  1. (A) Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis
  2. (B) Tracheoesophageal fistula
  3. (C) Congenital lobar emphysema
  4. (D) Respiratory distress syndrome
  5. (E) Pulmonary hypoplasia
AnswerB. Tracheoesophageal fistula
Explanation from the source
B. Tracheoesophageal fistula is an abnormal communication between the trachea and esophagus that results from an improper division of the foregut by the tracheoesophageal septum. It is generally associated with esophageal atresia and polyhydramnios.

Within hours after birth, a baby whose mother is diabetic had a rising respiratory rate and labored breathing. The baby became cyanotic and died. Postmortem histological examination revealed collapsed alveoli lined with eosinophilic material. What is the diagnosis?
  1. (A) Congenital emphysema
  2. (B) Respiratory distress syndrome
  3. (C) Cystic fibrosis
  4. (D) Tracheoesophageal fistula
  5. (E) Pulmonary carcinoma
AnswerB. Respiratory distress syndrome
Explanation from the source
B. Respiratory distress syndrome is common in premature infants and infants of diabetic mothers. It is caused by a deficiency or absence of surfactant. Collapsed alveoli and eosinophilic material consisting of fibrin (hyaline membrane) can be observed histologically, indicating associated hyaline membrane disease.

The trachea is lined with pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells. This epithelium is derived from
  1. (A) neuroectoderm
  2. (B) endoderm
  3. (C) ectoderm
  4. (D) visceral mesoderm
  5. (E) mesoderm of fourth and sixth pharyngeal arches
AnswerB. endoderm
Explanation from the source
B. The epithelial lining of the entire respiratory system (from tracheal epithelium to type I pneumocytes lining alveoli) is derived from endoderm.

Smooth muscle, connective tissue, and cartilage of primary bronchi are derived from which of the following sources?
  1. (A) Neuroectoderm
  2. (B) Endoderm
  3. (C) Ectoderm
  4. (D) Visceral mesoderm
  5. (E) Mesoderm of pharyngeal arches 4 and 6
AnswerD. Visceral mesoderm
Explanation from the source
D. The epithelium of primary bronchi is derived from endoderm; the other components are derived from visceral mesoderm.

117
Components of the blood–air barrier in the lung are derived from which of the following sources?
  1. (A) Ectoderm only
  2. (B) Visceral mesoderm only
  3. (C) Visceral mesoderm and ectoderm
  4. (D) Endoderm and ectoderm
  5. (E) Visceral mesoderm and endoderm
AnswerE. Visceral mesoderm and endoderm
Explanation from the source
E. The blood–air barrier comprises the structures through which gaseous exchange occurs between air in alveoli and blood in pulmonary capillaries. The attenuated pulmonary epithelium (type I pneumocytes) is derived from endoderm. The simple, squamous epithelium (endothelium) lining pulmonary capillaries is derived from visceral mesoderm.

118
The respiratory diverticulum initially is in open communication with the primitive foregut. Which of the following embryonic structures is responsible for separating these two structures?
  1. (A) Laryngotracheal groove
  2. (B) Posterior esophageal folds
  3. (C) Laryngotracheal diverticulum
  4. (D) Tracheoesophageal septum
  5. (E) Bronchopulmonary segment
AnswerD. Tracheoesophageal septum
Explanation from the source
D. When the tracheoesophageal folds fuse in the midline, they form the tracheoesophageal septum. This septum is responsible for separating the adult trachea ventrally from the esophagus dorsally.

119
Collapse of bronchi caused by failure of bronchial cartilage development is indicative of which one of the following congenital malformations?
  1. (A) Congenital bronchial cysts
  2. (B) Congenital neonatal emphysema
  3. (C) Tracheoesophageal fistula
  4. (D) Hyaline membrane disease
  5. (E) Pulmonary hypoplasia
AnswerB. Congenital neonatal emphysema
Explanation from the source
B. Congenital neonatal emphysema is a malformation involving the bronchi. One or more lobes of the lungs are overdistended with air because air can be inspired through collapsed bronchi but cannot be expired.
120
Pulmonary hypoplasia is commonly associated with which condition?
  1. (A) Hyaline membrane disease
  2. (B) Diaphragmatic hernia
  3. (C) Tracheoesophageal fistula
  4. (D) Congenital bronchial cysts
  5. (E) Congenital neonatal emphysema
AnswerB. Diaphragmatic hernia
Explanation from the source
B. During normal development, a space is provided for the prolific growth of the bronchial buds in a lateral and caudal direction. This space, which is part of the intraembryonic coelom, is called the primitive pleural cavity. If this space is reduced by herniation of abdominal viscera, lung development will be severely compromised.

Development of which of the following is the first sign of respiratory system development?
  1. (A) Tracheoesophageal septum
  2. (B) Hypobranchial eminence
  3. (C) Primitive foregut
  4. (D) Tracheoesophageal fistula
  5. (E) Respiratory diverticulum
AnswerE. Respiratory diverticulum
Explanation from the source
E. Development of the respiratory system begins in week 4; the first sign of development is formation of the respiratory diverticulum in the ventral wall of the primitive foregut.

122
In which stage of lung maturation is the blood–air barrier established?
  1. (A) Embryonic period
  2. (B) Pseudoglandular period
  3. (C) Canalicular period
  4. (D) Terminal sac period
  5. (E) Alveolar period
AnswerD. Terminal sac period
Explanation from the source
D. The simple cuboidal epithelium within the terminal sacs differentiates into pneumocytes within the terminal sac period. The rapidly proliferating capillary network makes intimate contact with the terminal sacs, and the blood–air barrier is established with type I pneumocytes. These events take place in the terminal sac period, which runs from embryonic week 24 until birth.

123
A congenital diaphragmatic hernia may result from failure of the
  1. (A) septum transversum to develop
  2. (B) pleuroperitoneal membranes to fuse in a normal fashion
  3. (C) pleuropericardial membrane to develop completely
  4. (D) dorsal mesentery of the esophagus to develop
  5. (E) body wall to form the peripheral part of the diaphragm
AnswerB. pleuroperitoneal membranes to fuse in a normal fashion
Explanation from the source
B. The formation of the diaphragm occurs through the fusion of tissue from four different sources. The pleuroperitoneal membranes normally fuse with the three other components during week 6 of development. Abnormal development or fusion of one or both of the pleuroperitoneal membranes causes a patent opening between the thorax and abdomen through which abdominal viscera may herniate.
Slides (2)
124
A congenital diaphragmatic hernia most commonly occurs
  1. (A) on the right anteromedial side
  2. (B) on the right posterolateral side
  3. (C) on the left anteromedial side
  4. (D) on the left posterolateral side
  5. (E) anywhere on the left side
AnswerD. on the left posterolateral side
Explanation from the source
D. Congenital diaphragmatic hernias occur most commonly on the left posterolateral side. The pleuroperitoneal membrane on the right side closes before the left for reasons that are not clear. Consequently, the patency on the left side remains unclosed for a longer time. The portion of the diaphragm formed by the pleuroperitoneal membrane in the newborn is located posterolateral.
Slide (1)
125
A congenital diaphragmatic hernia is usually life threatening because it is associated with
  1. (A) pulmonary hypoplasia
  2. (B) pulmonary hyperplasia
  3. (C) physiological umbilical hernia
  4. (D) liver hypoplasia
  5. (E) liver agenesis
AnswerA. pulmonary hypoplasia
Explanation from the source
A. The herniation of abdominal contents into the pleural cavity compresses the developing lung bud, resulting in pulmonary hypoplasia. Lung development on the ipsilateral (left) side of the herniation is most commonly affected, but lung development on the contralateral (right) side can also be compromised. The lungs may achieve normal size and function after surgical reduction of the hernia and repair of the diaphragm. However, mortality is high due to pulmonary hypoplasia.

126
An 8-day-old boy presents with a history of complete loss of breath at times and of turning blue on a number of occasions. If the baby is placed in an upright or sitting position, his breathing improves. Physical examination reveals an unusually flat stomach when the newborn is lying down; auscultation demonstrates no breath sounds on the left side of the thorax. What is the diagnosis?
  1. (A) Physiological umbilical herniation
  2. (B) Esophageal hiatal hernia
  3. (C) Tetralogy of Fallot
  4. (D) Congenital diaphragmatic hernia
  5. (E) Tricuspid atresia
AnswerD. Congenital diaphragmatic hernia
Explanation from the source
D. Loss of breath and cyanosis result from pulmonary hypoplasia associated with congenital diaphragmatic hernia. Placing the baby in an upright position will reduce the hernia somewhat and ease the pressure on the lungs, thereby increasing the baby’s comfort. The baby’s stomach is flat (instead of the plump belly of a normal newborn) because the abdominal viscera have herniated into the thorax. Auscultation reveals no breath sounds on the left side because of pulmonary hypoplasia.

127High-yield
During week 4, the developing diaphragm is located at
  1. (A) C3, C4, C5
  2. (B) T3, T4, T5
  3. (C) T8, T9, T10
  4. (D) L1, L2, L3
  5. (E) L4, L5, L6
AnswerA. C3, C4, C5
Explanation from the source
A. Although it may seem unusual, the adult diaphragm has its embryological beginning at the cervical level (C3, C4, C5). Nerve roots from C3, C4, and C5 enter the developing diaphragm, bringing both motor and sensory innervation. With the subsequent rapid growth of the neural tube, there is an apparent descent of the diaphragm to its adult levels (thoracic and lumbar). However, the diaphragm retains its innervation from C3, C4, and C5, which explains the unusually long phrenic nerves.

A mother brings in her newborn baby girl and says, “My baby coughs and gags every time I try to feed her; one time she even turned blue and it scared me.” The mother also indicates that her baby always has a “mouthful of saliva.” Relevant physical exam findings include a distended stomach, excessive saliva accumulation, a hint of pneumonitis, and inability to pass a catheter into the infant’s stomach.   1. A. Esophageal hiatal hernia
  2. B. Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis
  3. C. Tracheoesophageal fistula
  4. D. Respiratory distress syndrome
  5. E. Congenital diaphragmatic hernia
AnswerC. Tracheoesophageal fistula
Explanation from the source
C. Tracheoesophageal fistula. Tracheoesophageal fistula is an abnormal communication between the trachea and esophagus that results from improper division of foregut by the tracheoesophageal septum. It is generally associated with esophageal atresia and polyhydramnios. Clinical features include excessive accumulation of saliva or mucus in the nose and mouth; episodes of gagging and cyanosis after swallowing milk; abdominal distention after crying; and reflux of gastric contents into lungs, causing pneumonitis. Diagnostic features include inability to pass a catheter into the stomach and radiographs demonstrating air in the infant’s stomach. See Chapter 11, II.B.2.

A quick physical exam reveals that the baby has a barrel-shaped chest, a scaphoid-shaped abdomen, and absence of breath sounds on the left side, and the heartbeat is displaced to the right side. A chest radiograph reveals air/fluid containing bowel in the left-side hemithorax, no visible aerated lung on the left side, contralateral displacement of the heart and other mediastinal structures, compression of the contralateral lung, and reduced size of the abdomen. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
  1. A. Esophageal hiatal hernia
  2. B. Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis

  4. D. Respiratory distress syndrome
  5. E. Congenital diaphragmatic hernia
AnswerE. Congenital diaphragmatic hernia

E. A congenital diaphragmatic hernia is a herniation of abdominal contents into the pleural cavity caused by a failure of the pleuroperitoneal membrane to develop or fuse with other components of the diaphragm. Affected neonates usually present in the first few hours of life with respiratory distress that may be mild or so severe as to be incompatible with life. See Chapter 21, IV.A.

During early development of the respiratory system, the laryngotracheal tube maintains communication with the primitive foregut. Which of the following embryonic structures is most likely responsible for partitioning these two embryonic structures?
  1. (A) Tracheoesophageal folds
  2. (B) Tracheoesophageal fistula
  3. (C) Tracheoesophageal septum
  4. (D) Laryngotracheal diverticulum
  5. (E) Laryngotracheal septum
AnswerC. Tracheoesophageal septum
Explanation from the source
The answer is C. The tracheoesophageal septum is formed by the fusion of the tracheoesophageal folds in the midline. This septum divides the foregut into a ventral portion, the laryngotracheal tube (primordium of the larynx, trachea, bronchi, and lungs), and a dorsal portion (primordium of the oropharynx and esophagus).

A 7-day-old baby is diagnosed as having congenital neonatal emphysema, which is caused by collapsed bronchi because of failure of bronchial cartilage development. Bronchial cartilages are derived from which of the following derivations?
  1. (A) Ectoderm
  2. (B) Mesoderm
  3. (C) Endoderm
  4. (D) Proctodeum
  5. (E) Neuroectoderm
AnswerB. Mesoderm
Explanation from the source
The answer is B. Bronchial cartilages, smooth muscles, and connective tissue are derived from the mesoderm. The bronchial epithelium and glands are derived from the endoderm.

133
An infant, born at 28 weeks of gestation, rapidly gave evidence of respiratory distress. Clinical laboratory and imaging (X-ray) results supported the diagnosis of infant respiratory distress syndrome. Which of the following statements about this syndrome is true?
  1. A. It is unrelated to the baby’s premature birth.
  2. B. It is a consequence of too few type II pneumocytes.
  3. C. The lecithin/sphingomyelin ratio in the amniotic fluid is likely to be greater than two.
  4. D. The concentration of dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine in the amniotic fluid would be expected to be lower than that of a full-term baby.
  5. E. It is an easily treated disorder with low mortality.
  6. F. It is treated by administering surfactant to the mother just before she gives birth.
AnswerD. The concentration of dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine in the amniotic fluid would be expected to be lower than that of a full-term baby.
Explanation from the source
Correct answer = D. Dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC, or dipalmitoyl lecithin) is the lung surfactant found in mature, healthy lungs. Respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) can occur in lungs that make too little of this compound. If the lecithin/sphingomyelin ratio in amniotic is greater than two, a newborn’s lungs are considered to be sufficiently mature (premature lungs would be expected to have a ratio lower than two). The RDS would not be due to too few type II pneumocytes, which would simply be secreting sphingomyelin rather than DPPC at 28 weeks of gestation. The mother is given a glucocorticoid, not surfactant, prior to giving birth. Surfactant would be administered to the baby postnatally to reduce surface tension.

ANAT-2 Thoracic cage

162 questions · 45 high-yield
Learning questions 219

Sternal landmarks and vertebral levels

L1Learning
Which two opposing demands shape the design of the chest wall?
  1. A. Support the upper limbs
    Store red marrow for blood formation
  2. B. Protect the heart and lungs
    Change shape constantly for breathing
  3. C. Change shape constantly for breathing
    Stay rigid to anchor the diaphragm
AnswerB. Protect the heart and lungs
Change shape constantly for breathing
The wall must protect the heart and lungs yet move constantly to change thoracic volume; jointed ribs linked by flexible cartilage are the compromise.
Explanation

A rigid box would protect well but could not ventilate; a soft bag could ventilate but would not protect. The thoracic cage solves this with curved ribs joined to the vertebrae by synovial joints and to the sternum through flexible costal cartilages, so it is strong yet swings up and out with every breath.

  • Supporting the upper limbs and holding red marrow are real roles of the cage, but they do not pull against each other.
  • The cage never needs to stay rigid for the diaphragm: the diaphragm's rim attaches to the moving lower ribs and cartilages, and the diaphragm itself is the main moving part of inspiration.
Slide (1)
L2Learning
What is the sternal angle?
  1. A. The ridge where the manubrium meets the body of the sternum
  2. B. The notch between the medial ends of the clavicles
  3. C. The ridge where the body of the sternum meets the xiphoid process
AnswerA. The ridge where the manubrium meets the body of the sternum
The sternal angle (angle of Louis) is the palpable transverse ridge at the manubriosternal joint, where the manubrium meets the body of the sternum.
Explanation

The manubrium and the body of the sternum meet at a slight angle, so their joint (the manubriosternal joint, a symphysis) stands out as a transverse ridge you can feel under the skin about 4 cm below the top of the sternum. It is the key landmark of the front of the chest: the 2nd costal cartilage joins the sternum here.

  • The notch between the clavicles is the jugular (suprasternal) notch, at the top of the manubrium.
  • The body–xiphoid junction is the xiphisternal joint, at the lower end of the sternum (T9 level).
Slides (2)
L3Learning
Which rib's costal cartilage joins the sternum at the sternal angle?
  1. A. The 1st rib
  2. B. The 3rd rib
  3. C. The 2nd rib
AnswerC. The 2nd rib
The 2nd costal cartilage articulates at the sternal angle, so the angle identifies the 2nd rib, and the space below it is the 2nd intercostal space.
Explanation

The 2nd costal cartilage sits in a notch shared by the lower manubrium and the upper body of the sternum, exactly at the manubriosternal joint. Sliding a finger sideways from the sternal angle therefore lands on the 2nd rib; counting down from there gives each rib and intercostal space (each space is numbered for the rib above it).

  • The 1st rib joins the manubrium just below the sternoclavicular joint and is hidden behind the clavicle.
  • The 3rd rib is the first of the ribs (3–6) that join the body of the sternum directly, one level below the angle.
Slides (2)
L4Learning
Why does rib counting start at the sternal angle rather than at the 1st rib?
  1. A. The 1st rib lies hidden behind the clavicle and cannot be felt
  2. B. The 1st rib does not reach the sternum, so it has no front landmark
  3. C. The 1st rib is buried under pectoralis major and cannot be felt
AnswerA. The 1st rib lies hidden behind the clavicle and cannot be felt
The 1st rib lies behind the clavicle and cannot be palpated, so the examiner finds the 2nd rib at the sternal angle and counts down.
Explanation

The short, sharply curved 1st rib passes up under the clavicle to join the manubrium just below the sternoclavicular joint, so its front end cannot be felt. The sternal angle is easy to feel and always marks the 2nd costal cartilage, so it is the reliable starting point for counting ribs and spaces (for example, to place a stethoscope).

  • The 1st rib does reach the sternum: its cartilage joins the manubrium by a synchondrosis.
  • Pectoralis major covers the upper ribs in front, but ribs 2 to 6 can still be felt through it; muscle is not what hides the 1st rib.
Slides (2)
L5Learning
During a physical exam, the physician feels a midline depression at the top of the sternum, between the medial ends of the clavicles. Which landmark is this?
  1. A. Jugular (suprasternal) notch
  2. B. Sternal angle
  3. C. Clavicular notch
AnswerA. Jugular (suprasternal) notch
The jugular (suprasternal) notch is the midline dip in the upper border of the manubrium, between the medial ends of the clavicles.
Explanation

The jugular notch is the concave upper border of the manubrium; the trachea can be felt just above and behind it. It lies level with the lower border of T2, and the sternal angle is about 4 cm below it.

  • The sternal angle is a transverse ridge, not a notch, lower down at the manubriosternal joint (2nd rib).
  • The clavicular notches are the paired articular facets on each side of the manubrium that take the medial ends of the clavicles at the sternoclavicular joints; they are not the midline dip between them.
Slides (2)
L6Learning
At what vertebral level does the jugular notch lie?
  1. A. Lower border of T2
  2. B. Upper border of C7
  3. C. Lower border of T4
AnswerA. Lower border of T2
The jugular notch lies in the same horizontal plane as the inferior border of T2.
Explanation

The sternum slopes forward and down, so each sternal landmark sits several vertebrae lower than you might expect from its height on the front:

Jugular notchinferior border of T2
Sternal angleT4/T5 disc
Xiphisternal jointT9
  • C7 is the vertebra prominens at the base of the neck, above the thoracic inlet.
  • The lower border of T4 (the T4/T5 disc) is the level of the sternal angle, not the notch.
Slide (1)
L7Learning
About how far below the jugular notch is the sternal angle, and why?
  1. A. About 4 cm, because the manubrium is about 4 cm long
  2. B. About 8 cm, because the manubrium is about 8 cm long
  3. C. About 2 cm, because the manubrium is about 2 cm long
AnswerA. About 4 cm, because the manubrium is about 4 cm long
The jugular notch and sternal angle are the top and bottom of the manubrium, which is about 4 cm long.
Explanation

The manubrium runs from the jugular notch (upper border) to the manubriosternal joint (sternal angle). Because it is about 4 cm long, the sternal angle is felt about 4 cm below the notch. The lecture phrases this as the angle lying "about 4 cm inferior to the manubrium": it means below the top of the manubrium, the jugular notch.

  • 8 cm would put you on the body of the sternum, around the 3rd or 4th costal cartilage.
  • 2 cm is too short; the manubrium spans from the lower border of T2 to the T4/T5 disc.
Slides (2)
L8Learning
At what vertebral level does the sternal angle lie?
  1. A. T2/T3 intervertebral disc
  2. B. T6/T7 intervertebral disc
  3. C. T4/T5 intervertebral disc
AnswerC. T4/T5 intervertebral disc
A horizontal plane through the sternal angle passes back to the T4/T5 intervertebral disc (the transverse thoracic plane).
Explanation

The plane through the sternal angle and the T4/T5 disc (the transverse thoracic plane) is the most useful level in the thorax because several things happen in it: the aortic arch begins and ends, the trachea bifurcates, and the azygos vein joins the superior vena cava. A missile passing straight back through the sternal angle reaches the T4/T5 disc and the T4 body.

  • T2/T3 is near the jugular notch (inferior border of T2).
  • T6/T7 is too low: the body of the sternum spans T5–T9, and the xiphisternal joint is at T9.
Slide (1)
L9Learning
Which events take place at the level of the sternal angle?
  1. A. Brachiocephalic veins unite to form the superior vena cava
    Trachea bifurcates
    Thoracic duct joins the left subclavian vein
  2. B. Aortic arch begins and ends (descending aorta starts)
    Trachea bifurcates
    Azygos vein joins the superior vena cava
  3. C. Aortic arch begins and ends (descending aorta starts)
    Trachea bifurcates
    Hemiazygos vein joins the inferior vena cava
AnswerB. Aortic arch begins and ends (descending aorta starts)
Trachea bifurcates
Azygos vein joins the superior vena cava
At the sternal angle (T4/T5) the aortic arch begins and ends, the trachea bifurcates and the azygos vein arches forward into the superior vena cava.
Explanation

The plane of the sternal angle is a checklist of internal events:

  • the ascending aorta becomes the arch, and the arch becomes the descending (thoracic) aorta;
  • the trachea divides into the right and left main bronchi (carina);
  • the azygos vein arches over the root of the right lung to enter the superior vena cava.

Wrong choices: the brachiocephalic veins unite behind the right 1st costal cartilage, and the thoracic duct ends at the left venous angle in the root of the neck, both above this plane. The hemiazygos vein never joins the inferior vena cava; it crosses behind the aorta to the azygos vein at about T8–T9.

Slides (2)
L10Learning
A tumour is confined to the horizontal plane of the sternal angle. Which of these lies in that plane?
  1. A. Entry of the superior vena cava into the right atrium
  2. B. Inferior border of the heart
  3. C. Junction of the azygos vein with the superior vena cava
AnswerC. Junction of the azygos vein with the superior vena cava
The azygos vein arches over the right lung root and joins the superior vena cava at the T4/T5 level of the sternal angle.
Explanation

At the sternal angle the azygos arch, the end of the aortic arch and the tracheal bifurcation all sit in one plane, so a lesion there can involve any of them.

  • The superior vena cava enters the right atrium lower down, at about the level of the right 3rd costal cartilage.
  • The inferior border of the heart lies at the xiphisternal joint (T9), not at the sternal angle.

Tip: the highest point of the aortic arch is also above the sternal angle (behind the middle of the manubrium); only the arch's beginning and end are at the angle.

Slides (2)
L11Learning
Besides the aortic arch, the carina and the azygos arch, which further structures does the lecture place at the level of the sternal angle (T4/T5)?
  1. A. Bifurcation of the brachiocephalic trunk
    Ligamentum arteriosum with the right recurrent laryngeal nerve
    Transverse pericardial sinus
  2. B. Bifurcation of the pulmonary trunk
    Ligamentum arteriosum with the left recurrent laryngeal nerve
    Transverse pericardial sinus
  3. C. Bifurcation of the pulmonary trunk
    Union of the brachiocephalic veins into the superior vena cava
    Oblique pericardial sinus
AnswerB. Bifurcation of the pulmonary trunk
Ligamentum arteriosum with the left recurrent laryngeal nerve
Transverse pericardial sinus
The T4/T5 plane also passes through the pulmonary trunk bifurcation, the ligamentum arteriosum with the left recurrent laryngeal nerve, and the transverse pericardial sinus.
Explanation

The plane of the sternal angle runs back to the T4/T5 disc through the roots of the great vessels. Besides the start and end of the aortic arch, the tracheal bifurcation and the azygos arch entering the superior vena cava, the pulmonary trunk divides into right and left pulmonary arteries just under the arch. The ligamentum arteriosum ties the left pulmonary artery to the underside of the arch there, and the left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the arch beside it. The transverse pericardial sinus, behind the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk, is at the same level.
