  • The brachiocephalic trunk divides behind the right sternoclavicular joint, and the right recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks round the right subclavian artery in the neck: both above the plane.
  • The brachiocephalic veins unite behind the right 1st costal cartilage, above the plane; the oblique pericardial sinus lies lower, behind the left atrium.
Slide (1)
L12Learning
At what vertebral level does the xiphisternal joint lie?
  1. A. T11
  2. B. T9
  3. C. T7
AnswerB. T9
The xiphisternal joint, where the body of the sternum meets the xiphoid process, lies level with the T9 vertebra.
Explanation

The xiphisternal joint is the lower end of the sternal body; the body spans T5–T9, so its lower end is at T9. The 7th costal cartilage joins the sternum here, and the xiphoid tip hangs down to about T10.

  • T7 would be in the middle of the sternal body.
  • T11 is below the whole sternum, at the level of the floating ribs.
Slide (1)
L13Learning
Besides guiding hand placement in CPR, the xiphisternal joint is a midline marker for which structures?
  1. A. Lower limit of the liver
    Oesophageal hiatus of the diaphragm
    Apex of the heart
  2. B. Upper limit of the liver
    Bifurcation of the trachea
    Inferior border of the heart
  3. C. Upper limit of the liver
    Central tendon of the diaphragm
    Inferior border of the heart
AnswerC. Upper limit of the liver
Central tendon of the diaphragm
Inferior border of the heart
At the xiphisternal joint (T9) lie the upper limit of the liver, the central tendon of the diaphragm and the inferior border of the heart.
Explanation

The heart rests on the central tendon of the diaphragm, and the liver lies directly under the right dome, so all three meet at the level of the xiphisternal joint. This is also the lower limit of the central part of the thoracic cavity.

  • The lower limit of the liver is at the right costal margin, far below; the apex of the heart is in the left 5th intercostal space at the midclavicular line, and the oesophageal hiatus is at T10.
  • The tracheal bifurcation is at the sternal angle (T4/T5), not the xiphisternal joint.
Slides (2)
L14Learning
A hiker collapses and you prepare to start chest compressions. Which landmark do you palpate to place the heel of your hand correctly on the lower sternum?
  1. A. Xiphisternal joint (xiphoid process)
  2. B. Sternal angle
  3. C. Jugular notch
AnswerA. Xiphisternal joint (xiphoid process)
The xiphisternal joint marks the lower end of the sternal body; compressions go on the lower sternum just above it, not on the xiphoid.
Explanation

In cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) the hands go on the lower half of the sternum, which lies over the heart. Finding the xiphisternal joint (and the xiphoid process below it) shows where the sternal body ends, so the hands can sit just above it. Pressing on the xiphoid itself can break it and drive it into the liver below.

  • The sternal angle is too high: it marks the 2nd rib and the T4/T5 level, over the great vessels rather than the ventricles.
  • The jugular notch is the top of the manubrium, the highest point of the sternum.
Slides (2)
L15Learning
At what level is the tip of the xiphoid process, and when does it become easier to feel?
  1. A. About T12, more easily felt after about age 40
  2. B. About T10, more easily felt before about age 20
  3. C. About T10, more easily felt after about age 40
AnswerC. About T10, more easily felt after about age 40
The xiphoid tip lies at about T10; the xiphoid ossifies with age, so it is easier to palpate after about age 40.
Explanation

The xiphoid process is the small lowest part of the sternum, cartilaginous in young people and gradually ossified in adults. Once bony (usually after about 40) it can be felt as a hard point in the epigastric fossa and is sometimes mistaken for a mass.

  • T12 is too low: that is the level of the aortic hiatus and the 12th rib.
  • In young people the xiphoid is still mostly cartilage, so it is harder, not easier, to feel.
Slides (2)
L16Learning
What forms the costal margin?
  1. A. Costal cartilages of ribs 1–7
  2. B. Costal cartilages of ribs 7–10
  3. C. Costal cartilages of ribs 8–12
AnswerB. Costal cartilages of ribs 7–10
Each costal margin is the curved lower edge of the cage formed by the joined costal cartilages of ribs 7–10; it is the front border of the thoracic outlet.
Explanation

The cartilages of ribs 8, 9 and 10 join the cartilage above, and the 7th joins the sternum, so together they form one continuous curved edge on each side (the costal arch). The two margins meet at the xiphisternal joint to form the infrasternal angle and form the anterolateral border of the thoracic outlet.

  • The cartilages of ribs 1–6 run separately to the sternum above the margin; of ribs 1–7 only the 7th takes part, at the margin's upper end.
  • Ribs 11 and 12 are floating ribs with free ends; they do not join the margin, so 8–12 is wrong.
Slides (2)
L17Learning
What is the angle where the two costal margins meet?
  1. A. Costovertebral angle
  2. B. Infrasternal (subcostal) angle
  3. C. Sternal angle (angle of Louis)
AnswerB. Infrasternal (subcostal) angle
The right and left costal margins meet at the xiphisternal joint to form the infrasternal (subcostal) angle.
Explanation

The infrasternal angle is the inverted V below the sternum, with the xiphoid process in its apex and the epigastric fossa just below. It widens during inspiration as the lower ribs swing out (bucket-handle movement).

  • The costovertebral angle is on the back, between the 12th rib and the vertebral column (over the kidney).
  • The sternal angle is the manubriosternal joint at the 2nd rib, high on the sternum.
Slides (2)
L18Learning
Over which intercostal space does the nipple usually lie in men?
  1. A. 4th intercostal space
  2. B. 5th intercostal space
  3. C. 3rd intercostal space
AnswerA. 4th intercostal space
In men the nipple usually lies over the 4th intercostal space; in women breast size and shape make it unreliable.
Explanation

The 4th intercostal space lies between ribs 4 and 5 and is numbered for the rib above. The male nipple is a handy marker for it (and for the T4 dermatome). In women the nipple position varies with the size and shape of the breast, so it is not a reliable landmark.

  • The 5th intercostal space is one lower: the apex beat is found there at the midclavicular line.
  • The 3rd intercostal space is one higher, two spaces below the sternal angle's 2nd rib.
Slide (1)

Surface lines and axillary folds

L19Learning
What forms the anterior axillary fold?
  1. A. Lower border of latissimus dorsi
  2. B. Lower border of pectoralis major
  3. C. Lower border of pectoralis minor
AnswerB. Lower border of pectoralis major
The anterior axillary fold is the rounded lower (inferolateral) border of pectoralis major as it passes to the arm.
Explanation

Grip the front of your own armpit: the fleshy edge is pectoralis major running from the chest wall to the humerus. The anterior axillary line is drawn vertically along this fold.

  • Latissimus dorsi (with teres major) forms the posterior fold.
  • Pectoralis minor lies deep to pectoralis major and inserts on the coracoid process; it does not form a visible fold.
Slides (2)
L20Learning
Which muscles form the posterior axillary fold?
  1. A. Latissimus dorsi and teres minor
  2. B. Pectoralis major and latissimus dorsi
  3. C. Latissimus dorsi and teres major
AnswerC. Latissimus dorsi and teres major
The posterior axillary fold is formed by latissimus dorsi wrapping around teres major on their way to the humerus.
Explanation

The back of the armpit is a thick fold made by latissimus dorsi curling round teres major; both insert near the intertubercular groove of the humerus. The posterior axillary line runs vertically along this fold.

  • Teres minor is a rotator cuff muscle on the back of the scapula that inserts on the greater tubercle; it is not part of the fold.
  • Pectoralis major forms the anterior fold, so a pairing with latissimus dorsi mixes the two folds.
Slides (2)
L21Learning
At what level does the root (medial end) of the spine of the scapula lie?
  1. A. T7 spinous process (about the 7th rib)
  2. B. T3 spinous process (about the 3rd rib)
  3. C. T1 spinous process (about the 1st rib)
AnswerB. T3 spinous process (about the 3rd rib)
With the arm at the side, the root of the scapular spine lies level with the T3 spinous process, roughly at the 3rd rib.
Explanation

The scapula gives quick posterior landmarks when the arms hang at the sides:

Superior angleabout T2
Root of the spineT3 spinous process (3rd rib)
Inferior angleT7 spinous process (7th rib)
  • T7 is the level of the inferior angle, where the scapular lines are drawn.
  • T1 is above the scapula, just below the prominent C7 spine.

The landmarks shift when the arm is raised, because the scapula rotates.

Slide (1)
L22Learning
Which vertical line is where the median plane meets the front of the chest?
  1. A. Midclavicular line
  2. B. Anterior axillary line
  3. C. Anterior median line
AnswerC. Anterior median line
The anterior median line is the intersection of the median plane with the anterior thoracic wall, running down the middle of the sternum.
Explanation

Vertical lines let you describe where a finding lies on the chest. On the front: the anterior median line (midline), the midclavicular lines (through the midpoint of each clavicle, parallel to the median line) and the axillary lines at the sides. Its counterpart behind is the posterior median line along the spinous processes.

  • The midclavicular line runs through the midpoint of the clavicle, well lateral to the midline.
  • The anterior axillary line runs along the anterior axillary fold, at the side of the chest.
Slide (1)
L23Learning
Through which point does the midclavicular line pass?
  1. A. Midpoint of the clavicle
  2. B. Acromioclavicular joint
  3. C. Sternoclavicular joint
AnswerA. Midpoint of the clavicle
The midclavicular line drops vertically from the midpoint of the clavicle, parallel to the anterior median line.
Explanation

The midclavicular line is used to locate the apex beat (left 5th intercostal space) and to describe pleural and lung borders.

  • A line from the acromioclavicular joint would lie at the shoulder, lateral to the chest wall.
  • A line from the sternoclavicular joint would run along the edge of the sternum (the sternal line), much too medial.
Slides (2)
L24Learning
Along what does the anterior axillary line run?
  1. A. The anterior axillary fold
  2. B. The apex of the axilla
  3. C. The midpoint of the clavicle
AnswerA. The anterior axillary fold
The anterior axillary line runs vertically along the anterior axillary fold (lower border of pectoralis major); the posterior axillary line follows the posterior fold.
Explanation

The three axillary lines sit on the side of the chest:

  • anterior axillary line along the anterior axillary fold (pectoralis major);
  • midaxillary line down from the apex of the axilla;
  • posterior axillary line along the posterior axillary fold (latissimus dorsi and teres major).

Wrong choices: a line down from the apex of the axilla is the midaxillary line, and a line through the midpoint of the clavicle is the midclavicular line.

Slide (1)
L25Learning
From where does the midaxillary line run down?
  1. A. Apex of the axilla
  2. B. Tip of the acromion
  3. C. Coracoid process
AnswerA. Apex of the axilla
The midaxillary line runs vertically down from the apex (deepest point) of the axilla, halfway between the anterior and posterior axillary lines.
Explanation

With the arm raised, the midaxillary line drops straight down from the top of the armpit, parallel to the anterior axillary line. It matters clinically: the lateral cutaneous branches of the intercostal nerves emerge near it, and thoracentesis is done in the 9th intercostal space at this line.

  • The tip of the acromion is the point of the shoulder, lateral to the chest wall.
  • The coracoid process lies in front, below the lateral clavicle, medial to the axillary lines.
Slide (1)
L26Learning
Along what does the posterior median line run?
  1. A. Medial borders of the scapulae
  2. B. Tips of the spinous processes
  3. C. Tips of the transverse processes
AnswerB. Tips of the spinous processes
The posterior median line runs vertically along the tips of the spinous processes of the vertebrae.
Explanation

The posterior median line is the back's midline, the counterpart of the anterior median line. The scapular lines run parallel to it on each side.

  • The medial borders of the scapulae lie several centimetres lateral to the midline and move with the arm.
  • The transverse processes lie deep, a few centimetres either side of the spines; they cannot define a single midline.
Slide (1)
L27Learning
Through what do the scapular lines run?
  1. A. Superior angles of the scapulae
  2. B. Medial borders of the scapulae
  3. C. Inferior angles of the scapulae
AnswerC. Inferior angles of the scapulae
Each scapular line is a vertical line through the inferior angle of the scapula, parallel to the posterior median line.
Explanation

With the arms at the sides the inferior angle lies at about the T7 spinous process (7th rib), and the scapular line drops vertically through it. It is used to describe where findings lie on the back, for example when listening over the lower lobes.

  • The superior angle lies higher (about T2) and is not the reference point.
  • The medial border slants, so a line along it would not be vertical.
Slide (1)

Thoracic cage, sternum and vertebrae

L28Learning
What three components make up the thoracic cage?
  1. A. Sternum and costal cartilages (front)
    12 pairs of ribs (sides)
    12 thoracic vertebrae (behind)
  2. B. Sternum and costal cartilages (front)
    10 pairs of ribs (sides)
    10 thoracic vertebrae (behind)
  3. C. Sternum and costal cartilages (front)
    12 pairs of ribs (sides)
    7 cervical vertebrae (behind)
AnswerA. Sternum and costal cartilages (front)
12 pairs of ribs (sides)
12 thoracic vertebrae (behind)
The thoracic cage is the sternum and costal cartilages in front, 12 pairs of ribs at the sides and 12 thoracic vertebrae (with their discs) behind.
Explanation

The cage has two openings: the small thoracic inlet above (to the neck and upper limbs) and the large thoracic outlet below, almost closed by the diaphragm. Each of the 12 thoracic vertebrae carries a pair of ribs.

  • There are 12, not 10, pairs of ribs and thoracic vertebrae; ribs 11 and 12 are short floating ribs but still part of the cage.
  • The cervical vertebrae carry no ribs (an extra cervical rib is an anomaly) and lie above the cage.
Slide (1)
L29Learning
What are the functions of the thoracic cage?
  1. A. Protects heart, great vessels, lungs and trachea
    Passage between neck and abdomen
    Supports the pelvic girdle and lower limbs
  2. B. Protects heart, great vessels, lungs and trachea
    Separates the thorax from the abdomen
    Supports the upper limbs
  3. C. Protects heart, great vessels, lungs and trachea
    Passage between neck and abdomen
    Supports the upper limbs
AnswerC. Protects heart, great vessels, lungs and trachea
Passage between neck and abdomen
Supports the upper limbs
The cage protects the thoracic organs, provides a route between the neck and the abdomen, and gives attachment to and supports the upper limbs.
Explanation

The cage is a protective shell around the heart, great vessels, lungs and trachea. Its apertures let the trachea, oesophagus, vessels and nerves pass between the neck, thorax and abdomen. The clavicle and scapula (and muscles such as pectoralis major and serratus anterior) attach to it, so it carries the upper limbs.

  • Separating the thorax from the abdomen is the diaphragm's job; the bony cage is open below.
  • The pelvic girdle and lower limbs attach to the sacrum, not the thoracic cage.
Slide (1)
L30Learning
What are the three parts of the sternum, from top to bottom?
  1. A. Body → manubrium → xiphoid process
  2. B. Manubrium → body → xiphoid process
  3. C. Manubrium → xiphoid process → body
AnswerB. Manubrium → body → xiphoid process
The sternum is the manubrium above, the long body in the middle and the small xiphoid process at the bottom.
Explanation

The manubrium (handle) carries the jugular and clavicular notches and the 1st costal cartilages; it meets the body at the sternal angle (2nd rib). The body takes cartilages 3–6 directly and meets the xiphoid process at the xiphisternal joint (7th rib). The sternum protects much of the heart.

  • The manubrium is always the top part, so any order starting with the body is wrong.
  • The xiphoid is always the lowest, cartilaginous-to-bony tip; it never lies between the manubrium and body.
Slide (1)
L31Learning
Which notches does the manubrium carry, and what articulates with it?
  1. A. Jugular notch only
    Articulates with the 1st ribs but not the clavicles
  2. B. Jugular and clavicular notches
    Articulates with the clavicles and the 1st ribs
  3. C. Jugular and clavicular notches
    Articulates with the clavicles and the 3rd ribs
AnswerB. Jugular and clavicular notches
Articulates with the clavicles and the 1st ribs
The manubrium has the jugular notch and two clavicular notches, and takes the clavicles and the 1st costal cartilages.
Explanation

The clavicular notches form the sternoclavicular joints with the medial ends of the clavicles; just below each, the 1st costal cartilage joins the manubrium (synchondrosis). The 2nd costal cartilage sits at the lower edge, straddling the manubriosternal joint, which is why a manubrial fracture can involve the 1st and 2nd ribs.

  • Without the clavicular notches the clavicle could not articulate, and the sternoclavicular joint is the main joint linking the upper limb to the thorax.
  • The 3rd ribs join the body of the sternum, below the sternal angle.
Slide (1)
L32Learning
Opposite which vertebral levels does the manubrium lie?
  1. A. From C7 to the lower border of T2
  2. B. From the lower border of T2 to the T4/T5 disc
  3. C. From the T4/T5 disc to T9
AnswerB. From the lower border of T2 to the T4/T5 disc
The manubrium runs from the lower border of T2 (jugular notch) to the T4/T5 disc (sternal angle), about 4 cm.
Explanation

The top and bottom of the manubrium are the two best-known sternal landmarks, so its levels follow from them: jugular notch at the lower border of T2, sternal angle at the T4/T5 disc. The manubrium therefore lies in front of the bodies of T3 and T4.

  • C7 to T2 is above the sternum, at the thoracic inlet and root of the neck.
  • T4/T5 to T9 is the level of the body of the sternum (T5–T9), ending at the xiphisternal joint.
Slide (1)
L33Learning
Opposite which vertebrae does the body of the sternum lie?
  1. A. T5–T9
  2. B. T3–T6
  3. C. T1–T4
AnswerA. T5–T9
The body of the sternum lies opposite T5–T9, from the sternal angle (T4/T5 disc) down to the xiphisternal joint (T9).
Explanation

The body is the longest part of the sternum. Its upper end meets the manubrium at the sternal angle and its lower end meets the xiphoid at T9.

  • T1–T4 is roughly the level of the manubrium and the thoracic inlet above it.
  • T3–T6 starts too high: the body only begins at the T4/T5 disc.
Slide (1)
L34Learning
Which costal cartilages attach directly to the body of the sternum?
  1. A. Ribs 3–6
  2. B. Ribs 2–5
  3. C. Ribs 1–7
AnswerA. Ribs 3–6
Costal cartilages 3–6 join the body of the sternum; the 2nd joins at the sternal angle and the 7th at the xiphisternal joint.
Explanation

The lateral border of the body carries notches for the costal cartilages. Cartilages 3, 4, 5 and 6 sit wholly on the body. The 2nd and 7th sit at its two ends, at the manubriosternal and xiphisternal junctions, and the 1st joins the manubrium.

  • Ribs 2–5 wrongly includes the 2nd, which attaches at the sternal angle.
  • Ribs 1–7 adds the 1st, which joins the manubrium, and the 7th, which joins at the xiphisternal joint; neither sits on the body.
Slides (2)
L35Learning
Where do the 2nd and 7th costal cartilages attach to the sternum?
  1. A. 2nd at the jugular notch
    7th at the xiphoid tip
  2. B. 2nd at the sternal angle
    7th at the xiphisternal joint
  3. C. 2nd at the xiphisternal joint
    7th at the sternal angle
AnswerB. 2nd at the sternal angle
7th at the xiphisternal joint
The 2nd costal cartilage joins at the sternal angle and the 7th at the xiphisternal joint, the two ends of the sternal body.
Explanation

These two attachments make the joints between the sternal parts useful landmarks: the sternal angle finds the 2nd rib for counting, and the xiphisternal joint marks the 7th cartilage, the lowest one to reach the sternum.

  • Nothing articulates at the jugular notch (the clavicles and 1st cartilages join the sides of the manubrium), and the xiphoid tip is free.
  • The reverse pairing puts each rib at the wrong end of the sternum.
Slide (1)
L36Learning
Which feature identifies a vertebra as thoracic?
  1. A. Costal facets on its body and transverse processes
  2. B. Mammillary processes on its superior articular processes
  3. C. Foramina in its transverse processes
AnswerA. Costal facets on its body and transverse processes
Only thoracic vertebrae carry costal facets: on the body for the rib head and (T1–T10) on the transverse process for the rib tubercle.
Explanation

Ribs articulate only with thoracic vertebrae, so costal facets are the defining feature. The body facets (whole facets or demifacets) take the head of the rib; the transverse costal facets take the tubercle.

  • Mammillary processes are knobs on the superior articular processes of lumbar vertebrae.
  • Foramina transversaria (for the vertebral arteries) mark cervical vertebrae.

Tip: T11 and T12 have no transverse costal facets, because ribs 11 and 12 have no tubercles.

Slides (2)
L37Learning
Besides costal facets, which features mark a typical thoracic vertebra?
  1. A. Heart-shaped body
    Large triangular vertebral foramen
    Bifid spinous process
  2. B. Heart-shaped body
    Small vertebral foramen
    Long spinous process sloping downward
  3. C. Kidney-shaped body
    Small vertebral foramen
    Short, square spinous process
AnswerB. Heart-shaped body
Small vertebral foramen
Long spinous process sloping downward
A thoracic vertebra has a heart-shaped body, a small (round) vertebral foramen and a long spinous process sloping steeply downward.
Explanation

The long, downward-sloping spines overlap like roof tiles and limit extension of the thoracic spine; the small round foramen surrounds the thoracic spinal cord.

  • A large triangular foramen and a bifid spine are cervical features.
  • A kidney-shaped body and a short, square (hatchet-shaped) spine are lumbar features.
Slides (2)
L38Learning
Which thoracic vertebrae are typical, and what costal facets do their bodies carry?
  1. A. T5–T12, with a demifacet (half-facet) above and below on each body
  2. B. T1–T12, with a single whole facet on each body
  3. C. T2–T9, with a demifacet (half-facet) above and below on each body
AnswerC. T2–T9, with a demifacet (half-facet) above and below on each body
T2–T9 are typical: each body has a superior and an inferior demifacet, because each typical rib head spans two vertebrae.
Explanation

The superior demifacet of, say, T6 takes the head of rib 6; its inferior demifacet takes the head of rib 7. Together with the disc they form a socket for each rib head.

  • T10–T12 are atypical: they carry one whole facet for their own rib, so a typical range cannot run to T12.
  • T1 is atypical too: a whole facet above for rib 1 and a demifacet below for rib 2; not every vertebra carries a single whole facet.
Slides (2)
L39Learning
Why do typical thoracic vertebrae have demifacets?
  1. A. A typical rib tubercle touches two vertebrae
  2. B. A typical rib head touches two vertebrae
  3. C. A typical rib head touches only its own vertebra
AnswerB. A typical rib head touches two vertebrae
A typical rib head meets two vertebral bodies (its own and the one above) and their disc, so each body carries half a facet per rib.
Explanation

Each typical rib head has two facets separated by a crest: the inferior facet meets its own vertebra, the superior facet meets the vertebra above, and the crest is tied to the disc. Each vertebral body therefore needs two half-facets, one for the rib of its own number and one for the rib below.

  • The tubercle meets only the transverse process of its own vertebra, at one whole facet.
  • A head meeting only its own vertebra describes ribs 1, 10, 11 and 12, whose vertebrae carry whole facets instead.
Slides (2)
L40Learning
What costal facets does T1 have on its body?
  1. A. A whole facet for the 1st rib and an inferior demifacet for the 2nd rib
  2. B. A superior demifacet for the 1st rib and an inferior demifacet for the 2nd rib
  3. C. A whole facet for the 1st rib and a whole facet for the 2nd rib
AnswerA. A whole facet for the 1st rib and an inferior demifacet for the 2nd rib
T1 carries a whole superior facet for the head of rib 1 (which meets only T1) and an inferior demifacet for rib 2.
Explanation

The 1st rib has a single facet on its head and articulates with T1 alone, so T1 needs a whole facet above. The 2nd rib is typical in its head, spanning T1 and T2, so T1 has a demifacet below. The lecture's line "T1 has only inferior demifacets" means its only demifacet is the inferior one; the superior facet is whole.

  • A superior demifacet for rib 1 would imply rib 1 also meets C7, which it does not.
  • A whole inferior facet would imply rib 2 meets only T1; in fact it shares T1 and T2.
Slide (1)
L41Learning
What costal facets do the bodies of T10–T12 carry?
  1. A. No costal facets
  2. B. A demifacet above and below
  3. C. One whole facet each
AnswerC. One whole facet each
T10, T11 and T12 each carry one whole costal facet, because ribs 10–12 articulate with their own vertebra only.
Explanation

The heads of ribs 10, 11 and 12 have a single facet and meet only the vertebra of the same number, so each of these vertebrae has one whole facet for its own rib. T11 and T12 also lack transverse costal facets, because ribs 11 and 12 have no tubercles.

  • They are still thoracic vertebrae, so they do carry costal facets; a vertebra with no costal facets is cervical or lumbar.
  • Paired demifacets are the pattern of the typical vertebrae T2–T9.
Slide (1)

Ribs

L42Learning
In the lecture's classification by attachment, which ribs are true (vertebrosternal) ribs, attaching to the sternum directly by their own costal cartilages?
  1. A. Ribs 1–10
  2. B. Ribs 1–5
  3. C. Ribs 1–6
AnswerC. Ribs 1–6
True ribs attach to the sternum directly by their own costal cartilages; the lecture counts these as ribs 1–6 (most textbooks say 1–7).
Explanation

Ribs are classed by how their cartilages reach the sternum: true (directly, by their own cartilage), false (indirectly, by joining the cartilage above) and floating (not at all). The lecture's list gives true ribs 1–6, false ribs 7–9 (sometimes 10) and floating ribs 11–12 (sometimes 10); answer with this list on the exam.

Standard textbooks, and the cage figure in the same lecture, count 1–7 as true and 8–10 as false, because the 7th cartilage itself reaches the sternum at the xiphisternal joint. Know both: if 1–7 is offered without 1–6, it is the textbook answer.

  • Ribs 1–10 includes the lower ribs, whose cartilages reach the sternum only through the cartilage above.
  • Ribs 1–5 leaves out the 6th, whose own cartilage joins the body of the sternum.

The updated 2026 lecture shows only a labelled rib-cage figure, which marks ribs 1–7 as true ribs, the textbook count.

Slide (1)
L43Learning
Which ribs does the lecture classify as false (vertebrochondral) ribs, and how do they reach the sternum?
  1. A. Ribs 6–9: their cartilages join the cartilage of the rib below
  2. B. Ribs 8–12: their cartilages join the cartilage of the rib above
  3. C. Ribs 7–9 (sometimes 10): their cartilages join the cartilage of the rib above
AnswerC. Ribs 7–9 (sometimes 10): their cartilages join the cartilage of the rib above
In the lecture's list the false ribs are 7–9 (sometimes 10): each cartilage joins the cartilage of the rib above, so it reaches the sternum indirectly.
Explanation

A false rib has no sternal joint of its own: its cartilage joins the cartilage above, so it reaches the sternum only through the cartilages above it. The lecture lists the false ribs as the 7th–9th, with the 10th sometimes included (it may instead float).

Standard textbooks, and the lecture's own cage figure, give the false ribs as 8–10, because the 7th cartilage reaches the sternum itself at the xiphisternal joint. The cartilages of ribs 7–10 together form the costal margin.

  • Ribs 11 and 12 have no anterior connection at all (floating ribs), so "8–12 joining the rib above" is wrong in either scheme.
  • Cartilages join the rib above, never the one below, and the 6th rib reaches the sternum by its own cartilage.

The updated 2026 lecture's figure labels ribs 8–10 as false and 11–12 as floating, the textbook scheme.

Slide (1)
L44Learning
Which ribs are floating ribs, and where do they end?
  1. A. Ribs 10 and 11, ending in the muscles of the posterior abdominal wall
  2. B. Ribs 11 and 12, ending at the xiphoid process
  3. C. Ribs 11 and 12, ending in the muscles of the posterior abdominal wall
AnswerC. Ribs 11 and 12, ending in the muscles of the posterior abdominal wall
Ribs 11 and 12 are floating: their short cartilages do not reach the sternum even indirectly and end free in the posterior abdominal wall muscles.
Explanation

The floating (vertebral) ribs articulate only with their own vertebra behind and have free anterior tips buried in muscle. The 10th rib sometimes floats too, which is why the lecture adds "sometimes 10th".

  • Rib 10 usually joins the cartilage of rib 9, so the floating pair is 11 and 12, not 10 and 11.
  • Nothing attaches to the xiphoid process except the 7th cartilage region and muscles; floating ribs have no sternal connection.
Slide (1)
L45Learning
Although the lecture lists the 7th rib with the false ribs, standard textbooks count it as a true rib. On what basis?
  1. A. Its cartilage joins the cartilage of the 6th rib above
  2. B. Its cartilage meets the sternum at the sternal angle
  3. C. Its cartilage meets the sternum at the xiphisternal joint
AnswerC. Its cartilage meets the sternum at the xiphisternal joint
The 7th costal cartilage reaches the sternum itself, at the xiphisternal joint, so textbooks count the 7th as the last true rib.
Explanation

Whether a rib is true depends on its own cartilage touching the sternum. The 7th cartilage articulates at the junction of the sternal body and xiphoid (a synovial sternocostal joint), so standard texts and the lecture's cage figure count true ribs as 1–7. The lecture's list (true 1–6, false 7–9) puts the 7th with the false ribs; on the exam follow the list, but know why the textbooks differ.

  • Joining the 6th cartilage is how the lecture's list treats the 7th; textbooks reserve that pattern for ribs 8–10, and it would make a rib false, not true.
  • The sternal angle takes the 2nd costal cartilage, not the 7th.

The updated 2026 lecture's figure also counts the 7th as a true rib.

Slides (2)
L46Learning
By their bony features, which ribs are typical and which are atypical?
  1. A. Typical: 1–7
    Atypical: 8, 9, 10, 11, 12
  2. B. Typical: 3–12
    Atypical: 1 and 2
  3. C. Typical: 3–9
    Atypical: 1, 2, 10, 11, 12
AnswerC. Typical: 3–9
Atypical: 1, 2, 10, 11, 12
Ribs 3–9 are typical; 1, 2, 10, 11 and 12 are atypical because of unusual heads, shapes or missing parts.
Explanation

A typical rib has a two-faceted head, neck, tubercle, angle and a body with a costal groove. The atypical ones: 1st (broad, short, one facet, subclavian grooves), 2nd (thin, with a tuberosity for serratus anterior), 10th (one facet), 11th and 12th (short, one facet, no neck or tubercle).

  • 1–7 vs 8–12 mirrors the textbook attachment split (true vs false and floating ribs), not the bony one.
  • Ribs 10–12 have single-faceted heads, so they cannot be typical.
Slide (1)
L47Learning
What are the parts of a typical rib, from its vertebral end outward?
  1. A. Neck → head → tubercle → body (with angle and costal groove)
  2. B. Head → neck → tubercle → body (with angle and costal groove)
  3. C. Head → tubercle → neck → body (with angle and costal groove)
AnswerB. Head → neck → tubercle → body (with angle and costal groove)
A typical rib runs head → neck → tubercle → body; the body carries the angle and the costal groove.
Explanation

The head meets the vertebral bodies; the neck is the short stretch in front of the transverse process; the tubercle at the neck–body junction meets the transverse process; the thin, curved body (shaft) turns forward at the angle and has the costal groove on its inner lower edge.

  • The neck cannot come first: the head is the most medial part.
  • The tubercle lies lateral to the neck, at its junction with the body.
Slide (1)
L48Learning
What does the head of a typical rib look like?
  1. A. Wedge-shaped, with two facets separated by a crest
  2. B. Wedge-shaped, with one facet and a non-articular tubercle
  3. C. Flat, with three facets separated by two crests
AnswerA. Wedge-shaped, with two facets separated by a crest
A typical rib head is wedge-shaped, with two articular facets separated by a crest that fits against the intervertebral disc.
Explanation

The two facets let the head fit between two vertebral bodies: the inferior facet meets the vertebra of the same number, the superior facet meets the vertebra above, and the crest is attached to the disc by the intra-articular ligament.

  • One facet on the head is the atypical pattern of ribs 1, 10, 11 and 12; the tubercle is a separate part of the rib, not of the head.
  • No rib head has three facets; there are only two vertebrae to meet.
Slide (1)
L49Learning
Which vertebrae do the two facets on a typical rib head meet?
  1. A. Inferior facet → its own vertebra
    Superior facet → the vertebra above
  2. B. Inferior facet → the vertebra below
    Superior facet → its own vertebra
  3. C. Inferior facet → the vertebra above
    Superior facet → its own vertebra
AnswerA. Inferior facet → its own vertebra
Superior facet → the vertebra above
The inferior facet meets the vertebra of the same number; the superior facet meets the vertebra above (rib 5: T5 and T4).
Explanation

Each typical rib head sits at the level of the disc above its own vertebra. Its lower facet rests on the superior demifacet of its own vertebra, and its upper facet on the inferior demifacet of the vertebra above. So rib 6 meets T6 and T5, and rib 5 meets T5 and T4.

  • A rib head never reaches the vertebra below its own number.
  • The inferior facet cannot meet the vertebra above; the facets keep their up–down order.
Slides (2)
L50Learning
What does the facet on a typical rib's tubercle articulate with?
  1. A. Transverse process of the vertebra below
  2. B. Transverse process of its own vertebra
  3. C. Transverse process of the vertebra above
AnswerB. Transverse process of its own vertebra
The tubercle articulates with the transverse costal facet of its own vertebra (rib 7 tubercle → T7 transverse process) at the costotransverse joint.
Explanation

The head bridges two vertebrae, but the tubercle meets only one: the transverse process of the vertebra with the same number. Together the costovertebral and costotransverse joints set the axis about which the rib swings during breathing.

  • The vertebra above is met by the head's superior facet, not by the tubercle.
  • The vertebra below takes no part in the rib's joints.
Slides (2)
L51Learning
What is the angle of a rib, and what does it mark?
  1. A. Where the body turns forward; it marks the lateral limit of the deep back muscles
  2. B. Where the body turns backward; it marks the lateral limit of serratus anterior
  3. C. Where the body turns forward; it marks the medial limit of the deep back muscles
AnswerA. Where the body turns forward; it marks the lateral limit of the deep back muscles
The angle is where the rib body bends anterolaterally; it marks the lateral limit of attachment of the deep back muscles.
Explanation

Behind the angle the rib runs backward and laterally beside the vertebral column, covered by the erector spinae; at the angle it turns forward around the chest wall. The angle is also the weakest point region: ribs usually break just in front of it.

  • The rib turns forward, not backward, at the angle; serratus anterior attaches far forward on the lateral surfaces of the upper ribs.
  • The deep back muscles lie medial to the angles, so the angle is their lateral, not medial, edge.
Slide (1)
L52Learning
Where is the costal groove, and what does it shelter?
  1. A. Inner upper edge of the rib body; the intercostal vessels and nerve
  2. B. Inner lower edge of the rib body; the intercostal vessels and nerve
  3. C. Outer upper edge of the rib body; the intercostal vessels and nerve
AnswerB. Inner lower edge of the rib body; the intercostal vessels and nerve
The costal groove runs along the internal, inferior surface of the rib body and partly shields the intercostal vein, artery and nerve.
Explanation

The neurovascular bundle runs just under the lower border of each rib, in the groove, between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles. This is why needles and incisions are placed just above the rib below, away from the groove.

  • The upper edge of a rib has no groove; only small collateral branches run along it.
  • The outer surface is covered by the external intercostal muscle; the groove faces inward.
Slides (2)
L53Learning
How does the shape of the 1st rib compare with that of the other true ribs?
  1. A. Narrowest, shortest and most sharply curved
  2. B. Longest, narrowest and least curved
  3. C. Broadest, shortest and most sharply curved
AnswerC. Broadest, shortest and most sharply curved
The 1st rib is the broadest, shortest and most sharply curved; it lies almost flat, with its surfaces facing up and down.
Explanation

Its broad, flat shape forms the rim of the thoracic inlet and carries the subclavian vessels and the scalene muscles. Being short, curved and sheltered by the clavicle, it rarely breaks; a 1st-rib fracture signals severe trauma.

  • It is the broadest rib, not the narrowest.
  • The longest ribs are in the middle of the cage (about 7th), and the least curved are the lower ones.
Slide (1)
L54Learning
Why does the head of the 1st rib have only one facet?
  1. A. It meets only C7
  2. B. It meets T1 and T2 equally
  3. C. It meets only T1
AnswerC. It meets only T1
The 1st rib articulates with T1 alone, so its head needs only a single facet (matching the whole superior facet on T1).
Explanation

There is no rib-bearing vertebra above T1, so rib 1 cannot share a joint with the vertebra above as typical ribs do.

  • C7 carries no ribs (a cervical rib is an anomaly).
  • Rib 2, not rib 1, spans T1 and T2.
Slide (1)
L55Learning
Which grooves cross the upper surface of the 1st rib?
  1. A. Grooves for the internal thoracic artery and vein
  2. B. Grooves for the subclavian artery and subclavian vein
  3. C. Grooves for the brachiocephalic artery and vein
AnswerB. Grooves for the subclavian artery and subclavian vein
The upper surface of the 1st rib carries grooves for the subclavian vein (in front) and subclavian artery (behind), separated by the scalene tubercle.
Explanation

The anterior scalene muscle inserts on the scalene tubercle; the subclavian vein passes in front of it and the subclavian artery (with the lower trunk of the brachial plexus) behind it. This crowded spot is where a cervical rib or an abnormal anterior scalene compresses them in thoracic outlet syndrome.

  • The internal thoracic vessels run down behind the costal cartilages beside the sternum, not over the 1st rib.
  • The brachiocephalic trunk and veins lie behind the manubrium, medial to the 1st ribs.
Slides (2)
L56Learning
What marks the 2nd rib?
  1. A. A groove for the subclavian artery
  2. B. A rough area for pectoralis minor
  3. C. A rough area for serratus anterior
AnswerC. A rough area for serratus anterior
The 2nd rib has a roughened tuberosity for serratus anterior on its upper surface; it is also thinner, longer and less curved than the 1st.
Explanation

The 2nd rib is atypical mainly because of this tuberosity, where the upper digitation of serratus anterior arises. Its head is typical (two facets, meeting T1 and T2).

  • The subclavian artery groove is on the 1st rib.
  • Pectoralis minor arises from ribs 3–5 near their cartilages, not from the 2nd rib.
Slides (2)
L57Learning
What is atypical about the 10th rib?
  1. A. A single facet on its head
  2. B. Two facets separated by a crest
  3. C. No costal groove on its body
AnswerA. A single facet on its head
The 10th rib has a single facet on its head, because it articulates with T10 alone.
Explanation

Ribs 10, 11 and 12 each meet only their own vertebra, matching the single whole facets on T10–T12. Apart from its head, the 10th rib looks fairly ordinary: it has a neck, tubercle and costal groove, and its cartilage usually joins the 9th.

  • Two facets separated by a crest is the typical pattern, not what makes rib 10 atypical.
  • The 10th rib does have a costal groove; the 12th is the one that lacks a clear groove.
Slide (1)
L58Learning
What is atypical about the 11th and 12th ribs?
  1. A. Shortest ribs; two facets on the head; prominent costal groove
  2. B. Shortest ribs; one facet on the head; no neck or tubercle
  3. C. Longest ribs; two facets on the head; no neck or tubercle
AnswerB. Shortest ribs; one facet on the head; no neck or tubercle
Ribs 11 and 12 are the shortest, have a single facet on the head and have no neck or tubercle.
Explanation

Without a tubercle, ribs 11 and 12 form no costotransverse joint; they meet only their own vertebral body. Their short free ends float in the posterior abdominal wall.

  • They have one head facet, not two, and the 12th has little or no costal groove.
  • They are the shortest ribs, not the longest.
Slide (1)
L59Learning
A woman fractures her 5th rib. Its head meets two vertebral bodies and the disc between them, its tubercle meets a transverse process, and its cartilage joins the sternum. How is this rib classified?
  1. A. True and atypical
  2. B. True and typical
  3. C. False and typical
AnswerB. True and typical
Rib 5 joins the sternum by its own cartilage (true) and has a two-faceted head, neck, tubercle and angle (typical).
Explanation

The two classifications are independent. By attachment: true ribs reach the sternum by their own cartilage (1–6 in the lecture's list, 1–7 in textbooks), false ribs through the cartilage above (7–9, sometimes 10, in the lecture; 8–10 in textbooks), floating ribs (11–12) not at all. By bony features: typical ribs are 3–9; ribs 1, 2, 10, 11 and 12 are atypical.

  • Atypical would need a single-faceted head or another odd feature, as in ribs 1, 2, 10, 11, 12.
  • False would need the cartilage to reach the sternum only through the cartilage above, as in ribs 8 and 9.
Slides (2)

Joints of the cage

L60Learning
Which two joints does each typical rib make with the vertebral column, and of what type?
  1. A. Costovertebral and costotransverse; both synovial plane joints
  2. B. Costovertebral and costochondral; both synovial plane joints
  3. C. Costovertebral and costotransverse; both fibrous syndesmoses
AnswerA. Costovertebral and costotransverse; both synovial plane joints
A typical rib makes a costovertebral joint (head) and a costotransverse joint (tubercle); both are synovial plane joints.
Explanation

Both joints allow small gliding movements, and together they act as a hinge whose axis runs along the rib neck. Rotation about this axis produces the pump-handle movement of the upper ribs and the bucket-handle movement of the lower ribs.

  • The costochondral joint is at the front end of the rib, between bone and cartilage; it is not a vertebral joint.
  • The rib–vertebra joints are synovial, with joint cavities and capsules, not fibrous syndesmoses.
Slide (1)
L61Learning
What does the costovertebral joint connect?
  1. A. Rib head with two transverse processes and the ligament between them
  2. B. Rib tubercle with the transverse process of its own vertebra
  3. C. Rib head with two vertebral bodies and the disc between them
AnswerC. Rib head with two vertebral bodies and the disc between them
The costovertebral joint links the head of the rib with the demifacets of two adjacent vertebral bodies and the intervertebral disc between them.
Explanation

The crest of the head is tied to the disc by an intra-articular ligament, dividing the joint into two small synovial cavities. Ribs 1, 10, 11 and 12 articulate with a single vertebral body instead.

  • The rib head never reaches the transverse processes; the tubercle does.
  • Tubercle with transverse process is the costotransverse joint, the other posterior rib joint.
Slide (1)
L62Learning
What does the costotransverse joint connect?
  1. A. Rib head with the transverse process of its own vertebra
  2. B. Rib tubercle with the transverse process of its own vertebra
  3. C. Rib tubercle with the transverse process of the vertebra above
AnswerB. Rib tubercle with the transverse process of its own vertebra
The costotransverse joint joins the tubercle of a rib to the transverse costal facet of its own vertebra; it is a synovial plane joint.
Explanation

Ribs 1–10 have costotransverse joints; ribs 11 and 12 lack tubercles and so lack these joints. Strong costotransverse ligaments reinforce the joint.

  • The head meets vertebral bodies, not transverse processes.
  • The tubercle meets its own vertebra (rib 7 → T7), not the one above.
Slide (1)
L63Learning
With which vertebral bodies does the head of the 5th rib articulate?
  1. A. T5 (above) and T6 (below)
  2. B. T4 (above) and T5 (below)
  3. C. T3 (above) and T4 (below)
AnswerB. T4 (above) and T5 (below)
The 5th rib head meets T5 with its inferior facet and T4 (the vertebra above) with its superior facet, plus the T4/T5 disc.
Explanation

Rule for typical ribs: rib n meets the bodies of vertebra n and vertebra n − 1. So rib 5 sits on T4 and T5, and its tubercle meets the transverse process of T5.

  • T5 and T6 is the pair for rib 6, not rib 5.
  • T3 and T4 is the pair for rib 4.
Slides (2)
L64Learning
Which posterior joint do ribs 11 and 12 lack, and why?
  1. A. The costotransverse joint, because they have no tubercle
  2. B. The costovertebral joint, because they have no head
  3. C. The costotransverse joint, because they have no head facet
AnswerA. The costotransverse joint, because they have no tubercle
Ribs 11 and 12 have no tubercle, so they make no costotransverse joint; each meets only the body of its own vertebra.
Explanation

Their only posterior joint is a costovertebral joint between a single-faceted head and the whole facet on T11 or T12. With no tubercle (and no neck), there is nothing to articulate with the transverse process, and T11 and T12 accordingly lack transverse costal facets.

  • They do have a head, so they keep their costovertebral joints.
  • They do have a head facet (a single one); the missing part is the tubercle, which is what forms the costotransverse joint.
Slides (2)
L65Learning
What type of joint do the intervertebral discs form between thoracic vertebral bodies?
  1. A. Synchondroses
  2. B. Syndesmoses
  3. C. Symphyses
AnswerC. Symphyses
Intervertebral discs make symphyses (secondary cartilaginous joints): fibrocartilage between two hyaline-covered bones.
Explanation

In a symphysis the bones are covered with hyaline cartilage and joined by a pad of fibrocartilage; the disc (annulus fibrosus around the nucleus pulposus) is the classic example. Rib heads also attach to the disc between the two bodies they meet.

  • A synchondrosis (primary cartilaginous joint) joins bones by hyaline cartilage alone, as at the 1st sternocostal joint.
  • A syndesmosis is a fibrous joint joined by a ligament or membrane, such as the distal tibiofibular joint.
Slide (1)
L66Learning
What type of joint attaches the 1st costal cartilage to the manubrium?
  1. A. Synovial plane sternocostal joint
  2. B. Secondary cartilaginous joint (symphysis)
  3. C. Primary cartilaginous joint (synchondrosis)
AnswerC. Primary cartilaginous joint (synchondrosis)
The 1st sternocostal joint is a primary cartilaginous joint (synchondrosis): the cartilage is continuous with the manubrium and allows almost no movement.
Explanation

Fixing the 1st rib firmly to the manubrium gives a stable anchor for the upper chest and the sternoclavicular joint just above it. It is the only sternocostal joint without a synovial cavity.

  • Synovial plane sternocostal joints are the 2nd–7th.
  • A symphysis (fibrocartilage pad) describes the manubriosternal joint and intervertebral discs, not the 1st sternocostal joint.
Slide (1)
L67Learning
What joints do costal cartilages 2–7 form with the sternum?
  1. A. Synovial plane sternocostal (chondrosternal) joints
  2. B. Secondary cartilaginous sternocostal joints (symphyses)
  3. C. Synovial saddle sternocostal (chondrosternal) joints
AnswerA. Synovial plane sternocostal (chondrosternal) joints
Costal cartilages 2–7 make synovial plane sternocostal (chondrosternal) joints, which glide as the ribs rise and fall.
Explanation

These small gliding joints let the anterior ends of the true ribs move against the sternum during breathing. The 2nd joint has two cavities, one above and one below the manubriosternal junction.

  • They have joint cavities, so they are not symphyses; that type describes the manubriosternal joint.
  • Saddle describes the sternoclavicular joint, not the sternocostal joints.
Slide (1)
L68Learning
What are interchondral joints, and of what type are they?
  1. A. Joints between the cartilages of the false ribs; synovial plane
  2. B. Joints between ribs and their own cartilages; synovial plane
  3. C. Joints between the cartilages of the true ribs; symphyses
AnswerA. Joints between the cartilages of the false ribs; synovial plane
Interchondral joints link neighbouring costal cartilages of the lower (false) ribs along the costal margin; they are synovial plane joints.
Explanation

Where the cartilages of the lower ribs touch one another along the costal margin (from about the 6th–7th down to the 9th), small gliding joints form between them; the 9th–10th junction is usually fibrous. They let the costal margin flex as the lower ribs swing outward.

  • A rib joined to its own cartilage forms a costochondral joint.
  • Apart from the 6th–7th contact, the upper cartilages run separately to the sternum, and none of these joints is a symphysis.
Slide (1)
L69Learning
What is a costochondral joint?
  1. A. The joint where a costal cartilage meets the sternum
  2. B. The joint where a rib tubercle meets a transverse process
  3. C. The joint where a rib meets its own costal cartilage
AnswerC. The joint where a rib meets its own costal cartilage
A costochondral joint is the junction between the bony anterior end of a rib and its costal cartilage.
Explanation

The cup-shaped anterior end of each rib holds the end of its cartilage. The joint is a primary cartilaginous union with essentially no movement; the cartilage itself bends instead.

  • Cartilage meeting the sternum is a sternocostal (chondrosternal) joint.
  • Tubercle meeting the transverse process is the costotransverse joint at the back.
Slide (1)
L70Learning
What type of joint is the manubriosternal joint (at the sternal angle)?
  1. A. Primary cartilaginous joint (synchondrosis)
  2. B. Synovial plane joint
  3. C. Secondary cartilaginous joint (symphysis)
AnswerC. Secondary cartilaginous joint (symphysis)
The manubriosternal joint is a symphysis (secondary cartilaginous joint): a fibrocartilage pad between the manubrium and the body.
Explanation

The slight hinge movement at this symphysis lets the body of the sternum move forward as the ribs rise. In older people it may ossify. The lecture figure labels the xiphisternal joint a symphysis too; some texts call that one a synchondrosis.

  • A synchondrosis (hyaline cartilage only, no fibrocartilage pad) is the 1st sternocostal joint.
  • Synovial plane joints are the 2nd–7th sternocostal joints and the posterior rib joints.
Slides (2)
L71Learning
What type of joint is the sternoclavicular joint, and why does it matter?
  1. A. Saddle joint; the main joint between the upper limb and the thorax
  2. B. Plane joint; the main joint between the upper limb and the thorax
  3. C. Saddle joint; the main joint between the scapula and the thorax
AnswerA. Saddle joint; the main joint between the upper limb and the thorax
The sternoclavicular joint is a saddle-type synovial joint and the only bony joint between the upper limb and the axial skeleton.
Explanation

The medial clavicle articulates with the clavicular notch of the manubrium and the 1st costal cartilage, with an articular disc in between. Everything the arm does is transmitted to the trunk through this joint.

  • A plane joint describes the acromioclavicular joint, at the other end of the clavicle.
  • The scapula has no true joint with the thorax; it is held there by muscles and moves on the chest wall.
Slide (1)
L72Learning
Which posterior articulations does the 6th rib make?
  1. A. Bodies of T6 and T7 and the transverse process of T6
  2. B. Bodies of T5 and T6 and the transverse process of T5
  3. C. Bodies of T5 and T6 and the transverse process of T6
AnswerC. Bodies of T5 and T6 and the transverse process of T6
Rib 6: head on the bodies of T5 and T6 (and their disc); tubercle on the transverse process of T6.
Explanation

For any typical rib n: the head's inferior facet meets the superior demifacet of vertebra n, its superior facet meets the inferior demifacet of vertebra n − 1, and the tubercle meets the transverse process of vertebra n.

  • T6 and T7 belong to rib 7: the head never reaches the vertebra below its number.
  • The tubercle meets the transverse process of its own vertebra (T6), not the one above (T5).
Slides (2)
L73Learning
A climber falls and fractures the body of T4. Which part of which rib articulates with this vertebral body and is most likely also injured?
  1. A. Tubercle of the 5th rib
  2. B. Head of the 5th rib
  3. C. Head of the 3rd rib
AnswerB. Head of the 5th rib
The T4 body carries the heads of the 4th rib (its superior demifacet) and the 5th rib (its inferior demifacet), so the head of the 5th rib is involved.
Explanation

Each vertebral body is shared by two rib heads: the rib of the same number (on its upper edge) and the next rib down, number n + 1 (on its lower edge). So T4 meets the heads of ribs 4 and 5.

  • The tubercle of the 5th rib meets the transverse process of T5, not the body of T4.
  • The head of the 3rd rib meets T2 and T3; it does not reach T4.
Slides (2)

Breathing movements

L74Learning
Which thoracic diameters must every inspiration enlarge?
  1. A. Only the anteroposterior and transverse ones
  2. B. Only the vertical one; the others change in forced breathing only
  3. C. All three: vertical, anteroposterior and transverse
AnswerC. All three: vertical, anteroposterior and transverse
Inspiration enlarges the thorax in all three diameters: vertical (diaphragm), anteroposterior (pump-handle) and transverse (bucket-handle).
Explanation

The cage moves to increase thoracic volume in inspiration and decrease it in expiration:

Verticaldiaphragm contracts and descends
Anteroposteriorupper ribs (1–6) rise, sternum moves forward (pump-handle)
Transverseribs 7–10 swing outward (bucket-handle)
  • Leaving out the vertical diameter ignores the diaphragm, the main muscle of inspiration.
  • The rib movements are not limited to forced breathing: the ribs rise a little in every inspiration, much more in deep breaths.
Slides (2)
L75Learning
How does inspiration increase the vertical diameter of the thorax?
  1. A. The diaphragm contracts and pulls the abdominal viscera up
  2. B. The diaphragm relaxes and the abdominal viscera push it up
  3. C. The diaphragm contracts and presses the abdominal viscera down
AnswerC. The diaphragm contracts and presses the abdominal viscera down
The diaphragm contracts, its domes flatten and descend, and it compresses the abdominal viscera, lengthening the thorax vertically.
Explanation

The diaphragm's muscle fibres run up from the lower ribs, sternum and lumbar vertebrae to the central tendon. When they contract they pull the central tendon down, so the domes descend and flatten, the thoracic cavity gets taller, and the abdominal contents are pushed down and forward (the belly moves out). This is the main mechanism of quiet inspiration.

  • A contracting diaphragm moves down, so it cannot pull the viscera up.
  • A relaxing diaphragm rising under abdominal pressure describes expiration, which shortens the thorax.
Slides (2)
L76Learning
What is the pump-handle movement?
  1. A. The upper six ribs swing up about an axis through their necks, pushing the sternum forward and up
  2. B. The upper six ribs swing up about an axis through their tubercles, pushing the sternum downward
  3. C. The upper six ribs swing down about an axis through their necks, pulling the sternum backward
AnswerA. The upper six ribs swing up about an axis through their necks, pushing the sternum forward and up
In the pump-handle movement the upper six ribs rotate upward about an axis along their necks, lifting their front ends and driving the sternum forward and up.
Explanation

The front ends of the upper ribs lie lower than their back ends and are attached directly to the sternum. When the ribs rotate at the costovertebral and costotransverse joints, their anterior ends rise like the handle of an old water pump and carry the sternum forward and upward.

  • Rising ribs push the sternum up and forward, never downward.
  • Swinging down and pulling the sternum back is the reverse movement of expiration.
Slides (2)
L77Learning
Which thoracic diameter does the pump-handle movement increase?
  1. A. Anteroposterior
  2. B. Vertical
  3. C. Transverse
AnswerA. Anteroposterior
Pushing the sternum forward, the pump-handle movement of the upper ribs increases the anteroposterior diameter.
Explanation

Upper ribs (1–6) are attached to the sternum by their own cartilages, so when they rise the whole front of the chest moves forward and up, deepening the chest from front to back.

  • The vertical diameter is increased by descent of the diaphragm.
  • The transverse diameter is increased by the bucket-handle movement of ribs 7–10.
Slide (1)
L78Learning
What is the bucket-handle movement?
  1. A. Ribs 7–10 rise at their middles and swing outward
  2. B. The upper six ribs swing up about an axis through their necks
  3. C. Ribs 7–10 drop at their middles and swing inward
AnswerA. Ribs 7–10 rise at their middles and swing outward
In the bucket-handle movement ribs 7–10 lift their middle parts upward and outward, like a bucket handle raised from the side.
Explanation

The lower ribs are fixed at both ends (vertebra behind, costal margin in front), and their shafts hang lower in the middle than at the ends. Elevating them rotates the shaft about an axis running from front to back, so the middle swings up and out.

  • The upper six ribs swinging up about their necks is the pump-handle movement.
  • Middles dropping and swinging inward is what happens in expiration.
Slides (2)
L79Learning
Why does raising the lower ribs (7–10) widen the chest from side to side?
  1. A. Their front ends lie lower than their back ends, so lifting drives the sternum forward
  2. B. Their shafts sag lower in the middle than at the ends, so lifting swings the middle outward
  3. C. Their heads glide on the transverse processes, so lifting rotates the sternum sideways
AnswerB. Their shafts sag lower in the middle than at the ends, so lifting swings the middle outward
The lower ribs' shafts sag below their two ends; raising them swings the low middle part outward, increasing the transverse diameter.
Explanation

Think about the attachments. Ribs 7–10 are anchored behind at the vertebrae and in front at the costal margin, with the shaft drooping between the two. Lifting a drooping handle that is fixed at both ends swings it out to the side, which is the bucket-handle movement. The upper ribs instead have front ends lower than their back ends and attach straight to the sternum, so raising them moves the sternum forward (pump-handle).

  • Driving the sternum forward explains the anteroposterior increase of the upper ribs, not side-to-side widening.
  • The sternum does not rotate sideways; it rises and moves forward.
Slide (1)
L80Learning
A patient with emphysema shows only bucket-handle movements during deep inspiration. Which change in the thorax does this movement still produce?
  1. A. Increase in the vertical diameter
  2. B. Increase in the transverse diameter
  3. C. Increase in the anteroposterior diameter
AnswerB. Increase in the transverse diameter
The bucket-handle movement of ribs 7–10 swings their middles outward and increases the transverse diameter.
Explanation

In emphysema the chest is already held in an expanded, barrel shape, so the pump-handle movement adds little. Whatever the disease, each movement has its own diameter: bucket-handle → transverse; pump-handle → anteroposterior; diaphragm → vertical.

  • The vertical diameter depends on the diaphragm descending.
  • The anteroposterior diameter depends on the pump-handle movement of the upper ribs and sternum.
Slides (2)
L81Learning
How does enlarging the thoracic cavity in inspiration draw air into the lungs?
  1. A. Volume rises, intrapleural pressure becomes more negative, alveolar pressure falls below atmospheric
  2. B. Volume rises, intrapleural pressure becomes less negative, alveolar pressure rises above atmospheric
  3. C. Volume falls, intrapleural pressure becomes more negative, alveolar pressure falls below atmospheric
AnswerA. Volume rises, intrapleural pressure becomes more negative, alveolar pressure falls below atmospheric
A larger cavity makes intrapleural pressure more negative, the lungs expand, alveolar pressure drops below atmospheric, and air flows in.
Explanation

The lungs follow the chest wall because the thin pleural fluid layer couples them to it. When the diaphragm descends and the ribs rise, thoracic volume increases, the pressure in the pleural space falls further below atmospheric, the lungs are pulled outward, and gas in the alveoli expands to a pressure below atmospheric. Air moves down that pressure gradient into the lungs.

  • Alveolar pressure above atmospheric drives air out, as in expiration.
  • A falling thoracic volume is expiration, which makes intrapleural pressure less negative.
Slide (1)
L82Learning
What happens in quiet expiration?
  1. A. Diaphragm relaxes, intrapleural pressure becomes more negative, and air is pushed out
  2. B. Diaphragm contracts, intra-abdominal pressure rises, and the lungs recoil and expel the air
  3. C. Diaphragm relaxes, intra-abdominal pressure falls, and the lungs recoil and expel the air
AnswerC. Diaphragm relaxes, intra-abdominal pressure falls, and the lungs recoil and expel the air
In quiet expiration the diaphragm relaxes, intra-abdominal pressure falls, and the stretched lungs recoil, reducing thoracic volume and expelling air.
Explanation

Quiet expiration is passive: no muscle has to contract. As the diaphragm relaxes, the abdominal viscera it was compressing spring back, the domes rise, and the elastic tissue of the lungs and chest wall recoils. Thoracic volume falls, alveolar pressure rises above atmospheric, and air flows out. Forced expiration adds the internal intercostals and abdominal wall muscles.

  • Intrapleural pressure becomes less negative in expiration; more negative pressure would draw air in.
  • A contracting diaphragm is inspiration, not expiration.
Slide (1)

Rib fractures and other clinical correlates

L83Learning
Which ribs are fractured most often?
  1. A. The upper ribs
  2. B. The floating ribs
  3. C. The middle ribs
AnswerC. The middle ribs
The middle ribs break most often: they are long, exposed and least protected.
Explanation

Direct blows and crushing injuries usually land on the prominent middle part of the cage. Ribs usually break just in front of the angle, their weakest point.

  • The upper ribs are shielded by the clavicle and the shoulder girdle muscles; a 1st-rib fracture means severe trauma.
  • The floating ribs have free ends and move away from a blow rather than snapping, although when they do break they can injure the liver, spleen or kidney.
Slide (1)
L84Learning
Where is a rib weakest?
  1. A. At its costochondral junction
  2. B. Just in front of its angle
  3. C. Just behind its tubercle
AnswerB. Just in front of its angle
A rib is weakest just anterior to its angle, where the shaft is thin and turns sharply forward.
Explanation

At the angle the rib changes direction, so force applied to the chest concentrates there; this is where most rib fractures occur.

  • The costochondral junction is cushioned by flexible cartilage; it can separate in trauma, but it is not the usual fracture site.
  • Behind the tubercle the neck is short and braced by the costotransverse ligaments and deep back muscles.
Slides (2)
L85Learning
What does a fracture of the 1st rib signal, and why?
  1. A. Osteoporosis, because the 1st rib is the weakest rib
  2. B. Severe trauma, because the 1st rib is rarely fractured
  3. C. Minor trauma, because the 1st rib is the most often fractured
AnswerB. Severe trauma, because the 1st rib is rarely fractured
The 1st rib is short, broad, curved and hidden behind the clavicle, so it rarely breaks; a fracture means severe trauma.
Explanation

Breaking the 1st rib takes high-energy force, so it should prompt a search for injury to the structures crossing it: the subclavian artery and vein and the lower trunk of the brachial plexus.

  • It is one of the strongest ribs, not the weakest, so it is not a typical osteoporotic fracture site.
  • The middle ribs, not the 1st, are the most often fractured.
Slide (1)
L86Learning
What can broken lower ribs damage?
  1. A. The oesophagus and the thoracic duct
  2. B. The diaphragm and the trachea
  3. C. The diaphragm and the lung or heart
AnswerC. The diaphragm and the lung or heart
Broken lower ribs can tear the diaphragm or pierce the lung (or heart); the upper abdominal organs under them are also at risk.
Explanation

The lower ribs overlie the diaphragm, the lower lungs and pleural recesses, and, below the diaphragm, the liver, spleen and kidneys. A sharp fragment can tear the diaphragm (risking herniation of abdominal organs into the thorax) or puncture the pleura and lung, causing a pneumothorax or haemothorax.

  • The oesophagus and thoracic duct lie deep in the posterior midline, shielded by the vertebral column and aorta.
  • The trachea ends at the sternal angle, far above the lower ribs.
Slide (1)
L87Learning
What is a flail chest?
  1. A. Several rib fractures leave a loose segment of chest wall, which improves ventilation
  2. B. A single rib fracture that splints the chest wall, which reduces pain on breathing
  3. C. Several rib fractures leave a loose segment of chest wall, which impairs ventilation
AnswerC. Several rib fractures leave a loose segment of chest wall, which impairs ventilation
In flail chest several adjacent ribs break (each in two or more places), freeing a segment of chest wall that moves on its own and impairs ventilation.
Explanation

The loose segment is no longer pulled out with the rest of the cage, so it moves with the pressure changes inside the chest instead (paradoxical movement). This wastes part of each breath, and the injury is very painful because the intercostal nerves and parietal pleura are irritated.

  • The loose segment makes breathing less effective, never more.
  • A single rib fracture does not create a free segment.
Slide (1)
L88Learning
How does a flail segment move during breathing?
  1. A. Paradoxically: in on inspiration, out on expiration
  2. B. Normally: out on inspiration, in on expiration
  3. C. Paradoxically: out on inspiration, in on expiration
AnswerA. Paradoxically: in on inspiration, out on expiration
A flail segment moves paradoxically: it is sucked in during inspiration and pushed out during expiration.
Explanation

During inspiration the pressure inside the chest falls below atmospheric. The intact cage expands against it, but the detached segment simply follows the pressure and is drawn inward; in expiration the pressure rises and pushes it out.

  • Out on inspiration, in on expiration is how the normal chest wall moves, so it is not paradoxical.
  • Mixing the label "paradoxical" with the normal direction is the classic trap: paradoxical means opposite to the rest of the chest wall.
Slide (1)
L89Learning
By the lecture's definition, which injury produces a flail chest?
  1. A. Three or more adjacent ribs, each broken in at least two places
  2. B. Three or more adjacent ribs, each broken in one place
  3. C. Two or more adjacent ribs, each broken in one place
AnswerA. Three or more adjacent ribs, each broken in at least two places
A flail chest needs three or more ribs, each broken in two or more places, freeing a segment of chest wall that moves paradoxically.
Explanation

Two breaks in one rib leave the piece between them attached to nothing. When several neighbouring ribs break like this, a whole plate of chest wall floats free and is sucked in on inspiration and pushed out on expiration. Ordinary rib fractures hurt with breathing, coughing and sneezing but usually heal without splinting; a flail segment may need surgical fixation to anchor it. (Trauma texts often set the threshold at two or more adjacent ribs; the lecture uses three.)

  • With a single break per rib, however many ribs are broken, each fragment is still anchored, one to the vertebra and one to the sternum, so the wall stays stable: painful, but not flail.
Slide (1)
L90Learning
Notching of the ribs on a chest X-ray usually indicates which condition?
  1. A. Patent ductus arteriosus
  2. B. Thoracic outlet syndrome
  3. C. Coarctation of the aorta
AnswerC. Coarctation of the aorta
Rib notching is the classic X-ray sign of coarctation of the aorta: enlarged collateral intercostal arteries erode the ribs' lower borders.
Explanation

In coarctation the aorta is narrowed beyond the left subclavian artery. Blood reaches the lower body by detour: subclavian artery → internal thoracic artery → anterior intercostal arteries → (backwards through) posterior intercostal arteries → descending aorta below the narrowing. The enlarged, tortuous intercostal arteries notch the costal grooves.

  • Patent ductus arteriosus adds flow to the pulmonary circulation; it does not create intercostal collaterals.
  • Thoracic outlet syndrome compresses vessels and nerves at the 1st rib; it does not notch the ribs.
Slide (1)
L91Learning
Why does coarctation of the aorta notch the ribs?
  1. A. Blood rerouted around the narrowing enlarges the intercostal arteries
  2. B. Blood rerouted around the narrowing enlarges the internal thoracic veins
  3. C. Raised pressure in the intercostal veins erodes the upper borders of the ribs
AnswerA. Blood rerouted around the narrowing enlarges the intercostal arteries
Collateral flow from the internal thoracic arteries through the intercostal arteries to the aorta below the narrowing enlarges them, and their pulsations erode the ribs.
Explanation

The anterior and posterior intercostal arteries anastomose in each space. When the aorta is narrowed, flow reverses in the posterior intercostal arteries to fill the descending aorta. The dilated arteries lie in the costal grooves, so they notch the inferior borders of the ribs (typically ribs 3–9).

  • The collaterals are arteries; the veins are not part of the bypass.
  • The notches are on the lower borders, where the costal groove holds the vessels, and are caused by arterial, not venous, pressure.
Slide (1)
L92Learning
Which bone is used for bone marrow needle biopsy and marrow harvest, and why?
  1. A. Xiphoid process, because it is easy to reach below the costal margin
  2. B. Body of the sternum, because it is broad and just under the skin
  3. C. 1st rib, because it is broad and just under the clavicle
AnswerB. Body of the sternum, because it is broad and just under the skin
The body of the sternum is broad, subcutaneous and full of red marrow, so it is used for marrow biopsy and can be used for marrow harvest for transplantation.
Explanation

A needle passes easily through the thin outer layer of the sternal body into its marrow cavity, because only skin and fascia cover the bone in front. Care is needed not to pass through the thin posterior layer of bone, behind which lie the pericardium and heart.

  • The xiphoid is small, often cartilaginous and sits over the liver.
  • The 1st rib lies behind the clavicle and cannot be felt, so it is unreachable for a needle.
Slides (2)

Thoracic apertures and thoracic outlet syndrome

L93Learning
What are the boundaries of the thoracic inlet (superior thoracic aperture)?
  1. A. Behind: T1 vertebra
    Sides: 1st ribs and their cartilages
    Front: upper border of the manubrium
  2. B. Behind: T1 vertebra
    Sides: 1st ribs and their cartilages
    Front: xiphisternal joint
  3. C. Behind: T4 vertebra
    Sides: 2nd ribs and their cartilages
    Front: sternal angle
AnswerA. Behind: T1 vertebra
Sides: 1st ribs and their cartilages
Front: upper border of the manubrium
The thoracic inlet is ringed by T1 behind, the 1st ribs and cartilages at the sides and the upper border of the manubrium in front.
Explanation

The inlet is small and kidney-shaped and tilts down and forward, so the manubrium in front sits lower than T1 behind. It links the thorax with the neck and upper limbs, carrying the trachea, oesophagus, great vessels and nerves and holding the lung apices.

  • The xiphisternal joint is the front of the outlet (inferior aperture), at the bottom of the cage.
  • T4, the 2nd ribs and the sternal angle mark the plane of the sternal angle, well below the inlet.
Slide (1)
L94Learning
Apart from vessels and nerves, what passes through the thoracic inlet?
  1. A. Trachea
    Oesophagus
    Azygos vein
    Cisterna chyli
  2. B. Trachea
    Oesophagus
    Apices of the lungs
    Thoracic duct
  3. C. Trachea
    Oesophagus
    Bases of the lungs
    Thoracic duct
AnswerB. Trachea
Oesophagus
Apices of the lungs
Thoracic duct
The trachea, oesophagus and thoracic duct pass through the inlet, and the apices of the lungs (with the cervical pleura) rise into it.
Explanation

The inlet is the doorway between the root of the neck and the thorax. The lung apices bulge up through it behind the clavicles, which is why a stab wound just above the clavicle can cause a pneumothorax and why an apical (Pancoast) tumour can reach the structures crossing the 1st rib.

  • The azygos vein ends at T4 in the superior vena cava and the cisterna chyli lies in the abdomen at L1–L2; neither reaches the inlet.
  • The bases of the lungs rest on the diaphragm at the bottom of the chest.
Slides (2)
L95Learning
Which blood vessels pass through the thoracic inlet?
  1. A. Subclavian artery and vein
    Brachiocephalic artery
    Costocervical trunk
    Musculophrenic artery
  2. B. Axillary artery and vein
    Brachiocephalic artery
    Thyrocervical trunk
    Inferior epigastric artery
  3. C. Subclavian artery and vein
    Brachiocephalic artery
    Costocervical trunk
    Internal thoracic artery
AnswerC. Subclavian artery and vein
Brachiocephalic artery
Costocervical trunk
Internal thoracic artery
The inlet carries the subclavian artery and vein, the brachiocephalic artery, the costocervical trunk and the internal thoracic artery.
Explanation

These vessels pass between the arch of the aorta and the root of the neck and upper limb. The internal thoracic artery leaves the subclavian artery and descends behind the costal cartilages, and the costocervical trunk sends its superior intercostal branch over the neck of the 1st rib to the first two spaces.

  • The musculophrenic artery is a terminal branch of the internal thoracic artery along the costal margin, at the bottom of the cage.
  • The axillary vessels begin only at the outer border of the 1st rib, and the inferior epigastric artery is in the anterior abdominal wall.
Slides (2)
L96Learning
Which nerves pass through the thoracic inlet?
  1. A. Phrenic and accessory nerves
    Sympathetic chain
    Anterior ramus of T1
  2. B. Phrenic and vagus nerves
    Sympathetic chain
    Anterior ramus of T1
  3. C. Phrenic and vagus nerves
    Sympathetic chain
    Anterior ramus of C4
AnswerB. Phrenic and vagus nerves
Sympathetic chain
Anterior ramus of T1
The inlet transmits the phrenic and vagus nerves, the sympathetic chain and the anterior ramus of T1.
Explanation

The phrenic nerves (C3–C5) and vagus nerves descend from the neck into the thorax; the sympathetic trunks run down over the necks of the ribs; the T1 anterior ramus rises over the 1st rib to join the brachial plexus (lower trunk). That T1 ramus is the nerve compressed in thoracic outlet syndrome.

  • The accessory nerve (cranial nerve XI) supplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius and stays in the neck.
  • The C4 anterior ramus stays in the neck (cervical plexus); its fibres reach the thorax only within the phrenic nerve.
Slides (2)
L97Learning
What are the boundaries of the thoracic outlet (inferior thoracic aperture)?
  1. A. Behind: T12 vertebra
    Posterolaterally: ribs 11 and 12
    Anterolaterally: costal margins
    Front: xiphisternal joint
  2. B. Behind: T12 vertebra
    Posterolaterally: ribs 11 and 12
    Anterolaterally: costal margins
    Front: sternal angle
  3. C. Behind: L1 vertebra
    Posterolaterally: ribs 10 and 11
    Anterolaterally: costal margins
    Front: xiphisternal joint
AnswerA. Behind: T12 vertebra
Posterolaterally: ribs 11 and 12
Anterolaterally: costal margins
Front: xiphisternal joint
The thoracic outlet is bounded by T12, ribs 11 and 12, the costal margins (cartilages 7–10) and the xiphisternal joint.
Explanation

The outlet is the large, irregular lower opening of the cage. It is much larger than the inlet and is almost completely closed by the diaphragm, which attaches around its rim.

  • The sternal angle is high on the sternum; the lower front point of the outlet is the xiphisternal joint.
  • L1 and ribs 10–11 are one level off: the outlet's rim is the last thoracic vertebra and the last two ribs.
Slide (1)
L98Learning
What almost closes the thoracic outlet, and how does the outlet compare in size with the inlet?
  1. A. The diaphragm; the outlet is much larger than the inlet
  2. B. The diaphragm; the outlet is much smaller than the inlet
  3. C. The pericardium; the outlet is much larger than the inlet
AnswerA. The diaphragm; the outlet is much larger than the inlet
The diaphragm attaches around the rim of the large thoracic outlet and almost fills it, separating the thorax from the abdomen.
Explanation
