The outlet (bounded by T12, ribs 11–12, the costal margins and the xiphisternal joint) is far wider than the small kidney-shaped inlet. The diaphragm closes it except for its openings for the inferior vena cava, oesophagus and aorta (with structures passing behind it).

  • The outlet is the bigger aperture; the inlet is the narrow one.
  • The pericardium surrounds the heart and rests on the central tendon; it does not close the outlet.
Slide (1)
L99Learning
Which structures pass through or behind the diaphragm from the thorax into the abdomen?
  1. A. Aorta
    Trachea
    Inferior vena cava
    Azygos vein
    Thoracic duct
    Nerves
  2. B. Aorta
    Oesophagus
    Inferior vena cava
    Azygos vein
    Thoracic duct
    Nerves
  3. C. Aorta
    Oesophagus
    Superior vena cava
    Azygos vein
    Thoracic duct
    Nerves
AnswerB. Aorta
Oesophagus
Inferior vena cava
Azygos vein
Thoracic duct
Nerves
The aorta, oesophagus, inferior vena cava, azygos vein, thoracic duct and nerves (phrenic, vagal trunks) pass between thorax and abdomen at the outlet.
Explanation

They use the diaphragm's openings: the inferior vena cava (with the right phrenic nerve) through the caval opening (T8); the oesophagus with the vagal trunks through the oesophageal hiatus (T10); the aorta with the azygos vein and thoracic duct behind the median arcuate ligament, through the aortic hiatus (T12).

  • The trachea ends at the sternal angle by dividing into the main bronchi.
  • The superior vena cava drains the upper body and ends in the right atrium; it never crosses the diaphragm.
Slides (2)
L100Learning
Which anatomical aperture does thoracic outlet syndrome actually involve?
  1. A. The thoracic outlet (inferior thoracic aperture)
  2. B. The thoracic inlet (superior thoracic aperture)
  3. C. The plane of the sternal angle
AnswerB. The thoracic inlet (superior thoracic aperture)
Despite its name, thoracic outlet syndrome involves the anatomical thoracic inlet (superior aperture), where vessels and nerves leave for the upper limb.
Explanation

Clinicians call the superior aperture the "outlet" because the subclavian vessels and the T1 nerve come out of the thorax there to supply the neck and upper limb. Anatomically it is the inlet: T1, the 1st ribs and the manubrium. Some books therefore call it thoracic inlet syndrome.

  • The anatomical outlet (inferior aperture) is closed by the diaphragm and has nothing to do with the arm.
  • The sternal angle plane is inside the thorax at T4/T5, below the 1st rib where the compression happens.
Slide (1)
L101Learning
What causes thoracic outlet syndrome?
  1. A. A fractured clavicle or tight pectoralis major compressing the axillary vessels and/or the C5 nerve
  2. B. An extra cervical rib or an abnormal anterior scalene attachment compressing the subclavian vessels and/or the T1 nerve
  3. C. An extra cervical rib or an abnormal posterior scalene attachment compressing the brachiocephalic vessels and/or the phrenic nerve
AnswerB. An extra cervical rib or an abnormal anterior scalene attachment compressing the subclavian vessels and/or the T1 nerve
A supernumerary (cervical) rib or a variant anterior scalene narrows the space over the 1st rib, compressing the subclavian vessels and/or the T1 nerve.
Explanation

The subclavian artery and the lower trunk of the brachial plexus (C8, T1) cross the 1st rib between the anterior and middle scalene muscles; the subclavian vein crosses in front of the anterior scalene. A cervical rib (usually from C7, a congenital anomaly) or an abnormal scalene band raises the floor of this gap and squeezes them.

  • The axillary vessels and C5 lie beyond the 1st rib and higher in the plexus; they are not the classic structures.
  • The phrenic nerve descends on the front of the anterior scalene, and the brachiocephalic vessels lie deeper behind the manubrium.
Slides (2)
L102Learning
The T1 nerve compressed in thoracic outlet syndrome feeds which part of the brachial plexus?
  1. A. Middle trunk
  2. B. Upper trunk
  3. C. Lower trunk
AnswerC. Lower trunk
The T1 anterior ramus joins C8 to form the lower trunk of the brachial plexus, which crosses the 1st rib.
Explanation

The lower trunk supplies sensation to the medial forearm and hand (through the medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm and the ulnar nerve) and motor supply to the small muscles of the hand. Compressing it therefore causes medial forearm and hand pain or tingling and wasting of the intrinsic hand muscles.

  • The middle trunk is C7 alone.
  • The upper trunk is C5–C6, supplying the shoulder and lateral arm.
Slides (2)
L103Learning
What are the signs of thoracic outlet syndrome?
  1. A. Diminished radial pulse
    Poor blood flow to the arm
    Pain along the medial forearm and hand
    Wasting of the small muscles of the hand
  2. B. Diminished femoral pulse
    Poor blood flow to the leg
    Pain along the medial thigh
    Wasting of the small muscles of the foot
  3. C. Bounding radial pulse
    Increased blood flow to the arm
    Pain along the lateral forearm and thumb
    Wasting of the deltoid
AnswerA. Diminished radial pulse
Poor blood flow to the arm
Pain along the medial forearm and hand
Wasting of the small muscles of the hand
Compression of the subclavian artery weakens the radial pulse and arm blood flow; compression of the lower trunk (C8–T1) gives medial forearm and hand pain and intrinsic hand muscle wasting.
Explanation

The signs vary with which structure is squeezed. Vascular: a diminished radial pulse (often when the arm is raised or the head turned) and a cold, pale or discoloured hand. Neural: pain, tingling or numbness along the medial forearm and hand and weakness and wasting of the small hand muscles.

  • The syndrome affects the upper limb, never the leg.
  • The lateral forearm, thumb and deltoid belong to C5–C6 (upper trunk), and compression reduces, not increases, flow.
Slide (1)
L104Learning
A 22-year-old has tingling along the medial forearm and hand and wasting of the small hand muscles; her radial pulse weakens when her neck is turned. An X-ray shows a cervical rib. What is being compressed?
  1. A. Upper trunk of the brachial plexus (C5–C6) and the axillary artery
  2. B. Lower trunk of the brachial plexus (C8–T1) and the subclavian artery
  3. C. Phrenic nerve and the brachiocephalic vein
AnswerB. Lower trunk of the brachial plexus (C8–T1) and the subclavian artery
A cervical rib squeezes the lower trunk (C8–T1) and the subclavian artery as they cross the 1st rib: thoracic outlet syndrome.
Explanation

The medial forearm and hand symptoms and intrinsic hand muscle wasting point to C8–T1 (lower trunk); the weakening radial pulse points to the subclavian artery. Both cross the 1st rib behind the anterior scalene, exactly where a cervical rib or fibrous band from it crowds them.

  • The upper trunk would affect the shoulder and lateral arm, and the axillary artery starts beyond the 1st rib.
  • The phrenic nerve would cause diaphragm, not hand, problems, and the brachiocephalic vein is not in the gap over the 1st rib.
Slides (2)

Intercostal muscles

L105Learning
What are the three muscle layers in each intercostal space, from superficial to deep?
  1. A. Internal intercostal → external intercostal → innermost intercostal
  2. B. External intercostal → internal intercostal → innermost intercostal
  3. C. External intercostal → innermost intercostal → internal intercostal
AnswerB. External intercostal → internal intercostal → innermost intercostal
From outside in: external, internal, then innermost intercostal; the neurovascular bundle runs in the plane between the internal and innermost layers.
Explanation

Each of the 11 intercostal spaces is filled by three thin sheets of muscle, layered like the three flat muscles of the abdominal wall. The external intercostal is outermost, the internal intercostal lies just deep to it with its fibres at right angles, and the innermost intercostal is the deepest, lying against the endothoracic fascia and parietal pleura.

  • Putting the internal layer first reverses the two outer sheets.
  • Putting the innermost layer in the middle ignores its name: it is the deepest sheet, and the intercostal vessels and nerve separate it from the internal layer.
Slides (2)
L106Learning
What are the attachments of an intercostal muscle?
  1. A. Lower border of one rib → upper border of the rib two below
  2. B. Inner surface of one rib → inner surface of the 2nd or 3rd rib below
  3. C. Lower border of one rib → upper border of the rib below
AnswerC. Lower border of one rib → upper border of the rib below
All three intercostal layers span one space: from the lower border of the rib above to the upper border of the rib below.
Explanation

The external, internal and innermost intercostals all attach above to the inferior border of a rib and below to the superior border of the next rib, so each sheet closes exactly one intercostal space. All three are supplied by the intercostal nerve of that space.

  • Spanning two ribs is wrong for the intercostals; among the muscles of the spaces, that pattern belongs to the subcostals.
  • Running on the inner surface to the 2nd or 3rd rib below describes the subcostals, found low on the posterior wall near the rib angles.
Slides (2)
L107Learning
Which way do the fibres of the external intercostal muscles run?
  1. A. Downward and backward (inferoposterior)
  2. B. Vertically, straight from rib to rib
  3. C. Downward and forward (inferoanterior)
AnswerC. Downward and forward (inferoanterior)
External intercostal fibres run downward and forward from the rib above to the rib below, like hands slipped into front pockets, the same way as the external oblique.
Explanation

Seen from the side, each external intercostal fibre leaves the lower border of a rib and slopes inferoanteriorly to the rib below. This is the same direction as the external oblique of the abdomen, with which the layer is continuous below. Because the fibres pull on the lower rib at a point farther from its vertebral pivot, they raise the ribs in inspiration.

  • Downward and backward is the direction of the internal intercostals, at right angles to the externals.
  • Purely vertical fibres describe none of the three layers.
Slides (2)
L108Learning
How far does each external intercostal muscle extend, and what continues it in front?
  1. A. From the rib tubercles behind to the costochondral junctions in front; a membrane continues it to the sternum
  2. B. From the rib angles behind to the sternum in front; a membrane continues it to the tubercles
  3. C. From the vertebral bodies behind to the costochondral junctions in front; a membrane continues it to the sternum
AnswerA. From the rib tubercles behind to the costochondral junctions in front; a membrane continues it to the sternum
The external intercostal is muscular from the rib tubercles to the costochondral junctions; between the cartilages it is replaced by the external intercostal membrane.
Explanation

The external layer is muscular from the tubercles of the ribs at the back to where each rib meets its costal cartilage at the front. Between the costal cartilages the muscle is replaced by a thin aponeurotic sheet, the external intercostal membrane, through which the internal intercostal fibres can be seen.

  • Rib angles to the sternum is the extent of the internal intercostals, which are replaced by a membrane behind, medial to the angles.
  • No intercostal muscle reaches the vertebral bodies.

Hook: at each end, one layer is muscle where the other is membrane.

Slides (2)
L109Learning
Below the thorax, the external intercostals are continuous with which abdominal muscle?
  1. A. External oblique
  2. B. Internal oblique
  3. C. Transversus abdominis
AnswerA. External oblique
The external intercostals continue below as the external oblique: the same outermost layer, with the same downward-and-forward fibres.
Explanation

The thoracic and abdominal walls are built from the same three flat layers. The outermost thoracic layer, the external intercostal, is continuous inferiorly with the outermost abdominal layer, the external oblique, and their fibres run the same way (inferoanteriorly).

  • The internal oblique continues the internal intercostals (middle layer).
  • Transversus abdominis continues the deepest layer, transversus thoracis.
Slides (2)
L110Learning
Which way do the fibres of the internal intercostal muscles run?
  1. A. Downward and forward (inferoanterior), parallel to the externals
  2. B. Downward and backward (inferoposterior), at right angles to the externals
  3. C. Horizontally, parallel to the ribs above and below
AnswerB. Downward and backward (inferoposterior), at right angles to the externals
Internal intercostal fibres run downward and backward, crossing the external fibres at right angles.
Explanation

Deep to the external layer, the internal intercostals slope inferoposteriorly from the lower border of a rib to the upper border of the rib below. The two layers form a crossed lattice, as the external and internal obliques do in the abdomen, which keeps the space from being sucked in or blown out during breathing.

  • Downward and forward is the external intercostal direction.
  • Horizontal fibres, parallel to the ribs, could not draw one rib toward the next; no intercostal layer runs that way.
Slides (2)
L111Learning
How far does each internal intercostal muscle extend, and what replaces it at the back?
  1. A. From the costochondral junctions in front to the rib tubercles behind; a membrane replaces it in front
  2. B. From the sternum in front to the rib angles behind; medial to the angles a membrane replaces it
  3. C. From the sternum in front to the rib tubercles behind; no membrane replaces it
AnswerB. From the sternum in front to the rib angles behind; medial to the angles a membrane replaces it
The internal intercostals run from the sternum to the rib angles; medial to the angles they are replaced by the internal intercostal membrane.
Explanation

The internal layer is fully muscular at the front, right up to the sternum, including between the costal cartilages. Posteriorly it stops at the angles of the ribs; from there to the vertebral column the space is closed only by the thin internal intercostal membrane, which lies deep to the external intercostal muscle.

  • Costochondral junctions to tubercles is the extent of the external layer.
  • Saying no membrane replaces it ignores the internal intercostal membrane between the angles and the vertebrae.
Slides (2)
L112Learning
Below the thorax, the internal intercostals are continuous with which abdominal muscle?
  1. A. External oblique
  2. B. Transversus abdominis
  3. C. Internal oblique
AnswerC. Internal oblique
The middle thoracic layer, the internal intercostals, continues below as the middle abdominal layer, the internal oblique.
Explanation

The pattern is layer for layer: external intercostal → external oblique, internal intercostal → internal oblique, transversus thoracis → transversus abdominis. The internal intercostals and the internal oblique share both their depth (middle layer) and their fibre direction, at right angles to the outer layer.

  • The external oblique continues the external intercostals.
  • Transversus abdominis continues transversus thoracis, the deepest layer.
Slides (2)
L113Learning
How do the internal intercostals compare with the externals in strength and timing?
  1. A. Weaker → most active in expiration
  2. B. Stronger → most active in inspiration
  3. C. Weaker → most active in quiet inspiration
AnswerA. Weaker → most active in expiration
The lecture describes the internal intercostals as weaker than the externals and most active during expiration.
Explanation

The interosseous part of the internal intercostals pulls the ribs down, which shrinks the thorax, so their main work is in expiration, especially forced expiration such as coughing or blowing out candles, together with the abdominal muscles. The external intercostals, working with the diaphragm, carry the inspiratory load.

  • Stronger and inspiratory describes the external intercostals.
  • Quiet inspiration is done by the diaphragm and external intercostals, not by the internal layer.
Slide (1)
L114Learning
What are the innermost intercostal muscles?
  1. A. The most superficial fibres of the external layer, split off by the external intercostal membrane
  2. B. The deepest fibres of transversus thoracis, split off by the endothoracic fascia
  3. C. The deepest fibres of the internal layer, split off by the neurovascular bundle
AnswerC. The deepest fibres of the internal layer, split off by the neurovascular bundle
The innermost intercostals are really the deepest part of the internal intercostals; the intercostal vessels and nerve passing through them make them look like a separate muscle.
Explanation

Technically the innermost and internal intercostals are one layer. The intercostal neurovascular bundle runs through it, peeling off a thin deep sheet that is described as a separate muscle, the innermost intercostal. That is why the bundle is said to run 'between the internal and innermost intercostals', and why the innermost layer has the same fibre direction as the internal one.

  • The external layer is outermost and is not split into a separate muscle.
  • Transversus thoracis is a separate deep muscle on the back of the sternum, not the source of the innermost intercostals.
Slide (1)
L115Learning
What is the action of the innermost intercostals?
  1. A. Clearly the same as the external intercostals: they elevate the ribs
  2. B. Probably the same as the internal intercostals, but still not established
  3. C. Clearly the same as transversus thoracis: they depress the sternum
AnswerB. Probably the same as the internal intercostals, but still not established
Being part of the internal layer, the innermost intercostals probably act like the internal intercostals, but their action is still undetermined.
Explanation

The lecture is cautious: the innermost intercostals 'likely have similar action as internal intercostals but still undetermined'. The muscle table groups them with the internal intercostals (interosseous part depresses the ribs, interchondral part elevates them, in forced breathing).

  • Saying they clearly elevate the ribs like the externals overstates what is known and ignores their internal-type fibre direction.
  • Depressing the sternum is not a described action of any intercostal; transversus thoracis only weakly depresses the ribs.
Slide (1)
L116Learning
What do the external intercostal muscles do?
  1. A. Elevate the ribs → inspiration
  2. B. Depress the ribs → expiration
  3. C. Hold the ribs still → no change in thoracic volume
AnswerA. Elevate the ribs → inspiration
The external intercostals elevate the ribs, enlarging the thorax in inspiration: pump handle in the upper ribs, bucket handle in the lower ribs.
Explanation

Contracting external intercostals lift each rib toward the one above. In the upper ribs this swings the sternum forward (pump handle → anteroposterior diameter); in ribs 7–10 it swings the rib shafts outward (bucket handle → transverse diameter). The lecture lists them with the diaphragm as the muscles of quiet inspiration, and the muscle table adds that they elevate the ribs in forced inspiration.

  • Depressing the ribs in expiration is the job of the internal intercostals (interosseous part), with the abdominal muscles in forced expiration.
  • The intercostals do stiffen the spaces, but the externals also actively change thoracic volume.
Slides (2)
L117Learning
What do the internal and innermost intercostals do to the ribs in forced breathing?
  1. A. Interosseous part elevates the ribs; interchondral part depresses them
  2. B. Interosseous part depresses the ribs; interchondral part elevates them
  3. C. Both parts depress the ribs, including the part between the cartilages
AnswerB. Interosseous part depresses the ribs; interchondral part elevates them
Between the bony ribs (interosseous part) they depress the ribs; between the costal cartilages (interchondral part) they elevate them.
Explanation

The internal intercostals reach the sternum, so part of each muscle lies between the costal cartilages (interchondral) and part between the bony ribs (interosseous). The interosseous fibres pull the ribs down in forced expiration. Beside the sternum the geometry reverses, and the interchondral fibres (the 'parasternal intercostals') help raise the ribs in inspiration. The lecture table gives the innermost intercostals the same actions.

  • Swapping the two parts reverses their actions.
  • Saying both parts depress ignores the interchondral fibres, which are inspiratory.
Slides (2)

Other thoracic wall muscles

L118Learning
Which group lists only true muscles of the thoracic wall?
  1. A. Pectoralis major and minor, serratus anterior, scalenes, intercostals
  2. B. Serratus posterior, levatores costarum, intercostals, subcostals, transversus thoracis
  3. C. Intercostals, subcostals, transversus thoracis, serratus anterior, latissimus dorsi
AnswerB. Serratus posterior, levatores costarum, intercostals, subcostals, transversus thoracis
The true thoracic wall muscles are serratus posterior, levatores costarum, the intercostals, subcostals and transversus thoracis; pectorals, serratus anterior and scalenes merely attach.
Explanation

'True' wall muscles belong to the thoracic cage itself. Several upper limb and neck muscles also attach to the ribs (pectoralis major and minor, serratus anterior, scalenes). They act on the arm or neck, but in forced inspiration they can pull the ribs up as accessory muscles of respiration.

  • The list with pectoralis, serratus anterior and scalenes mixes in the accessory muscles.
  • Serratus anterior and latissimus dorsi are upper limb muscles, so the third list is also mixed.
Slides (2)
L119Learning
Where are the subcostal muscles, and how do they attach?
  1. A. Inner surface of the lower ribs near their angles → upper border of the 2nd or 3rd rib below
  2. B. Outer surface of the upper ribs near their tubercles → upper border of the rib immediately below
  3. C. Back of the lower sternum → inner surface of costal cartilages 2–6
AnswerA. Inner surface of the lower ribs near their angles → upper border of the 2nd or 3rd rib below
The subcostals lie on the inner posterior wall, best developed low down, running from near the rib angles to the 2nd or 3rd rib below.
Explanation

The subcostals are thin slips in the same deep plane as the innermost intercostals, but each crosses one or two intercostal spaces. They are best developed in the lower thorax, their fibres run in the same direction as the internal intercostals, and they probably act like them.

  • The subcostals are internal and low; nothing in the deep layer lies on the outer surface of the upper ribs.
  • Back of the lower sternum → cartilages 2–6 is transversus thoracis, the anterior member of the deep layer.
Slides (2)
L120Learning
What are the attachments and action of transversus thoracis?
  1. A. Front of the upper sternum → costal cartilages 2–6 → strongly elevates the ribs
  2. B. Inner surface of the lower ribs → 2nd or 3rd rib below → strongly elevates the ribs
  3. C. Back of the lower sternum → costal cartilages 2–6 → weakly depresses the ribs
AnswerC. Back of the lower sternum → costal cartilages 2–6 → weakly depresses the ribs
Transversus thoracis fans up and out from the posterior surface of the lower sternum to costal cartilages 2–6; its action is only weakly expiratory.
Explanation

This is the anterior part of the deepest layer of the chest wall, on the inner surface of the sternum and cartilages just outside the parietal pleura. Its fibres run superolaterally, so contraction pulls the cartilages down slightly: a weak expiratory action (the lecture table adds 'proprioception?').

  • The muscle lies on the back of the sternum, inside the cage; the pectoralis major on the front is a limb muscle.
  • The inner lower ribs → 2nd or 3rd rib below attachment belongs to the subcostals.
Slides (2)
L121Learning
Below the thorax, transversus thoracis is continuous with which abdominal muscle?
  1. A. Internal oblique
  2. B. Rectus abdominis
  3. C. Transversus abdominis
AnswerC. Transversus abdominis
The deepest thoracic layer, transversus thoracis, continues inferiorly as the deepest abdominal layer, transversus abdominis.
Explanation

The layer-for-layer rule: external intercostal → external oblique, internal intercostal → internal oblique, transversus thoracis → transversus abdominis. Both 'transversus' muscles lie deepest, just outside the serous lining (parietal pleura above, peritoneum below).

  • The internal oblique continues the internal intercostals.
  • Rectus abdominis is a vertical strap muscle in the rectus sheath with no counterpart in this series.
Slides (2)
L122Learning
Which vessels run just anterior to transversus thoracis, on the inner surface of the front chest wall?
  1. A. Lateral thoracic artery and vein
  2. B. Internal thoracic artery and vein
  3. C. Posterior intercostal artery and vein
AnswerB. Internal thoracic artery and vein
The internal thoracic artery and vein descend just lateral to the sternum, in front of transversus thoracis and behind the costal cartilages.
Explanation

The internal thoracic vessels run about 1 cm lateral to the sternal border, between the costal cartilages and internal intercostals in front and transversus thoracis behind. A surgeon harvesting the internal thoracic artery for coronary bypass therefore has to divide transversus thoracis. In the 6th intercostal space the artery divides into the superior epigastric and musculophrenic arteries, which supply the anterior abdominal wall and the lower spaces.

  • The lateral thoracic vessels run on the outer surface of serratus anterior, far from the sternum.
  • The posterior intercostal vessels come from behind in the costal grooves; they do not run vertically beside the sternum.
Slides (2)
L123Learning
Which thoracic wall muscles are thought to act mainly as proprioceptors rather than as breathing muscles?
  1. A. External intercostals and interchondral parts of the internal intercostals
  2. B. Serratus posterior superior and inferior; levatores costarum
  3. C. Subcostals and innermost intercostals of the lower spaces
AnswerB. Serratus posterior superior and inferior; levatores costarum
Serratus posterior (superior and inferior) and levatores costarum add little to breathing; they are thought to be mainly proprioceptive.
Explanation

Their attachments suggest that serratus posterior superior should raise the ribs and serratus posterior inferior lower them, but they contribute little to respiration. They are thought to act mainly as sense organs (proprioception) and can be a source of chronic pain in myofascial pain syndromes. Levatores costarum are also believed to be mostly proprioceptive; they help move the vertebral column and can elevate the ribs.

  • The external intercostals and the interchondral internal intercostals are true breathing muscles that elevate the ribs.
  • Subcostals and innermost intercostals probably act like the internal intercostals.
Slide (1)
L124Learning
What are the attachments of serratus posterior superior?
  1. A. Nuchal ligament and spines of C7–T3 → upper borders of ribs 2–4
  2. B. Spines of T11–L2 → lower borders of ribs 8–12
  3. C. Transverse processes of C7–T11 → the rib below each
AnswerA. Nuchal ligament and spines of C7–T3 → upper borders of ribs 2–4
Serratus posterior superior runs from the nuchal ligament and spines of C7–T3 down and out to ribs 2–4.
Explanation

Its fibres slope inferolaterally from the midline of the lower neck and upper back to the upper borders of ribs 2–4, so in theory it raises those ribs; in practice it is thought to be mainly proprioceptive. It is supplied by intercostal nerves 2–5.

  • T11–L2 → ribs 8–12 is serratus posterior inferior, its mirror image at the bottom of the cage.
  • Transverse processes → rib below is levatores costarum.
Slide (1)
L125Learning
Which nerves supply serratus posterior superior?
  1. A. Anterior rami of T9–T12
  2. B. Dorsal scapular nerve
  3. C. Intercostal nerves 2–5
AnswerC. Intercostal nerves 2–5
Serratus posterior superior lies on the back but is supplied by intercostal nerves 2–5 (anterior rami), like the ribs it attaches to.
Explanation

Although it lies on the posterior thorax under the rhomboids, serratus posterior superior is not a deep back muscle: it is supplied by anterior rami, the 2nd to 5th intercostal nerves.

  • Anterior rami of T9–T12 supply serratus posterior inferior.
  • The dorsal scapular nerve supplies the rhomboids and levator scapulae, which lie just superficial to it.
Slides (2)
L126Learning
What are the attachments of serratus posterior inferior?
  1. A. Spines of T6–T10 → lower borders of ribs 4–8
  2. B. Spines of T11–L2 → the iliac crest
  3. C. Spines of T11–L2 → lower borders of ribs 8–12
AnswerC. Spines of T11–L2 → lower borders of ribs 8–12
Serratus posterior inferior runs from the spines of T11–L2 up and out to the lower borders of ribs 8–12, near their angles.
Explanation

Its fibres pass superolaterally from the thoracolumbar junction to the lower ribs, so in theory it pulls them down; like serratus posterior superior it is thought to be mainly proprioceptive. It is supplied by the anterior rami of T9–T12.

  • The two serratus posterior muscles cap the top (ribs 2–4) and bottom (ribs 8–12) of the cage; there is no muscle from T6–T10 to ribs 4–8.
  • The iliac crest is not a rib; serratus posterior inferior acts on the lower ribs.
Slide (1)
L127Learning
Which nerves supply serratus posterior inferior?
  1. A. Posterior rami of T9–T12
  2. B. Anterior rami of T9–T12
  3. C. Anterior rami of L1–L3
AnswerB. Anterior rami of T9–T12
Serratus posterior inferior is supplied by the anterior rami of T9–T12, not by the posterior rami that supply the deep back muscles around it.
Explanation

Both serratus posterior muscles are supplied by anterior rami: the superior one by intercostal nerves 2–5, the inferior one by T9–T12 (lower intercostal and subcostal nerves). This marks them as body-wall muscles that migrated onto the back, not true deep back muscles.

  • Posterior rami supply the erector spinae and the other deep back muscles, plus levatores costarum.
  • The L1–L3 anterior rami form the lumbar plexus for the lower abdominal wall and thigh.
Slides (2)
L128Learning
What are the attachments and action of levatores costarum?
  1. A. Transverse processes → the rib below → elevate the ribs
  2. B. Transverse processes → the rib above → depress the ribs
  3. C. Spinous processes → the rib below → elevate the ribs
AnswerA. Transverse processes → the rib below → elevate the ribs
Levatores costarum ('rib raisers') run from the tips of the transverse processes to the rib below, between its tubercle and angle, and elevate the ribs.
Explanation

These are 12 pairs of small fan-shaped muscles beside the vertebral column, from the transverse processes of C7 and T1–T11 (the lecture table prints 'T7–11') to the rib below, between its tubercle and angle. They can raise the ribs, help move the vertebral column and are thought to be largely proprioceptive. They are supplied by posterior rami of C8–T11.

  • Running to the rib above and depressing it would make them anything but 'levatores'.
  • Spinous processes give origin to the serratus posterior muscles, not to levatores costarum.
Slides (2)
L129Learning
Which nerves supply levatores costarum?
  1. A. Anterior rami of C8–T11
  2. B. Intercostal nerves 2–5
  3. C. Posterior rami of C8–T11
AnswerC. Posterior rami of C8–T11
Levatores costarum are supplied by posterior rami of C8–T11, the only true thoracic wall muscles supplied by posterior rami.
Explanation

Levatores costarum lie beside the vertebral column among the deep back muscles, and like them they are supplied by posterior (dorsal) rami. All the other true wall muscles (serratus posterior, intercostals, subcostals, transversus thoracis) are supplied by anterior rami.

  • The anterior rami of C8–T11 mostly form the intercostal nerves (and C8 joins the brachial plexus).
  • Intercostal nerves 2–5 supply serratus posterior superior.
Slides (2)
L130Learning
Which nerves supply the intercostal, subcostal and transversus thoracis muscles?
  1. A. Intercostal nerves
  2. B. Phrenic nerves
  3. C. Posterior rami of the thoracic spinal nerves
AnswerA. Intercostal nerves
All the muscles in the intercostal spaces, plus the subcostals and transversus thoracis, are supplied by the intercostal nerves (anterior rami of T1–T11).
Explanation

The intercostal nerve of each space runs in the plane between the internal and innermost layers and gives motor branches to all three intercostal muscles; the deep layer on the inner wall (subcostals, transversus thoracis) is supplied by the same nerves.

  • The phrenic nerves (C3–C5) supply the diaphragm, not the chest wall muscles.
  • Posterior rami supply the deep back muscles and, of the wall muscles, only levatores costarum.
MuscleFrom → toNerveAction
Serratus posterior superiorNuchal ligament, spines C7–T3 → ribs 2–4Intercostal nerves 2–5Proprioception (elevates)
Serratus posterior inferiorSpines T11–L2 → ribs 8–12Anterior rami T9–T12Proprioception (depresses)
Levatores costarumTransverse processes → rib belowPosterior rami C8–T11Elevate ribs
IntercostalsRib → rib belowIntercostal nervesExternal elevate; internal and innermost depress (interchondral part elevates)
SubcostalsLower ribs → 2nd or 3rd rib belowIntercostal nervesAs internal intercostals
Transversus thoracisBack of lower sternum → cartilages 2–6Intercostal nervesWeakly depresses ribs
Slides (2)

Intercostal spaces and the neurovascular bundle

L131Learning
How many intercostal spaces are there on each side, and how is each one numbered?
  1. A. 11 → each named for the rib below it
  2. B. 11 → each named for the rib above it
  3. C. 12 → each named for the rib above it
AnswerB. 11 → each named for the rib above it
12 ribs leave 11 intercostal spaces; each is named for the rib above, so the 4th space lies between ribs 4 and 5.
Explanation

There is a space between each pair of adjacent ribs, so 12 ribs make 11 spaces. A space takes the number of the rib forming its upper border: the 4th intercostal space is between the 4th and 5th ribs. These numbers are how you say where to put a stethoscope or a thoracentesis needle (the 9th space, just above the 10th rib).

  • Naming by the rib below would shift every space by one.
  • The region below the 12th rib is not a 12th intercostal space; it is the subcostal space.
Slides (2)
L132Learning
What is the space below the 12th rib called?
  1. A. 12th intercostal space
  2. B. Lumbar space
  3. C. Subcostal space
AnswerC. Subcostal space
Below the 12th rib there is no rib to close an intercostal space; the area is the subcostal space, with the subcostal nerve and vessels.
Explanation

The subcostal space lies below the 12th rib. Its nerve is the anterior ramus of T12, the subcostal nerve; the matching artery is the subcostal artery from the aorta, and the subcostal vein helps begin the azygos and hemiazygos veins.

  • There is no 12th intercostal space: an intercostal space needs a rib above and a rib below.
  • 'Lumbar space' is not the term used for this region.
Slide (1)
L133Learning
Where does the main intercostal neurovascular bundle run?
  1. A. In the costal groove on the lower border of the rib above, between the internal and innermost intercostals
  2. B. In the costal groove on the lower border of the rib above, between the external and internal intercostals
  3. C. Along the upper border of the rib below, between the internal and innermost intercostals
AnswerA. In the costal groove on the lower border of the rib above, between the internal and innermost intercostals
The main bundle hugs the lower border of each rib in the costal groove, in the plane between the internal and innermost intercostals.
Explanation

The costal groove is a channel on the internal, inferior surface of each rib body. The intercostal vein, artery and nerve run in it, sheltered by the overhanging lower edge of the rib, in the neurovascular plane that separates the internal intercostal from the innermost intercostal. A typical intercostal nerve follows this same plane round the chest.

  • Between the external and internal layers is the wrong plane; the bundle lies deeper.
  • The upper border of the rib below carries only the smaller collateral branches.
Slides (2)
L134Learning
What is the order of structures in the main intercostal neurovascular bundle, from top to bottom?
  1. A. Vein → artery → nerve
  2. B. Nerve → artery → vein
  3. C. Artery → vein → nerve
AnswerA. Vein → artery → nerve
Top to bottom in the costal groove: Vein, Artery, Nerve (VAN); the vein sits highest and the nerve lowest, least protected.
Explanation

Under each rib the bundle is stacked with the intercostal vein highest in the groove, the artery below it and the nerve lowest, often hanging just below the rib edge. So the nerve is the structure most exposed to a needle or blade passing just under a rib.

  • Nerve → artery → vein is the reverse ('NAV'), which the lecture gives for the collateral branches on the rib below.
  • Artery → vein → nerve swaps the two vessels.

Hook: the VAN parks under the rib.

Slide (1)
L135Learning
A shard of glass enters the neurovascular bundle directly beneath the 5th rib. Which structure in the bundle lies lowest and is least sheltered by the costal groove?
  1. A. Intercostal vein
  2. B. Intercostal nerve
  3. C. Intercostal artery
AnswerB. Intercostal nerve
In the VAN stack under a rib the nerve lies lowest, partly below the shelter of the costal groove.
Explanation

Directly under a rib the order is vein, artery, nerve from top to bottom, so the most inferior structure is the intercostal nerve. The vein and artery are tucked up in the groove; the nerve may hang below the rib edge and is the least protected. If the wound were just above the 6th rib instead, it would reach the collateral branches, whose order the lecture gives reversed (nerve on top).

  • The vein is the highest structure, deepest in the groove.
  • The artery lies between the vein and the nerve.
Slides (2)
L136Learning
Where do the collateral branches of the intercostal vessels and nerve run?
  1. A. Along the upper border of the rib below, between the external and internal intercostals
  2. B. Across the middle of the space, between the internal and innermost intercostals
  3. C. Along the upper border of the rib below, between the internal and innermost intercostals
AnswerC. Along the upper border of the rib below, between the internal and innermost intercostals
The collateral branches run along the upper border of the rib below, in the same internal–innermost plane as the main bundle.
Explanation

Near the rib angle the intercostal nerve and posterior intercostal artery give off collateral branches (with a companion vein) that cross the space and run forward along the superior border of the rib below. Both bundles lie between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles. The lecture summary stresses it: in any thoracic procedure, remember the collateral bundle on the upper border of the lower rib of every space.

  • The collaterals do not change planes into the external–internal interval.
  • The middle of the space is the zone between the two bundles, which is why thoracotomy incisions go there.
Slides (2)
L137Learning
According to the lecture, in what order do the collateral branches lie, from top to bottom?
  1. A. Nerve → artery → vein (the reverse of the main bundle)
  2. B. Vein → artery → nerve (the same as the main bundle)
  3. C. Artery → nerve → vein (the artery on top)
AnswerA. Nerve → artery → vein (the reverse of the main bundle)
The lecture says the collateral bundle on the rib below is flipped to NAV: nerve, artery, vein from top to bottom.
Explanation

The main bundle under a rib is vein–artery–nerve (VAN). The lecture teaches that the collateral bundle, on the upper border of the rib below, is the mirror image, nerve–artery–vein (NAV), so in both bundles the nerve lies farthest from its rib. Standard atlases rarely state the order of the collateral branches, so learn it as the lecture gives it.

  • VAN is the order of the main bundle, not the collateral one.
  • Artery on top fits neither bundle.
Slide (1)
L138Learning
A thoracentesis needle passes through the lateral chest wall into the pleural cavity. In what order does it cross the layers?
  1. A. External intercostal → innermost intercostal → internal intercostal → endothoracic fascia → parietal pleura
  2. B. External intercostal → internal intercostal → innermost intercostal → parietal pleura → endothoracic fascia
  3. C. External intercostal → internal intercostal → innermost intercostal → endothoracic fascia → parietal pleura
AnswerC. External intercostal → internal intercostal → innermost intercostal → endothoracic fascia → parietal pleura
Outside in: external, internal, innermost intercostal, then endothoracic fascia, then parietal pleura, the last layer before the pleural cavity.
Explanation

After the skin and superficial fascia, the needle crosses the three intercostal layers in order. The endothoracic fascia is the thin connective tissue lining the inner surface of the cage that binds the parietal pleura to it. Piercing the parietal pleura enters the pleural cavity; the needle should not reach the visceral pleura on the lung. The parietal pleura is pain-sensitive (intercostal nerves), so it is the deepest layer to anaesthetise.

  • Putting the innermost before the internal layer reverses the two deep sheets.
  • Putting the pleura before the fascia reverses the lining: the fascia lies outside the pleura.
Slides (2)
L139Learning
Where in an intercostal space should a needle be inserted to avoid the main neurovascular bundle?
  1. A. Just below the lower border of the rib above
  2. B. Just above the upper border of the rib below
  3. C. Anywhere in the space, provided it passes between the external and internal intercostals
AnswerB. Just above the upper border of the rib below
The main VAN bundle hides under the rib above, so needles go in just above the rib below, in the lower part of the space.
Explanation

The large vein, artery and nerve of each space run in the costal groove on the lower border of the rib above. Entering over the superior border of the rib below keeps the needle as far as possible from them. Thoracentesis is therefore done 'above the rib', for example in the 9th space at the midaxillary line just above the 10th rib.

  • Just below the rib above aims straight at the main bundle.
  • The bundle lies between the internal and innermost layers, so choosing a muscle plane does not protect it; only the position in the space does.
Slides (2)
L140Learning
Thoracentesis is planned in the 9th intercostal space at the midaxillary line. Exactly where should the needle enter?
  1. A. Immediately above the 10th rib
  2. B. Immediately below the 9th rib
  3. C. Immediately above the 9th rib
AnswerA. Immediately above the 10th rib
The 9th space lies between ribs 9 and 10; the needle goes in just above the 10th rib, away from the bundle under the 9th.
Explanation

Spaces are numbered for the rib above, so the 9th space is bounded by rib 9 above and rib 10 below. The main bundle runs under rib 9, so the safe entry is over the upper border of rib 10, angled slightly upward to stay clear of the diaphragm and liver. The 9th space at the midaxillary line is used because it opens onto the costodiaphragmatic recess, where fluid collects in an upright patient.

  • Below the 9th rib is exactly where the vein, artery and nerve lie.
  • Above the 9th rib is in the 8th space, not the 9th.
Slides (2)
L141Learning
Why is a thoracentesis needle passed just above the rib below, but not scraping along that rib's edge?
  1. A. Above the rib avoids the collateral branches; staying off the rib edge spares the main bundle
  2. B. Above the rib avoids the parietal pleura; staying off the rib edge spares the periosteum
  3. C. Above the rib avoids the main bundle under the rib above; staying off the rib edge spares the collateral branches
AnswerC. Above the rib avoids the main bundle under the rib above; staying off the rib edge spares the collateral branches
Going above the rib below avoids the main bundle; not hugging that rib's edge spares the collateral branches running along it.
Explanation

Each space has two neurovascular bundles: the large main bundle under the rib above and the smaller collateral branches along the upper border of the rib below. The lecture's instruction is to insert the needle superior to the rib, but far enough above it to avoid the collateral branches.

  • Swapping the bundles puts the main bundle on the wrong rib.
  • The needle must pierce the parietal pleura to drain the pleural cavity, so avoiding the pleura is not the aim.
Slides (2)
L142Learning
How is a thoracotomy incision placed to spare the intercostal neurovascular bundles?
  1. A. Along the costal groove under the rib above, or, for wider access, through the neurovascular bundle
  2. B. Along the upper border of the rib below, or, for wider access, through the muscles of two adjacent spaces
  3. C. Midway between the ribs, or, for wider access, through the periosteum of a resected piece of rib
AnswerC. Midway between the ribs, or, for wider access, through the periosteum of a resected piece of rib
A thoracotomy goes midway between the ribs, clear of both bundles; for wider access a piece of rib is removed and the incision made through its periosteum.
Explanation

A thoracotomy is a surgical opening into the pleural cavity. The middle of the space lies between the main bundle (under the rib above) and the collateral branches (on the rib below), so it is the least dangerous line. When more room is needed, a segment of rib is excised and the surgeon enters through the bed of its periosteum, which leaves the neurovascular bundles intact.

  • The costal groove is exactly where the main bundle runs.
  • The upper border of the rib below carries the collateral branches.
Slide (1)

Intercostal nerves and dermatomes

L143Learning
What are the intercostal nerves?
  1. A. Posterior rami of spinal nerves T1–T11
  2. B. Anterior rami of spinal nerves T1–T11
  3. C. Anterior rami of spinal nerves T1–T12
AnswerB. Anterior rami of spinal nerves T1–T11
The intercostal nerves are the anterior (ventral) rami of T1–T11; the anterior ramus of T12 is the subcostal nerve.
Explanation

Each thoracic spinal nerve divides just outside the intervertebral foramen into a posterior and an anterior ramus. The anterior rami of T1–T11 run in the intercostal spaces as the intercostal nerves, supplying the intercostal muscles, the parietal pleura and the skin of the lateral and anterior chest (T7–T11 also the abdominal wall). They carry motor, sensory and postganglionic sympathetic fibres.

  • Posterior rami supply the deep back muscles and the skin over them.
  • The anterior ramus of T12 runs below the 12th rib, so it is the subcostal nerve, not an intercostal nerve.
Slide (1)
L144Learning
What is the anterior ramus of T12 called?
  1. A. Iliohypogastric nerve
  2. B. 12th intercostal nerve
  3. C. Subcostal nerve
AnswerC. Subcostal nerve
T12's anterior ramus runs below the 12th rib, so it is the subcostal nerve; the lecture adds that it is part of the lumbar plexus.
Explanation

With no rib below it, T12 has no intercostal space: its anterior ramus follows the lower border of the 12th rib as the subcostal nerve and supplies the lower abdominal wall. It usually sends a communicating branch to L1, which is why the lecture counts it with the lumbar plexus.

  • The iliohypogastric nerve is a branch of L1 (with a T12 contribution), not the T12 ramus itself.
  • There is no '12th intercostal nerve', just as there is no 12th intercostal space.
Slide (1)
L145Learning
What do the posterior rami of the thoracic spinal nerves supply?
  1. A. The intercostal muscles and the skin over them
  2. B. Serratus anterior and the skin over it
  3. C. The deep back muscles and the skin over them
AnswerC. The deep back muscles and the skin over them
Posterior rami of T1–T11 supply the deep (true) back muscles and the overlying skin of the back.
Explanation

The thoracic wall is supplied by both rami of T1–T11. The posterior ramus turns backward to supply the erector spinae and other deep back muscles (and levatores costarum) and the strip of skin over them. Pain from a cut in the skin of the back therefore travels in posterior rami.

  • The intercostal muscles are supplied by anterior rami (the intercostal nerves).
  • Serratus anterior is an upper limb muscle supplied by the long thoracic nerve.
Slide (1)
L146Learning
Which intercostal nerves are typical, and which are atypical?
  1. A. Typical: T3–T6
    Atypical: T1–T2 and T7–T11
  2. B. Typical: T2–T5
    Atypical: T1 and T6–T11
  3. C. Typical: T1–T6
    Atypical: T7–T12
AnswerA. Typical: T3–T6
Atypical: T1–T2 and T7–T11
T3–T6 are typical: they stay within their spaces. T1–T2 (upper limb links) and T7–T11 (abdominal wall) are atypical.
Explanation

A typical intercostal nerve runs its whole course within one space and ends beside the sternum as an anterior cutaneous branch; nerves 3–6 do this. The rest are atypical: most of T1 goes to the brachial plexus; nerves 1 and 2 run on the inner surface of their ribs, and the 2nd gives the intercostobrachial nerve to the axilla and arm; nerves 7–11 leave the spaces to supply the abdominal wall as thoracoabdominal nerves.

  • T2–T5 wrongly includes T2 and leaves out T6.
  • T1–T6 wrongly includes T1 and T2, and T12 is the subcostal nerve, not an intercostal nerve.
Slide (1)
L147Learning
In what order does a typical intercostal nerve give off its branches, from back to front?
  1. A. Lateral cutaneous branch (rib angle) → collateral branch (midaxillary line) → anterior cutaneous branch (beside the sternum)
  2. B. Collateral branch (rib angle) → anterior cutaneous branch (midaxillary line) → lateral cutaneous branch (beside the sternum)
  3. C. Collateral branch (rib angle) → lateral cutaneous branch (midaxillary line) → anterior cutaneous branch (beside the sternum)
AnswerC. Collateral branch (rib angle) → lateral cutaneous branch (midaxillary line) → anterior cutaneous branch (beside the sternum)
Back to front: collateral branch at the rib angle, lateral cutaneous at the midaxillary line, anterior cutaneous beside the sternum.
Explanation

A typical nerve (T3–T6) enters its space between the internal and innermost intercostals. At the angle of the rib it gives a collateral branch that runs along the upper border of the rib below. At the midaxillary line the lateral cutaneous branch pierces the muscles and splits into anterior and posterior twigs to the skin of the side of the chest. Near the sternum the nerve turns forward as the anterior cutaneous branch. Along the way it supplies the intercostal muscles and parietal pleura.

  • The other two orders misplace the branches, whose names already say where they are: lateral cutaneous on the side, anterior cutaneous at the front.
Slides (2)
L148Learning
Besides the skin, what does a typical intercostal nerve supply along its course?
  1. A. Intercostal muscles and visceral pleura
  2. B. Intercostal muscles and costal parietal pleura
  3. C. Deep back muscles and costal parietal pleura
AnswerB. Intercostal muscles and costal parietal pleura
Along its course a typical intercostal nerve supplies the intercostal muscles (motor) and the costal parietal pleura (sensory, pain-sensitive).
Explanation

The intercostal nerve is mixed. Its motor fibres supply the intercostal layers (and subcostals and transversus thoracis); its sensory fibres supply the skin and the costal parietal pleura lining the inner surface of the wall (the lower nerves also the peripheral diaphragmatic pleura). That is why pain from the costal pleura is sharp and well localised to the chest wall.

  • The visceral pleura has only autonomic innervation and is insensitive to pain.
  • The deep back muscles are supplied by posterior rami.
Slides (2)
L149Learning
How does the anterior ramus of T1 divide?
  1. A. Small upper part → brachial plexus
    Large lower part → 1st intercostal nerve
  2. B. Large upper part → cervical plexus
    Small lower part → 1st intercostal nerve
  3. C. Large upper part → brachial plexus
    Small lower part → 1st intercostal nerve
AnswerC. Large upper part → brachial plexus
Small lower part → 1st intercostal nerve
Most of T1 goes to the brachial plexus (large superior part); only a small inferior part becomes the 1st intercostal nerve.
Explanation

The T1 anterior ramus first splits: its large superior part joins C8 in the lower trunk of the brachial plexus to supply the upper limb (especially the small muscles of the hand); its small inferior part runs in the 1st intercostal space as the 1st intercostal nerve. That is why T1 compression in thoracic outlet syndrome affects the hand and medial forearm.

  • Reversing the sizes makes the 1st intercostal nerve the main branch; it is in fact small.
  • The cervical plexus is formed by C1–C4, not T1.
Slide (1)
L150Learning
How does the course of the 1st and 2nd intercostal nerves differ from that of a typical intercostal nerve?
  1. A. They run along the upper border of their ribs instead of the lower border
  2. B. They run on the internal surface of their ribs instead of along the lower border
  3. C. They run outside the cage, on the external surface of their ribs
AnswerB. They run on the internal surface of their ribs instead of along the lower border
The 1st and 2nd intercostal nerves run on the internal surface of their ribs, not along the inferior margin in a costal groove.
Explanation

The first two ribs are short, broad and sharply curved, and their nerves follow the inner (pleural) surfaces of the ribs rather than lying in a costal groove along the lower margin, as typical intercostal nerves do. This is one of the features that make nerves 1 and 2 atypical.

  • No intercostal nerve's main trunk runs along the upper border of a rib; that is the course of a collateral branch.
  • Running on the external surface would put the nerves outside the cage, among the shoulder muscles.
Slide (1)
L151Learning
Which intercostal nerve usually has no anterior cutaneous branch?
  1. A. The 2nd
  2. B. The 6th
  3. C. The 1st
AnswerC. The 1st
The small 1st intercostal nerve (the leftover lower part of T1) usually has no anterior cutaneous branch.
Explanation

Because most of T1 goes to the brachial plexus, the 1st intercostal nerve is small and usually ends without an anterior cutaneous branch; the skin over the upper sternum is supplied by the supraclavicular nerves (C3–C4) and the 2nd intercostal nerve. This is one reason T1 is atypical.

  • The 2nd nerve is atypical for another reason: its lateral cutaneous branch becomes the intercostobrachial nerve.
  • The 6th is a typical nerve that ends as an anterior cutaneous branch beside the sternum.
Slide (1)
L152Learning
What is the intercostobrachial nerve?
  1. A. Lateral cutaneous branch of the 2nd intercostal nerve → floor of the axilla and medial arm
  2. B. Anterior cutaneous branch of the 2nd intercostal nerve → skin over the sternum
  3. C. Lateral cutaneous branch of the 1st intercostal nerve → floor of the axilla and medial arm
AnswerA. Lateral cutaneous branch of the 2nd intercostal nerve → floor of the axilla and medial arm
The intercostobrachial nerve is the lateral cutaneous branch of the 2nd intercostal nerve (T2); it pierces serratus anterior at the midaxillary line to supply the axillary floor and medial arm.
Explanation

It emerges through serratus anterior at the midaxillary line, crosses the axilla and supplies the skin of the axillary floor and upper medial arm. It is sensory (with sympathetic fibres to sweat glands), so injury causes numbness, not weakness; it is at risk in axillary lymph node dissection. Its T2 origin is why cardiac pain can be felt down the medial arm.

  • The anterior cutaneous branch of T2 supplies skin beside the sternum, not the axilla.
  • The 1st intercostal nerve is small and gives no such branch.
Slide (1)
L153Learning
What are the thoracoabdominal nerves?
  1. A. Intercostal nerves 7–11 → continue into the diaphragm to supply its muscle
  2. B. Intercostal nerves 7–11 → continue into the abdominal wall to supply its skin and muscles
  3. C. Intercostal nerves 3–6 → continue into the abdominal wall to supply its skin and muscles
AnswerB. Intercostal nerves 7–11 → continue into the abdominal wall to supply its skin and muscles
Intercostal nerves 7–11 run on past the costal margin into the abdominal wall, supplying its skin and muscles: the thoracoabdominal nerves.
Explanation

The lower spaces open forward into the abdominal wall, so after giving off their lateral cutaneous branches nerves 7–11 continue between the internal oblique and transversus abdominis. Their anterior cutaneous branches pierce rectus abdominis close to the midline. This is why T10 supplies the skin around the umbilicus.

  • The lower intercostal nerves are only sensory to the peripheral diaphragm; all its motor supply is phrenic.
  • 3–6 are the typical nerves that stay in the thorax.
Slide (1)
L154Learning
What is a dermatome?
  1. A. The group of muscles supplied by one spinal nerve
  2. B. The strip of skin supplied by one spinal nerve
  3. C. The segment of bone supplied by one spinal nerve
AnswerB. The strip of skin supplied by one spinal nerve
A dermatome is the strip of skin whose sensation is carried by one spinal nerve (on the trunk, one intercostal nerve).
Explanation

On the thorax the dermatomes are neat bands, because each intercostal nerve wraps round the chest in its own space. Knowing a few landmark levels lets you localise a spinal or nerve lesion from a band of numbness or a shingles rash.

  • The muscles supplied by one spinal nerve form a myotome.
  • The bone derived from one segment is a sclerotome.
Slide (1)
L155Learning
According to the lecture, which dermatome lies at the clavicles?
  1. A. C5
  2. B. T2
  3. C. C7
AnswerA. C5
The lecture's landmark is C5 at the clavicles (many charts put the C4/C5 border here).
Explanation

The lecture lists four landmark dermatomes: C5 at the clavicles, T4 at the nipple, T10 at the umbilicus and L1 at the inguinal region. Many dermatome charts draw C4 over the clavicle with C5 just lateral, over the shoulder; for this exam use the lecture's C5. Just below the clavicle the cervical bands give way to T2, because C5–T1 are drawn out into the upper limb.

  • T2 lies below the clavicle, on the upper chest.
  • C7 lies on the middle finger and the back of the arm, not on the trunk.
Slide (1)
L156Learning
Which dermatome lies at the nipple?
  1. A. T2
  2. B. T6
  3. C. T4
AnswerC. T4
The nipple lies in the T4 dermatome (4th intercostal space, 4th intercostal nerve).
Explanation

The T4 band crosses the nipple, which in men lies over the 4th intercostal space and is supplied by the 4th intercostal nerve. Useful pair: T4 at the nipple, T10 at the umbilicus, with the bands in between in order.

  • T2 lies higher, below the clavicle and over the upper sternum.
  • T6 lies lower, around the lower sternum and xiphoid.
Slide (1)
L157Learning
Which dermatome lies at the umbilicus?
  1. A. T10
  2. B. T8
  3. C. T12
AnswerA. T10
The umbilicus lies in the T10 dermatome, supplied by the 10th intercostal (thoracoabdominal) nerve.
Explanation

The 10th intercostal nerve continues into the abdominal wall as a thoracoabdominal nerve and supplies the band of skin round the umbilicus. Classic uses: shingles round the umbilicus means the T10 spinal ganglion; early appendicitis pain is felt round the umbilicus because the appendix's visceral afferents enter at about T10.

  • T8 lies higher, between the xiphoid and the umbilicus.
  • T12 lies lower, just above the inguinal ligament (suprapubic region).
Slide (1)
L158Learning
Which dermatome lies at the inguinal region?
  1. A. T12
  2. B. L3
  3. C. L1
AnswerC. L1
The inguinal region lies in the L1 dermatome (iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves).
Explanation

Below the umbilicus the bands continue: T11 and T12 between the umbilicus and the groin, then L1 over the inguinal region and the root of the thigh, through the iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves.

  • T12 lies just above the inguinal ligament.
  • L3 lies over the front of the thigh down to the knee.
Slide (1)
L159Learning
Why is complete loss of sensation over one whole dermatome rare?
  1. A. Neighbouring dermatomes overlap
  2. B. The sympathetic chain takes over the sensation
  3. C. Sensory nerve fibres regenerate within days
AnswerA. Neighbouring dermatomes overlap
Adjacent dermatomes overlap, so each patch of skin gets fibres from more than one spinal nerve; cutting one nerve only reduces sensation.
Explanation

The territory of each intercostal nerve overlaps those of the nerves above and below, so a point on the chest wall is usually supplied by two or three adjacent spinal nerves. Interrupting a single nerve causes at most a narrow band of reduced feeling, rarely complete anaesthesia. The same overlap is why several adjacent nerves must be blocked to numb an area.

  • The sympathetic chain does not carry touch or pain from the skin in place of the spinal nerves.
  • Peripheral nerves regenerate at about 1 mm a day, over weeks to months, not days.
Slide (1)
L160Learning
Why does a herpes zoster (shingles) rash stay within one dermatome?
  1. A. The virus lies latent in one ventral horn and travels out along its motor axons
  2. B. The virus lies latent in one sympathetic chain ganglion and travels out along its postganglionic axons
  3. C. The virus lies latent in one spinal (dorsal root) ganglion and travels out along that ganglion's sensory axons
AnswerC. The virus lies latent in one spinal (dorsal root) ganglion and travels out along that ganglion's sensory axons
Varicella zoster virus hides in a spinal (dorsal root) ganglion; reactivated, it travels along that ganglion's sensory axons, so the rash maps one dermatome.
Explanation

After chickenpox the virus stays dormant in the cell bodies of sensory neurons in a spinal ganglion. Reactivation (with age or immune suppression) sends virus down the peripheral sensory axons of that one spinal nerve to the skin, producing a painful, band-like vesicular rash on one side of the trunk that follows the dermatome of the infected ganglion.

  • Ventral horn neurons are motor; zoster is a disease of the sensory ganglion.
  • Sympathetic chain ganglia contain autonomic neurons, not the sensory cell bodies that harbour the virus.
Slide (1)
L161Learning
A patient has a painful band of vesicles running round one side of the trunk through the umbilicus. Where is the reactivated virus?
  1. A. Spinal (dorsal root) ganglion of T12
  2. B. Spinal (dorsal root) ganglion of T10
  3. C. Ventral horn of the T10 spinal cord segment
AnswerB. Spinal (dorsal root) ganglion of T10
A band through the umbilicus is the T10 dermatome, so the virus is in the T10 spinal (dorsal root) ganglion.
Explanation

Two steps: find the dermatome (umbilicus = T10), then recall where zoster lives (the sensory spinal ganglion of that nerve). The same logic gives the T4 ganglion for a band across the nipple.

  • T12 would put the band lower, just above the inguinal ligament.
  • The ventral horn contains motor neurons; the virus resides in the sensory ganglion.
Slides (2)
L162Learning
Why must several adjacent intercostal nerves be blocked to anaesthetise one area of the chest wall?
  1. A. Neighbouring dermatomes overlap, so adjacent nerves also supply the area
  2. B. Each intercostal nerve supplies only the front or the back of its dermatome
  3. C. Local anaesthetic cannot cross the costal groove to reach the nerve
AnswerA. Neighbouring dermatomes overlap, so adjacent nerves also supply the area
Because dermatomes overlap, each area also gets fibres from the nerves above and below, so an intercostal nerve block must include adjacent nerves.
Explanation

In an intercostal nerve block, local anaesthetic is injected around the nerve near the lower border of the rib. Each strip of skin is also supplied by the neighbouring intercostal nerves, so blocking one nerve only reduces sensation; full anaesthesia needs the nerves above and below too. Care is taken not to puncture the neurovascular bundle.

  • Each nerve supplies its band all the way round through its lateral and anterior cutaneous branches, not just half of it.
  • The injection is placed right next to the nerve at the rib's lower border, so the anaesthetic does reach it.
Slide (1)

Intercostal arteries and veins

L163Learning
From which two directions does each upper intercostal space receive its arterial supply?
  1. A. Posterior intercostal artery from behind (mostly from the aorta)
    Anterior intercostal arteries from in front (from the internal thoracic artery)
  2. B. Posterior intercostal artery from behind (from the internal thoracic artery)
    Anterior intercostal arteries from in front (mostly from the aorta)
  3. C. Posterior intercostal artery from behind (mostly from the aorta)
    Anterior intercostal arteries from in front (from the lateral thoracic artery)
AnswerA. Posterior intercostal artery from behind (mostly from the aorta)
Anterior intercostal arteries from in front (from the internal thoracic artery)
Each space is fed from behind by a posterior intercostal artery (mostly from the aorta) and from in front by anterior intercostal arteries (from the internal thoracic artery).
Explanation

The thoracic wall has two arterial sources: the subclavian artery (through the internal thoracic artery in front, and the superior intercostal artery for spaces 1–2) and the thoracic aorta. The posterior and anterior intercostal arteries run toward each other in the space and meet, forming an arterial ring in each of spaces 1–9.

  • Swapping the sources puts the aorta at the front of the chest; the internal thoracic artery runs beside the sternum.
  • The lateral thoracic artery (from the axillary artery) runs on serratus anterior and supplies the lateral breast; it gives no anterior intercostal arteries.
Slides (2)
L164Learning
What is the internal thoracic artery a branch of, and where does it run?
  1. A. Subclavian artery → runs down along the midclavicular line, superficial to the ribs
  2. B. Axillary artery → runs down just lateral to the sternum, deep to the costal cartilages
  3. C. Subclavian artery → runs down just lateral to the sternum, deep to the costal cartilages
AnswerC. Subclavian artery → runs down just lateral to the sternum, deep to the costal cartilages
The internal thoracic artery arises from the subclavian artery and descends about 1 cm lateral to the sternum, behind the costal cartilages.
Explanation

It leaves the first part of the subclavian artery, enters the thorax through the inlet and runs vertically down the inside of the anterior wall, behind the costal cartilages and in front of transversus thoracis. It gives the anterior intercostal arteries of spaces 1–6, then divides into the superior epigastric and musculophrenic arteries. Because it is long, accessible and resistant to atherosclerosis, it is the artery most often harvested for coronary artery bypass grafting (its other name is the internal mammary artery).

  • The midclavicular line is far too lateral.
  • The axillary artery gives the lateral thoracic and thoracoacromial arteries, not the internal thoracic.
Slides (2)
L165Learning
Which intercostal spaces receive anterior intercostal arteries directly from the internal thoracic artery?
  1. A. Spaces 1–9
  2. B. Spaces 1–6
  3. C. Spaces 7–9
AnswerB. Spaces 1–6
The internal thoracic artery itself gives the anterior intercostal arteries of spaces 1–6; spaces 7–9 get theirs from its musculophrenic branch.
Explanation

Running beside the sternum, the internal thoracic artery sends anterior intercostal branches (usually two per space) into the upper six spaces. At about the 6th space it divides, and its musculophrenic branch then supplies spaces 7–9. Spaces 10 and 11 have no anterior intercostal arteries.

  • 1–9 is the total of spaces with anterior intercostals, counting the musculophrenic ones.
  • 7–9 are the spaces supplied by the musculophrenic artery.
Slide (1)
L166Learning
What are the two terminal branches of the internal thoracic artery?
  1. A. Superior epigastric artery and musculophrenic artery
  2. B. Inferior epigastric artery and musculophrenic artery
  3. C. Superior epigastric artery and lateral thoracic artery
AnswerA. Superior epigastric artery and musculophrenic artery
At about the 6th space the internal thoracic artery divides into the superior epigastric (into the rectus sheath) and the musculophrenic (along the costal margin).
Explanation

The superior epigastric continues the straight downward line into the rectus sheath; the musculophrenic artery turns laterally along the costal margin, supplying the lower anterior intercostal spaces and the diaphragm.

  • The inferior epigastric artery comes from the external iliac artery and climbs to meet the superior epigastric.
  • The lateral thoracic artery is a branch of the axillary artery.
Slide (1)
L167Learning
Where does the superior epigastric artery go, and with what does it anastomose?
  1. A. Down through the rectus sheath → inferior epigastric artery (from the internal iliac artery)
  2. B. Down through the rectus sheath → inferior epigastric artery (from the external iliac artery)
  3. C. Along the costal margin → musculophrenic artery (from the internal thoracic artery)
AnswerB. Down through the rectus sheath → inferior epigastric artery (from the external iliac artery)
The superior epigastric runs down in the rectus sheath to anastomose with the inferior epigastric, a branch of the external iliac artery.
Explanation

Behind rectus abdominis the two epigastric arteries meet, linking the subclavian and external iliac territories. This anastomosis is a collateral route: in coarctation of the aorta it carries blood round the narrowing, and if the internal thoracic artery is used for a bypass graft, rectus abdominis keeps its supply through increased flow in the inferior epigastric artery.

  • The inferior epigastric arises from the external, not the internal, iliac artery.
  • Running along the costal margin describes the musculophrenic artery, the other terminal branch.
Slide (1)
L168Learning
What is the course of the musculophrenic artery, and which spaces does it supply?
  1. A. Along the costal margin → posterior intercostal arteries of spaces 7–9
  2. B. Along the costal margin → anterior intercostal arteries of spaces 7–9
  3. C. Down the rectus sheath → anterior intercostal arteries of spaces 10–11
AnswerB. Along the costal margin → anterior intercostal arteries of spaces 7–9
The musculophrenic artery follows the costal margin, giving the anterior intercostal arteries of spaces 7–9 and branches to the diaphragm.
Explanation

As its name says, it supplies muscle (the lower intercostals and upper abdominal wall) and the diaphragm (phrenic). Running along the costal margin, it gives anterior intercostal branches to the 7th, 8th and 9th spaces.

  • Posterior intercostal arteries come from behind (superior intercostal artery and aorta), never from the internal thoracic system.
  • Spaces 10–11 have no anterior intercostal arteries, and the rectus sheath carries the superior epigastric.
Slide (1)
L169Learning
Why do intercostal spaces 10 and 11 have no anterior intercostal arteries?
  1. A. They are supplied by the superior epigastric artery instead
  2. B. The diaphragm covers them in front, so they need no anterior supply
  3. C. The cage is open in front: these spaces run on into the abdominal wall
AnswerC. The cage is open in front: these spaces run on into the abdominal wall
Ribs 11 and 12 end free and the costal margin rises to the xiphoid: the cage is open in front, so spaces 10–11 run into the abdominal wall.
Explanation

The lecture's hint is to think of the shape of the cage. The costal margin climbs from the 10th cartilage to the xiphoid, and ribs 11 and 12 end in the abdominal wall. The 10th and 11th spaces therefore have no anterior part beside the costal margin for the musculophrenic artery to supply; their posterior intercostal arteries continue forward into the abdominal wall instead.

  • The superior epigastric artery runs in the rectus sheath and gives no intercostal branches.
  • The diaphragm arises from the inner surfaces of the lower cartilages and ribs; it does not replace the arteries.
Slides (2)
L170Learning
Roughly how much of each intercostal space do the posterior intercostal arteries supply?
  1. A. About two-thirds
  2. B. About one-third
  3. C. About half
AnswerA. About two-thirds
The posterior intercostal artery supplies about two-thirds of its space; the anterior intercostal arteries supply the front third.
Explanation

The posterior intercostal artery enters from behind and runs most of the way round in the costal groove before meeting the much smaller anterior intercostal arteries, which supply only the anterior third. On the way it gives a dorsal branch to the back, a collateral branch and a lateral cutaneous branch.

  • One-third is the anterior intercostal arteries' share.
  • Half would make the two equal partners; the posterior artery is the larger.
Slide (1)
L171Learning
Where do the posterior intercostal arteries of spaces 1 and 2 come from?
  1. A. Superior (supreme) intercostal artery ← thyrocervical trunk ← subclavian artery
  2. B. The thoracic aorta directly, like those of spaces 3–11
  3. C. Superior (supreme) intercostal artery ← costocervical trunk ← subclavian artery
AnswerC. Superior (supreme) intercostal artery ← costocervical trunk ← subclavian artery
Spaces 1–2 get their posterior intercostals from the superior (supreme) intercostal artery, a branch of the costocervical trunk of the subclavian artery.
Explanation

The descending thoracic aorta begins at T4/T5, below the first two spaces, so these are supplied from above: subclavian artery → costocervical trunk → superior (supreme) intercostal artery, which descends in front of the necks of ribs 1 and 2.

  • The thyrocervical trunk supplies the thyroid, neck and scapular region, not the intercostal spaces.
  • Only spaces 3–11 receive posterior intercostals directly from the thoracic aorta.
Slides (2)
L172Learning
Where do the posterior intercostal arteries of spaces 3–11 come from?
  1. A. Internal thoracic artery
  2. B. Thoracic aorta
  3. C. Costocervical trunk
AnswerB. Thoracic aorta
Posterior intercostal arteries 3–11 (and the subcostal arteries) are paired branches of the thoracic aorta.
Explanation

The descending thoracic aorta gives off nine pairs of posterior intercostal arteries for spaces 3–11 and a pair of subcostal arteries below the 12th rib. A block at the origin of the descending aorta would therefore cut flow to these posterior intercostals, while spaces 1–2 (supplied from the costocervical trunk) would be spared.

  • The internal thoracic artery gives the anterior intercostals.
  • The costocervical trunk supplies only spaces 1–2, through the superior intercostal artery.
Slide (1)
L173Learning
Why are the right posterior intercostal arteries longer than the left?
  1. A. The heart lies to the left, so the right arteries must reach farther round the chest
  2. B. The aorta lies to the left of the midline, so the right arteries must cross the vertebral bodies
  3. C. The azygos vein lies on the right, so the right arteries must loop around it
AnswerB. The aorta lies to the left of the midline, so the right arteries must cross the vertebral bodies
The descending aorta lies to the left of the vertebral bodies, so the right posterior intercostal arteries must cross in front of the vertebrae to reach their spaces.
Explanation

The thoracic aorta descends on the left side of the vertebral bodies. The left posterior intercostal arteries pass straight into their spaces, but the right ones first cross the front of the vertebral bodies, behind the oesophagus, thoracic duct and azygos vein, which makes them longer.

  • The heart does not set the length of these arteries; they arise behind it, from the aorta.
  • The right arteries pass behind the azygos vein on their way, but they do not loop around it.
Slide (1)
L174Learning
In which intercostal spaces do anterior and posterior intercostal arteries anastomose?
  1. A. Spaces 1–9
  2. B. Spaces 1–6
  3. C. Spaces 1–11
AnswerA. Spaces 1–9
Anterior intercostal arteries exist only in spaces 1–9, so that is where they join the posterior intercostals; spaces 10–11 have posterior arteries only.
Explanation

In spaces 1–6 the anterior arteries come from the internal thoracic artery, in 7–9 from the musculophrenic artery; in all nine they anastomose with the posterior intercostal arteries. The ring matters clinically: if the internal thoracic artery is harvested for a bypass graft, or a posterior supply is cut, the space stays perfused through the other side of the loop; in coarctation of the aorta these channels enlarge and notch the ribs.

  • 1–6 counts only the internal thoracic branches and forgets the musculophrenic ones.
  • 1–11 forgets that spaces 10–11 have no anterior intercostal arteries.
Slide (1)
L175Learning
Into which venous system do the posterior intercostal veins mainly drain?
  1. A. Azygos system
  2. B. Hepatic portal system
  3. C. Inferior vena cava directly
AnswerA. Azygos system
The thoracic wall drains into the azygos system, a set of veins running parallel to the venae cavae on the posterior wall.
Explanation

The azygos system (azygos vein on the right; hemiazygos and accessory hemiazygos veins on the left; the superior intercostal veins above) runs beside the vertebral column, parallel to the inferior and superior venae cavae. While the caval system drains the limbs and organs, the azygos system drains the posterior abdominal wall and the thoracic wall, emptying finally into the superior vena cava. The anterior intercostal veins drain forward into the internal thoracic veins.

  • The portal system drains the gut to the liver.
  • The posterior intercostal veins do not enter the inferior vena cava; the azygos system ends in the superior vena cava.
Slide (1)
L176Learning
How does the azygos system begin in the lumbar region?
  1. A. Ascending lumbar vein + subcostal vein → hemiazygos vein on the right, azygos vein on the left
  2. B. Ascending lumbar vein + subcostal vein → azygos vein on the right, hemiazygos vein on the left
  3. C. Renal vein + subcostal vein → azygos vein on the right, accessory hemiazygos vein on the left
AnswerB. Ascending lumbar vein + subcostal vein → azygos vein on the right, hemiazygos vein on the left
On each side the ascending lumbar vein joins the subcostal vein: on the right it becomes the azygos, on the left the hemiazygos.
Explanation

The ascending lumbar veins run up the posterior abdominal wall linking the lumbar veins. Once each receives the subcostal vein it passes into the thorax under a new name: azygos on the right, hemiazygos on the left. ('Azygos' means unpaired: there is only one, on the right.)

  • Swapping the sides is wrong: the azygos is the right-sided vessel.
