  • The accessory hemiazygos begins higher, in the thorax (spaces 5–8), and the renal veins drain into the inferior vena cava.
Slide (1)
L177Learning
Where does the 1st posterior intercostal vein drain on each side?
  1. A. Brachiocephalic vein of the same side
  2. B. Superior vena cava directly
  3. C. Superior intercostal vein of the same side
AnswerA. Brachiocephalic vein of the same side
The 1st posterior intercostal vein on each side drains into the brachiocephalic vein of its own side.
Explanation

The top space lies at the level of the brachiocephalic veins, so its vein drains straight into the nearest one: right 1st → right brachiocephalic, left 1st → left brachiocephalic. Spaces 2–4 are the ones collected by the superior intercostal veins.

  • No intercostal vein enters the superior vena cava directly; the azygos vein is the vessel that does.
  • The superior intercostal veins collect spaces 2–4, not space 1.
Slides (2)
L178Learning
Where do the right 2nd–4th posterior intercostal veins drain?
  1. A. Right superior intercostal vein → right internal jugular vein
  2. B. Right superior intercostal vein → azygos vein or right brachiocephalic vein
  3. C. Directly into the superior vena cava
AnswerB. Right superior intercostal vein → azygos vein or right brachiocephalic vein
Right spaces 2–4 drain into the right superior intercostal vein, which empties into the azygos (or the right brachiocephalic) vein.
Explanation

A short right superior intercostal vein collects spaces 2–4 and usually ends in the azygos vein just before the azygos arches into the superior vena cava; the lecture notes it can drain into the right brachiocephalic vein instead. So tumour cells entering the right 3rd posterior intercostal vein reach the right superior intercostal vein first.

  • The internal jugular vein drains the head and neck.
  • No posterior intercostal vein enters the superior vena cava directly.
Slide (1)
L179Learning
Where do the left 2nd–4th posterior intercostal veins drain?
  1. A. Left superior intercostal vein → azygos vein or right brachiocephalic vein
  2. B. Hemiazygos vein → azygos vein
  3. C. Left superior intercostal vein → left brachiocephalic vein or accessory hemiazygos vein
AnswerC. Left superior intercostal vein → left brachiocephalic vein or accessory hemiazygos vein
Left spaces 2–4 drain into the left superior intercostal vein, which ends in the left brachiocephalic vein (or the accessory hemiazygos).
Explanation

The left superior intercostal vein collects spaces 2–4 and crosses the left side of the aortic arch to empty into the left brachiocephalic vein; the lecture notes it can drain into the accessory hemiazygos instead. The left 2nd posterior intercostal vein therefore drains directly into the left superior intercostal vein.

  • Azygos or right brachiocephalic is where the right superior intercostal vein ends.
  • The hemiazygos vein collects spaces 9–11, not 2–4.
Slide (1)
L180Learning
Where do the 5th–8th posterior intercostal veins drain on each side?
  1. A. Right → azygos vein
    Left → hemiazygos vein → crosses to the azygos
  2. B. Right → azygos vein
    Left → accessory hemiazygos vein → crosses to the azygos
  3. C. Right → right superior intercostal vein
    Left → left superior intercostal vein
AnswerB. Right → azygos vein
Left → accessory hemiazygos vein → crosses to the azygos
Right 5th–8th → azygos; left 5th–8th → accessory hemiazygos, which crosses the vertebrae to the azygos.
Explanation

On the right, every posterior intercostal vein from the 5th down (5th–11th) goes straight into the azygos. On the left, the middle group (5th–8th) is collected by the accessory hemiazygos, which crosses behind the aorta at about T7–T8 to join the azygos. So blood from the left 7th intercostal vein reaches the heart by accessory hemiazygos → azygos → superior vena cava.

  • The hemiazygos takes the lower left group (9th–11th).
  • The superior intercostal veins take spaces 2–4.
Slides (2)
L181Learning
Where do the 9th–11th posterior intercostal, subcostal and lumbar veins drain on each side?
  1. A. Right → azygos vein
    Left → accessory hemiazygos vein → crosses to the azygos
  2. B. Right → azygos vein
    Left → hemiazygos vein → crosses to the azygos
  3. C. Right → inferior vena cava
    Left → hemiazygos vein → left renal vein
AnswerB. Right → azygos vein
Left → hemiazygos vein → crosses to the azygos
The right lower group drains into the azygos; the left 9th–11th, subcostal and lumbar veins drain into the hemiazygos, which crosses to the azygos.
Explanation

The hemiazygos begins from the left ascending lumbar and subcostal veins, collects the left 9th–11th posterior intercostal veins and crosses behind the aorta at about T9 to end in the azygos. An infection spreading up the left lumbar veins reaches the hemiazygos first.

  • The accessory hemiazygos takes the left 5th–8th.
  • These veins do not drain into the inferior vena cava or a renal vein; the azygos system ends in the superior vena cava.
Posterior intercostal veinsRightLeft
1stRight brachiocephalicLeft brachiocephalic
2nd–4thRight superior intercostal → azygos or right brachiocephalicLeft superior intercostal → left brachiocephalic or accessory hemiazygos
5th–8thAzygosAccessory hemiazygos → azygos
9th–11th, subcostal, lumbarAzygosHemiazygos → azygos
Slides (2)
L182Learning
Where does the azygos vein end?
  1. A. It arches over the root of the left lung → left brachiocephalic vein
  2. B. It arches under the root of the right lung → right atrium directly
  3. C. It arches over the root of the right lung → superior vena cava
AnswerC. It arches over the root of the right lung → superior vena cava
The arch of the azygos hooks forward over the root of the right lung at about T4 to enter the superior vena cava.
Explanation

After collecting the right intercostal veins and the hemiazygos and accessory hemiazygos from the left, the azygos vein climbs on the right side of the vertebral bodies and, at about the level of the sternal angle (T4/T5), arches forward over the superior aspect of the right lung root to empty into the back of the superior vena cava. It leaves an impression on the mediastinal surface of the right lung.

  • The left lung root is arched over by the aortic arch, not the azygos.
  • The azygos passes over the root, not under it, and joins the superior vena cava, not the right atrium.
Slide (1)

Diaphragm: structure and openings

L183Learning
What is the diaphragm?
  1. A. A flat fibrous sheet separating the thoracic and abdominal cavities
  2. B. A purely muscular dome separating the abdominal and pelvic cavities
  3. C. A musculotendinous dome separating the thoracic and abdominal cavities
AnswerC. A musculotendinous dome separating the thoracic and abdominal cavities
The diaphragm is a musculotendinous dome (muscular periphery, central tendon) between the thorax and abdomen; it is the main muscle of inspiration.
Explanation

It closes almost all of the thoracic outlet. Its muscle fibres arise round the margins of the outlet (xiphoid, lower six costal cartilages, upper lumbar vertebrae and arcuate ligaments) and converge on an aponeurotic central tendon. It bulges up into the thorax as right and left domes.

  • It is not flat and not purely fibrous: the muscular periphery is what contracts.
  • It is not purely muscular (its centre is tendon), and the abdominal and pelvic cavities are continuous, with no diaphragm between them.
Slide (1)
L184Learning
Which dome of the diaphragm sits higher, and why?
  1. A. Right → pushed up by the liver beneath it
  2. B. Left → pushed up by the stomach and spleen beneath it
  3. C. Right → pulled up by the larger right lung
AnswerA. Right → pushed up by the liver beneath it
The right dome sits higher because the bulky liver lies under it.
Explanation

The liver fills most of the right upper abdomen and holds the right dome up; the left dome, over the stomach and spleen, sits a little lower, and the heart rests on the central tendon between them. On a chest X-ray the right hemidiaphragm is normally slightly higher than the left.

  • The stomach and spleen under the left dome do not lift it as high as the liver lifts the right.
  • The lungs rest on the domes; they do not set their height.
Slides (2)
L185Learning
In expiration, to what levels do the right and left domes of the diaphragm rise?
  1. A. Right → 5th intercostal space
    Left → 5th rib
  2. B. Right → 5th rib
    Left → 5th intercostal space
  3. C. Right → 7th rib
    Left → 7th intercostal space
AnswerB. Right → 5th rib
Left → 5th intercostal space
At the end of expiration the right dome rises to the 5th rib and the left to the 5th intercostal space, slightly lower.
Explanation

The domes rise surprisingly high, to about nipple level, which is why a stab wound of the lower chest can pass through the diaphragm into the liver or spleen. The right is higher (a rib) than the left (the space just below that rib), consistent with the liver holding the right dome up. In inspiration both descend.

  • Swapping them would make the left dome the higher one.
  • The 7th rib level is too low for the domes in expiration.
Slides (2)
L186Learning
What are the three muscular parts of the diaphragm and their origins?
  1. A. Sternal → manubrium
    Costal → upper six costal cartilages
    Lumbar → arcuate ligaments + upper three lumbar vertebrae
  2. B. Sternal → xiphoid process (not always present)
    Costal → lower six costal cartilages
    Lumbar → iliac crests + lower three lumbar vertebrae
  3. C. Sternal → xiphoid process (not always present)
    Costal → lower six costal cartilages
    Lumbar → arcuate ligaments + upper three lumbar vertebrae
AnswerC. Sternal → xiphoid process (not always present)
Costal → lower six costal cartilages
Lumbar → arcuate ligaments + upper three lumbar vertebrae
Sternal part from the xiphoid, costal part from the lower six cartilages, lumbar part from the arcuate ligaments and L1–L3; all converge on the central tendon.
Explanation

The muscle arises all round the inferior thoracic aperture. The small sternal slips (sometimes absent) come from the back of the xiphoid; the broad costal part from the inner surfaces of the lower six costal cartilages and adjacent ribs; the lumbar part from the medial and lateral arcuate ligaments and, as the crura, from the bodies of the upper lumbar vertebrae.

  • The manubrium and the upper cartilages lie far above the outlet.
  • The iliac crests and lower lumbar vertebrae give origin to abdominal and back muscles, not the diaphragm.
Slide (1)
L187Learning
Where do all three muscular parts of the diaphragm insert?
  1. A. Xiphoid process
  2. B. Central tendon
  3. C. Median arcuate ligament
AnswerB. Central tendon
Every muscular part of the diaphragm converges on the central tendon, its aponeurotic centre.
Explanation

Sternal, costal and lumbar fibres all rise from the margins of the outlet and insert into the trefoil-shaped central tendon at the top of the dome. When they contract they pull the tendon down, increasing the vertical diameter of the thorax.

  • The xiphoid is an origin (of the sternal part), not the insertion.
  • The median arcuate ligament is also an origin: it unites the crura in front of the aorta.
Slide (1)
L188Learning
What is the central tendon of the diaphragm fused to?
  1. A. The inferior surface of the fibrous pericardium
  2. B. The upper surface of the liver capsule
  3. C. The inferior surface of the visceral (serous) pericardium
AnswerA. The inferior surface of the fibrous pericardium
The central tendon is fused to the fibrous pericardium, so the heart sits on it and moves down with it in inspiration.
Explanation

The tough outer fibrous pericardium blends with the central tendon. The level of the xiphisternal joint marks the central tendon and the inferior border of the heart.

  • The liver lies under the right dome, separated from it by peritoneum except at its bare area; it is not fused to the central tendon.
  • The visceral serous pericardium (epicardium) covers the heart itself, inside the pericardial cavity, so it cannot fuse with the diaphragm.
Slides (2)
L189Learning
Which part of the diaphragm forms the crura, and which crus is larger?
  1. A. Lumbar part → the left crus is larger and longer
  2. B. Costal part → the right crus is larger and longer
  3. C. Lumbar part → the right crus is larger and longer
AnswerC. Lumbar part → the right crus is larger and longer
The crura are the 'legs' of the lumbar part; the right crus is larger and longer (reaching L3) and forms the oesophageal hiatus.
Explanation

The two crura arise from the front of the upper lumbar vertebral bodies (right L1–L3, left L1–L2) and climb to the central tendon. The bigger right crus splits to encircle the oesophageal hiatus.

  • The left crus is the smaller, shorter one.
  • The costal part arises from the lower six costal cartilages and has no crura.
Slide (1)
L190Learning
What unites the two crura, and what does it arch in front of?
  1. A. Median arcuate ligament → arches in front of the aorta
  2. B. Median arcuate ligament → arches in front of the oesophagus
  3. C. Medial arcuate ligament → arches in front of the aorta
AnswerA. Median arcuate ligament → arches in front of the aorta
The median arcuate ligament joins the right and left crura in the midline and arches in front of the aorta at about T12.
Explanation

The aorta does not pierce the diaphragm: it slips behind the median arcuate ligament, between the crura, and changes from thoracic to abdominal aorta there. That is why the aortic hiatus is described as posterior to the diaphragm, and why contraction of the diaphragm does not squeeze the aorta.

  • The oesophagus passes through the muscular right crus at T10, higher up.
  • The medial arcuate ligaments (one on each side) arch over psoas major; the lateral ones over quadratus lumborum. Neither unites the crura.
Slide (1)
L191Learning
What happens to the central tendon when the diaphragm contracts?
  1. A. The peripheral muscle pushes it up, increasing the vertical diameter of the thorax
  2. B. The peripheral muscle pulls it down, increasing the vertical diameter of the thorax
  3. C. It stays fixed while only the costal margins move
AnswerB. The peripheral muscle pulls it down, increasing the vertical diameter of the thorax
Contracting peripheral fibres pull the central tendon down, the domes flatten and the vertical diameter of the thorax increases: the diaphragm is the main muscle of inspiration.
Explanation

As the muscle round the periphery shortens, the central tendon descends, the domes flatten and the abdominal viscera are pressed down. Thoracic volume rises, intrapleural and alveolar pressures fall below atmospheric, and air flows in. In relaxation (quiet expiration) the domes rise again.

  • A muscle can only pull; contraction cannot push the tendon up.
  • The tendon does not stay fixed: its descent is the main inspiratory movement.
Slides (2)
L192Learning
Where is the caval opening of the diaphragm, and at what vertebral level?
  1. A. In the central tendon → T8
  2. B. In the right crus → T10
  3. C. Behind the diaphragm → T12
AnswerA. In the central tendon → T8
The caval opening pierces the central tendon at T8; the tendon holds it open, so inspiration does not squeeze the inferior vena cava.
Explanation

Mnemonic: 'I (IVC) ate (8) ten (10) eggs (oesophagus) at (aorta) twelve (12)'. The caval opening is the highest of the three, just right of the midline, in tendon, so contraction of the diaphragm tends to widen rather than close it, helping venous return.

  • Right crus at T10 is the oesophageal hiatus.
  • Behind the diaphragm at T12 is the aortic hiatus.
Slides (2)
L193Learning
What passes through the caval opening?
  1. A. Inferior vena cava
    Right phrenic nerve
    Lymphatic vessels
  2. B. Inferior vena cava
    Left phrenic nerve
    Thoracic duct
  3. C. Inferior vena cava
    Right vagus nerve
    Azygos vein
AnswerA. Inferior vena cava
Right phrenic nerve
Lymphatic vessels
The caval opening (T8) transmits the inferior vena cava, the right phrenic nerve and lymphatic vessels.
Explanation

The right phrenic nerve runs down on the inferior vena cava and passes through the caval opening to supply the underside of the right dome. The left phrenic nerve pierces the muscle of the left dome on its own.

  • The thoracic duct passes through the aortic hiatus (T12).
  • The vagal trunks pass through the oesophageal hiatus and the azygos vein through the aortic hiatus.
Slide (1)
L194Learning
Where is the oesophageal hiatus, and at what vertebral level?
  1. A. In the left crus → T10
  2. B. In the central tendon → T8
  3. C. In the right crus → T10
AnswerC. In the right crus → T10
The oesophageal hiatus is a slit in the muscular right crus at T10.
Explanation

Fibres of the right crus loop round the oesophagus, forming a muscular sling that constricts it when the diaphragm contracts (part of the mechanism that resists reflux). An endoscope advanced to the hiatus reaches about the T10 level.

  • The hiatus is formed by the right, larger crus, even though it lies slightly left of the midline.
  • The central tendon at T8 holds the caval opening.
Slides (2)
L195Learning
What passes through the oesophageal hiatus?
  1. A. Oesophagus
    Anterior and posterior vagal trunks
    Thoracic duct
  2. B. Oesophagus
    Right and left phrenic nerves
    Oesophageal branches of the left gastric vessels
  3. C. Oesophagus
    Anterior and posterior vagal trunks
    Oesophageal branches of the left gastric vessels
AnswerC. Oesophagus
Anterior and posterior vagal trunks
Oesophageal branches of the left gastric vessels
The oesophageal hiatus (T10) transmits the oesophagus, the anterior and posterior vagal trunks and oesophageal branches of the left gastric vessels.
Explanation

The vagus nerves form a plexus on the oesophagus and leave the thorax as two trunks on its front and back, so they are at risk in surgery at the hiatus (for example repair of a hiatal hernia). The left gastric artery sends oesophageal branches up through the hiatus to the lower oesophagus.

  • The thoracic duct passes through the aortic hiatus.
  • The phrenic nerves do not use the hiatus: the right goes with the inferior vena cava, the left pierces the left dome.
Slide (1)
L196Learning
Where is the aortic hiatus, and at what vertebral level?
  1. A. Behind the diaphragm, between the crura → L2
  2. B. Behind the diaphragm, between the crura → T12
  3. C. In the central tendon → T8
AnswerB. Behind the diaphragm, between the crura → T12
The aortic hiatus is not a hole in the muscle: the aorta passes behind the diaphragm, under the median arcuate ligament, at T12.
Explanation

Because the aorta runs behind the diaphragm, between the crura and behind the median arcuate ligament, contraction of the diaphragm does not compress it. The azygos vein and the thoracic duct share this route.

  • L2 is too low: by then the aorta is well inside the abdomen.
  • Central tendon at T8 is the caval opening.
Slides (2)
L197Learning
What passes through the aortic hiatus?
  1. A. Aorta
    Azygos vein
    Thoracic duct
  2. B. Aorta
    Inferior vena cava
    Thoracic duct
  3. C. Aorta
    Azygos vein
    Vagal trunks
AnswerA. Aorta
Azygos vein
Thoracic duct
The aortic hiatus (T12) transmits the aorta, the azygos vein and the thoracic duct.
Explanation

All three run up the posterior abdominal wall in front of the vertebral column and slip behind the median arcuate ligament together.

  • The inferior vena cava goes through the central tendon at T8.
  • The vagal trunks go with the oesophagus at T10.
OpeningLevelPasses
Caval (central tendon)T8Inferior vena cava, right phrenic nerve, lymphatics
Oesophageal hiatus (right crus)T10Oesophagus, anterior and posterior vagal trunks, oesophageal branches of left gastric vessels
Aortic hiatus (behind the diaphragm)T12Aorta, azygos vein, thoracic duct
Slide (1)
L198Learning
An aortic aneurysm at the level of the aortic hiatus compresses the structures that share the opening. Which two are at risk?
  1. A. Oesophagus and vagal trunks
  2. B. Inferior vena cava and right phrenic nerve
  3. C. Azygos vein and thoracic duct
AnswerC. Azygos vein and thoracic duct
The aorta shares the aortic hiatus (T12) with the azygos vein and the thoracic duct, so an aneurysm there can compress both.
Explanation

Work it out from the opening: aortic hiatus = T12 = aorta, azygos vein, thoracic duct. Compressing the thoracic duct obstructs the return of lymph; compressing the azygos vein obstructs venous return from the posterior wall.

  • The oesophagus and vagal trunks pass at T10, through the right crus.
  • The inferior vena cava and right phrenic nerve pass at T8, through the central tendon.
Slides (2)
L199Learning
Why does contraction of the diaphragm constrict the oesophagus but not the aorta?
  1. A. Muscle of the right crus surrounds the oesophageal hiatus; the aorta passes behind the diaphragm
  2. B. Muscle of the left crus surrounds the oesophageal hiatus; the aorta passes through the central tendon
  3. C. Muscle of the right crus surrounds the aortic hiatus; the oesophagus passes through the central tendon
AnswerA. Muscle of the right crus surrounds the oesophageal hiatus; the aorta passes behind the diaphragm
The oesophagus passes through muscle (right crus) and is squeezed; the aorta passes behind the diaphragm and is not; the inferior vena cava passes through tendon and is held open.
Explanation

The wall of each opening decides what happens in inspiration. The muscular oesophageal hiatus acts like a pinchcock, helping prevent gastric reflux. The aortic hiatus is a gap behind the median arcuate ligament, so aortic flow is unaffected. The caval opening in the central tendon is pulled open, aiding venous return.

  • The hiatus is formed by the right crus, and the aorta does not pierce the central tendon.
  • The aortic hiatus is not ringed by crural muscle, and the oesophagus does not pass through tendon.
Slides (2)

Diaphragm: nerves, breathing and clinical

L200Learning
Which nerve supplies the diaphragm, and from which spinal levels?
  1. A. Phrenic nerve → C5, C6, C7
  2. B. Phrenic nerve → C3, C4, C5
  3. C. Lower intercostal nerves → T7–T11
AnswerB. Phrenic nerve → C3, C4, C5
The phrenic nerve (C3–C5) is the diaphragm's motor nerve: 'C3, 4 and 5 keep the diaphragm alive'.
Explanation

Each phrenic nerve arises in the neck from the anterior rami of C3–C5 (mainly C4), descends on anterior scalene, enters the thorax through the inlet, passes in front of the lung root and reaches the diaphragm. A cord injury above C3–C5 paralyses the diaphragm; one below C5 spares it.

  • C5–C7 are the roots of the long thoracic nerve to serratus anterior.
  • The lower intercostal nerves carry only sensation from the periphery of the diaphragm; they give it no motor fibres.
Slide (1)
L201Learning
Why does the nerve to the diaphragm arise so high, in the neck?
  1. A. The diaphragm forms in the abdomen, and its nerve grows upward to reach the cervical cord
  2. B. The diaphragm starts development at cervical levels and descends, taking its nerve with it
  3. C. The nerve must first pass through the brachial plexus to collect its motor fibres
AnswerB. The diaphragm starts development at cervical levels and descends, taking its nerve with it
The diaphragm begins at cervical levels (septum transversum opposite C3–C5) and descends during development, dragging the phrenic nerve with it.
Explanation

Early in development the septum transversum, which forms the central tendon, lies opposite the upper cervical segments, and the diaphragm's muscle receives its nerve supply from C3–C5 there. As the heart and lungs grow and the body elongates, the diaphragm descends to its adult position and pulls the nerves down with it, which explains their long course through the neck and thorax.

  • The nerve does not grow upward: its cord segments are fixed in the neck from the start.
  • The phrenic nerve is separate from the brachial plexus; it is not a branch of it.
Slide (1)
L202Learning
What does the phrenic nerve supply in the diaphragm?
  1. A. Motor to the whole diaphragm
    Sensory to its central part
  2. B. Motor to the whole diaphragm
    Sensory to its periphery only
  3. C. Motor to its central part only
    Sensory to the whole diaphragm
AnswerA. Motor to the whole diaphragm
Sensory to its central part
The phrenic nerve is motor to the entire diaphragm (its only motor supply) and sensory to its central part; the periphery's sensation goes in the lower intercostal nerves.
Explanation

Each phrenic nerve supplies all the muscle of its own half; the two halves are innervated separately. Its sensory fibres carry pain and proprioception from the central tendon area, including the overlying pleura and underlying peritoneum, and it also supplies the mediastinal pleura. Sensation from the peripheral (costal) diaphragm is carried by the lower five intercostal nerves.

  • Sensory to the periphery is the job of the intercostal nerves.
  • The phrenic is motor to all of the muscle, not just the centre (which is tendon).
Slide (1)
L203Learning
Which nerves carry sensation from the periphery of the diaphragm?
  1. A. Phrenic nerves
  2. B. Lower five intercostal nerves
  3. C. Greater splanchnic nerves
AnswerB. Lower five intercostal nerves
The lower five intercostal nerves carry sensation from the peripheral diaphragm; they give it no motor supply.
Explanation

The peripheral, costal part of the diaphragm is attached to the lower ribs and cartilages, the territory of the lower intercostal nerves, which carry its pain fibres (and those of the pleura above and peritoneum below it). The lecture says the lower five intercostal nerves; Moore gives the lower six or seven intercostal nerves plus the subcostal nerve.

  • The phrenic nerve is sensory to the central part.
  • The greater splanchnic nerves are visceral (sympathetic) nerves to the abdominal organs that merely pierce the crura.
Slide (1)
L204Learning
Where is pain referred from irritation of the central versus the peripheral diaphragm?
  1. A. Central → the shoulder region
    Periphery → skin over the costal margin
  2. B. Central → skin over the costal margin
    Periphery → the shoulder region
  3. C. Central → the epigastrium
    Periphery → the shoulder region
AnswerA. Central → the shoulder region
Periphery → skin over the costal margin
Central irritation → shoulder (phrenic nerve, C3–C5); peripheral irritation → skin over the costal margin (lower intercostal nerves).
Explanation

Referred pain is felt in the skin supplied by the same spinal segments as the irritated structure. Central diaphragmatic pain travels in the phrenic nerve to C3–C5; the skin of the shoulder (supraclavicular nerves, C3–C4) shares those segments, so the pain is felt there. Peripheral diaphragmatic pain travels in the lower intercostal nerves, which also supply the skin of the lower chest and costal margin.

  • Swapping the two reverses the nerves.
  • The epigastrium is not where central diaphragmatic pain is referred.
Slide (1)
L205Learning
Which muscles act in quiet inspiration?
  1. A. Diaphragm and external intercostals
  2. B. Diaphragm and internal intercostals
  3. C. Diaphragm and abdominal wall muscles
AnswerA. Diaphragm and external intercostals
Quiet inspiration uses the diaphragm (main muscle) and the external intercostals; accessory muscles join only in forced breathing.
Explanation

The diaphragm descends (vertical diameter) and the external intercostals raise the ribs (pump handle above, bucket handle below), so all three diameters of the thorax increase, intrathoracic pressure falls and air flows in.

  • The internal intercostals (interosseous part) depress the ribs and are expiratory; the lecture gives their interchondral part a rib-raising role only in forced breathing.
  • The abdominal wall muscles push the diaphragm up in forced expiration; in quiet inspiration they relax.
Slide (1)
L206Learning
According to the lecture, what produces quiet expiration?
  1. A. Active diaphragm contraction, plus external intercostal contraction
  2. B. Passive lung recoil and diaphragm relaxation, plus internal intercostal contraction
  3. C. Abdominal wall muscle contraction, plus external intercostal contraction
AnswerB. Passive lung recoil and diaphragm relaxation, plus internal intercostal contraction
Quiet expiration is mainly passive: the lungs recoil and the diaphragm relaxes; the lecture adds the internal intercostals.
Explanation

Once the inspiratory muscles relax, the elastic recoil of the stretched lungs and chest wall shrinks the thorax, alveolar pressure rises above atmospheric and air flows out; no muscle work is essential. The lecture slide adds contraction of the internal intercostals, but the TA review and most textbooks treat quiet expiration as purely passive and bring in the internal intercostals and abdominal muscles only in forced expiration. An answer of 'elastic recoil' alone is also right.

  • The diaphragm contracts in inspiration, not expiration.
  • The abdominal muscles drive forced, not quiet, expiration.

The updated 2026 lecture describes quiet expiration as passive (muscle relaxation plus elastic recoil of the lungs), with no internal intercostal contraction, as most textbooks do.

Slide (1)
L207Learning
Which accessory muscles join the diaphragm and external intercostals in forced inspiration?
  1. A. Pectoralis major and minor, serratus anterior, scalenes
  2. B. Internal intercostals, rectus abdominis, internal obliques
  3. C. Transversus thoracis, subcostals, serratus posterior inferior
AnswerA. Pectoralis major and minor, serratus anterior, scalenes
In forced inspiration the pectoralis major and minor, serratus anterior and scalenes help lift the ribs and sternum.
Explanation

These upper limb and neck muscles normally move the arm or neck, but with the arms or head fixed they can pull up on the ribs, as in a breathless patient leaning on a table. The scalenes raise the 1st and 2nd ribs, and sternocleidomastoid raises the sternum. Visible use of accessory muscles is a sign of respiratory distress.

  • Internal intercostals, rectus abdominis and obliques are expiratory: they pull the ribs down or push the diaphragm up.
  • Transversus thoracis, subcostals and serratus posterior inferior depress the ribs, if anything.
Slides (2)
L208Learning
According to the lecture, how do the scalene muscles assist breathing?
  1. A. They depress the 1st and 2nd ribs, so the intercostal muscles can pull the lower ribs down
  2. B. They fix the 11th and 12th ribs, so the intercostal muscles can pull the lower ribs down
  3. C. They fix the 1st and 2nd ribs, so the intercostal muscles can lift the ribs below them
AnswerC. They fix the 1st and 2nd ribs, so the intercostal muscles can lift the ribs below them
The scalenes act as fixators: holding the 1st and 2nd ribs steady gives the intercostals a fixed top from which to lift the ribs below.
Explanation

A muscle moves one bone only if the other is held still. The intercostals run from rib to rib, so to raise the cage they need a stable top rib to pull from. The scalenes, running from the cervical vertebrae down to the 1st and 2nd ribs, anchor those ribs (and raise them in deep breaths). The lecture sorts the accessory muscles by job: elevators (pectoralis major, pectoralis minor, serratus anterior) lift the ribs when the arms are fixed; fixators (scalenes) steady the top of the cage; serratus posterior superior and inferior are mainly proprioceptive.

  • The scalenes attach above the ribs and pull upward; they cannot depress the upper ribs.
  • The scalenes end on the 1st and 2nd ribs and never reach the 11th and 12th ribs.
Slide (1)
L209Learning
Which muscles drive forced expiration?
  1. A. Scalenes and sternocleidomastoid
  2. B. Diaphragm and external intercostals
  3. C. Muscles of the abdominal wall
AnswerC. Muscles of the abdominal wall
Forced expiration (coughing, blowing out candles) is driven by the abdominal wall muscles, which push the viscera and diaphragm up; the internal intercostals help.
Explanation

Contracting rectus abdominis, the obliques and transversus abdominis raise intra-abdominal pressure, forcing the relaxed diaphragm up into the thorax and pulling the lower ribs down, so air is expelled quickly. The internal intercostals (interosseous part) assist by depressing the ribs.

  • Scalenes and sternocleidomastoid are accessory muscles of inspiration.
  • The diaphragm and external intercostals are the muscles of inspiration.
InspirationExpiration
QuietDiaphragm + external intercostalsPassive lung recoil + diaphragm relaxation (lecture adds internal intercostals)
ForcedAdds pectoralis major and minor, serratus anterior, scalenesAbdominal wall muscles (+ internal intercostals)
Slides (2)
L210Learning
What happens to the diaphragm when one phrenic nerve is cut?
  1. A. That half is paralysed → its dome stays permanently flattened (low) on chest X-ray, and the muscle atrophies
  2. B. That half is paralysed → its dome stays permanently elevated on chest X-ray, and the muscle atrophies
  3. C. That half keeps working → the lower intercostal nerves take over its motor supply
AnswerB. That half is paralysed → its dome stays permanently elevated on chest X-ray, and the muscle atrophies
Each half has its own phrenic nerve; cutting one paralyses that half, whose dome stays elevated (and moves paradoxically), and the muscle atrophies.
Explanation

A paralysed hemidiaphragm cannot contract, so it is pushed up by abdominal pressure and drawn up by the negative intrathoracic pressure produced by the working side: on X-ray it sits permanently high. On fluoroscopy it may even rise during inspiration (paradoxical movement). The other half is unaffected because the two phrenic nerves do not cross over.

  • A low, flat dome is the opposite finding, seen with hyperinflated lungs, not paralysis.
  • The intercostal nerves give the diaphragm only sensory fibres, so they cannot take over its motor supply.
Slide (1)
L211Learning
After a car crash, fluoroscopy shows the right hemidiaphragm rising instead of descending during inspiration, while the left moves normally. Which nerve is injured?
  1. A. Right phrenic nerve
  2. B. Left phrenic nerve
  3. C. Lower five intercostal nerves on the right
AnswerA. Right phrenic nerve
Paradoxical rise of the right hemidiaphragm means loss of its motor supply: the right phrenic nerve.
Explanation

Each hemidiaphragm is supplied only by its own phrenic nerve. When the healthy left side contracts, intrathoracic pressure falls and the paralysed right dome is sucked upward: paradoxical movement. The left phrenic nerve must be intact, because the left side moves normally.

  • A left phrenic injury would paralyse the left side.
  • The lower intercostal nerves are only sensory to the diaphragm, so injuring them causes no paralysis.
Slide (1)
L212Learning
Diaphragmatic paralysis from a phrenic nerve injury changes inspiration mainly in which way?
  1. A. Reduced ability to increase thoracic volume
  2. B. A larger fall in intrapleural pressure
  3. C. Air trapped by a rise in alveolar pressure
AnswerA. Reduced ability to increase thoracic volume
Without the diaphragm the thorax cannot enlarge its vertical diameter, so the patient has a reduced ability to increase thoracic volume and draw air in.
Explanation

Inspiration works by enlarging the thorax: the diaphragm adds vertical diameter, the ribs add anteroposterior and transverse diameter. The larger volume makes intrapleural and alveolar pressures fall below atmospheric, and air flows in. Losing the main muscle of inspiration means a smaller volume change, a smaller pressure drop and less air per breath.

  • Intrapleural pressure falls less, not more, when the diaphragm is paralysed.
  • A rise in alveolar pressure that traps air describes a problem of expiration (airway obstruction), not a weak inspiratory muscle.
Slides (2)
L213Learning
After a complete spinal cord transection at C6, how is breathing affected?
  1. A. The diaphragm is paralysed; the intercostal muscles still work
  2. B. All breathing muscles are paralysed, so the patient needs a ventilator
  3. C. The diaphragm still works; the intercostal muscles are paralysed
AnswerC. The diaphragm still works; the intercostal muscles are paralysed
The phrenic nerve (C3–C5) arises above a C6 lesion, so the diaphragm keeps working; the intercostals (T1–T11) are cut off from the brain.
Explanation

Breathing after a high spinal injury depends on whether the C3–C5 segments and their connection to the brainstem survive. At C6 they do, so diaphragmatic breathing continues, although weaker without the intercostal and abdominal muscles, whose motor neurons in the thoracic cord lie below the lesion. A transection above C3 would paralyse the diaphragm too and require a ventilator.

  • The reverse pattern is impossible: the intercostal segments lie below a C6 lesion.
  • Total paralysis of the breathing muscles needs a lesion above C3–C5.
Slides (2)
L214Learning
A patient in respiratory distress shows vigorous rib movements but almost no movement of the abdominal wall with each breath. Which nerves are most likely failing?
  1. A. Phrenic nerves
  2. B. Intercostal nerves
  3. C. Medial and lateral pectoral nerves
AnswerA. Phrenic nerves
Ribs moving but abdomen still means the diaphragm is not descending: the phrenic nerves have failed, and the vertical diameter no longer increases.
Explanation

When the diaphragm contracts it pushes the abdominal viscera down and the abdominal wall out; without it the abdomen hardly moves. Here the intercostal and accessory muscles are working hard (the ribs move vigorously), so their nerves are intact; what is lost is the muscle that increases the vertical dimension of the thorax, supplied by the phrenic nerves. A demyelinating neuropathy such as Guillain–Barré syndrome can do this.

  • Failing intercostal nerves would stop the rib movements (pump handle and bucket handle).
  • The pectoral nerves supply accessory muscles only; their loss would not stop the diaphragm.
Slides (2)
L215Learning
A man with inflammation of the pleura over the central part of the diaphragm feels sharp pain radiating to his right shoulder. Which nerve carries this pain?
  1. A. Intercostal nerves
  2. B. Vagus nerve
  3. C. Phrenic nerve
AnswerC. Phrenic nerve
Pleura over the central diaphragm is supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3–C5), so its pain is referred to the shoulder.
Explanation

The diaphragmatic pleura over the central tendon and the mediastinal pleura are supplied by the phrenic nerve. Its sensory fibres enter the cord at C3–C5, the segments that also supply the skin of the shoulder, so the pain is felt at the shoulder tip. The same happens when the underside of the central diaphragm is irritated from below, for example by a liver abscess, an inflamed gallbladder or blood from a ruptured spleen.

  • The intercostal nerves supply the costal pleura and the peripheral diaphragm; their pain is felt on the chest wall and costal margin.
  • The vagus nerve does not carry somatic pain from the pleura.
Slides (2)
L216Learning
How can the diaphragm herniate?
  1. A. Only through a rupture (most after minor coughing)
  2. B. Congenitally, or through a rupture (most after major trauma)
  3. C. Only congenitally, never through a rupture
AnswerB. Congenitally, or through a rupture (most after major trauma)
A diaphragmatic hernia can be congenital (a developmental defect) or follow a rupture, usually from major trauma.
Explanation

Congenital diaphragmatic hernia results from failure of the left pleuroperitoneal membrane to close, leaving a posterolateral defect; abdominal organs enter the thorax and compress the developing lung. Traumatic hernias follow a tear of the diaphragm from severe blunt trauma (a sudden rise in abdominal pressure, as in a steering-wheel injury), penetrating wounds or fractures of the lower ribs.

  • Minor coughing does not rupture a normal diaphragm.
  • Ruptures certainly happen: they are the usual acquired cause.
Slide (1)
L217Learning
On which side do most traumatic ruptures of the diaphragm occur, and why?
  1. A. Right → the liver makes the right dome rigid and brittle
  2. B. Left → the heart weakens the left dome
  3. C. Left → the liver buttresses the right dome
AnswerC. Left → the liver buttresses the right dome
Most traumatic ruptures are left-sided: the bulky liver lies under the right dome and protects it.
Explanation

The lecture states that most ruptures occur on the left after major trauma. The usual explanation (Moore) is that the liver lies against the right dome and absorbs and spreads the force, so the left dome, over the more mobile stomach and spleen, gives way more often.

  • The liver protects the right side; it does not make the dome brittle.
  • The heart rests on the central tendon and does not weaken the left dome.
Slides (2)
L218Learning
According to the lecture, which organs may herniate into the thorax through a diaphragmatic rupture?
  1. A. Stomach, small intestine, transverse colon and left kidney
  2. B. Stomach, pancreas, descending colon and liver
  3. C. Stomach, small intestine, transverse colon and spleen
AnswerC. Stomach, small intestine, transverse colon and spleen
Through a (usually left) diaphragmatic defect the stomach, small intestine, transverse colon and spleen can enter the chest.
Explanation

Mobile organs under the left dome slip through the tear: the stomach, loops of small bowel, the transverse colon and the spleen. Signs include bowel sounds over the chest, reduced breath sounds and a shift of the mediastinum away from the hernia.

  • The kidneys and pancreas are retroperitoneal and fixed, so they do not herniate this way.
  • The descending colon is also fixed to the posterior wall, and the liver lies under the right dome, the side that usually holds.
Slide (1)
L219Learning
After her abdomen strikes the steering wheel, a woman is breathless; breath sounds are absent over the left chest, bowel sounds are heard there, and the mediastinum is shifted to the right. What is the most likely diagnosis?
  1. A. Left tension pneumothorax
  2. B. Traumatic diaphragmatic hernia
  3. C. Left haemothorax
AnswerB. Traumatic diaphragmatic hernia
Bowel sounds in the chest after blunt abdominal trauma mean gut has herniated through a ruptured left hemidiaphragm.
Explanation

A sudden rise in abdominal pressure (a steering-wheel blow) can tear the diaphragm, usually on the left. Stomach and bowel move into the left chest, compress the lung (absent breath sounds) and push the mediastinum to the right. The decisive clue is bowel sounds over the thorax.

  • A tension pneumothorax also silences the lung and shifts the mediastinum, but air gives a hyperresonant chest, not bowel sounds.
  • A haemothorax gives dullness and absent breath sounds, but no bowel sounds.

The thoracic wall is innervated by:
  1. A. Dorsal primary rami
  2. B. Intercostal nerves
  3. C. Lateral pectoral nerves
  4. D. Medial pectoral nerves
  5. E. Thoracodorsal nerves
AnswerB. Intercostal nerves
Explanation from the source
Intercostal nerves are the ventral primary rami of spinal nerves T1-T11. They provide motor innervation to intercostal muscles, abdominal wall muscles (via T7-T11) and muscles of the forearm and hand (via T1). They provide sensory innervation to the skin of the chest and abdomen on the anterior and lateral sides. The other nerves listed do not innervate the chest wall. Dorsal primary rami provide motor innervation to true back muscles and sensory innervation to the skin on the back. The lateral pectoral nerve provides motor innervation to pectoralis major only, while the medial pectoral nerve provides motor innervation to pectoralis major and minor. The thoracodorsal nerve provides motor innervation to latissimus dors

The tubercle of the 7th rib articulates with which structure?
  1. A. Body of vertebra T6
  2. B. Body of vertebra T7
  3. C. Body of vertebra T8
  4. D. Transverse process of vertebra T6
  5. E. Transverse process of vertebra T7
AnswerE. Transverse process of vertebra T7
Explanation from the source
The tubercle of a rib is a projection located posteroinferior and lateral to the neck of the rib. It articulates with the transverse process of the vertebra of the same number. So, the tubercle of rib 7 should articulate with the transverse process of the T7 vertebra. The head of the rib is the part of the rib that articulates with the demifacets of two adjacent vertebral bodies. So, the head of rib 7 should articulate with the 6th vertebra superiorly and the 7th vertebra inferiorly

A 24-year-old patient suffered a lower back strain after a severe fall while skiing. MRI studies reveal injury to the muscles responsible for extending and laterally bending the trunk. What arteries provide blood supply for these muscles?
  1. A. Subscapular

  3. C. Anterior intercostal
  4. D. Suprascapular
  5. E. Posterior intercostal
AnswerE. Posterior intercostal
Explanation from the source
E. Posterior intercostal arteries supply the deep back muscles, which are responsible for extending and laterally bending the trunk. The subscapular artery supplies the subscapularis muscle, the thoracodorsal artery supplies the latissimus dorsi, the anterior intercostal supplies the upper nine intercostal spaces, and the suprascapular artery supplies the supraspinatus and infraspinatus muscles. These muscles are not responsible for extension and lateral flexion of the trunk.
Answer is the posterior intercostal arteries (ANAT-2 thoracic-wall arteries), but the target is the deep back muscles (Foundations back unit).

A 38-year-old man is admitted to the emergency department after a car collision. During physical examination several lacerations to the back are discovered. Pain from lacerations or irritations of the skin of the back is conveyed to the central nervous system by which of the following?
  1. A. Dorsal primary rami
  2. B. B. Communicating rami
  3. C. C. Ventral primary rami
  4. D. D. Ventral roots
  5. E. E. Intercostal nerves
AnswerA. Dorsal primary rami
Explanation from the source
A. General somatic afferent fibers are conveyed from the skin of the back via the dorsal primary rami. Communicating rami contain general visceral efferent (sympathetic) fibers and general visceral afferent fibers of the autonomic nervous system. Ventral primary rami convey mixed spinal nerves to/from all other parts of the body excluding the back, and parts of the head innervated by cranial nerves. The ventral roots contain only efferent (motor) fibers. Intercostal nerves are the ventral rami of T1 to T11. The ventral ramus of T12 is the subcostal nerve.
Back skin is supplied by posterior (dorsal) rami — stated on the CP1 thoracic-wall innervation slide; the question itself is set in the back (Foundations) unit.

A 65-year-old woman who has been otherwise well presents to her physician with complaints of a group of painful blisters over her back in the distribution of the T9 dermatome. She noticed that a few days prior to the eruption of the blisters she experienced an intense burning sensation over her skin. She was diagnosed with herpes zoster (shingles). Where are the neural cell bodies located that are responsible for the pain sensation?
  1. A. Dorsal horn
  2. B. Lateral horn
  3. C. Dorsal root ganglia
  4. D. Sympathetic chain ganglia
  5. E. White rami communicans
AnswerC. Dorsal root ganglia
Explanation from the source
C. Somatic afferent fibers convey localized pain, typically from the body wall and limbs and the cell bodies are found in the dorsal root ganglia. The dorsal horn is found at all spinal cord levels and is comprised of sensory nuclei that receive and process incoming somatosensory information. The lateral horn comprises autonomic neurons innervating visceral and pelvic organs. The sympathetic chain ganglia deliver the sympathetic information to the body. White rami communicans carry preganglionic sympathetic fibers and are called white because the fibers it contains are myelinated.

A 35-year-old man pedestrian is crossing a busy intersection and is hit by a truck. He is admitted to the emergency department, and a CT scan reveals a dislocation of the fourth thoracic vertebra. Which of the following costal structures is most likely also involved in the injury?

AnswerE. Head of the fifth rib
Explanation from the source
E. The T4 thoracic vertebra articulates with the head of the fifth rib. The head of the rib has two facets. The rib articulates with the superior facet on the body of its own vertebra (the fourth rib articulates with the superior facet T4 vertebra) and with the inferior facet on the body of the vertebra above (the fourth rib articulates with the inferior facet of T3 vertebra). Taking the T4 vertebra into consideration, the superior facet of this vertebra articulates with the head of the fourth rib and the inferior facet articulates with the head of the fifth rib. The head of the fourth rib has two points of articulation (a joint with the vertebral body and a costotransverse joint) on T4, so when it is injured it moves as a unit, whereas the fifth rib has only one articulation with T4. Which structures were most likely damaged to result in these signs?

  2. B. Ventral roots
  3. C. Cutaneous branches of dorsal rami
  4. D. Cutaneous branches of ventral rami
  5. E. Rami communicans
AnswerD. Cutaneous branches of ventral rami
Explanation from the source
D. Ventral rami contain both sensory and motor fibers and also sympathetics to the body wall, supplying all areas of the body wall except for tissues of the back. In this case both sensory fibers (numbness) and sympathetics (anhydrosis) are disrupted at the midaxillary line; therefore, cutaneous ventral rami is the only correct choice. The dorsal roots carry somatic and visceral sensory information from the periphery. Because only cutaneous sensation is lost the deficit cannot be the dorsal roots. The ventral roots of the spinal cord carry only somatic and visceral efferents. Because no motor functions are disrupted, this is not the correct answer. The branches of dorsal rami provide cutaneous and postural muscle innervation to the back and thus have no relation to the midaxillary line. The rami communicans are components of the sympathetic nervous system and are not involved with general somatic afferent sensation. GAS 60-61; N 188; McM 182

A 34-year-old man with a complaint of sharp, localized pain over the thoracic wall is diagnosed with pleural effusion. A chest tube is inserted to drain the effusion through an intercostal space. Where should the chest tube be inserted?
  1. A. Just superior to the upper border of the rib
  2. B. Just inferior to the lower border of the rib
  3. C. At the middle of the intercostal space
  4. D. Between the internal and external intercostal muscles
  5. E. Between the intercostal muscles and the posterior intercostal membrane
AnswerA. Just superior to the upper border of the rib
Explanation from the source
A. By placing a chest tube just superior to the upper border of the rib, the important neurovascular bundle is avoided. The bundle consists of intercostal vein, artery, and nerve running through the superior portion of the intercostal space. In each space, the vein is the most superior structure and is highest in the costal groove. The artery is inferior to the vein and the nerve is inferior to the artery and may not be protected by the costal groove on the lower border of the rib. Entrance through the middle of the space does not remove the possibility of damaging the neurovascular bundle. Neither passage between the internal and external intercostal muscles, nor between the intercostal muscles and the posterior intercostal membrane would allow entry to the pleural cavity. A 49-year-old woman who had suffered a myocardial infarction must undergo a bypass graft procedure using the internal thoracic artery. Which vessels will most likely continue to supply blood to the anterior part of the upper intercostal spaces?

  5. E. Thoracodorsal

Explanation from the source
C. The anterior intercostal arteries are twelve small arteries, two in each of the upper six intercostal spaces at the upper and lower borders. The upper artery lying in each space anastomoses with the posterior intercostal arteries, whereas the lower one usually joins the collateral branch of the posterior intercostal artery. The musculophrenic artery is a terminal branch of the internal thoracic artery (also known as the internal mammary artery), and it supplies the pericardium, diaphragm, and muscles of the abdominal wall. It anastomoses with the deep circumflex iliac artery. The superior epigastric artery is the other terminal branch of the internal thoracic artery, and it supplies the diaphragm, peritoneum, and the anterior abdominal wall and anastomoses with the inferior epigastric artery. The lateral thoracic artery runs along the lateral border of the pectoralis minor muscle and supplies the pectoralis major, pectoralis minor, and serratus anterior. The thoracodorsal artery accompanies the thoracodorsal nerve in supplying the latissimus dorsi muscle and lateral thoracic wall. GAS 155; N 188; McM 183

A 17-year-old girl has suffered from a painful discoloration of her hand for the past year. A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan revealed “thoracic outlet” syndrome. Which symptom would most likely result from this syndrome?

AnswerD. Numbness in the upper limb
Explanation from the source
D. Thoracic outlet syndrome is characterized by the presence of a cervical rib, accessory muscles, or connective tissue bands that constrict the limited dimensions of the thoracic outlet. The cervical rib is usually located on the C7 vertebra and can impinge on the brachial plexus, resulting in loss of some feeling to the upper limb. There would be no impingement on the phrenic nerve because it leaves C3 to C5 directly parallel with the vertebral column. The syndrome does not include reduction of blood flow to the thoracic wall because of extensive anastomoses between the vessels that supply blood to the anterior thoracic wall. Venous return from the head and neck is mainly through the internal jugular vein and would not be affected because of this vein’s location near the midline of the body; thus, it would not be occluded or distended. AnswerD. Numbness in the upper extremity
Explanation from the source

Obstruction actually occurs outside the aperture in the root of the neck, and the manifestations of the syndromes involve the upper limb through this aperture. A supernumerary (extra cervical) rib or a fibrous connection extending from its tip to the first thoracic rib may elevate and place pressure on structures that emerge from the superior thoracic aperture, notably the subclavian artery or inferior trunk of the brachial plexus, and may cause symptoms. Other etiologies could include an elongated transverse process of the C7 vertebra and muscular abnormalities (e.g., in the scalenus anterior muscle, a sickle-shaped scalenus medius). Most common symptoms include discoloration of the hands, one hand colder than the other hand, weakness of the hand and arm muscles, and tingling. GAS 31-33; N 109-112; McM 69-72

251High-yield
A 22-year-old woman visits the outpatient clinic with pain in her left upper limb. She has a long history of pain in this limb and difficulty with fine motor tasks of the hand. Physical examination reveals paraesthesia along the medial surface of the forearm and palm and weakness and atrophy of gripping muscles (“long flexors”) and the intrinsic muscles of the hand. The radial pulse is diminished when her neck is rotated to the ipsilateral side (positive Adson’s test). What is the most likely diagnosis?
  1. A. Erb-Duchenne paralysis
  2. B. Aneurysm of the brachiocephalic artery, with plexus compression
  3. C. Thoracic outlet syndrome
  4. D. Carpal tunnel syndrome
  5. E. Injury to the medial cord of the brachial plexus
AnswerC. Thoracic outlet syndrome
Explanation from the source
C. The patient is suffering from thoracic outlet syndrome, involving neural and vascular elements. This results from any condition that decreases the dimensions of the superior thoracic aperture (the formal name of the thoracic outlet). It could be a result of a cervical rib, accessory muscles, and/or atypical connective tissue bands at the root of the neck. In this case, symptoms involve the arm, forearm, and hand. Paraesthesia along the medial forearm and hand and atrophy of long flexors and intrinsic muscles point to a possible compression or traction problem of the lower trunk (C8, T1) rather than a lesion of either the median or ulnar nerve. The lateral palm has no sensory problem, which tends to rule out median nerve involvement. Changes in the radial artery pulse point to vascular compression. Erb-Duchenne paralysis of the upper trunk would affect proximal limb functions, such as arm rotation, abduction, and so on. This lesion is on the left side, so the brachiocephalic artery could not be involved because it arises from the right side of the aortic arch; moreover, it would not compress the brachial plexus. Carpal tunnel syndrome would not explain the problems of the forearm and medial hand, or the long flexor atrophy. An isolated medial cord lesion would not explain the atrophy of all long flexors and intrinsic muscles and does not explain the radial pulse characteristics. The ischemic pain in the arm is due to vascular compression.
Slides (2)
252
A 32-year-old man who is an expert target shooter reports pain in his right upper limb and slight tingling and numbness of all digits of the ipsilateral hand. However, the tingling and numbness of the fourth and fifth digits is the most severe. The man states that the problem usually occurs when he is firing his gun with his hand overhead. Radiographic studies reveal the presence of a cervical rib and accessory scalene musculature. Which of the following structures is most likely being compressed?
  1. A. Axillary artery
  2. B. Upper trunk of brachial plexus
  3. C. Subclavian artery
  4. D. Lower trunk of brachial plexus
  5. E. Brachiocephalic artery and lower trunk of brachial plexus
AnswerD. Lower trunk of brachial plexus
Explanation from the source
D. A cervical rib (usually found at C7) may cause thoracic outlet syndrome, which is a condition characterized by weak muscle tone in the hand and loss of radial pulse when the upper limb is abducted above the shoulder. The mechanism of injury with the gun being fired overhead suggests a lower trunk injury to the brachial plexus. The axillary artery supplies the shoulder muscles, and there is no loss of function to these muscles. The upper trunk of the brachial plexus also supplies innervation to the shoulder muscles, which are unaffected based on the patient’s presenting abnormalities. The subclavian artery is located anterior to the brachial plexus until the plexus separates into cords as it passes under the clavicle. The brachiocephalic artery and lower trunk of the brachial plexus is only partially correct; the brachiocephalic artery is not directly associated with the brachial plexus due to its location at the midline of the body behind the sternum.

D. In thoracic outlet syndrome—sometimes caused by a cervical rib or a cervical band—ventral rami or trunks of the brachial plexus can be compressed by these structures as they travel from the neck to the axilla. In this case the inferior trunk of the brachial plexus is being compressed by a cervical rib. The anterior division of the inferior trunk continues as the medial cord of the brachial plexus. The medial brachial cutaneous nerve (medial cutaneous nerve of the arm) and medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve (medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm) are branches of the medial cord of the plexus, with the ulnar nerve as its terminal branch. Additionally, there is medial cord contribution to the median nerve. Compression of the inferior cord of the brachial plexus therefore presents with numbness and paraesthesia on the medial part of the arm, forearm, and hand.

22. A 77-year-old man presents with shingles on his anterolateral abdomen and umbilicus, as shown in the figure. Shingles (or herpes zoster) is caused by the varicella zoster virus, which resides latent in sensory ganglia in the body for many years. When a patient is immunocompromised, this virus can cause a painful skin rash called shingles, which usually presents unilaterally along the infected nerve’s dermatome distribution. Given the location of the rash, what ganglion is most likely affected in this patient?
  1. (A) Paravertebral ganglion
  2. (B) Prevertebral ganglion
  3. (C) Lumbar ganglion
  4. (D) Spinal ganglion of T10
  5. (E) Spinal ganglion of L2
AnswerD. Spinal ganglion of T10
Explanation from the source
The answer is D: Spinal ganglion of T10. In this patient, herpes zoster, or shingles, is a painful skin rash affecting the dermatome distribution pattern of the left 10th thoracic (T10) nerve, as evidenced by the involvement of the umbilicus. Shingles is seen in patients who have had previous exposure to the varicella zoster virus, which causes chickenpox in children or young adults. After the initial exposure to chickenpox, this virus can reside latent in ganglia of an individual for years. If this individual becomes immunocompromised, the skin (or dermatomes supplied by the infected ganglia) can develop shingles, a painful skin rash, which blisters, breaks open, crusts over, and then disappears. In this patient, the herpetic lesions were found in the sensory distribution of the left T10 nerve, which means the virus resides in this nerve’s sensory ganglion, or the spinal ganglion of T10. Remember that two types of ganglia exist: sensory (afferent) and autonomic. The sensory ganglia, which are most often affected by shingles, are equivalent to the spinal (dorsal root) ganglia of spinal nerves in that they house typical pseudounipolar cell bodies of afferent neurons and do not contain synapses. If a spinal ganglion were infected by the varicella zoster virus, shingles may present in its dermatome distribution patterns when the patient is immunocompromised. Choice A (Paravertebral ganglion) is incorrect. The paravertebral (sympathetic) ganglia are located within the sympathetic trunk. They receive efferent ﬁbers from the presynaptic (preganglionic) sympathetic neurons originating in the intermediolateral (IML) cell column of the thoracic and upper lumbar segments (T1-L2). Due to their location, these sympathetic ganglia are called paravertebral ganglia. Before it causes shingles (or herpes zoster), the varicella zoster virus resides latent in sensory ganglia for many years. Because the paravertebral ganglia are autonomic ganglia, it is unlikely they would be responsible for the skin rash in this patient. Choice B (Prevertebral ganglion) is incorrect. The prevertebral ganglia are sympathetic ganglia that receive their name as they are located anterior to the vertebral column, as distinguished from the ganglia of the sympathetic trunk (paravertebral ganglia). Prevertebral ganglia exist near major branches of the abdominal aorta in the abdominopelvic cavity. These ganglia send postsynaptic (postganglionic) sympathetic ﬁbers to the abdominopelvic organs with periarterial plexuses. Before it causes shingles (or herpes zoster), the varicella zoster virus resides latent in sensory ganglia for many years. Because the prevertebral ganglia are autonomic ganglia, it is unlikely they would be responsible for the skin rash in this patient. Choice C (Lumbar ganglion) is incorrect. The lumbar ganglia are paravertebral ganglia located in the abdominopelvic part of the sympathetic trunk. Before it causes shingles (or herpes zoster), the varicella zoster virus resides latent in sensory ganglia for many years. Because the lumbar ganglia are autonomic ganglia, it is unlikely they would be responsible for the skin rash in this patient. Choice E (Spinal ganglion of L2) is incorrect. The spinal (posterior root) ganglion is a sensory ganglion, so it could be infected by the varicella zoster virus and present with a painful, skin rash along its dermatome distribution pattern. The sensory distribution of L2 would extend along the back, hip, and extend into the anterior and medial aspects of the thigh. Because this patient presents with a skin rash at the level of the umbilicus, the spinal ganglion of T10 would be the source of this painful skin rash.

A 56-year-old construction worker comes to his family physician complaining of pain in the neck and shoulder, numbness and tingling in the right fingers, and a weak grip in his right hand. His symptoms are exacerbated by carrying heavy objects on his right shoulder. The given plain X-ray film indicates the presence of a right cervical (C7) rib in close approximation to the proximal part of the first rib. Given the signs and symptoms of this patient, what structure is most likely impinged by the cervical rib?
Show figure
  1. (A) Right common carotid artery
  2. (B) Brachiocephalic trunk
  3. (C) Right subclavian artery
  4. (D) Vertebral artery
  5. (E) Right brachiocephalic vein
AnswerC. Right subclavian artery
Explanation from the source
Right subclavian artery. The right subclavian artery arises off the brachiocephalic trunk (a direct branch off of the arch of the aorta) and runs to the lateral border of the first rib. At this location, the subclavian artery becomes the axillary artery, which continues on to supply the upper limb. The right cervical rib (C7), depicted on the given X-ray, extends inferiorly in close relationship to the first rib. The subclavian artery typically passes over the cervical rib, causing the vessel to take a steeper route. When the shoulder is depressed (e.g., when carrying a heavy load), the subclavian artery may be compressed against the cervical rib, leading to the symptoms present in the patient and resulting in thoracic outlet syndrome. Thoracic outlet syndrome causes pain, numbness, and paresthesia (tingling) in the neck and shoulder as well as the fingers of the hand. Moreover, the poor circulation in the right upper limb, due to the compression of the right subclavian artery, is causing the weakness (paresis) of the muscles of the hand. Choice A (Right common carotid artery) is incorrect. The right common carotid artery arises off the brachiocephalic trunk, which is a direct branch off of the arch of the aorta. The right common carotid artery ascends into the neck to split into the internal and external carotid arteries at the fourth cervical vertebra (C4). However, the common carotid is not closely associated with the first rib, so it will not be compromised by the presence of the right cervical rib (C7). Furthermore, compression of the right common carotid artery would lead to symptoms in the head and neck as well as affect the anterior circulation of the brain. However, the symptoms of this patient were localized to the right upper limb, so the right common carotid artery was not affected. Choice B (Brachiocephalic trunk) is incorrect. The brachiocephalic trunk, a direct branch off the arch of the aorta, gives rise to the right subclavian and common carotid arteries. If this artery were compressed by the right cervical rib (C7), the symptoms of the patient would include head and neck effects due to the involvement of the right common carotid artery. Choice D (Vertebral artery) is incorrect. The vertebral artery is the first branch off the subclavian artery, but this artery ascends through the cervical vertebral column to supply the posterior circulation of the brain. Compression of this artery would not explain the right upper limb symptoms, or the thoracic outlet syndrome, seen in this patient. Choice E (Right brachiocephalic vein) is incorrect. Compression of the right brachiocephalic vein would cause the superficial veins of the neck to become engorged due to the backflow of venous return to the heart. This sign is often seen in patients with congestive heart failure. However, compression of the right brachiocephalic vein would not explain the thoracic outlet syndrome seen in this patient because the right upper limb would still be receiving its arterial supply. Therefore, blockage of this vein would not cause the symptoms seen in this patient.

An anesthesiologist administers an anesthetic solution into the axillary sheath of a 19-year-old college baseball player in preparation for repair of the ulnar collateral ligament of the elbow. After 5 minutes, the patient experiences numbness and paresthesia distal to the middle aspect of the arm; however, the medial aspect of the arm and elbow remain sensitive to pain. What nerve provides sensory innervation to the sensitive area and was not blocked by the anesthetic solution?
  1. (A) Long thoracic nerve
  2. (B) Median nerve
  3. (C) Medial cutaneous nerve of the arm
  4. (D) Intercostobrachial nerve
  5. (E) Ulnar nerve
AnswerD. Intercostobrachial nerve
Explanation from the source
Intercostobrachial nerve. The intercostobrachial nerve is the lateral cutaneous branch of the second intercostal nerve. As its name implies, it leaves the thorax by exiting between the second and third ribs (between the ribs = intercosto-) to supply cutaneous innervation to the axilla and medial aspect of the arm (brachium). In some instances, it may also supply skin distal to the elbow. The anesthetic solution would block all of the distal branches of the brachial plexus residing within the axillary sheath, thus sparing the intercostobrachial nerve. Choice A (Long thoracic nerve) is incorrect. The long thoracic nerve does not have a cutaneous distribution and provides only motor innervation to the serratus anterior. Because the long thoracic nerve arises from the ventral rami of C5-C7, it would not be affected by the anesthetic solution, especially if an occlusive tourniquet was utilized to retain the solution. Such a procedure is used to prevent spread of the anesthetic into the neck where it could affect the phrenic nerve and negatively affect respiration. Choice B (Median nerve) is incorrect. The median nerve does not branch proximal to the elbow, and its sensory distribution is limited to distal to the wrist. Furthermore, this nerve would be blocked by effective administration of the anesthetic reagent. Choice C (Medial cutaneous nerve of the arm) is incorrect. The medial cutaneous nerve of the arm arises from the medial cord of the brachial plexus, and it would be blocked by effective administration of the anesthetic solution into the axillary sheath. This nerve would also provide sensation to the area (medial aspect of the arm) that remains sensitive to pain, but it should be blocked by the drug. Choice E (Ulnar nerve) is incorrect. The ulnar nerve does not branch proximal to the elbow, and its sensory distribution is limited to distal to the wrist. Furthermore, this nerve would be blocked by effective administration of the anesthetic solution.

Typical Ribs - Posterior articulations All typical ribs articulate with the thoracic vertebrae of the same number (n) and the one above it (n-1) Two types of posterior articulations - costotransverse- tubercle of rib and transverse process of the vertebrae - absent in ribs 11& 12 costovertebral- rib head and demifacets of vertebral body

Which of the follow does not attach to rib 1?
  1. A. Anterior scalenes
  2. B. Middle scalenes
  3. C. Posterior scalene

First Rib anterior scalene muscle: scalene tubercle middle scalene muscle: between groove for the subclavian artery and transverse tubercle intercostal muscles: from the outer border subclavius muscle: arises from distal shaft and first costal cartilage first digitation of the serratus anterior muscle parietal pleura: from the inner border costoclavicular ligament: anterior to the groove for the subclavian vein https://radiopaedia.org/articles/first-rib
288Borderline
A 16-year-old patient received a laceration of the posterior intercostal nerves by a penetrated knife blade. A pathologist obtained needle biopsy tissues and observed numerous degenerated cell bodies of the unipolar or pseudounipolar neurons. Which of the following structures would most likely provide the abnormal cell morphology?
  1. (A) Ventral horn of the spinal cord
  2. (B) Lateral horn of the spinal cord
  3. (C) Dorsal horn of the spinal cord
  4. (D) Dorsal root ganglion
  5. (E) Sympathetic chain ganglion
AnswerD. Dorsal root ganglion
Explanation from the source
The answer is D. Ventral, lateral, and dorsal horns and sympathetic chain ganglia contain multipolar neurons, whereas the dorsal root ganglion contains unipolar or pseudounipolar neurons. A laceration of the intercostal nerve injures GSE, postganglionic sympathetic general visceral efferent (GVE), general visceral afferent (GVA), and general somatic afferent (GSA) fibers, whose cell bodies are located in the anterior horn, sympathetic chain ganglia, and dorsal root ganglia.
Intercostal-nerve setting, but the tested fact (pseudounipolar sensory neurons in the dorsal root ganglion) is general neuroanatomy (Foundations).

289
A 33-year-old patient is suffering from a sudden occlusion at the origin of the descending (thoracic) aorta. This condition would most likely decrease blood flow in which of the following intercostal arteries?
  1. (A) Upper six anterior
  2. (B) All of the posterior
  3. (C) Upper two posterior
  4. (D) Lower anterior
  5. (E) Lower six posterior
AnswerE. Lower six posterior
Explanation from the source
The answer is E. The first two posterior intercostal arteries are branches of the highest (superior) intercostal artery of the costocervical trunk; the remaining nine branches are from the thoracic aorta. The internal thoracic artery gives off the upper six anterior intercostal arteries and is divided into the superior epigastric and musculophrenic arteries, which gives off anterior intercostal arteries in the 7th, 8th, and 9th intercostal spaces and ends in the 10th intercostal space where it anastomoses with the deep circumflex iliac artery.

290
A 62-year-old woman who is a heavy smoker has an advanced lung cancer that spread into her right third posterior intercostal space posterior to the midaxillary line. If cancer cells are carried in the venous drainage, they would travel first to which of the following veins?
  1. (A) SVC
  2. (B) Right superior intercostal vein
  3. (C) Right brachiocephalic vein
  4. (D) Azygos vein
  5. (E) Hemiazygos vein
AnswerB. Right superior intercostal vein
Explanation from the source
The answer is B. The superior intercostal vein is formed by the union of the second, third, and fourth posterior intercostal veins and drains into the azygos vein on the right and the brachiocephalic vein on the left. The azygos vein drains into the SVC. The hemiazygos vein usually drains into the azygos vein.

291Borderline
A 37-year-old man is brought to the emergency department complaining of severe chest pain. His angiogram reveals thromboses of both brachiocephalic veins just before entering the superior vena cava. This condition would most likely cause a dilation of which of the following veins?
  1. (A) Azygos
  2. (B) Hemiazygos
  3. (C) Right superior intercostal
  4. (D) Left superior intercostal
  5. (E) Internal thoracic
AnswerD. Left superior intercostal
Explanation from the source
The answer is D. The left superior intercostal vein is formed by the second, third, and fourth posterior intercostal veins and drains into the left brachiocephalic vein. The right superior intercostal vein drains into the azygos vein, which in turn drains into the SVC. The hemiazygos vein drains into the azygos vein, whereas the internal thoracic vein empties into the brachiocephalic vein.
Uses the superior intercostal vein drainage (IN) in a caval-obstruction collateral scenario (CP2).

292
A patient has a small but solid tumor in the mediastinum, which is confined at the level of the sternal angle. Which of the following structures would most likely be found at this level?
  1. (A) Bifurcation of the trachea
  2. (B) Beginning of the ascending aorta
  3. (C) Middle of the aortic arch
  4. (D) Articulation of the third rib with the sternum
  5. (E) Superior border of the superior mediastinum
AnswerA. Bifurcation of the trachea
Explanation from the source
The answer is A. The sternal angle is the junction of the manubrium and the body of the sternum. It is located at the level where the second rib articulates with the sternum, the trachea bifurcates into the right and left bronchi, and the aortic arch begins and ends. It marks the end of the ascending aorta and the beginning of the descending aorta, and it forms the inferior border of the superior mediastinum.

A 37-year-old house painter fell from a ladder and fractured his left third rib and the structures with which it articulated. Which of the following structures would most likely be damaged?
  1. (A) Manubrium of the sternum
  2. (B) Body of the second thoracic vertebra
  3. (C) Spinous process of the third thoracic vertebra
  4. (D) Body of the fourth thoracic vertebra
  5. (E) Transverse process of the second thoracic vertebra
AnswerB. Body of the second thoracic vertebra
Explanation from the source
The answer is B. The third rib articulates with the body of the sternum, bodies of the second and third thoracic vertebrae, and transverse process of the third thoracic vertebra.
