294
A 32-year-old patient has a tension pneumothorax that can be treated with needle aspiration. To avoid an injury of the intercostal neurovascular bundle, the needle may be inserted in which of the following locations?
  1. (A) Above the upper border of the ribs
  2. (B) Deep to the upper border of the ribs
  3. (C) Beneath the lower border of the ribs
  4. (D) Between the external and internal intercostals
  5. (E) Through the transversus thoracis muscle
AnswerA. Above the upper border of the ribs
Explanation from the source
The answer is A. The intercostal veins, arteries, and nerves run in the costal groove beneath the inferior border of the ribs between the internal and innermost layers of muscles. The transversus thoracis muscles are situated in the internal surface of the lower anterior thoracic wall.
Slides (2)
295
A 55-year-old woman presents with ulceration and pain in the skin around and including her right nipple. Her physician correctly identifies the affected area as that of the T4 dermatome. The pain this woman is suffering could be related to which of the following spinal segmental levels?
  1. (A) T3 only
  2. (B) T4 only
  3. (C) T3 and T4
  4. (D) T4 and T5
  5. (E) T3, T4, and T5
AnswerE. T3, T4, and T5
Explanation from the source
The answer is E: T3, T4, and T5. A dermatome is the area of skin innervated by sensory fibers (i.e., by the dorsal root) from a single spinal segment. The classic anatomical dermatome map shown in the illustration indicates a barber-pole-like distribution of discrete bands of cutaneous territories. However, this standard map is somewhat deceiving in that there is actually considerable overlap between the dermatomes supplied by adjacent spinal cord segments. Thus, any one dermatome is actually supplied by three spinal segments: one major supplying segment plus two smaller supplying adjacent segments that overlap with the main segment. Choice A (T3 only) is incorrect. While this spinal segment contributes to the supply of the T4 dermatome (with T4 the major component), it does not account for the entire innervation. Choice B (T4 only) is incorrect. Damage to only the T4 dermatome would be hard to detect due to the overlap of innervation from the T3 and T5 spinal nerves. Choice C (T3 and T4) is incorrect. While this combination of damaged nerves more fully accounts for the supply of the T4 dermatome, it does not account for the entire supply due to the overlap of innervation from T5. Choice D (T4 and T5) is incorrect. While this combination of damaged nerves more fully accounts for the supply of the T4 dermatome, it does not account for the entire supply due to the overlap of innervation from T3.

ANAT-3 Breast

62 questions · 15 high-yield
Learning questions 55

Position and bed

L1Learning
In which layer of the chest wall does the breast lie?
  1. A. Superficial fascia (subcutaneous tissue) → superficial to the pectoral fascia
  2. B. Deep fascia → beneath the pectoral fascia, on the surface of pectoralis major
  3. C. Superficial fascia (subcutaneous tissue) → beneath pectoralis major, on the ribs
AnswerA. Superficial fascia (subcutaneous tissue) → superficial to the pectoral fascia
The mammary gland develops in the subcutaneous tissue (superficial fascia) of the anterior chest wall and rests superficial to the pectoral fascia.
Explanation

The superficial fascia is the fatty subcutaneous layer between the skin and the deep fascia. The breast is a skin appendage that grows within it. The pectoral fascia is the deep fascia that invests pectoralis major; the breast sits on it, separated by the loose retromammary space.

  • Deep to the pectoral fascia would bind the gland to the muscle; normally it slides freely over it, and fixation to the fascia is a sign of cancer invasion.
  • Beneath pectoralis major is the plane of pectoralis minor and the ribs; no gland tissue lies there.
Slides (2)
L2Learning
Which muscles does the breast lie on?
  1. A. Pectoralis minor and the intercostal muscles
  2. B. Pectoralis major and latissimus dorsi
  3. C. Pectoralis major and serratus anterior
AnswerC. Pectoralis major and serratus anterior
The breast lies in the subcutaneous tissue over pectoralis major (medially and above) and serratus anterior (inferolaterally).
Explanation

The bed of the breast is formed by the fascia of pectoralis major (the larger, medial and upper part) and of serratus anterior (the inferolateral part, toward the midaxillary line). The gland is well developed in females and rudimentary in males.

  • Pectoralis minor lies deep to pectoralis major and never touches the breast; the intercostal muscles are deeper still, between the ribs.
  • Latissimus dorsi forms the posterior axillary fold, behind the bed's lateral limit (the midaxillary line).
Slides (2)
L3Learning
What is the extent of the bed of the breast?
  1. A. Midline of sternum → anterior axillary line
    1st → 4th rib
  2. B. Lateral border of sternum → posterior axillary line
    3rd → 8th rib
  3. C. Lateral border of sternum → midaxillary line
    2nd → 6th rib
AnswerC. Lateral border of sternum → midaxillary line
2nd → 6th rib
The breast bed runs from the lateral border of the sternum to the midaxillary line, and vertically from the 2nd to the 6th rib.
Explanation

The bed of the breast is the part of the chest wall the gland rests on. Horizontally it reaches from the lateral sternal border to the midaxillary line (the vertical line from the apex of the axilla, between the anterior and posterior axillary lines). Vertically it spans ribs 2–6.

  • The breast does not cross the sternal midline, and it reaches well below the 4th rib.
  • The posterior axillary line and the 8th rib lie beyond the bed, and the bed starts at the 2nd rib, not the 3rd.

The axillary tail is the only part that extends beyond this bed, toward the axilla.

Slides (2)
L4Learning
What forms the bed of the breast, and in what proportion?
  1. A. ~2/3 pectoralis major and its fascia
    ~1/3 serratus anterior and its fascia
  2. B. ~1/3 pectoralis major and its fascia
    ~2/3 serratus anterior and its fascia
  3. C. ~2/3 pectoralis minor and its fascia
    ~1/3 serratus anterior and its fascia
AnswerA. ~2/3 pectoralis major and its fascia
~1/3 serratus anterior and its fascia
About two-thirds of the breast bed is pectoralis major and its fascia; the remaining one-third is serratus anterior and its fascia.
Explanation

Pectoralis major covers the upper and medial chest, so it carries most of the gland (~2/3). Serratus anterior covers the lateral chest wall on ribs 1–8 and forms the inferolateral third of the bed.

  • The swapped proportions are wrong: the larger, medial part of the breast lies on pectoralis major.
  • Pectoralis minor is deep to pectoralis major and takes no part in the bed.
Slides (2)
L5Learning
What is the axillary process (tail) of the breast?
  1. A. An extension of the inferomedial breast toward the sternum
  2. B. A separate accessory breast lying in the axillary fossa
  3. C. An extension of the superolateral breast toward the axilla
AnswerC. An extension of the superolateral breast toward the axilla
The axillary process (tail of Spence) is a prolongation of the superolateral part of the gland along the edge of pectoralis major toward the axillary fossa.
Explanation

The axillary tail is part of the normal gland, continuous with the superolateral quadrant. It runs along the inferolateral edge of pectoralis major into the axilla, next to the axillary nodes and the long thoracic nerve.

Clinically, it must be palpated in every breast examination; it adds glandular tissue to the superolateral quadrant, the site of most cancers.

  • No part of the gland extends toward the sternum: the bed stops at the lateral sternal border.
  • An accessory breast in the axilla is a separate structure on the milk line, not the axillary process.
Slides (2)
L6Learning
What is the retromammary space, and what does it allow?
  1. A. Loose plane between pectoralis major and pectoralis minor → lets the two muscles slide on each other
  2. B. Potential space between the skin and the breast → lets the skin move over the gland
  3. C. Potential space between the breast and the pectoral fascia → lets the breast move on the chest wall
AnswerC. Potential space between the breast and the pectoral fascia → lets the breast move on the chest wall
The retromammary space (bursa) is a potential space of loose connective tissue between the gland and the pectoral fascia; it lets the breast move.
Explanation

A potential space is a plane of loose tissue whose walls normally touch but can be separated. Behind the gland, this loose, almost fat-free layer lets the breast glide over pectoralis major.

It matters clinically: a simple mastectomy removes the breast down to this plane, and a tumour that crosses it into the pectoral fascia fixes the breast to the chest wall.

  • The plane between the pectoral muscles is deep to the pectoral fascia and has nothing to do with the breast.
  • The skin is firmly bound to the gland by the suspensory ligaments; there is no loose space there.
Slides (2)
L7Learning
From superficial to deep, what is the order of layers over the breast region of the chest wall?
  1. A. Skin → superficial fascia with gland → pectoral fascia → retromammary space → pectoralis major → ribs and intercostals
  2. B. Skin → superficial fascia with gland → retromammary space → pectoral fascia → pectoralis major → ribs and intercostals
  3. C. Skin → retromammary space → superficial fascia with gland → pectoral fascia → pectoralis major → ribs and intercostals
AnswerB. Skin → superficial fascia with gland → retromammary space → pectoral fascia → pectoralis major → ribs and intercostals
Skin → superficial fascia containing the gland → retromammary space → pectoral fascia → pectoralis major → ribs and intercostal muscles.
Explanation

The gland lies in the superficial fascia. Directly behind it (retro-mammary) is the loose retromammary space, and behind that the pectoral fascia, the deep fascia that invests pectoralis major. The muscle lies on the ribs and intercostal muscles.

  • Putting the space deep to the pectoral fascia is wrong: the space separates the gland from the fascia, which is why the breast moves on the fascia and why a tumour that reaches the fascia becomes fixed.
  • Putting the space between the skin and the gland is wrong: as its name says, it lies behind the gland.
Slides (2)

Internal structure

L8Learning
What kind of gland is the breast?
  1. A. An endocrine gland, enclosed in a thick capsule
  2. B. A modified sebaceous gland, enclosed in a thin capsule
  3. C. A modified sweat gland, with no capsule or sheath
AnswerC. A modified sweat gland, with no capsule or sheath
The mammary gland is a modified (apocrine) sweat gland and has no special capsule or sheath; it blends with the surrounding subcutaneous fat.
Explanation

Like sweat glands, the breast is an exocrine skin gland that grows down from the epidermis into the subcutaneous tissue; histologically it is a modified apocrine sweat gland of compound tubuloalveolar form. It has no capsule: its lobes are held by fibrous septa (the suspensory ligaments) set in fat.

  • It is not endocrine: it delivers milk through ducts onto the skin.
  • Sebaceous glands are present, but in the areola, not as the mammary gland itself.
Slide (1)
L9Learning
How many lobes of glandular tissue does the breast contain?
  1. A. 5–10
  2. B. 15–20
  3. C. 30–40
AnswerB. 15–20
The suspensory ligaments divide the gland into 15–20 lobes, each drained by its own lactiferous duct.
Explanation

Each lobe is a separate tree of ducts ending in many small lobules, which hold the milk-secreting alveoli. Each lobe drains through one lactiferous duct to the nipple, so the nipple has 15–20 duct openings.

The lecture slide calls these 15–20 units "lobules"; in strict terms they are lobes, each made of many lobules. The number 15–20 is the same either way.

Slides (2)
L10Learning
During lactation, what route does milk take to the nipple?
  1. A. Alveoli → lactiferous duct → lactiferous sinus → nipple, each duct opening separately
  2. B. Alveoli → lactiferous sinus → lactiferous duct → nipple, each duct opening separately
  3. C. Alveoli → lactiferous duct → lactiferous sinus → one common duct opening on the nipple
AnswerA. Alveoli → lactiferous duct → lactiferous sinus → nipple, each duct opening separately
Milk made in the alveoli flows into the lobe's lactiferous duct, which widens into a lactiferous sinus under the areola and then opens independently on the nipple.
Explanation

The alveoli are the secretory units in the lobules. Each lobe's ducts join into one lactiferous duct. Just deep to the areola the duct dilates into a lactiferous sinus, a small reservoir where milk collects, before the duct narrows again and opens on the tip of the nipple.

  • The sinus lies after the duct, close to the nipple, not before it.
  • The 15–20 ducts never merge into one common duct; each opens separately, so the nipple has 15–20 openings.
Slides (2)
L11Learning
What makes up most of the size of the non-lactating breast, and what grows in pregnancy?
  1. A. Fat (laid down at puberty) → in pregnancy the glandular tissue enlarges
  2. B. Glandular tissue (laid down at puberty) → in pregnancy the fat enlarges
  3. C. Fibrous tissue (laid down at birth) → in pregnancy the suspensory ligaments enlarge
AnswerA. Fat (laid down at puberty) → in pregnancy the glandular tissue enlarges
Breast size depends on the fat deposited at puberty; in pregnancy the breast grows because the glandular tissue develops.
Explanation

At puberty, oestrogen drives fat deposition and some duct growth, so the size of the resting breast is mostly fat. In pregnancy, the ducts branch and the alveoli multiply and enlarge, ready to secrete milk; the figure contrasts small resting lobules with large lactating ones.

  • The resting gland has relatively little glandular tissue; growth in pregnancy is glandular, not fatty.
  • The suspensory ligaments are support bands; they do not grow to enlarge the breast (they stretch when it sags).
Slide (1)
L12Learning
What are the suspensory ligaments (of Cooper)?
  1. A. Smooth-muscle bands from the nipple to the areola that erect the nipple
  2. B. Elastic bands from the clavicle to the breast that hang it from above
  3. C. Fibrous bands from the skin through the gland to the deep fascia, separating the lobes
AnswerC. Fibrous bands from the skin through the gland to the deep fascia, separating the lobes
The suspensory ligaments (of Cooper) are fibrous septa that run from the dermis through the gland to the deep fascia and divide it into lobes.
Explanation

These connective-tissue bands anchor the gland to the overlying skin and pass between the lobes, separating them. They are the breast's main support.

  • Smooth muscle exists in the nipple and areola, but it is not the suspensory ligament system.
  • The ligaments do not come from the clavicle, and they are fibrous, not elastic. (This mistake appears in some review-book explanations.)

Clinical link: a tumour that pulls on them dimples the skin, and when they stretch with age the breast sags (ptosis).

Slides (2)
L13Learning
What do the suspensory ligaments do, and where are they best developed?
  1. A. Bind the gland firmly to the overlying skin → best developed in the upper breast
  2. B. Bind the gland firmly to pectoralis major → best developed in the lower breast
  3. C. Bind the gland loosely to the ribs → best developed in the medial breast
AnswerA. Bind the gland firmly to the overlying skin → best developed in the upper breast
The suspensory ligaments attach the gland firmly to the overlying skin and are best developed in the superior part of the breast, where they help support it.
Explanation

Because the ligaments tie the gland to the dermis, anything that shortens them pulls the skin inward. They are strongest superiorly, where they carry the gland's weight.

  • The gland is not bound to pectoralis major: the retromammary space lets it slide over the muscle.
  • It is not attached to the ribs at all; the pectoral muscles and fascia lie in between.
Slides (2)
L14Learning
Which glands make the areola rich, and what do they do?
  1. A. Eccrine sweat glands → cool the nipple during breastfeeding
  2. B. Sebaceous glands → keep the areola and nipple from cracking during breastfeeding
  3. C. Mucous glands → produce the first milk (colostrum) during breastfeeding
AnswerB. Sebaceous glands → keep the areola and nipple from cracking during breastfeeding
The areola is rich in sebaceous glands (the areolar glands or tubercles of Montgomery), whose oily secretion keeps the areola and nipple from cracking during lactation.
Explanation

The areola is the circle of darker skin around the nipple. Its areolar glands (of Montgomery) are modified sebaceous glands. They raise small bumps on the areola and secrete an oily lubricant that protects the skin from the friction of suckling.

  • Eccrine sweat glands secrete watery sweat for cooling; they are not the areola's special glands.
  • Colostrum is made by the mammary alveoli, not by any mucous glands in the areola.
Slide (1)
L15Learning
Where can supernumerary nipples appear?
  1. A. Only in the axilla, never below the normal breasts
  2. B. Anywhere along a line from the axilla to the groin, above or below the normal breasts
  3. C. Anywhere along the anterior midline, from the sternum to the umbilicus
AnswerB. Anywhere along a line from the axilla to the groin, above or below the normal breasts
Supernumerary nipples can appear anywhere along the line from the axilla to the groin (the milk line), above or below the normal breasts, and are usually rudimentary.
Explanation

In the embryo, a mammary ridge (milk line) runs on each side from the axilla to the groin. Normally only the pectoral part persists. If other parts persist, an extra nipple (polythelia) or, rarely, extra breast tissue (polymastia) forms along that line. Most are rudimentary and are easily mistaken for a mole.

  • The axilla is a common site, but extra nipples also occur below the breasts, down to the groin.
  • The lines are paired and lateral, so the midline is not on them.
Slides (2)

Arteries, veins and nerves

L16Learning
What are the four arterial sources of the breast?
  1. A. Internal thoracic artery (medial mammary + anterior intercostal branches)
    Suprascapular artery
    Thyrocervical trunk
    Posterior intercostal arteries
  2. B. Internal thoracic artery (medial mammary + anterior intercostal branches)
    Lateral thoracic artery
    Thoracoacromial trunk
    Posterior intercostal arteries
  3. C. Internal thoracic artery (medial mammary + anterior intercostal branches)
    Lateral thoracic artery
    Thoracoacromial trunk
    Superior epigastric arteries
AnswerB. Internal thoracic artery (medial mammary + anterior intercostal branches)
Lateral thoracic artery
Thoracoacromial trunk
Posterior intercostal arteries
The breast is supplied by the internal thoracic artery, the lateral thoracic artery, the thoracoacromial trunk and the posterior intercostal arteries.
Explanation
  • Internal thoracic artery (from the subclavian artery): medial mammary branches of its perforating branches, plus anterior intercostal branches. Medial breast.
  • Lateral thoracic artery (from the axillary artery): lateral mammary branches. Lateral breast.
  • Thoracoacromial trunk (axillary artery): pectoral branches, through pectoralis major.
  • Posterior intercostal arteries (from the aorta), 2nd–4th spaces: lateral mammary branches of their lateral cutaneous branches.

Wrong: the suprascapular artery and thyrocervical trunk supply the neck and scapula. The superior epigastric artery continues the internal thoracic artery into the rectus sheath, below the breast.

Slides (2)
L17Learning
Which artery gives rise to the medial mammary branches?
  1. A. Lateral thoracic artery
  2. B. Thoracoacromial trunk
  3. C. Internal thoracic artery
AnswerC. Internal thoracic artery
The medial mammary branches come from the perforating branches of the internal thoracic artery, which runs just lateral to the sternum.
Explanation

The internal thoracic artery leaves the subclavian artery and descends behind the costal cartilages, about 1 cm from the sternal edge. Its perforating branches pierce the upper intercostal spaces next to the sternum, and their medial mammary branches enter the medial part of the breast.

  • The lateral thoracic artery gives the lateral mammary branches, which supply the lateral breast.
  • The thoracoacromial trunk reaches the breast through its pectoral branches, which pass through pectoralis major.
Slides (2)
L18Learning
Where does venous blood from the breast drain?
  1. A. Mostly → axillary vein
    Smaller part → internal thoracic vein
  2. B. Mostly → internal thoracic vein
    Smaller part → axillary vein
  3. C. Mostly → cephalic vein
    Smaller part → external jugular vein
AnswerA. Mostly → axillary vein
Smaller part → internal thoracic vein
Most venous blood from the breast drains to the axillary vein; a smaller part drains to the internal thoracic vein.
Explanation

The veins follow the arteries. The lateral and larger part of the breast drains through the lateral thoracic and other tributaries into the axillary vein. The medial part drains through perforating veins into the internal thoracic vein. Some blood also reaches the posterior intercostal veins, a link to the vertebral venous plexus.

  • The swapped proportions are wrong: the axillary route is the main one, as it is for the lymph.
  • The cephalic vein drains the lateral upper limb and the external jugular vein drains the scalp and face; neither is a main breast route.
Slide (1)
L19Learning
Which nerves supply the breast?
  1. A. 1st–3rd intercostal nerves
  2. B. 4th–6th intercostal nerves
  3. C. 7th–9th intercostal nerves
AnswerB. 4th–6th intercostal nerves
The breast is innervated by the 4th–6th intercostal nerves, which reach the gland and skin through the pectoral fascia.
Explanation

The anterior and lateral cutaneous branches of the 4th–6th intercostal nerves pass through the pectoral fascia to the breast tissue and the overlying skin. This fits the T4 dermatome at the nipple.

  • The upper intercostal nerves (with the supraclavicular nerves) supply skin above the breast. One TA table lists T2–T6; the lecture's answer is 4th–6th.
  • The 7th–9th intercostal nerves are thoracoabdominal nerves that supply the lower chest and the abdominal wall.
Slides (2)
L20Learning
Which intercostal nerve supplies the nipple and areola?
  1. A. 4th intercostal nerve (through its anterior and lateral cutaneous branches)
  2. B. 2nd intercostal nerve (through its intercostobrachial branch)
  3. C. 6th intercostal nerve (through its anterior and lateral cutaneous branches)
AnswerA. 4th intercostal nerve (through its anterior and lateral cutaneous branches)
The nipple lies in the T4 dermatome: the anterior and lateral cutaneous branches of the 4th intercostal nerve supply the nipple and areola.
Explanation

The nipple sits at about the 4th intercostal space in men, within the T4 dermatome. The 4th intercostal nerve reaches it through its lateral cutaneous branch (from the side) and its anterior cutaneous branch (from the front). Injuring the lateral cutaneous branch, for example during breast augmentation, can leave the nipple numb.

  • The intercostobrachial nerve (from the 2nd intercostal nerve) supplies the floor of the axilla and the medial arm, not the nipple.
  • The 6th intercostal nerve supplies the lower breast and the skin below it.
Slide (1)
L21Learning
What do the intercostal nerves carry to and from the breast?
  1. A. Motor fibres to pectoralis major
    Parasympathetic fibres to the glandular tissue
  2. B. Sensory fibres from the overlying skin
    Parasympathetic fibres that drive milk secretion
  3. C. Sensory fibres from the overlying skin
    Sympathetic fibres to blood vessels and to smooth muscle of skin and nipple
AnswerC. Sensory fibres from the overlying skin
Sympathetic fibres to blood vessels and to smooth muscle of skin and nipple
The 4th–6th intercostal nerves carry sensation from the overlying skin and sympathetic fibres to the breast's blood vessels and to the smooth muscle of the skin and nipple.
Explanation

Their branches pass through the pectoral fascia to the gland and skin. The sympathetic fibres they carry constrict blood vessels and contract smooth muscle in the skin and nipple (for example, nipple erection).

  • The breast has no parasympathetic supply. Milk secretion and ejection are controlled by hormones (prolactin and oxytocin), not by nerves to the gland.
  • Pectoralis major is supplied by the medial and lateral pectoral nerves, not by the intercostal nerves.
Slides (2)

Quadrants

L22Learning
How is the breast divided to describe the position of a lump?
  1. A. Medial and lateral halves, divided along the midclavicular line
  2. B. Four quadrants, divided by a horizontal and a vertical line through the nipple, plus clock-face positions
  3. C. Six sectors that follow the lactiferous ducts, numbered from the axilla
AnswerB. Four quadrants, divided by a horizontal and a vertical line through the nipple, plus clock-face positions
Lines through the nipple divide the breast into four quadrants; a clock face gives finer positions for a tumour or cyst.
Explanation

A horizontal and a vertical line crossing at the nipple give the superolateral, superomedial, inferolateral and inferomedial quadrants. The axillary tail belongs to the superolateral quadrant. For finer detail, clinicians give a clock position and the distance from the nipple. On the figure (right breast, facing the patient), 9 o'clock is lateral and 3 o'clock is medial; on the left breast this is reversed.

  • Two halves would be too coarse, and the lecture's system uses the nipple, not the midclavicular line.
  • No clinical system uses duct sectors.
Slides (2)
L23Learning
Why do the breast quadrants matter clinically?
  1. A. They have separate arterial supplies
    Cancers are spread evenly among them
  2. B. They all drain to the same nodes
    Cancers are not spread evenly among them
  3. C. They drain to different nodes
    Cancers are not spread evenly among them
AnswerC. They drain to different nodes
Cancers are not spread evenly among them
The quadrants matter because they have different lymph drainage and are used to locate a tumour or cyst, and cancers cluster in the superolateral quadrant.
Explanation

The lecture gives two reasons: the difference in lymph drainage (lateral → pectoral axillary nodes, medial → parasternal nodes, superior → supraclavicular, inferior → abdominal), and their use to describe where a tumour or cyst is. Cancers are not spread evenly: about 60% arise in the superolateral quadrant.

  • The arteries overlap freely across quadrants, and cancers are not evenly spread.
  • If all quadrants drained to the same nodes, quadrant would not predict where cancer spreads.
Slides (2)
L24Learning
Which breast quadrant is the site of most cancers, and what share?
  1. A. Superolateral → about 25%
  2. B. Superolateral → about 60%
  3. C. Inferolateral → about 40%
AnswerB. Superolateral → about 60%
About 60% of breast cancers arise in the superolateral (upper outer) quadrant.
Explanation

The lecture's quadrant figure puts ~60% of cancers in the superolateral quadrant, which includes the axillary tail. The other quadrants are much lower: superomedial ~15%, inferolateral ~10%, inferomedial ~5%. These add up to about 90%; the rest arise centrally, under the areola.

  • 25% is far too low for the superolateral quadrant. (25% is the share of breast lymph that goes to the parasternal nodes.)
  • The inferolateral quadrant has only about 10%.
Slides (2)
L25Learning
Why does the superolateral quadrant get the most breast cancers?
  1. A. It has the most fat, being furthest from the nipple
  2. B. It has the most glandular tissue, including the axillary tail
  3. C. It has the fewest lymphatics, so tumour cells are cleared slowly
AnswerB. It has the most glandular tissue, including the axillary tail
The superolateral quadrant holds the most glandular tissue, including the axillary tail. Breast cancer arises from duct epithelium, so more gland means more cancers.
Explanation

Breast carcinoma is mostly an adenocarcinoma of the duct epithelium, so cancers arise where there is most epithelium. Much of the gland, plus the axillary process, lies in the upper outer quadrant.

  • Fat does not give rise to carcinoma, and more fat would not increase the cancer rate.
  • The lateral breast is not short of lymphatics: it drains richly to the axillary nodes, which is why it spreads there first.
Slide (1)
L26Learning
What share of breast cancers arise in the other three quadrants?
  1. A. Superomedial ~10%
    Inferolateral ~15%
    Inferomedial ~5%
  2. B. Superomedial ~15%
    Inferolateral ~10%
    Inferomedial ~5%
  3. C. Superomedial ~5%
    Inferolateral ~10%
    Inferomedial ~15%
AnswerB. Superomedial ~15%
Inferolateral ~10%
Inferomedial ~5%
After the superolateral quadrant (~60%) come the superomedial ~15%, the inferolateral ~10% and the inferomedial ~5%.
Explanation

On the lecture's clock-face figure, the shares fall away from the upper outer quadrant: 60 → 15 → 10 → 5. The two upper quadrants (60 + 15) carry most of the gland, and the inferomedial quadrant has the least.

  • The other two options swap the numbers between quadrants. Hook: the share falls as you move away from the axillary tail, and the upper inner quadrant comes second.
Slides (2)

Lymphatic drainage

L27Learning
Where does most of the breast's lymph drain, and how much?
  1. A. Axillary nodes → more than 75%
  2. B. Parasternal nodes → more than 75%
  3. C. Axillary nodes → about 25%
AnswerA. Axillary nodes → more than 75%
More than 75% of breast lymph drains to the axillary nodes, mostly from the lateral quadrants.
Explanation

Lymph starts in the subareolar lymphatic plexus and in the gland's lymphatics. Most of it runs laterally to the axillary nodes, first the pectoral (anterior) group. The rest, about 25% and mainly from the medial quadrants, goes to the parasternal nodes; small amounts go to the opposite breast and the abdomen.

That is why the axilla is always examined and sampled in breast cancer.

  • The parasternal nodes receive the smaller medial share, not 75%.
  • 25% is the parasternal share, not the axillary one.
Slides (2)
L28Learning
Which group of axillary nodes receives breast lymph first?
  1. A. Central group
  2. B. Apical group
  3. C. Anterior (pectoral) group
AnswerC. Anterior (pectoral) group
Lymph from the lateral breast drains first to the anterior (pectoral) axillary nodes.
Explanation

The pectoral (anterior) nodes lie on the medial wall of the axilla, along the lateral thoracic vessels at the lower border of pectoralis minor. They are the first stop for most breast lymph and the usual sentinel nodes.

  • The central nodes, deep in the axillary fat, are the second stop: they collect from the pectoral, humeral and subscapular groups.
  • The apical nodes, at the apex of the axilla below the clavicle, are the last axillary stop before the subclavian lymphatic trunk.
Slides (2)
L29Learning
After the pectoral nodes, what route does breast lymph usually take?
  1. A. Central axillary nodes → apical axillary nodes → subclavian lymphatic trunk
  2. B. Apical axillary nodes → central axillary nodes → subclavian lymphatic trunk
  3. C. Humeral nodes → subscapular nodes → jugular lymphatic trunk
AnswerA. Central axillary nodes → apical axillary nodes → subclavian lymphatic trunk
From the pectoral nodes, lymph passes to the central and then the apical axillary nodes, whose efferents form the subclavian lymphatic trunk.
Explanation

The lecture figure shows all five axillary groups: pectoral, subscapular, humeral, central and apical. The pectoral, humeral and subscapular groups all drain into the central group, which drains into the apical group at the apex of the axilla. The apical nodes (with the infraclavicular and supraclavicular nodes) send lymph into the subclavian trunk, which joins the venous system near the venous angle.

  • The order is reversed in the second option: the apical nodes come last.
  • The humeral and subscapular nodes drain the upper limb and the posterior axillary wall, not the main breast route.
Slides (2)
L30Learning
According to the lecture, where does lymph from the medial quadrants drain?
  1. A. Parasternal (internal thoracic) nodes → superficial vessels can also cross to the opposite side
  2. B. Supraclavicular nodes → superficial vessels can also cross to the opposite side
  3. C. Abdominal (subdiaphragmatic) nodes → the lymph always stays on the same side
AnswerA. Parasternal (internal thoracic) nodes → superficial vessels can also cross to the opposite side
The medial quadrants drain to the parasternal (internal thoracic) nodes; superficial lymphatics can also reach the contralateral parasternal nodes.
Explanation

The parasternal nodes lie along the internal thoracic vessels, just beside the sternum in the upper intercostal spaces. They take about 25% of breast lymph, mainly from the medial quadrants. Superficial lymphatics of the medial breast cross the midline, so cancer can spread to the opposite parasternal nodes and breast.

  • The supraclavicular nodes are the lecture's target for the superior quadrants.
  • The abdominal nodes are the target for the inferior quadrants.
Slides (2)
L31Learning
Where can lymph from the upper and lower quadrants of the breast drain?
  1. A. Upper quadrants → abdominal nodes
    Lower quadrants → supraclavicular nodes
  2. B. Upper quadrants → supraclavicular nodes
    Lower quadrants → abdominal nodes
  3. C. Upper quadrants → apical axillary nodes only
    Lower quadrants → parasternal nodes only
AnswerB. Upper quadrants → supraclavicular nodes
Lower quadrants → abdominal nodes
Per the lecture, the superior quadrants can drain to the supraclavicular nodes and the inferior quadrants to the abdominal group of nodes.
Explanation

The lecture's four-way rule: lateral → pectoral, medial → parasternal, superior → supraclavicular, inferior → abdominal. The lower breast drains through the anterior abdominal wall toward the subdiaphragmatic nodes (and, via the diaphragm, toward the liver), which is how breast cancer can reach the abdomen.

  • The first option swaps the two routes.
  • The third option is wrong: the lecture sends the superior quadrants to the supraclavicular nodes and the inferior quadrants to the abdominal nodes, and no quadrant drains to a single group "only" (the lateral parts of both drain mainly to the axillary nodes, the medial parts to the parasternal nodes).

The updated 2026 lecture names the abdominal group the inferior phrenic nodes.

Slides (2)
L32Learning
Through which channel does most lymph from the right breast finally enter the blood?
  1. A. Thoracic duct → left venous angle
  2. B. Right lymphatic duct → right venous angle
  3. C. Thoracic duct → right venous angle
AnswerB. Right lymphatic duct → right venous angle
Lymph from the right breast reaches the blood through the right lymphatic duct at the right venous angle.
Explanation

A venous angle is the junction of the internal jugular and subclavian veins. The right lymphatic duct drains the right upper quadrant of the body (right head, neck, upper limb and thorax, including the right breast) into the right venous angle. Sometimes its trunks open into the veins separately. The thoracic duct drains the rest of the body, including the left breast, into the left venous angle.

  • Thoracic duct → left venous angle is the route for the left breast, not the right; lymph from both breasts does not end in the thoracic duct.
  • Thoracic duct → right venous angle is wrong because the thoracic duct ends on the left, never at the right venous angle.
Slides (2)
L33Learning
A sentinel node biopsy is planned for a cancer in the lateral half of the breast. What is the sentinel node, and where is it usually found?
  1. A. The first node to receive lymph from the tumour → anterior (pectoral) axillary group
  2. B. The last node before lymph enters the veins → apical axillary group
  3. C. The largest node draining the breast → central axillary group
AnswerA. The first node to receive lymph from the tumour → anterior (pectoral) axillary group
The sentinel node is the first node to receive lymph from a tumour; for the lateral breast it is usually in the anterior (pectoral) axillary group.
Explanation

In a sentinel node biopsy, dye or a radiotracer is injected near the tumour and followed to the first node it reaches. That node is removed and examined. Because lateral breast lymph drains first to the pectoral nodes, the sentinel node is usually there.

If the sentinel node is free of tumour, the other axillary nodes are unlikely to be involved, so a full axillary dissection and its risk of arm lymphoedema can be avoided.

  • The apical nodes come last in the axillary chain, not first.
  • "Sentinel" means first in line, not largest. The central nodes are the second stop.
Slide (1)
L34Learning
A firm, fixed lump is found in the superolateral quadrant of a woman's breast. Using the lecture's quadrant rules, where would palpable nodes most likely be?
  1. A. Pectoral (axillary) and supraclavicular nodes
  2. B. Parasternal and supraclavicular nodes
  3. C. Pectoral (axillary) and abdominal nodes
AnswerA. Pectoral (axillary) and supraclavicular nodes
A lateral lump drains to the pectoral axillary nodes and a superior lump to the supraclavicular nodes, so a superolateral lump points to both.
Explanation

Apply the lecture's rules to each half of the location: lateral → pectoral nodes of the axilla (the main route, >75% of breast lymph) and superior → supraclavicular nodes. The axilla is examined first.

  • Parasternal nodes go with the medial quadrants.
  • Abdominal nodes go with the inferior quadrants.
Slides (2)
L35Learning
A cancer in the inferomedial quadrant of the right breast is found in parasternal nodes to the left of the sternum. What explains this spread?
  1. A. Tumour cells travel in the internal thoracic veins to the opposite parasternal nodes
  2. B. Deep lymphatics in the retromammary space cross the midline to the opposite axillary nodes
  3. C. Superficial lymphatics of the medial breast cross the midline to the opposite parasternal nodes
AnswerC. Superficial lymphatics of the medial breast cross the midline to the opposite parasternal nodes
Superficial lymphatics of the medial breast cross the midline, so medial cancers can reach the contralateral parasternal nodes and the opposite breast.
Explanation

The medial quadrants drain to the parasternal nodes, and if the lymphatics are superficial enough they communicate across the sternum with those of the other side. This is how a medial cancer can appear in the opposite parasternal nodes and the opposite breast.

  • No route runs from the retromammary space to the opposite axilla; the axillary nodes receive lymph from their own side.
  • Veins drain into the venous system and do not deliver tumour cells to lymph nodes.
Slides (2)

Breast cancer: signs and spread

L36Learning
How does a breast cancer cause dimpling of the overlying skin?
  1. A. It invades the gland and shortens the suspensory ligaments → pulls the overlying skin inward
  2. B. It shortens the lactiferous ducts → pulls the overlying skin inward
  3. C. It blocks the superficial lymphatics → swells the overlying skin
AnswerA. It invades the gland and shortens the suspensory ligaments → pulls the overlying skin inward
Skin dimpling occurs when cancer invades the glandular tissue and shortens the suspensory ligaments, which tether the skin and pull it inward.
Explanation

The suspensory ligaments run from the dermis into the gland. When tumour grows along them, fibrosis shortens them and the skin over the tumour is drawn in to form a dimple. It shows best when the patient raises her arms or presses her hands on her hips.

  • Shortened lactiferous ducts pull in the nipple (nipple retraction), not the general skin.
  • Blocked superficial lymphatics cause skin oedema: peau d'orange.
Slides (2)
L37Learning
What causes the peau d'orange appearance of the breast?
  1. A. Shortened suspensory ligaments → dimpled, tethered skin
  2. B. Blocked lactiferous ducts → swollen, cystic skin
  3. C. Blocked superficial lymphatics → oedematous, puffy, pitted skin
AnswerC. Blocked superficial lymphatics → oedematous, puffy, pitted skin
Peau d'orange (orange-peel skin) results from cancer blocking the superficial lymphatics, so fluid builds up in the subcutaneous tissue and the skin becomes puffy and pitted.
Explanation

When tumour cells block the skin's lymphatics, interstitial fluid collects (lymphoedema of the skin). The skin swells, but the points where hair follicles and sweat ducts tether it stay down, so it looks like the pitted skin of an orange. The lecture's "puffy and dimpled" means these small pits, not the large single dimple of ligament traction.

  • Shortened suspensory ligaments cause a single skin dimple.
  • Duct shortening retracts the nipple; blocked ducts do not make the skin oedematous.
Slide (1)
L38Learning
What causes nipple retraction in breast cancer?
  1. A. A cancer deep in the breast invades pectoralis major → pulls the nipple in
  2. B. A cancer under the areola blocks the superficial lymphatics → pulls the nipple in
  3. C. A cancer under the areola shortens the lactiferous ducts → pulls the nipple in
AnswerC. A cancer under the areola shortens the lactiferous ducts → pulls the nipple in
A subareolar cancer shortens and tightens the lactiferous ducts, which converge on the nipple and pull it inward.
Explanation

The 15–20 lactiferous ducts all converge on the nipple. A cancer just behind the areola infiltrates and fibroses them, shortening them, so the nipple is drawn in (retraction) and may point to one side (deviation). The breast's contour may also change.

  • Invasion of pectoralis major fixes the breast to the chest wall; it does not pull on the nipple.
  • Blocked lymphatics cause skin oedema (peau d'orange), not traction.

Some review books attribute nipple inversion to the suspensory ligaments; the lecture's answer is the lactiferous ducts.

Slide (1)
L39Learning
A breast lump no longer moves over the chest wall but stays fixed to it. What does this indicate?
  1. A. The cancer has shortened the suspensory ligaments into the skin
  2. B. The cancer has crossed the retromammary space and invaded the pectoral fascia and muscle
  3. C. The cancer has blocked the superficial lymphatics of the skin
AnswerB. The cancer has crossed the retromammary space and invaded the pectoral fascia and muscle
A lump fixed to the chest wall has crossed the retromammary space and invaded the pectoral fascia (and pectoralis major).
Explanation

Normally the loose retromammary space lets the breast, and any lump in it, slide over the pectoral fascia. A cancer that crosses this space and invades the pectoral fascia and pectoralis major binds the breast to the muscle. When the patient contracts pectoralis major (hands pressed on the hips), the lump moves with the muscle. A lump that moves freely is still confined to the breast.

  • Tethering by the suspensory ligaments fixes the lump to the skin (dimpling), not to the chest wall.
  • Blocked lymphatics cause peau d'orange, not fixation.
Slides (2)
L40Learning
What type of tumour is breast cancer usually, and where does it arise?
  1. A. Adenocarcinoma → from the epithelium of the lactiferous ducts
  2. B. Adenocarcinoma → from the myoepithelial cells around the alveoli
  3. C. Squamous cell carcinoma → from the skin of the nipple
AnswerA. Adenocarcinoma → from the epithelium of the lactiferous ducts
Breast cancer, the most common cancer in women, is usually an adenocarcinoma arising from the epithelium of the lactiferous ducts.
Explanation

An adenocarcinoma is a cancer of glandular epithelium. In the breast it usually starts in the lining cells of the ducts (with some lobular cancers starting in the lobules). It spreads easily along the lymph drainage routes, so the drainage map is also the map of spread.

  • Myoepithelial cells are contractile cells around the alveoli and ducts that eject milk; they are not the usual source of carcinoma.
  • Squamous cancer of the nipple skin is rare and is not the typical breast cancer.
Slide (1)
L41Learning
Where does breast cancer spread?
  1. A. Most often directly into pectoralis major
    Also the ribs, lung and opposite axilla
  2. B. Most often to the parasternal nodes
    Also the inguinal nodes, opposite axilla and brain
  3. C. Most often to the axillary nodes
    Also the supraclavicular nodes, opposite breast and abdomen
AnswerC. Most often to the axillary nodes
Also the supraclavicular nodes, opposite breast and abdomen
Breast cancer spreads most often to the axillary nodes, and can also reach the supraclavicular nodes, the opposite breast and the abdomen.
Explanation

The spread follows the lymph routes: lateral (and most) lymph → axillary nodes; superior → supraclavicular; medial → parasternal nodes and across to the opposite breast; inferior → abdominal nodes.

  • Direct invasion of pectoralis major happens, but it is not the most common route; lymphatic spread is.
  • The parasternal nodes take only the smaller medial share (~25%), and the inguinal nodes drain the lower limb and lower abdominal wall, not the breast.
Slide (1)
L42Learning
Breast cancer can reach the vertebrae and brain without passing through the lungs. Which feature of the internal vertebral venous plexus (of Batson) allows this?
  1. A. Its veins are largely valveless, so blood can flow in either direction
  2. B. Its veins have one-way valves that direct blood upward to the brain
  3. C. Its veins lie in the subarachnoid space, bathed in cerebrospinal fluid
AnswerA. Its veins are largely valveless, so blood can flow in either direction
The vertebral venous plexus is largely valveless, so blood (and tumour cells) can flow backward into it from the posterior intercostal veins and up to the brain.
Explanation

Some breast veins drain into the posterior intercostal veins, which connect with the internal vertebral venous plexus. This plexus runs the whole length of the vertebral canal, in the epidural (extradural) space, and continues into the dural venous sinuses of the skull. Its veins are largely valveless. When intrathoracic or abdominal pressure rises (coughing, straining), blood can flow backward into it, carrying tumour cells to the vertebrae and brain without passing through the lung capillaries.

  • The plexus has no valves to direct flow.
  • It lies in the epidural space, not the subarachnoid space.
Slide (1)
L43Learning
About what share of breast cancer cases occur in men?
  1. A. About 0.05%
  2. B. About 1.5%
  3. C. About 25%
AnswerB. About 1.5%
About 1.5% of breast cancers occur in men (about 1,000 men a year in the US), as the updated 2026 lecture and Moore state.
Explanation

Male breast cancer is uncommon. The updated 2026 lecture gives about 1.5% (roughly 1,000 men a year in the US), the same figure as Moore; epidemiological data put it near 1%. The older lecture slide said 4.5%: if an exam question offers 4.5% but not 1.5%, that is the answer it wants. Either way it is a small minority, often found late because men do not expect it.

  • 0.05% is far too low: male breast cancer is uncommon but not vanishingly rare.
  • 25% is far too high.
Slides (2)
L44Learning
How does breast cancer in men typically behave?
  1. A. It stays confined to the nipple for years → usually found early
  2. B. It infiltrates the pectoral fascia, pectoralis major and axillary nodes → often found only after extensive spread
  3. C. It spreads mainly to the opposite breast → rarely reaches the axillary nodes
AnswerB. It infiltrates the pectoral fascia, pectoralis major and axillary nodes → often found only after extensive spread
Male breast cancer tends to infiltrate the pectoral fascia, pectoralis major and axillary nodes, and is often not detected until it has metastasized extensively.
Explanation

The male breast is rudimentary: there is very little gland and fat between the nipple and the chest wall. A tumour therefore reaches the pectoral fascia and pectoralis major quickly, and soon the axillary nodes. Because few men examine their breasts or expect breast cancer, it is often found late.

  • It does not stay small and confined; it is usually found late.
  • Like female breast cancer, its main lymphatic route is the axillary nodes.
Slide (1)
L45Learning
What share of males with Klinefelter syndrome develop gynaecomastia, and when?
  1. A. About 40% → at puberty
  2. B. About 40% → in infancy
  3. C. About 80% → in old age
AnswerA. About 40% → at puberty
About 40% of males with Klinefelter syndrome develop gynaecomastia (enlarged breast tissue) during puberty.
Explanation

Gynaecomastia is enlargement of the male breast tissue. In Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY), the small testes make too little testosterone relative to oestrogen, so breast tissue grows when puberty starts. The lecture gives about 40% of affected males. The typical patient is a tall adolescent with small, firm testes.

  • The rise comes at puberty, when sex hormones surge, not in infancy.
  • In old age is wrong: the gynaecomastia of Klinefelter syndrome appears at puberty, and the lecture's figure is 40%.
Slide (1)

Imaging and surgery

L46Learning
What is the most commonly used method for breast cancer screening?
  1. A. Fine-needle aspiration
  2. B. Mammography
  3. C. Ultrasound
AnswerB. Mammography
Mammography is the most commonly used preventive method, used to screen for tumours before they become evident.
Explanation

A mammogram is a low-dose X-ray of the compressed breast. It can show a mass or microcalcifications before a lump can be felt, so it is the screening test.

  • Fine-needle aspiration samples a lump that has already been found; it is a diagnostic test, not screening.
  • Ultrasound is an add-on for dense breasts and for telling cysts from solid masses.
Slide (1)
L47Learning
What is ultrasound used for in breast imaging?
  1. A. Routine population screening
    Planning treatment of a known tumour
  2. B. Structures mammograms show best, as in fatty breasts
    Staging distant metastases
  3. C. Structures mammograms show poorly, as in dense breasts
    Telling a fluid-filled cyst from a solid mass
AnswerC. Structures mammograms show poorly, as in dense breasts
Telling a fluid-filled cyst from a solid mass
Ultrasound examines what mammograms show poorly, for example dense breast tissue, and tells fluid-filled cysts from solid masses.
Explanation

Dense glandular tissue looks white on a mammogram, just like a tumour, which hides masses. Ultrasound uses sound waves instead of X-rays, so density matters less. Fluid transmits sound, so a cyst is black with sharp walls, while a solid mass returns echoes.

  • Routine screening is mammography, and treatment planning is a use of MRI.
  • Fatty breasts are where mammograms work best, so ultrasound is not needed there; distant staging uses other imaging.
Slide (1)
L48Learning
What is MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) used for in breast cancer?
  1. A. Routine yearly screening of average-risk women
    Replacing biopsy as proof of cancer
  2. B. First test for any new lump
    Telling a cyst from a solid mass at the bedside
  3. C. Further examining a detected tumour
    Ruling out false positives
    Planning treatment
AnswerC. Further examining a detected tumour
Ruling out false positives
Planning treatment
MRI is used to examine a tumour already detected, to rule out false positives, and to plan treatment.
Explanation

MRI gives detailed images of the soft tissue. Once a lesion is found, it shows its extent, any other lesions, and whether a suspicious mammogram finding is real (ruling out a false positive). That guides the choice and extent of surgery.

  • Routine screening is done with mammography, and a biopsy is still needed to prove cancer.
  • Telling a cyst from a solid mass at the bedside is the job of ultrasound.
Slide (1)
L49Learning
What does a simple mastectomy remove?
  1. A. The breast and pectoralis minor, down to the ribs
  2. B. The lump alone, with a rim of normal tissue
  3. C. The breast tissue, down to the retromammary space
AnswerC. The breast tissue, down to the retromammary space
A simple mastectomy removes the breast tissue down to the retromammary space, leaving the pectoral fascia and muscles.
Explanation

The retromammary space is the natural cleavage plane behind the gland, so the surgeon can lift the whole breast off the pectoral fascia there. The muscles stay.

  • Taking chest-wall muscle belongs to the radical mastectomy, which removes the pectoral muscles; a simple mastectomy leaves them.
  • Removing the lump with a margin is a lumpectomy, a breast-conserving operation.

The updated 2026 lecture also lists the axillary nodes under simple mastectomy; in standard terms, removing the breast and axillary nodes while sparing the pectoral muscles is a modified radical mastectomy.

Slides (2)
L50Learning
What does a radical mastectomy remove?
  1. A. The breast, pectoral muscles, fat, fascia, and as many axillary and pectoral-region nodes as needed
  2. B. The breast, serratus anterior, latissimus dorsi and the long thoracic nerve
  3. C. The breast alone, down to the retromammary space
AnswerA. The breast, pectoral muscles, fat, fascia, and as many axillary and pectoral-region nodes as needed
A radical mastectomy removes the breast, the pectoral muscles, fat, fascia and as many lymph nodes as needed in the axilla and pectoral region.
Explanation

The radical operation clears the breast together with the tissues the cancer spreads into first: the pectoral muscles and fascia (deep to the retromammary space) and the axillary and pectoral-region nodes. Mastectomies of either kind are less common now than they were.

  • Serratus anterior, latissimus dorsi and the long thoracic nerve are preserved; injuring the long thoracic nerve is a complication, not a goal.
  • The breast alone down to the retromammary space is a simple mastectomy.
Slides (2)
L51Learning
Which breast cancer operations are more common today?
  1. A. Bilateral mastectomy → followed by hormone therapy
  2. B. Radical mastectomy → followed by chemotherapy
  3. C. Lumpectomy or quadrantectomy → usually followed by radiation therapy
AnswerC. Lumpectomy or quadrantectomy → usually followed by radiation therapy
Today, breast-conserving surgery (lumpectomy or quadrantectomy) is more common than mastectomy and is usually followed by radiation therapy.
Explanation

A lumpectomy removes the tumour with a rim of normal tissue; a quadrantectomy removes the quadrant (a segment) of breast containing it. Radiation then treats any cancer cells left in the remaining breast.

  • Bilateral mastectomy is reserved for special cases (for example, high inherited risk); it is not the usual operation.
  • Radical mastectomy is now uncommon: the lecture stresses that mastectomies are "not as common as they once were".
Slide (1)
L52Learning
Breast surgery involving the lateral quadrants leaves a patient with a winged scapula. Which nerve was injured?
  1. A. Thoracodorsal nerve
  2. B. Long thoracic nerve
  3. C. Medial pectoral nerve
AnswerB. Long thoracic nerve
Any breast surgery involving the lateral quadrants puts the long thoracic nerve at risk; its injury causes a winged scapula.
Explanation

The long thoracic nerve runs down the lateral chest wall on the outer surface of serratus anterior, about at the midaxillary line. It lies just deep to the lateral breast, the axillary tail and the axillary nodes, so lateral-quadrant and axillary surgery can cut or stretch it.

  • The thoracodorsal nerve can also be injured in axillary surgery, but it supplies latissimus dorsi; losing it does not wing the scapula.
  • The medial pectoral nerve (pectoralis minor and part of pectoralis major) can also be injured in mastectomy, but its loss weakens the pectoral muscles; it does not wing the scapula.
Slides (2)
L53Learning
After a mastectomy with axillary dissection, a woman cannot raise her arm above her head and her scapula wings. Which muscle has lost its nerve supply?
  1. A. Latissimus dorsi
  2. B. Pectoralis minor
  3. C. Serratus anterior
AnswerC. Serratus anterior
A winged scapula after lateral breast or axillary surgery means the long thoracic nerve was injured and serratus anterior is paralysed.
Explanation

Serratus anterior holds the scapula flat against the thoracic wall and rotates it upward, which is needed to lift the arm above the head. When the long thoracic nerve is cut, the medial border of the scapula lifts off the chest wall (winging) and the arm cannot be raised fully overhead.

  • Latissimus dorsi (thoracodorsal nerve) extends, adducts and medially rotates the arm; its loss does not cause winging.
  • Pectoralis minor depresses and protracts the scapula; it is supplied by the medial pectoral nerve.
Slide (1)
L54Learning
Why is lymphoedema of the arm common after breast cancer treatment?
  1. A. Removing the axillary nodes spreads tumour cells into the arm → tumour builds up in the limb
  2. B. Removing or irradiating the axillary nodes interrupts the arm's lymph drainage → fluid builds up in the limb
  3. C. Removing the pectoral muscles cuts the arm's venous return → blood pools in the limb
AnswerB. Removing or irradiating the axillary nodes interrupts the arm's lymph drainage → fluid builds up in the limb
The axillary nodes drain the upper limb as well as the breast, so removing or irradiating them blocks the arm's lymph flow and causes lymphoedema of the same-side arm.
Explanation

Lymphoedema is swelling from interstitial fluid that the lymphatics cannot clear. Nearly all lymph from the upper limb passes through the axillary nodes (humeral group → central → apical). Excising these nodes, or scarring them with radiation, breaks that path. Fluid filtered from the capillaries then collects in the ipsilateral arm.

  • The swelling is fluid, not tumour spreading into the arm.
  • It is a lymphatic problem: the axillary vein, which carries venous return, is preserved.
Slides (2)
L55Learning
After axillary node dissection, a woman has numbness of the axilla and the medial side of her upper arm. Which nerve was injured?
  1. A. Long thoracic nerve
  2. B. Thoracodorsal nerve
  3. C. Intercostobrachial nerve
AnswerC. Intercostobrachial nerve
The intercostobrachial nerve, the lateral cutaneous branch of the 2nd intercostal nerve, crosses the axilla to the medial arm and is easily cut in axillary dissection.
Explanation

The 2nd intercostal nerve's lateral cutaneous branch emerges through serratus anterior at the midaxillary line, crosses the floor of the axilla through the fat that holds the axillary nodes, and supplies the skin of the axillary floor and the medial upper arm. Removing that fat and its nodes often injures it, leaving numbness or pain in this area.

  • The long thoracic and thoracodorsal nerves are motor nerves (serratus anterior and latissimus dorsi). Their injury causes weakness, not skin numbness.

A 39-year-old woman complains of an inability to reach the top of her head to brush her hair with her right hand. History reveals that she had undergone a mastectomy procedure of her right breast 2 months earlier. Physical examination demonstrates winging of her right scapula. Which nerves were most likely damaged during surgery?
  1. A. Axillary
  2. B. Spinal accessory
  3. C. Long thoracic
  4. D. Dorsal scapular
  5. E. Thoracodorsal
AnswerC. Long thoracic
Explanation from the source
C. The long thoracic nerve innervates the serratus anterior, which is responsible for elevation and protraction of the scapula beyond the horizontal level while maintaining its position against the thoracic wall. Along with the thoracodorsal nerve, the long thoracic nerve runs superficially along the thoracic wall and is subject to injury during a mastectomy procedure. The axillary nerve, the spinal accessory nerve, and the thoracodorsal nerve supply the deltoid muscle, trapezius muscle, and latissimus dorsi muscles, respectively. The dorsal scapular nerve is responsible for innervation of the rhomboids and levator scapulae. Aside from the long thoracic and thoracodorsal nerves, the remaining nerves do not course along the lateral thoracic wall.

A 38-year-old woman with a history of carcinoma of the left breast and who had had a lumpectomy 2 years previously, presents to her surgeon with complaints of a hard mass in the left breast. On ultrasound examination, a 3 cm × 4 cm hard mass is discovered in the upper outer quadrant extending in the axillary tail (of Spence). A radical mastectomy is performed successfully and the tumor is removed. Three weeks postoperatively the patient complains of difficulty raising her left arm above her head. Which of the following is most likely expected to be found during physical examination?
  1. A. Protraction of the both scapulae
  2. B. Protrusion of the medial border of the left scapula when hands are pushed against the wall
  3. C. Weak abduction of the left upper limb in the 15 to 90 degree range
  4. D. Weak retraction of the scapula
  5. E. Weak adduction of the humerus
AnswerB. Protrusion of the medial border of the left scapula when hands are pushed against the wall
Explanation from the source
B. During surgery the long thoracic nerve was damaged which supplies the serratus anterior muscle. During abduction of the arm, serratus anterior elevates and laterally rotates the scapulae to allow for full abduction, such as when the ability to lift the hand above the head. The serratus anterior is responsible for protracting the scapula and therefore holding it against the thoracic wall. If the nerve supply to this muscle is damaged this will not be achieved when the patient pushes her hands against the wall, resulting in what is called a “winged scapula”.

A 35-year-old woman is admitted to a surgical ward with a palpable mass in her right breast and swollen lymph nodes in the ipsilateral axilla. Radiologic studies and biopsy reveal carcinoma of the breast. Which group of axillary lymph nodes is the first to receive lymph drainage from the secretory tissue of the breast and therefore most likely to contain metastasized tumor cells?

  3. C. Apical
  4. D. Anterior (pectoral)
  5. E. Posterior (subscapular)

Explanation from the source
D. Lymphatic drainage of the breast is typically to the axillary nodes, more specifically to the anterior (pectoral) nodes. Lymphatic vessels from the pectoral nodes continue into the central axillary nodes, the drainage of which passes farther into the apical node, just inferior to the clavicle in the deltopectoral triangle. From these nodes lymph passes to the “sentinel,” or scalene, nodes and the subclavian lymph trunk. The lateral and posterior axillary nodes do not normally receive lymph drainage from the breast but do receive lymph from the upper limb. (This is the reason for the edema of the upper limb that occurs after a mastectomy, in which there may be a total removal of axillary lymph nodes.) GAS 140-141; N 182; McM 179

  3. C. C
  4. D. D
  5. E. E
AnswerC. C
Explanation from the source
C. The long thoracic nerve arises from the C5, C6, and C7 ventral rami and innervates the serratus anterior muscle. Injury of this nerve will result in a characteristic winged scapula. A is the lateral pectoral nerve, which innervates the pectoralis major muscle. B is the suprascapular nerve, which innervates the supraspinatus and infraspinatus muscles. D is the thoracodorsal nerve, which innervates latissimus dorsi. E is the lower subscapular nerve that innervates the lower part of the subscapularis muscle and the teres major. GAS 728, 738, 804; N 185; McM 138
Winged scapula after axillary dissection -> long thoracic nerve (IN via breast surgery), but answering requires locating the nerve on a plexus drawing (MSK I).

A 47-year-old woman patient’s right breast exhibited peau d’orange characteristics. This condition is primarily a result of which of the following occurrences?
  1. A. Blockage of cutaneous lymphatic vessels
  2. B. Shortening of the suspensory ligaments by cancer in the axillary tail of the breast
  3. C. Contraction of the retinacula cutis of the areola and nipple
  4. D. Invasion of the pectoralis major by metastatic cancer
  5. E. Ipsilateral (same side) inversion of the nipple from cancer of the duct system of the breast
AnswerA. Blockage of cutaneous lymphatic vessels
Explanation from the source
A. Blockage of cutaneous lymphatic vessels results in edema of the skin surrounding the hair follicles, leading to an appearance like an orange peel (peau d’orange). Shortening of the suspensory ligaments leads to dimpling of the overlying skin, not peau d’orange. Contraction of retinacula cutis results in retraction and inversion of the nipple and/or areola. Pectoralis major involvement has nothing to do with this condition but can result in fixing the tumor firmly to the chest wall. GAS 141; N 182; McM 179

A 35-year-old woman patient has a hard tumor about 1 cm in diameter slightly above, and lateral, to her right areola. A specific dye was injected into the tissue around the tumor which was taken up by the lymph vessels, draining the area. An incision was made to expose the lymphatic vessels which were then visible to the naked eye. The vessels were traced to surgically expose the lymph nodes receiving the lymph from the tumor. Which nodes will most likely first receive lymph from the tumor?
  1. A. Anterior axillary (pectoral)
  2. B. Lateral axillary
  3. C. Parasternal
  4. D. Central axillary
  5. E. Apical (infraclavicular)
AnswerA. Anterior axillary (pectoral)
Explanation from the source
A. The lateral quadrants of the breast drain into the anterior axillary (pectoral), which is approximately 75% of the lymphatic drainage. The medial quadrants drain into the parasternal nodes with some drainage to the parasternal nodes of the opposite breast. There is also a small amount of drainage of the inferior part of the breast into lymph nodes of the anterior abdominal wall. The central and apical axillary nodes receive lymphatic from the pectoral, lateral, and posterior axillary nodes. GAS 140-141; N 182; McM 179

A 41-year-old woman is examined in the outpatient surgical clinic for a lump in her right breast. Physical examination reveals dimpling of skin of the breast over the mass. A CT scan of the breast reveals a 3-cm mass at the right upper quadrant of her right breast with multiple calcifications. The dimpling of the breast is most likely caused by invasion of the tumor into which of the following structure(s)?
  1. A. Lactiferous ducts
  2. B. Mammary and apical lymph nodes
  3. C. Suspensory ligaments
  4. D. Deltopectoral fascia
  5. E. Medial and lateral pectoral nerves
AnswerC. Suspensory ligaments
Explanation from the source
C. The suspensory ligaments (of Cooper) are well-defined condensations of connective tissue that run from the clavicle to the dermis of the skin overlying the breast. They support and suspend the breast from the chest wall. Carcinoma of the breast produces tension on these ligaments and causes dimpling of the breast. Invasion of the axillary lymph nodes results in stagnation and fibrosis of lymph resulting in the peau d’orange appearance of the overlying skin. GAS 140-141; N 179; McM 179

A 45-year-old woman is being examined as a candidate for cosmetic breast surgery. The surgeon notes that both of her breasts sag considerably. Which structure(s) has most likely become stretched to result in this condition?
  1. A. Scarpa’s fascia
  2. B. Pectoralis major muscle
  3. C. Pectoralis minor muscle
  4. D. Suspensory (Cooper’s) ligaments
  5. E. Serratus anterior muscle
AnswerD. Suspensory (Cooper’s) ligaments
Explanation from the source
D. The suspensory ligaments of the breast, also known as Cooper’s ligaments, are fibrous bands that run from the dermis of the skin to the deep layer of superficial fascia and are primary supports for the breasts against gravity. Ptosis of the breast is usually due to the stretching of these ligaments and can be repaired with plastic surgery. Scarpa’s fascia is the deep membranous layer of superficial fascia of the anterior abdominal wall. The pectoralis major and pectoralis minor are muscles that move the upper limb and lie deep to the breast but do not provide any direct support structure to the breast. The serratus anterior muscle is involved in the movements of the scapula. GAS 131, 139; N 179; McM 179

The 35-year-old woman has a hard breast nodule about 1 cm in diameter slightly above and lateral to the right areola of her right breast. A specific dye is injected into the tissue around the tumor, and an incision is made to expose the lymphatic vessels draining the area, for the lymphatic vessels to take up the dye, which is visible to the eye. The vessels can then be traced to surgically expose the lymph nodes receiving the lymph from the tumor. Which of the following nodes will most likely first encounter the lymph from the tumor?
  1. A. Anterior axillary (pectoral) nodes
  2. B. Rotter’s interpectoral nodes
  3. C. Parasternal nodes along the internal thoracic artery and vein
  4. D. Central axillary nodes
  5. E. Apical or infraclavicular nodes
AnswerA. Anterior axillary (pectoral) nodes
Explanation from the source
A. The anterior axillary (or anterior pectoral) nodes are the first lymph nodes to receive most of the lymph from the breast parenchyma, areola, and nipple. From there, lymph flows through central axillary, apical, and supraclavicular nodes in sequence. The interpectoral Rotter’s nodes lie between the pectoral muscles and are, unfortunately, an alternate route in some patients, speeding the rate of metastasis. The parasternal nodes receive lymph from the medial part of the breast and lie along the internal thoracic artery and vein. GAS 748; N 403; McM 179

A 47-year-old woman’s right breast exhibited characteristics of peau d’orange, that is, the skin resembled an orange peel. This condition is primarily a result of which of the following?
  1. A. Shortening of the suspensory ligaments by cancer in the axillary tail (of Spence) of the breast
  2. B. Blockage of cutaneous lymphatic vessels
  3. C. Contraction of the retinacula cutis of the areola and nipple
  4. D. Invasion of the pectoralis major by the cancer
  5. E. Ipsilateral (same side) inversion of the periareolar skin from ductular cancer
AnswerB. Blockage of cutaneous lymphatic vessels
Explanation from the source
B. When cutaneous lymphatics of the breast are blocked by cancer, the skin becomes edematous, except where hair follicles cause small indentations of the skin, giving an overall resemblance to orange peel. Shortening of the suspensory ligaments (of Cooper) or retinacula cutis leads to pitting of the overlying skin, pitting that is intensified if the patient raises her arm above her head. Invasion of the pectoralis major by cancer can result in fixation of the breast, seen upon elevation of the ipsilateral limb. Inversion of areolar skin with involvement of the ducts would also be due to involvement of the retinacula cutis. GAS 748; N 181; McM 179

(M1.BC.14.71) A 16-year-old presents to the primary care physician because he has noticed an increase in the size of his breast tissue over the past 3 years. He states that he is significantly taller than his entire class at school although he feels increasingly weak and uncoordinated. He performs at the bottom of his grade level academically. On physical exam the patient has marked gynecomastia with small firm testes. The physician decides to perform a karyotype on the patient. What is the most likely outcome of this test?
  1. 1 47, XXY
  2. 2 46, XY
  3. 3 47, XY
  4. 4 45, XO
  5. 5 47, XXX
Answer1. 47, XXY
Explanation from the source
This patient has the typical features of Klinefelter syndrome (47, XXY) including tall stature, gynecomastia, small testes, and mild mental retardation. Klinefelter syndrome is often diagnosed during adolescence when patients begin to exhibit the above characteristics. The severity and presentation of the syndrome can often vary based on mosaicism. It often occurs secondary to an event of nondisjunction during gametogenesis. There is little treatment for these patients. Gynecomastia can be addressed surgically and psychosocial issues can be intervened upon through therapy. Many patients can go on to live normal adult lives.
Deciding fact is the karyotype of Klinefelter syndrome (genetics; the scope document says Klinefelter genetics is not Anatomy). Kept as borderline because the CP1 breast lecture teaches gynecomastia in ~40% of males with Klinefelter syndrome at puberty, the key clue here.

An 80-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a lump in her right breast. Physical examination shows a 2-cm mass in the right breast with dimpling of the overlying skin and peau d’orange (edema of the breast with the skin assuming the appearance of an orange peel). Examination of a biopsy specimen confirms a diagnosis of carcinoma. Involvement of what structure is the most likely cause of this patient’s skin dimpling?
  1. (A) Clavipectoral fascia
  2. (B) Suspensory ligaments
  3. (C) Lactiferous ducts
  4. (D) Retromammary space
  5. (E) Pectoralis major
AnswerB. Suspensory ligaments
Explanation from the source
Suspensory Ligaments. Fibrous lobar septa are connective tissue partitions that separate the glandular lobes of the breast and compartmentalize breast tissue. These septa run through the depth of the breast from the dermis of the skin to the underlying pectoral fascia and are most pronounced in the superior aspect of the breast, where they are termed suspensory (Cooper’s) ligaments of the breast. Edema and/or tumor growth within the breast can apply traction on the suspensory ligaments, and this tension causes dimpling of the skin that resembles an orange peel. Choice A (Clavipectoral fascia) is incorrect. This sleeve of connective tissue extends from the clavicle to the deep fascia of the axilla and envelopes the subclavius and pectoralis minor muscles. It does not enter the breast. Choice C (Lactiferous ducts) is incorrect. Each of the 15 to 20 glandular lobes of the breast is drained by a lactiferous duct that opens in the lactiferous sinus and then onto the nipple. Edema and/or tumor growth within the breast may apply traction to these ducts. However, the result of such traction is typically inversion of the nipple rather than dimpling of the skin. Choice D (Retromammary space) is incorrect. The retromammary space (or bursa) is a loose connective tissue plane between the breast and pectoral fascia, which contains a small amount of fat and allows the breast some degree of mobility on the pectoral fascia. It does not send connective tissue extensions into the substance of the breast and would not lead to dimpling of the skin due to the presence of an abnormal growth within the breast. Choice E (Pectoralis major muscle) is incorrect. The pectoralis major underlies the breast but does not send fibers into the breast. It does not influence the appearance of the skin of the breast.

A 48-year-old woman is diagnosed with a malignant tumor in the superolateral quadrant of the right breast, including the axillary tail. If it metastasizes, this cancer will most likely spread first to which of the following locations?
  1. (A) Lateral axillary lymph nodes
  2. (B) Anterior axillary lymph nodes
  3. (C) Deep cervical lymph nodes
  4. (D) Parasternal lymph nodes
  5. (E) Contralateral breast lymph nodes
AnswerB. Anterior axillary lymph nodes
Explanation from the source
Anterior axillary lymph nodes. The primary lymphatic drainage route for the lateral half of the breast (including the axillary tail) plus part of the medial half of the breast is first into the anterior (pectoral; Level 1) axillary lymph nodes. These lymph nodes are located along the lateral border of the pectoralis minor muscle. Further metastasis would spread progressively to the central axillary (Level 2) nodes, then the apical axillary (Level 3) nodes. Choice A (Lateral axillary lymph nodes) is incorrect. These nodes, located along the distal segment of the axillary vein, collect the lymphatic drainage from most of the upper limb. They drain to the central axillary (Level 2) nodes. Choice C (Deep cervical lymph nodes) is incorrect. These nodes are located in the neck, along the internal jugular vein, and collect lymph from the head and neck. Choice D (Parasternal lymph nodes) is incorrect. The parasternal (internal thoracic) nodes lie along the internal thoracic vessels within the chest. Most of the medial half of the breast sends its lymphatic drainage primarily to these nodes. Choice E (Contralateral breast lymph nodes) is incorrect. Small areas of the medial aspect of the breast may send an accessory lymphatic drainage across the midline to the contralateral nodes of the opposite breast. Due to the site of the tumor, this lymphatic drainage pattern is unlikely.

354
Organization of the axillary lymph nodes into Levels I, II, and III for breast cancer treatment is based on the location of the nodes relative to which of the following muscles?
  1. (A) Pectoralis minor
  2. (B) Pectoralis major
  3. (C) Latissimus dorsi
  4. (D) Serratus anterior
  5. (E) Subscapularis
Answer(A) Pectoralis minor
Explanation from the source
Pectoralis minor. The pectoralis minor muscle forms a portion of the anterior axillary wall and is used as a marker to organize the contained groups of axillary lymph nodes. In a clinical context, the axillary nodes are organized into three major groups (Level 1, 2, and 3) that denote the progressive lymph drainage of the breast. Level 1 (anterior; pectoral) nodes are located along the lateral border of the pectoralis minor. Level 2 (central; deep) nodes are situated in the center of the axilla, deep (posterior) to the pectoralis minor. Level 3 (apical; medial) nodes are positioned in the apex of the axilla, superior to the upper medial border of the pectoralis minor. Detection of cancer cells in each increasing number level of nodes indicates progressively greater metastasis of the disease out of the breast. Choice B (Pectoralis major) is incorrect. The pectoralis major and minor form the anterior axillary wall. However, the pectoralis major muscle is not used to classify the positions of the axillary lymph nodes or levels of metastasis. Choice C (Latissimus dorsi) is incorrect. The latissimus dorsi muscle helps to form the posterior wall of the axilla along with the subscapularis and teres major muscles. Due to its posterior location, it is not an important landmark for classification of axillary lymph nodes in breast cancer. Choice D (Serratus anterior) is incorrect. This muscle contributes to the formation of the medial wall of the axilla, along with the thoracic cage. This muscle is not an important landmark for classification of axillary lymph nodes in breast cancer. Choice E (Subscapularis) is incorrect. The subscapularis muscle helps to form the posterior wall of the axilla along with the latissimus dorsi and teres major muscles. Due to its posterior location, this muscle is not an important landmark for classification of axillary lymph nodes in breast cancer.
