ANAT-4 Pleura & lungs

239 questions · 59 high-yield
Learning questions 132

The pleura and the pleural cavity

L1Learning
How is the thoracic cavity divided into compartments?
  1. A. Two pleural cavities, one per lung, with the mediastinum between them
  2. B. Two pleural cavities, one per lung, with the diaphragm between them
  3. C. One pleural cavity around both lungs, with the mediastinum inside it
AnswerA. Two pleural cavities, one per lung, with the mediastinum between them
The thoracic cavity holds two separate pleural cavities (one per lung) with the mediastinum between them; the heart has its own sac, the pericardium.
Explanation

The thoracic cavity has three compartments: a right and a left pulmonary (pleural) cavity, each lined by its own pleural sac, and the central mediastinum, which holds the heart, great vessels, trachea and oesophagus. Each organ has a two-layered serous lining: pleura for the lungs, pericardium for the heart.

  • The diaphragm is the floor under both pleural cavities; it does not separate them from each other.
  • There is no single pleural cavity: the two sacs are completely separate, so air in one side (pneumothorax) does not collapse the other lung.
Slide (1)
L2Learning
What is the visceral pleura?
  1. A. The pleura stuck tightly to the lung surface
  2. B. The pleura lining the inside of the chest wall
  3. C. The fascia separating the pleura from the ribs
AnswerA. The pleura stuck tightly to the lung surface
The visceral pleura is fused to the lung itself ("visceral" = on the organ) and cannot be peeled off it.
Explanation

Each serous membrane has two layers: the visceral layer, intimately attached to the organ's surface, and the parietal layer, lining the wall of the cavity (Latin paries = wall). They are one continuous sheet, folded back on itself at the root of the lung.

  • The pleura lining the chest wall is the parietal layer (its costal part).
  • The fascia between pleura and ribs is the endothoracic fascia, a connective-tissue layer, not pleura.

Hook: VISceral = VISiting the lung; PARietal = PART of the wall.

Slides (2)
L3Learning
What does the parietal pleura line?
  1. A. The lung surface, including the fissures between the lobes
  2. B. The inside of the chest wall, the diaphragm and the mediastinum
  3. C. The surface of the heart and the roots of the great vessels
AnswerB. The inside of the chest wall, the diaphragm and the mediastinum
The parietal pleura lines the walls of each pulmonary cavity: the chest wall, the upper surface of the diaphragm and the side of the mediastinum.
Explanation

The parietal pleura is named by what it touches: costal (ribs and intercostal spaces), diaphragmatic, mediastinal and cervical (the dome over the lung apex). It is separated from the chest wall by the endothoracic fascia.

  • The lung surface and fissures are covered by the visceral pleura, which dips into the fissures.
  • The heart and great vessel roots are covered by the serous pericardium, the heart's own lining; mediastinal pleura lies only on the lateral side of the pericardial sac.
Slides (2)
L4Learning
In the "fist pushed into a balloon" model of the pleura, what does each part represent?
  1. A. Fist = lung
    Balloon wall touching fist = parietal pleura
    Rest of balloon = visceral pleura
    Squashed space between = pleural cavity
  2. B. Fist = heart
    Balloon wall touching fist = visceral pleura
    Rest of balloon = parietal pleura
    Squashed space between = mediastinum
  3. C. Fist = lung
    Balloon wall touching fist = visceral pleura
    Rest of balloon = parietal pleura
    Squashed space between = pleural cavity
AnswerC. Fist = lung
Balloon wall touching fist = visceral pleura
Rest of balloon = parietal pleura
Squashed space between = pleural cavity
Fist = lung; balloon wall touching the fist = visceral pleura; outer balloon wall = parietal pleura; the squashed space between = pleural cavity.
Explanation

Push a fist into a soft balloon: the balloon wraps the fist in two layers that are continuous where the wrist goes in. The lung bud grows into its pleural sac in the same way in the embryo.

  • The layer in contact with the organ is always visceral; the outer layer is parietal. Swapping them is the classic error.
  • The wrist corresponds to the root of the lung, where the two layers meet.
  • The heart has the same arrangement with the pericardium, but the space there is the pericardial cavity, not the mediastinum (the mediastinum is the whole middle compartment of the chest).
Slide (1)
L5Learning
Where are the visceral and parietal pleura continuous with each other?
  1. A. At the apex of the lung, under the cupula
  2. B. Around the root of the lung at the hilum
  3. C. Along the inferior border of the lung
AnswerB. Around the root of the lung at the hilum
The two layers turn into each other in a sleeve around the root of the lung at the hilum; below the root the sleeve hangs down as the pulmonary ligament.
Explanation

The hilum is the area where bronchus, vessels, nerves and lymphatics enter the lung; the bundle of these structures is the root. Visceral pleura cannot cover this area, so it turns back around the root and becomes mediastinal parietal pleura. Below the root this loose sleeve forms a double fold, the pulmonary ligament, so the layers are continuous there too.

  • At the apex, the visceral pleura lies against the cervical parietal pleura (cupula) across the pleural cavity; the layers do not join.
  • At the inferior border, the lung lies above the costodiaphragmatic recess, which keeps the layers apart.
Slides (2)
L6Learning
What is the pleural cavity?
  1. A. A potential space between visceral and parietal pleura, holding a thin film of fluid
  2. B. A potential space between parietal pleura and endothoracic fascia, holding fat
  3. C. A real air-filled space between lung and chest wall, holding no fluid
AnswerA. A potential space between visceral and parietal pleura, holding a thin film of fluid
The pleural cavity is a potential space between visceral and parietal pleura that contains only a thin film of serous fluid.
Explanation

A potential space is one whose walls normally touch: the two pleural layers are separated only by a capillary film of serous pleural fluid. The space becomes real only when something collects in it: air (pneumothorax), blood, watery fluid or lymph.

  • It holds no air normally; air there is a pneumothorax and the lung collapses.
  • The layer between parietal pleura and chest wall is the endothoracic fascia, a connective-tissue plane outside the pleural sac, not the pleural cavity.

The pleural cavity is not a third layer; it is the gap between the two layers.

Slides (2)
L7Learning
What is the normal job of the serous fluid in the pleural cavity?
  1. A. Lubricates the pleural layers so they slide over each other in breathing
  2. B. Cushions the lung against the ribs as a shock absorber
  3. C. Supplies surfactant that lowers surface tension in the alveoli
AnswerA. Lubricates the pleural layers so they slide over each other in breathing
The thin film of pleural fluid is a lubricant: it lets the visceral pleura glide over the parietal pleura as the lung expands and recoils.
Explanation

With each breath the lung surface moves against the chest wall and diaphragm. The film of serous fluid removes friction, so the layers slide silently. The same film also makes the layers cling together (like two wet glass slides), so the lung follows the chest wall outward.

  • The film is far too thin to act as a shock absorber.
  • Surfactant is made by type II pneumocytes inside the alveoli; pleural fluid has nothing to do with it.

When the pleura is inflamed (pleuritis) the lubrication fails and a friction rub can be heard.

Slides (2)
L8Learning
Why does the lung collapse when the parietal pleura is pierced?
  1. A. Air enters the alveoli → surface tension rises → the chest wall springs outward
  2. B. Air enters the pleural cavity → the layers separate → the elastic lung recoils toward the hilum
  3. C. Blood enters the pleural cavity → the layers stick → the diaphragm pushes the lung up
AnswerB. Air enters the pleural cavity → the layers separate → the elastic lung recoils toward the hilum
Air entering the pleural cavity breaks the fluid seal between lung and wall; the lung's own elastic recoil then shrinks it toward the hilum: a pneumothorax.
Explanation

The lung is elastic and always tends to recoil inward; it stays expanded only because the pleural fluid film keeps the visceral pleura stuck to the parietal pleura on the chest wall. Once air enters the potential space, the layers separate and the lung collapses toward its root.

  • Air in the alveoli is normal; it does not collapse the lung.
  • Blood in the cavity (haemothorax) separates the layers too; it does not make them stick, and the diaphragm does not push the lung up.

Because each lung has its own sac, only the punctured side collapses.

Slide (1)

Parietal pleura, cupula and reflections

L9Learning
Name the four parts of the parietal pleura (named by what they line).
  1. A. Cervical
    Costal
    Diaphragmatic
    Pericardial
  2. B. Cervical
    Sternal
    Diaphragmatic
    Vertebral
  3. C. Cervical
    Costal
    Diaphragmatic
    Mediastinal
AnswerC. Cervical
Costal
Diaphragmatic
Mediastinal
Parietal pleura is named by what it lines: cervical (the cupula), costal, diaphragmatic and mediastinal.
Explanation

The four parts form one continuous sheet:

  • Costal: lines the ribs, costal cartilages and intercostal spaces.
  • Diaphragmatic: covers the upper surface of the diaphragm.
  • Mediastinal: covers the side of the mediastinum and turns into visceral pleura at the root.
  • Cervical (cupula): the dome rising into the neck over the lung apex.

Pericardial is not a part: pleura lying on the pericardium is still mediastinal pleura. Sternal and vertebral are names of reflection lines (where costal pleura turns into mediastinal pleura), not parts.

Slides (2)
L10Learning
What layer separates the parietal pleura from the chest wall?
  1. A. Transversalis fascia
  2. B. Endothoracic fascia
  3. C. Pretracheal fascia
AnswerB. Endothoracic fascia
A thin layer of endothoracic fascia lies between the costal parietal pleura and the inner surface of the ribs and intercostal muscles.
Explanation

The endothoracic fascia is the loose connective tissue lining the inside of the thoracic cage. It gives a cleavage plane along which surgeons can strip the parietal pleura off the wall. It is thickened over the cupula as the suprapleural membrane and continues on the diaphragm as the phrenicopleural fascia.

  • Transversalis fascia is its counterpart inside the abdominal wall.
  • Pretracheal fascia is a layer of deep cervical fascia around the trachea and thyroid in the neck.
Slides (2)
L11Learning
What is the cupula?
  1. A. Cervical parietal pleura, rising into the root of the neck over the lung apex
  2. B. Visceral pleura covering the lung apex inside the thoracic inlet
  3. C. Mediastinal parietal pleura folding around the root of the lung
AnswerA. Cervical parietal pleura, rising into the root of the neck over the lung apex
The cupula (cervical pleura) is the dome of parietal pleura that rises through the superior thoracic aperture into the neck, above the first rib, capping the lung apex.
Explanation

The cupula projects about an inch (2–3 cm) above the medial third of the clavicle into the root of the neck. It is reinforced by the suprapleural membrane (thickened endothoracic fascia), and the subclavian artery arches over its front.

  • The pleura stuck on the lung apex is visceral; the cupula is parietal.
  • The fold of mediastinal pleura around the root is where parietal pleura turns into visceral pleura, not the cupula.
Slides (2)
L12Learning
What is the suprapleural membrane?
  1. A. A thickening of cervical parietal pleura that seals the pleural cavity at the thoracic inlet
  2. B. A fold of visceral pleura that holds the lung apex to the first rib
  3. C. A thickening of endothoracic fascia that roofs the cupula, attached to the 1st rib and C7
AnswerC. A thickening of endothoracic fascia that roofs the cupula, attached to the 1st rib and C7
The suprapleural membrane (Sibson fascia) is endothoracic fascia thickened over the cupula, running from the inner border of the 1st rib to the C7 transverse process.
Explanation

It reinforces the dome of cervical pleura and stops the cupula bulging up into the neck as intrathoracic pressure changes. It is fascia, not pleura: it lies outside the parietal pleura, just as the endothoracic fascia does everywhere else on the wall.

  • Calling it part of the parietal pleura is the classic trap.
  • No fold of visceral pleura anchors the apex; visceral pleura is stuck to the lung only.
Slides (2)
L13Learning
A stab wound just above the middle of the right clavicle is followed by collapse of the right lung. Which part of the pleura was breached?
  1. A. Costal parietal pleura
  2. B. Cervical parietal pleura (cupula)
  3. C. Mediastinal parietal pleura
AnswerB. Cervical parietal pleura (cupula)
The cupula rises above the clavicle into the root of the neck, so a wound there opens the pleural cavity and causes a pneumothorax.
Explanation

Because the lung apex and its cervical pleura project about an inch above the clavicle, the pleural cavity can be entered from the neck: by stab or bullet wounds, or by a needle aimed at the subclavian vein or the brachial plexus. Air then enters the pleural cavity and the lung collapses.

  • The costal pleura lines the ribs below the clavicle; a supraclavicular wound does not reach it first.
  • The mediastinal pleura lies deep in the middle of the chest beside the mediastinum.
Slides (2)
L14Learning
What are the lines of pleural reflection?
  1. A. Lines where visceral pleura turns into parietal pleura
  2. B. Lines where one part of the parietal pleura turns into the next
  3. C. Lines that mark the lung's inferior border in quiet breathing
AnswerB. Lines where one part of the parietal pleura turns into the next
Lines of pleural reflection are where the parietal pleura changes direction from one part to the next, e.g. costal into mediastinal or diaphragmatic.
Explanation

The parietal pleura is one sheet; where the wall it lines changes direction, the pleura bends sharply. These bends outline the pleural sac on the body surface:

  • Sternal line: costal → mediastinal, anteriorly.
  • Costal line: costal → diaphragmatic, inferiorly.
  • Vertebral line: costal → mediastinal, posteriorly.

Visceral pleura turns into parietal pleura only at the root of the lung, which is not a reflection line. The lung's inferior border lies about two ribs higher than the costal line; the gap is the costodiaphragmatic recess.

Slide (1)
L15Learning
At the sternal and vertebral lines of pleural reflection, what does the costal pleura turn into?
  1. A. Mediastinal pleura
  2. B. Diaphragmatic pleura
  3. C. Cervical pleura
AnswerA. Mediastinal pleura
At the sternal (front) and vertebral (back) lines the costal pleura turns medially to become mediastinal pleura.
Explanation

Follow the costal pleura round the chest: in front it reaches the sternum and turns back along the side of the mediastinum (sternal line); behind it reaches the vertebral bodies and turns forward onto the mediastinum (vertebral line). Both lines therefore join costal and mediastinal pleura.

  • Costal → diaphragmatic happens at the costal line, inferiorly.
  • Costal → cervical is a smooth continuation at the thoracic inlet with no named reflection line.
Slide (1)
L16Learning
At the costal line of pleural reflection, what does the costal pleura turn into, and where is the line?
  1. A. Mediastinal pleura, anteriorly
  2. B. Visceral pleura, posteriorly
  3. C. Diaphragmatic pleura, inferiorly
AnswerC. Diaphragmatic pleura, inferiorly
The costal line is the lower edge of the pleural sac: there the costal pleura turns onto the diaphragm as diaphragmatic pleura.
Explanation

The costal line runs round the lower chest at about the 8th rib in the midclavicular line, the 10th rib in the midaxillary line and T12 beside the spine. It lies about two rib levels below the lung's inferior border, so the costodiaphragmatic recess lies just above it.

  • Costal → mediastinal happens at the sternal (anterior) and vertebral (posterior) lines.
  • Parietal pleura never turns into visceral pleura at a reflection line; that happens only at the lung root.
Slide (1)
L17Learning
What is the pulmonary ligament?
  1. A. A loose double fold of visceral pleura within the oblique fissure, running from the hilum toward the base
  2. B. A fibrous band of endothoracic fascia below the lung root, anchoring the lung to the diaphragm
  3. C. A loose double fold of mediastinal pleura below the lung root, running from the hilum toward the diaphragmatic surface
AnswerC. A loose double fold of mediastinal pleura below the lung root, running from the hilum toward the diaphragmatic surface
The pulmonary ligament is the loose, empty double fold of mediastinal pleura that hangs below the lung root toward the diaphragmatic surface.
Explanation

The pleural sleeve around the root is roomier than the root itself. Below the root its front and back walls come together as a two-layered fold containing only a little connective tissue. It runs from the hilum down the mediastinal surface toward the base of the lung, and parietal and visceral layers are continuous along it.

  • It is not in the oblique fissure: each lobe's visceral pleura simply lines the fissure.
  • It is pleura, not fascia, and despite its name it does not firmly anchor the lung to the diaphragm.
Slides (2)
L18Learning
What is the function of the pulmonary ligament?
  1. A. Anchors the lung firmly to the diaphragm
  2. B. Drains pleural fluid toward the hilum
  3. C. Gives the root structures room to expand
AnswerC. Gives the root structures room to expand
The slack of the pulmonary ligament gives the root's vessels room to expand, for example when venous return rises during exercise.
Explanation

When blood flow through the lungs rises, the pulmonary veins in the root distend. The loose pleural sleeve below the root lets them enlarge downward instead of being squeezed by a tight collar of pleura.

  • Despite being called a ligament, it is too thin and loose to anchor the lung to the diaphragm.
  • Pleural fluid is absorbed by pleural capillaries and lymphatics; the ligament is not a drainage channel.

The updated 2026 lecture gives a second role: the slack fold lets the root structures move up and down with each breath.

Slide (1)
L19Learning
Which description fits the visceral pleura?
  1. A. Shiny and inseparable from the lung; covers all lung surfaces, fissures included, except the hilum
  2. B. Rough and easily stripped from the lung; covers all surfaces except the fissures and hilum
  3. C. Shiny and inseparable from the lung; covers the costal surface only, not the fissures
AnswerA. Shiny and inseparable from the lung; covers all lung surfaces, fissures included, except the hilum
Visceral pleura is shiny, cannot be separated from the lung, and covers every lung surface, dipping into the fissures, except the hilum.
Explanation

The visceral pleura is fused to the lung tissue, so it cannot be dissected off. It gives the lung its glossy surface and follows the lung into the horizontal and oblique fissures, so each lobe has a complete pleural covering. The only bare area is the hilum, where the root structures enter and the visceral pleura turns into parietal pleura.

  • It is the parietal pleura that can be stripped (from the wall, along the endothoracic fascia).
  • Covering only the costal surface would leave the diaphragmatic and mediastinal surfaces bare; they are covered too.
Slide (1)

Pleural recesses

L20Learning
What is a pleural recess?
  1. A. Part of the pleural cavity the lung fills, where visceral pleura lines a fissure
  2. B. Part of the pleural cavity the lung does not fill, where two parts of parietal pleura meet
  3. C. The point at the hilum where parietal pleura turns back into visceral pleura
AnswerB. Part of the pleural cavity the lung does not fill, where two parts of parietal pleura meet
Pleural recesses are parts of the pleural cavity that the lung does not fill in quiet breathing, so two parietal surfaces lie against each other.
Explanation

The parietal pleura follows the chest wall and diaphragm, but the lungs are smaller than their pleural sacs. Where the lung stops short, the cavity continues as a slit between two parietal layers: costal against diaphragmatic below (costodiaphragmatic recess) and costal against mediastinal in front (costomediastinal recess). The lung slides into them only in deep inspiration.

  • The fissures have lung on both sides, lined by visceral pleura; they are not recesses.
  • The turning of parietal into visceral pleura at the hilum forms the root sleeve and pulmonary ligament.
Slides (2)
L21Learning
Where is the costomediastinal recess?
  1. A. Above the lung apex, where cervical pleura meets costal pleura
  2. B. Behind the lung root, where mediastinal pleura meets the vertebral bodies
  3. C. Behind the sternum, where costal pleura meets mediastinal pleura
AnswerC. Behind the sternum, where costal pleura meets mediastinal pleura
The costomediastinal recess lies anteriorly, behind the sternum and costal cartilages, where costal pleura meets mediastinal pleura at the sternal line.
Explanation

The anterior borders of the lungs stop just short of the sternal lines of reflection, leaving a narrow slit of pleural cavity behind the sternum. It is largest on the left, opposite the cardiac notch, where the lung edge swings away from the heart. It is the smaller of the two recesses.

  • Above the apex there is no recess: the lung fills the cupula.
  • Behind the root and beside the vertebral bodies, the costal pleura turns onto the mediastinum at the vertebral line; the costomediastinal recess is the anterior one, behind the sternum.
Slides (2)
L22Learning
Where is the costodiaphragmatic recess?
  1. A. Below the lung root, between the two layers of the pulmonary ligament
  2. B. Below the inferior border of the lung, between costal and diaphragmatic pleura
  3. C. Above the lung apex, between cervical and costal pleura
AnswerB. Below the inferior border of the lung, between costal and diaphragmatic pleura
The costodiaphragmatic recess is the slit of pleural cavity below the lung's inferior border, between costal and diaphragmatic pleura: the lowest part of the cavity.
Explanation

The diaphragm's dome rises steeply from its costal attachment, so costal and diaphragmatic pleura meet at an acute angle round the lower chest. The lung's thin inferior border stops about two ribs above that angle, leaving a deep gutter of pleural cavity with no lung in it. It is the largest recess and, in an upright person, the lowest point of the pleural cavity.

  • The pulmonary ligament is a pleural fold below the root, not a space.
  • Above the apex, cervical pleura caps the lung directly; there is no recess.
Slides (2)
L23Learning
Which ribs does the costodiaphragmatic recess span in the midaxillary line?
  1. A. Roughly 6th → 8th ribs
  2. B. Roughly 10th → 12th ribs
  3. C. Roughly 8th → 10th ribs
AnswerC. Roughly 8th → 10th ribs
In the midaxillary line the lung ends at the 8th rib and the pleura at the 10th, so the recess spans ribs 8–10.
Explanation

The recess is the gap between the lung's inferior border and the pleura's costal line; it is about two ribs deep all round:

LineRecess spans
Midclavicularribs 6 → 8
Midaxillaryribs 8 → 10
ParavertebralT10 → T12

6 → 8 is the midclavicular span; 10 → 12 mixes up the posterior (vertebral) levels. The 8–10 span in the midaxillary line is why thoracentesis goes through the 9th intercostal space there.

Slides (2)
L24Learning
When does the lung expand down into the costodiaphragmatic recess?
  1. A. Throughout quiet breathing
  2. B. Only during forced expiration
  3. C. During deep inspiration
AnswerC. During deep inspiration
In quiet breathing the recess stays empty; only in deep inspiration does the lung's inferior border slide down into it (partly).
Explanation

As the diaphragm descends strongly in deep inspiration, the costodiaphragmatic angle opens and the expanding lung edge moves down into the recess, so the empty recess is actually smaller in inspiration. In expiration the lung edge withdraws upward and the two parietal layers fall back together.

  • In quiet breathing the lung border stays at about ribs 6/8/T10, above the recess; that is what makes the recess a safe needle target.
  • In forced expiration the lung retreats even further up, away from the recess.
Slide (1)
L25Learning
In a patient sitting upright, where does a pleural effusion collect first, and why?
  1. A. Costomediastinal recess: the lowest point of the cavity
  2. B. Costodiaphragmatic recess: the lowest point of the cavity
  3. C. Cupula: the point where the pleura is thinnest
AnswerB. Costodiaphragmatic recess: the lowest point of the cavity
Fluid sinks: in an upright patient the costodiaphragmatic recess is the lowest part of the pleural cavity, so effusions fill it first.
Explanation

A pleural effusion is excess fluid in the pleural cavity. Gravity carries it to the most dependent part: in a standing or sitting patient that is the costodiaphragmatic recess, where the peripheral diaphragmatic pleura meets the lowest costal pleura. On an upright chest X-ray this blunts the costophrenic angle, and it is where the fluid is tapped by thoracentesis.

  • The costomediastinal recess is anterior and high, behind the sternum.
  • The cupula is the highest point; fluid reaches it last.
Slides (2)

Nerves of the pleura and pleural pain

L26Learning
What nerves supply the parietal pleura, and how pain-sensitive is it?
  1. A. Autonomic (phrenic and splanchnic nerves) → exquisitely pain-sensitive
  2. B. Somatic (intercostal and phrenic nerves) → exquisitely pain-sensitive
  3. C. Somatic (intercostal and vagus nerves) → poorly localised dull pain only
AnswerB. Somatic (intercostal and phrenic nerves) → exquisitely pain-sensitive
The parietal pleura gets somatic sensory fibres from the intercostal and phrenic nerves, so it is very sensitive to pain.
Explanation

Parietal pleura is part of the body wall, so it shares the wall's somatic sensory supply: intercostal nerves for the costal and peripheral diaphragmatic pleura, and the phrenic nerve (C3–C5) for the mediastinal and central diaphragmatic pleura. Somatic fibres carry sharp, well-localised pain that worsens with breathing.

  • The phrenic nerve is somatic (motor and sensory), not autonomic; splanchnic nerves serve the abdominal viscera.
  • The vagus nerve carries autonomic fibres to the lung and visceral pleura; it does not supply the parietal pleura.
Slide (1)
L27Learning
What is the nerve supply of the visceral pleura, and is it pain-sensitive?
  1. A. Autonomic only → insensitive to pain
  2. B. Somatic intercostal nerves → sensitive to pain
  3. C. Phrenic nerve → sensitive to pain
AnswerA. Autonomic only → insensitive to pain
The visceral pleura is supplied by autonomic fibres of the pulmonary plexus, like the lung itself, so it is insensitive to pain.
Explanation

Visceral pleura develops with the lung and shares its autonomic supply from the pulmonary plexus (vagal and sympathetic fibres). These visceral afferents respond to stretch but carry no sharp pain, so disease confined inside the visceral pleura is painless until it reaches the parietal pleura.

  • Intercostal nerves supply the costal and peripheral diaphragmatic parietal pleura.
  • The phrenic nerve supplies the mediastinal and central diaphragmatic parietal pleura.

The updated 2026 lecture adds that its visceral afferents, which run with the sympathetic fibres, respond to stretch and may give vague referred pain, but never the sharp, localised pain of the parietal pleura.

Slide (1)
L28Learning
Which nerves supply the costal pleura and the peripheral part of the diaphragmatic pleura?
  1. A. Intercostal nerves
  2. B. Pulmonary plexus
  3. C. Phrenic nerves
AnswerA. Intercostal nerves
The intercostal nerves supply the costal pleura and the periphery of the diaphragmatic pleura; pain from there is felt in the chest (or abdominal) wall.
Explanation

Each intercostal nerve runs in its intercostal space just outside the costal pleura and sends sensory twigs to it. The rim of the diaphragm is supplied by the lower intercostal nerves, and its pleura shares that supply. Pain from these parts is sharp and felt over the overlying chest wall; the lower nerves can refer it to the abdominal wall.

  • The phrenic nerves supply the mediastinal and the central diaphragmatic pleura.
  • The pulmonary plexus is autonomic and supplies the lung and visceral pleura.
Slide (1)
L29Learning
Which nerve supplies the mediastinal pleura and the central part of the diaphragmatic pleura?
  1. A. Phrenic nerve
  2. B. Sympathetic trunk
  3. C. Vagus nerve
AnswerA. Phrenic nerve
The phrenic nerve (C3–C5) supplies the mediastinal and central diaphragmatic pleura, so pain from there is referred to the shoulder.
Explanation

The phrenic nerve descends on the side of the mediastinum, in front of the lung root, to the diaphragm. On the way it gives sensory fibres to the mediastinal pleura and, from the centre of the diaphragm, to the central diaphragmatic pleura. A cut phrenic nerve therefore removes sensation from the mediastinal pleura as well as paralysing that half of the diaphragm.

  • The vagus nerve and sympathetic trunk are autonomic; they supply the lung and visceral pleura, not parietal pleura.

Hook: "C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive", and its sensory fibres explain shoulder-tip pain.

Slides (2)
L30Learning
According to the review lecture, which nerves supply the cervical pleura (the cupula)?
  1. A. Intercostal nerves on its medial side; phrenic nerve on its lateral side
  2. B. Phrenic nerve on its medial side; intercostal nerves on its lateral side
  3. C. Vagus nerve on its medial side; intercostal nerves on its lateral side
AnswerB. Phrenic nerve on its medial side; intercostal nerves on its lateral side
The cervical pleura takes the phrenic nerve medially and the intercostal nerves laterally: each part of the parietal pleura is supplied by the somatic nerve of what it touches.
Explanation

The cupula is the dome of parietal pleura rising above the 1st rib into the root of the neck. Like all parietal pleura it has somatic, pain-sensitive supply. The review slide splits it by contact: its medial side faces the root of the neck and the mediastinum, where the phrenic nerve passes down in front of the dome into the thorax; its lateral side lies against the 1st rib and the upper intercostal space, supplied by intercostal nerves. The same rule gives the costal pleura intercostal supply and the mediastinal pleura phrenic supply.

  • Swapping the two reverses the anatomy: the phrenic nerve runs medially, beside the mediastinum, not on the lateral chest wall.
  • The vagus is autonomic; it supplies the lung and visceral pleura, not parietal pleura.

Textbooks often give no separate supply for the cervical pleura; this split is the lecturer's.

Slide (1)
L31Learning
A patient has sharp, well-localised chest pain that worsens on deep inspiration. Which layer of pleura is the source?
  1. A. Visceral pleura
  2. B. Parietal pleura
  3. C. Pulmonary ligament
AnswerB. Parietal pleura
Sharp pain that worsens with breathing is pleuritic pain: it comes from the somatically innervated parietal pleura.
Explanation

Each breath stretches the pleura and slides the layers over each other. Only the parietal layer has somatic pain fibres (intercostal and phrenic nerves), so inflammation reaching it produces sharp, localisable pain that catches on inspiration.

  • The visceral pleura has only autonomic supply and is insensitive to pain; disease limited to it is painless.
  • The pulmonary ligament is a fold of mediastinal pleura below the root, not a source of chest-wall pain.
Slides (2)
L32Learning
Where are the cell bodies of the sensory neurons that carry sharp pain from the costal pleura?
  1. A. Sympathetic chain ganglia
  2. B. Lateral horn of the spinal cord
  3. C. Dorsal root ganglia
AnswerC. Dorsal root ganglia
Pain from the costal pleura travels in the intercostal nerves; like all spinal sensory neurons, their cell bodies lie in the dorsal root ganglia.
Explanation

Intercostal nerves are the ventral rami of T1–T11. Their sensory fibres belong to pseudounipolar neurons: one process runs out to the pleura and chest wall, the other enters the spinal cord through the dorsal root, and the cell body sits in the dorsal root ganglion of that segment.

  • Sympathetic chain ganglia hold postganglionic sympathetic motor neurons, not sensory cell bodies.
  • The lateral horn (T1–L2) holds preganglionic sympathetic neurons. The sensory fibres synapse in the dorsal horn, but their cell bodies are outside the cord.
Slide (1)
L33Learning
A man with pneumonia has a pleural rub and sharp pain on breathing over the lateral chest wall. Which nerves should be blocked with local anaesthetic to relieve the pain?
  1. A. Intercostal nerves
  2. B. Phrenic nerve
  3. C. Vagus nerve
AnswerA. Intercostal nerves
Pleuritic pain over the lateral chest wall comes from the costal parietal pleura, whose pain fibres run in the intercostal nerves; blocking them relieves it.
Explanation

The pleural rub shows inflamed pleural layers rubbing together. The painful layer is the parietal pleura, and over the lateral chest wall that is costal pleura, supplied segment by segment by the intercostal nerves. Local anaesthetic around the intercostal nerves of the affected spaces blocks the pain.

  • The phrenic nerve carries pain only from the mediastinal and central diaphragmatic pleura (felt in the shoulder), and blocking it would paralyse the hemidiaphragm.
  • The vagus nerve carries autonomic fibres from the lung and visceral pleura, not sharp chest-wall pain.
Slides (2)
L34Learning
Inflammation of the pleura over the central part of the diaphragm causes pain felt where, and through which nerve?
  1. A. Over the lower chest wall, through the intercostal nerves
  2. B. Between the scapulae, through the sympathetic trunk
  3. C. In the shoulder, through the phrenic nerve
AnswerC. In the shoulder, through the phrenic nerve
Central diaphragmatic pleura is supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3–C5); the brain refers that pain to the shoulder, whose skin is supplied by the same segments.
Explanation

Referred pain is pain felt away from its source because both share spinal cord segments. The phrenic nerve's sensory fibres enter the cord at C3–C5; the supraclavicular nerves (C3–C4) supply the skin over the shoulder. So irritation of the mediastinal or central diaphragmatic pleura is felt as shoulder-tip pain.

  • The intercostal nerves supply the peripheral diaphragmatic pleura; that pain is felt over the lower chest or abdominal wall.
  • The sympathetic trunk carries no somatic pleural pain, and pain between the scapulae is not the phrenic pattern.
Slides (2)

Blood vessels and lymph of the pleura

L35Learning
Which arteries supply the parietal pleura?
  1. A. Internal thoracic and posterior intercostal arteries
  2. B. Internal thoracic and bronchial arteries
  3. C. Pulmonary and posterior intercostal arteries
AnswerA. Internal thoracic and posterior intercostal arteries
Parietal pleura shares the chest wall's supply: internal thoracic artery branches in front and posterior intercostal arteries behind.
Explanation

Parietal pleura belongs to the body wall, so it is fed by the wall's arteries: the internal thoracic artery and its anterior intercostal branches in front, and the posterior intercostal arteries from the aorta behind.

  • Bronchial arteries supply the lung's own tissues and the visceral pleura.
  • Pulmonary arteries carry poorly oxygenated blood to the alveolar capillaries for gas exchange; they do not supply the pleura.

Rule: parietal = wall vessels; visceral = lung (bronchial) vessels.

Slide (1)
L36Learning
Where do the veins of the parietal pleura drain?
  1. A. Hemiazygos and pulmonary veins
  2. B. Brachiocephalic and pulmonary veins
  3. C. Azygos and internal thoracic veins
AnswerC. Azygos and internal thoracic veins
Parietal pleura drains with the chest wall: through intercostal veins to the azygos system behind and to the internal thoracic veins in front.
Explanation

Its veins follow the arteries: posterior intercostal veins run back to the azygos (and hemiazygos) system; anterior intercostal veins run forward to the internal thoracic veins, which end in the brachiocephalic veins.

  • The pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood from the alveoli to the left atrium; parietal pleura does not drain into them.
  • Any choice that includes the pulmonary veins is therefore wrong.
Slide (1)
L37Learning
What blood vessels supply and drain the visceral pleura?
  1. A. The chest wall's vessels: internal thoracic arteries; internal thoracic veins → brachiocephalic veins
  2. B. The lung's own bronchial vessels: bronchial arteries; bronchial veins → azygos system or left superior intercostal vein
  3. C. The intercostal vessels: posterior intercostal arteries; intercostal veins → azygos system
AnswerB. The lung's own bronchial vessels: bronchial arteries; bronchial veins → azygos system or left superior intercostal vein
The visceral pleura is fed like the lung's supporting tissue: bronchial arteries, with bronchial veins draining to the azygos system or left superior intercostal vein.
Explanation

Visceral pleura is part of the lung, so it uses the lung's nutritive (bronchial) circulation, not the chest-wall vessels. Bronchial arteries come from the thoracic aorta (on the right often through a posterior intercostal artery); bronchial veins drain to the azygos vein on the right and the hemiazygos or left superior intercostal vein on the left.

  • Internal thoracic and posterior intercostal vessels supply the parietal pleura together with the chest wall.

Answer as the lecture does. Anatomy texts add that bronchial veins drain mainly the region near the root; most blood from the visceral pleura and the peripheral lung returns through the pulmonary veins.

Slides (2)
L38Learning
Where does lymph from the parietal pleura drain?
  1. A. Tracheobronchial and deep cervical nodes
  2. B. Parasternal, mediastinal and intercostal nodes
  3. C. Bronchopulmonary (hilar) and pulmonary nodes
AnswerB. Parasternal, mediastinal and intercostal nodes
Parietal pleura lymph follows the chest wall to the parasternal, mediastinal and intercostal nodes (the "superficial" group in the lecture summary).
Explanation

Lymph from the parietal pleura drains with the wall: anteriorly along the internal thoracic vessels to parasternal nodes, posteriorly to intercostal nodes near the rib heads, and from the mediastinal and diaphragmatic parts to mediastinal nodes.

  • Bronchopulmonary (hilar) and pulmonary nodes take lymph from the lung and visceral pleura (the "deep" group).
  • Tracheobronchial nodes are the next station after the hilar nodes; deep cervical nodes drain the head and neck.
Slide (1)
L39Learning
Where does lymph from the visceral pleura drain?
  1. A. Bronchopulmonary (hilar) nodes
  2. B. Parasternal nodes
  3. C. Intercostal nodes
AnswerA. Bronchopulmonary (hilar) nodes
The visceral pleura drains with the lung, through the subpleural plexus, to the bronchopulmonary (hilar) nodes.
Explanation

A subpleural lymphatic plexus just under the visceral pleura collects lymph from the lung surface and runs to the hilum, where it joins the deep plexus at the bronchopulmonary (hilar) nodes. From there lymph goes on to the tracheobronchial nodes and the bronchomediastinal trunks.

  • Parasternal and intercostal nodes receive lymph from the parietal pleura and chest wall.
Slide (1)

Lungs: lobes, fissures, surfaces and borders

L40Learning
Why does healthy lung float in water while a stillborn baby's lungs sink?
  1. A. Healthy lung contains fat that is lighter than water; a stillborn's lungs lack fat
  2. B. Healthy lung is spongy and air-filled; a stillborn's lungs were never aerated
  3. C. Healthy lung has thin pleura; a stillborn's pleura is thick and heavy
AnswerB. Healthy lung is spongy and air-filled; a stillborn's lungs were never aerated
Air in the alveoli makes healthy lung spongy and buoyant; a stillborn never breathed, so its lungs are solid and sink.
Explanation

Lung tissue itself is denser than water; it floats only because of the air trapped in millions of alveoli, which also gives it a spongy feel. Before birth the lungs are filled with fluid, not air, so the lungs of a baby who never took a breath are solid and sink.

  • Lung contains very little fat; buoyancy comes from air.
  • The pleura is a thin membrane whose thickness makes no difference to buoyancy.
Slide (1)
L41Learning
How does the colour of the lung change with age?
  1. A. Pink at birth → grey from years of inhaled carbon
  2. B. Pink at birth → dark red from congestion with blood
  3. C. Grey at birth → pink from increasing blood supply
AnswerA. Pink at birth → grey from years of inhaled carbon
Lungs are pink at birth and become mottled grey with age as inhaled carbon particles collect in the tissue and lymphatics.
Explanation

Alveolar macrophages (dust cells) swallow inhaled carbon and soot; much of it ends up stored in the connective tissue under the pleura and along the lymphatics, giving the adult lung a grey, mottled surface, darker in city dwellers and smokers. Carbon also blackens the hilar lymph nodes.

  • Grey at birth is the reverse of reality: the newborn lung has had no exposure.
  • Dark red congestion is a sign of disease (e.g. heart failure), not normal ageing.
Slide (1)
L42Learning
How do the right and left lungs differ in size and shape?
  1. A. Right: long and narrow, deep cardiac impression
    Left: larger, heavier, short and wide, shallow cardiac impression
  2. B. Right: larger, heavier, short and wide, shallow cardiac impression
    Left: long and narrow, deep cardiac impression
  3. C. Right: larger, heavier, long and narrow, deep cardiac impression
    Left: short and wide, shallow cardiac impression
AnswerB. Right: larger, heavier, short and wide, shallow cardiac impression
Left: long and narrow, deep cardiac impression
The right lung is larger, heavier, short and wide (the liver pushes the right dome up); the left is long and narrow, with a deep cardiac impression.
Explanation

The right dome of the diaphragm sits higher over the liver, so the right lung is shorter but broader. The heart bulges to the left, so the left lung is narrower and smaller, with a deep cardiac impression and a cardiac notch.

RightLeft
Short, wide, largerLong, narrow, smaller
3 lobes, 2 fissures2 lobes, 1 fissure
Shallow cardiac impressionDeep impression, notch, lingula
1 bronchial artery2 bronchial arteries

Lobes and fissures vary between people.

Slides (2)
L43Learning
How many lobes and which fissures does the right lung have?
  1. A. 3 lobes; oblique and horizontal fissures
  2. B. 3 lobes; horizontal fissure only
  3. C. 2 lobes; oblique fissure only
AnswerA. 3 lobes; oblique and horizontal fissures
The right lung has 3 lobes (superior, middle, inferior) separated by 2 fissures: oblique and horizontal.
Explanation

The oblique fissure, present in both lungs, cuts off the inferior lobe. The horizontal fissure, found only on the right, splits the part in front of the oblique fissure into superior and middle lobes.

  • A horizontal fissure alone would leave no separate inferior lobe; the oblique fissure is the one both lungs share.
  • 2 lobes with an oblique fissure only is the left lung.

Hook: right = 3 lobes, 2 fissures; left = 2 lobes, 1 fissure. Counting fissures by touch tells a right lung from a left one.

Slides (2)
L44Learning
How many lobes and which fissures does the left lung have?
  1. A. 3 lobes; oblique and horizontal fissures
  2. B. 2 lobes; oblique fissure only
  3. C. 2 lobes; horizontal fissure only
AnswerB. 2 lobes; oblique fissure only
The left lung has 2 lobes (superior and inferior) separated by the oblique fissure only; the horizontal fissure is right-sided.
Explanation

The space taken by the heart leaves no middle lobe on the left. Instead, the superior lobe has a cardiac notch in its anterior border and a tongue-like lingula below the notch, roughly the counterpart of the right middle lobe.

  • 3 lobes with two fissures is the right lung.
  • The horizontal fissure exists only in the right lung; the left lung's single fissure is oblique.
Slides (2)
L45Learning
What does the oblique fissure of the right lung separate?
  1. A. The superior lobe from the middle lobe
  2. B. The inferior lobe from both the superior and middle lobes
  3. C. The inferior lobe from the middle lobe only
AnswerB. The inferior lobe from both the superior and middle lobes
On the right, the oblique fissure separates the inferior lobe from both lobes in front of it; the horizontal fissure separates superior from middle.
Explanation

The oblique fissure runs from the back of the lung (level of the T2 spine) down and forward to the 6th costal cartilage, cutting off the whole inferior lobe behind and below it. The horizontal fissure branches forward from it at the level of the 4th rib, dividing the part in front into superior and middle lobes. On the left, the oblique fissure separates superior from inferior lobe.

  • Superior from middle is the horizontal fissure's job.
  • Inferior from middle only ignores the upper, posterior stretch of the fissure, which borders the superior lobe.
Slides (2)
L46Learning
Which pair of features does the left lung have that the right lung lacks?
  1. A. Hilum
    Lingula
  2. B. Cardiac notch
    Horizontal fissure
  3. C. Cardiac notch
    Lingula
AnswerC. Cardiac notch
Lingula
The cardiac notch is a deep indentation in the anterior border of the left lung beside the heart's apex; the tongue-like lingula projects below it.
Explanation

The heart lies to the left, so the anterior border of the left superior lobe is cut away as the cardiac notch, leaving part of the pericardium uncovered by lung. Below the notch the superior lobe sends a thin tongue, the lingula (Latin "little tongue"), round in front of the heart.

  • The hilum is where the root enters; both lungs have one.
  • The horizontal fissure is only in the right lung.
Slides (2)
L47Learning
The lingula is part of which lobe?
  1. A. Left superior lobe
  2. B. Left inferior lobe
  3. C. Right middle lobe
AnswerA. Left superior lobe
The lingula is a tongue-like projection of the left superior lobe, lying just below the cardiac notch.
Explanation

The left lung has no middle lobe; the lingula, at the lower front of the superior lobe below the cardiac notch, is its rough equivalent and has its own lingular bronchus and segments. A tumour beside the cardiac notch or in the lingula is therefore removed with the left superior lobe.

  • The left inferior lobe lies behind and below the oblique fissure, away from the notch.
  • The right middle lobe is the right-sided counterpart, but the lingula itself is only on the left.
Slides (2)
L48Learning
How high does the apex of the lung rise, and which artery lies against it?
  1. A. About an inch into the root of the neck, under the cervical pleura; against the subclavian artery
  2. B. Level with the clavicle, not above it, under the costal pleura; against the subclavian artery
  3. C. About an inch into the root of the neck, under the cervical pleura; against the common carotid artery
AnswerA. About an inch into the root of the neck, under the cervical pleura; against the subclavian artery
The apex rises about an inch above the clavicle into the root of the neck, capped by cervical pleura, and is grooved by the subclavian artery.
Explanation

Each lung is a cone whose apex fills the cupula. The subclavian artery arches over the front of the cupula and grooves the apex. This position explains why the apex can be injured by neck wounds and why an apical (Pancoast) tumour can involve the lower trunk of the brachial plexus, the sympathetic trunk and the subclavian vessels.

  • The apex lies above the clavicle, and the pleura over it is cervical, not costal.
  • The common carotid artery runs up the neck medial to the apex and does not groove it.
Slides (2)
L49Learning
What marks the costal surface of the lung?
  1. A. Impressions of the ribs
  2. B. Impressions of the heart
  3. C. Impressions of the oesophagus
AnswerA. Impressions of the ribs
The large, convex costal surface lies against the costal pleura and ribs, which leave rib impressions on the fixed lung.
Explanation

The costal surface is the biggest surface, facing the ribs and intercostal spaces through the costal pleura. In an embalmed lung the ribs leave shallow parallel grooves on it.

  • The heart marks the mediastinal surface (cardiac impression).
  • The oesophagus also grooves the mediastinal surface, behind the hilum.
Slide (1)
L50Learning
What lies under the diaphragmatic surface of the right lung, on the other side of the diaphragm?
  1. A. Stomach and spleen
  2. B. Left lobe of the liver
  3. C. Right lobe of the liver
AnswerC. Right lobe of the liver
The concave diaphragmatic surface of the right lung sits on the right dome of the diaphragm, which is pushed up by the right lobe of the liver.
Explanation

The base of each lung is concave, moulded to its dome of the diaphragm. The right dome rides higher because of the bulky right lobe of the liver beneath it, which is also why the right lung is shorter.

  • Stomach and spleen lie under the left dome.
  • The left lobe of the liver extends under the left dome, beneath the left lung.
Slide (1)
L51Learning
What lies under the diaphragmatic surface of the left lung, on the other side of the diaphragm?
  1. A. Left lobe of the liver
    Stomach
    Pancreas
  2. B. Right lobe of the liver
    Stomach
    Spleen
  3. C. Left lobe of the liver
    Stomach
    Spleen
AnswerC. Left lobe of the liver
Stomach
Spleen
Under the left dome lie the left lobe of the liver, the stomach and the spleen.
Explanation

The diaphragm separates the base of the left lung from the upper abdominal organs on the left: the left lobe of the liver medially, the fundus of the stomach, and the spleen posterolaterally. This is why percussion below the left lung base is dull over the spleen.

  • The pancreas lies much lower and further back, behind the stomach.
  • The right lobe of the liver lies under the right dome.
Slide (1)
L52Learning
What does the mediastinal surface of the lung face, and what lies in its middle?
  1. A. Vertebrae in front, mediastinum behind; cardiac notch in the middle
  2. B. Vertebrae behind, mediastinum in front; hilum in the middle
  3. C. Sternum in front, mediastinum behind; hilum in the middle
AnswerB. Vertebrae behind, mediastinum in front; hilum in the middle
The mediastinal surface has a posterior vertebral part against the vertebrae and an anterior mediastinal part against the mediastinum, with the hilum in its centre.
Explanation

The medial surface wraps around the midline structures: its back part lies against the vertebral bodies and discs, its front part against the mediastinum (heart, great vessels, trachea, oesophagus), which grooves it. The hilum, where the root enters, lies near the middle of this surface.

  • The vertebrae are behind, not in front.
  • The cardiac notch is on the anterior border of the left lung, not in the centre of the medial surface.
  • The sternum faces the anterior border and costal surface, not the mediastinal surface.
Slide (1)
L53Learning
At which border of the lung do the diaphragmatic and costal surfaces meet?
  1. A. Anterior border
  2. B. Posterior border
  3. C. Inferior border
AnswerC. Inferior border
The inferior border is where the diaphragmatic surface meets the costal surface; the anterior and posterior borders join costal and mediastinal surfaces.
Explanation

The lung has three surfaces (costal, diaphragmatic, mediastinal) and three borders:

  • Anterior: costal meets mediastinal surface in front; thin and sharp, notched on the left.
  • Posterior: costal meets mediastinal surface behind; thick and rounded, beside the spine.
  • Inferior: diaphragmatic meets costal surface below; rounded, and it slips into the costodiaphragmatic recess in deep inspiration.
Slide (1)
L54Learning
How do the anterior and posterior borders of the lung compare?
  1. A. Anterior: thick, shorter
    Posterior: thin, beside the spine from C7 to T10
  2. B. Anterior: thin, shorter
    Posterior: thick, beside the spine from T1 to T12
  3. C. Anterior: thin, shorter
    Posterior: thick, beside the spine from C7 to T10
AnswerC. Anterior: thin, shorter
Posterior: thick, beside the spine from C7 to T10
The anterior border is thin, sharp and shorter; the posterior border is thick, rounded and ill-defined, lying beside the spine from C7 to T10.
Explanation

In front the lung tapers to a thin edge that slides into the costomediastinal recess; behind, the lung fills the deep gutter beside the vertebral bodies, so its posterior border is thick and rounded. That border runs alongside the spine from about the C7 spinous process (level of the apex) down to T10 (the lung's lower limit beside the spine).

  • Thick anterior / thin posterior is the swap.
  • T12 is the lower limit of the pleura beside the spine, two levels below the lung.
Slide (1)

Root of the lung and mediastinal impressions

L55Learning
Which main structures make up the root of each lung?
  1. A. 1 main bronchus
    1 pulmonary artery
    1 pulmonary vein
  2. B. 1 main bronchus
    2 pulmonary arteries
    1 pulmonary vein
  3. C. 1 main bronchus
    1 pulmonary artery
    2 pulmonary veins
AnswerC. 1 main bronchus
1 pulmonary artery
2 pulmonary veins
Each root carries one main bronchus, one pulmonary artery and two pulmonary veins (superior and inferior), plus bronchial vessels, nerves and lymphatics.
Explanation

The root is the bundle of structures joining lung to mediastinum; the hilum is the area on the mediastinal surface where they enter. Each lung has a superior and an inferior pulmonary vein, so four pulmonary veins reach the left atrium. Smaller root structures: bronchial arteries and veins, the pulmonary plexus of nerves, lymphatics and the bronchopulmonary (hilar) nodes.

  • One vein per lung is the common slip: there are two.
  • There is only one pulmonary artery per lung (the right or left branch of the pulmonary trunk).
Slides (2)
L56Learning
Which structures are the most anterior and inferior at the hilum of both lungs?
  1. A. Main bronchi
  2. B. Pulmonary arteries
  3. C. Pulmonary veins
AnswerC. Pulmonary veins
On both sides the pulmonary veins are the most anterior and inferior structures at the hilum.
Explanation

The veins leave the front and bottom of the hilum and run toward the left atrium, which lies in front of and below the lung roots. The bronchus is posterior on both sides, and the artery lies in front of the bronchus on the right and above it on the left ("RALS").

  • Main bronchi are the most posterior structures in each root.
  • Pulmonary arteries are anterior (right) or superior (left), never the lowest.
Slides (2)
L57Learning
At the right hilum, where does the pulmonary artery lie relative to the main bronchus?
  1. A. Anterior
  2. B. Superior
  3. C. Inferior
AnswerA. Anterior
RALS: on the Right the pulmonary artery is Anterior to the bronchus; on the Left it is Superior.
Explanation

On the right, the pulmonary artery lies in front of the main bronchus; only the superior lobar (eparterial) bronchus leaves above the level of the artery. On the left, the artery arches over the main bronchus and so lies above it. The pulmonary veins are anterior and inferior on both sides.

  • Superior is the left-sided relation.
  • Inferior to the bronchus lie the pulmonary veins (and below them the pulmonary ligament), not the artery.
Slides (2)
L58Learning
At the left hilum, where does the pulmonary artery lie relative to the main bronchus?
  1. A. Superior
  2. B. Inferior
  3. C. Anterior
AnswerA. Superior
On the left the pulmonary artery arches over the main bronchus, so it is the highest structure at the hilum (RALS: left = superior).
Explanation

The left pulmonary artery is the highest structure in the left root, with the main bronchus below and behind it and the two pulmonary veins at the front and bottom. On a lung on the table: artery on top = left lung; a bronchus on top (the eparterial bronchus) = right lung.

  • Anterior is the right-sided relation.
  • Inferior would put the artery below the bronchus; on the left it is the bronchus that lies below the artery.
Slides (2)
L59Learning
What is the eparterial bronchus?
  1. A. The right superior lobar bronchus, arising above the level of the right pulmonary artery
  2. B. The right inferior lobar bronchus, passing below the right pulmonary artery
  3. C. The left superior lobar bronchus, arising above the left pulmonary artery
AnswerA. The right superior lobar bronchus, arising above the level of the right pulmonary artery
The eparterial bronchus is the right superior lobar bronchus: it leaves the right main bronchus above the level of the pulmonary artery ("ep-arterial" = upon the artery).
Explanation

The right main bronchus gives off its branch to the superior lobe almost at once, before the right pulmonary artery crosses in front; this branch is therefore above the artery. The rest of the right main bronchus continues as the intermediate bronchus to the middle and inferior lobes. All the other lobar bronchi arise below the level of their artery ("hyparterial").

  • The inferior lobar bronchus is hyparterial.
  • On the left, the pulmonary artery arches over the main bronchus, so no left bronchus is eparterial.
Slides (2)
L60Learning
On both sides, which nerve passes in front of the lung root and which behind it?
  1. A. Vagus nerve in front
    Phrenic nerve behind
  2. B. Phrenic nerve in front
    Vagus nerve behind
  3. C. Sympathetic trunk in front
    Vagus nerve behind
AnswerB. Phrenic nerve in front
Vagus nerve behind
On both sides the phrenic nerve passes anterior to the root and the vagus nerve posterior to it.
Explanation

The phrenic nerve (C3–C5, somatic) descends on the side of the pericardium in front of the root to reach the diaphragm. The vagus nerve (parasympathetic) passes behind the root, giving branches to the posterior pulmonary plexus, and continues onto the oesophagus.

  • Swapping them is the classic error. Hook: Phrenic = Pre-hilar.
  • The sympathetic trunk lies far back on the heads of the ribs beside the vertebrae, never in front of the root.
Slides (2)
L61Learning
A tumour invades the surface of the lung just anterior to the hilum, and the patient becomes short of breath. Which nerve is most likely compressed?
  1. A. Vagus nerve
  2. B. Recurrent laryngeal nerve
  3. C. Phrenic nerve
AnswerC. Phrenic nerve
The phrenic nerve runs just in front of the hilum; compressing it weakens that half of the diaphragm, the main muscle of inspiration, causing dyspnoea.
Explanation

A mass in front of the root meets the phrenic nerve on its way to the diaphragm. Loss of phrenic function paralyses that hemidiaphragm, which rises and fails to descend in inspiration, so breathing becomes difficult.

  • The vagus nerve passes behind the root.
  • The recurrent laryngeal nerves loop under the aortic arch (left) or subclavian artery (right), above the root, and supply the larynx; compressing one causes hoarseness, not diaphragm weakness.
Slides (2)
L62Learning
Which set of impressions is found on the mediastinal surface of the right lung?
  1. A. Left brachiocephalic vein
    Superior vena cava
    Azygos vein and its arch
    Oesophagus
    Trachea
    Descending aorta
  2. B. Right brachiocephalic vein
    Superior vena cava
    Azygos vein and its arch
    Oesophagus
    Trachea
    Inferior vena cava
  3. C. Right brachiocephalic vein
    Left subclavian artery
    Azygos vein and its arch
    Oesophagus
    Trachea
    Inferior vena cava
AnswerB. Right brachiocephalic vein
Superior vena cava
Azygos vein and its arch
Oesophagus
Trachea
Inferior vena cava
The right lung is grooved by the venous side of the mediastinum: right brachiocephalic vein, superior vena cava, azygos vein and arch, inferior vena cava, plus oesophagus and trachea.
Explanation

The right side of the mediastinum is dominated by large veins: the right brachiocephalic vein and superior vena cava above and in front of the hilum, the arch of the azygos vein hooking over the root, the azygos vein behind, and the inferior vena cava at the base. The oesophagus and trachea also groove the right lung, which has only a shallow cardiac impression.

  • The descending aorta and left subclavian artery groove the left lung.
  • The left brachiocephalic vein grooves the left lung.

Hook: right lung = veins (azygos, venae cavae); left lung = aorta.

Slides (2)
L63Learning
A CT scan shows a tumour just superior to the root of the right lung. Blood flow in which vein is most likely compressed?
  1. A. Arch of the azygos vein
  2. B. Hemiazygos vein
  3. C. Left brachiocephalic vein
AnswerA. Arch of the azygos vein
The arch of the azygos vein hooks over the root of the right lung into the superior vena cava, so a mass just above the right root compresses it.
Explanation

The azygos vein climbs on the right side of the vertebral bodies, then at about T4 arches forward over the right main bronchus and root to empty into the back of the superior vena cava. Its arch grooves the right lung just above the hilum.

  • The hemiazygos vein runs on the left side of the lower thoracic vertebrae and crosses behind the aorta to the azygos; it is far from the right root.
  • The left brachiocephalic vein crosses high in front of the aortic arch toward the right; it does not touch the right root.
Slides (2)
L64Learning
You are handed a lung with three lobes separated by two fissures. Which structure has left an impression on its mediastinal surface?
  1. A. Arch of the aorta
  2. B. Arch of the azygos vein
  3. C. Left subclavian artery
AnswerB. Arch of the azygos vein
Three lobes and two fissures identify a right lung; of the choices, only the arch of the azygos vein grooves the right lung.
Explanation

A two-step question: first identify the side (3 lobes + horizontal and oblique fissures = right), then recall that side's impressions. The right lung bears the azygos vein and its arch, the superior vena cava, the right brachiocephalic vein, the inferior vena cava, the oesophagus and the trachea.

  • The arch of the aorta passes over the left root and grooves the left lung.
  • The left subclavian artery grooves the upper part of the left lung.
Slides (2)
L65Learning
A tumour lies just posterior to the root of the left lung at the level of T4. Which vessel is most likely compressed?
  1. A. Arch of the azygos vein
  2. B. Ascending aorta
  3. C. Arch of the aorta
AnswerC. Arch of the aorta
The arch of the aorta passes over the left root and turns down behind it at T4, so a mass behind the left root there presses on it.
Explanation

The aortic arch runs from front to back over the left main bronchus and pulmonary artery, then becomes the descending (thoracic) aorta beside the T4 vertebra, behind the left root. Both leave grooves on the left lung: the arch above the hilum and the descending aorta behind it.

  • The arch of the azygos vein hooks over the right root.
  • The ascending aorta lies in front, inside the pericardium, not behind the left root.
Slides (2)
L66Learning
Which set of impressions is found on the mediastinal surface of the left lung?
  1. A. Aortic arch and descending aorta
    Left subclavian artery
    Left brachiocephalic vein
    Oesophagus
    Trachea
    Heart (apex, left ventricle, auricle)
  2. B. Aortic arch and descending aorta
    Left subclavian artery
    Left brachiocephalic vein
    Oesophagus
    Trachea
    Azygos vein and its arch
  3. C. Superior vena cava
    Left subclavian artery
    Left brachiocephalic vein
    Oesophagus
    Trachea
    Heart (apex, left ventricle, auricle)
AnswerA. Aortic arch and descending aorta
Left subclavian artery
Left brachiocephalic vein
Oesophagus
Trachea
Heart (apex, left ventricle, auricle)
The left lung is grooved by the aorta (arch and descending), the left subclavian artery, the left brachiocephalic vein, oesophagus, trachea and the heart (apex, left ventricle, auricle).
Explanation

The aortic arch curves over the left root and the descending aorta runs down behind it, cutting a long groove; the left subclavian artery grooves the upper part. The apex of the heart, the left ventricle and the left auricle make the deep cardiac impression in front of the hilum.

  • The azygos arch and the superior vena cava lie on the right and groove the right lung.
Slides (2)

Surface markings of the lungs and pleura

L67Learning
What is the surface marking of the oblique fissure?
  1. A. Spine of T4 behind → 4th costal cartilage in front
  2. B. Spine of T2 behind → 6th costal cartilage in front
  3. C. Spine of T2 behind → 8th costal cartilage in front
AnswerB. Spine of T2 behind → 6th costal cartilage in front
The oblique fissure runs from about the T2 spinous process behind, round and down the chest wall to the 6th costal cartilage in front.
Explanation

Because it starts high at the back and ends low at the front, everything below and behind it is lower lobe: most of the posterior chest wall overlies the lower lobes, while the front of the chest overlies the upper (and, on the right, middle) lobes.

  • The 4th costal cartilage is where the horizontal fissure meets the front of the chest.
  • The 8th costal cartilage is too low: in front the lung's lower border is only at the 6th rib in the midclavicular line.
Slides (2)
L68Learning
What is the surface marking of the horizontal fissure?
  1. A. Forward from the oblique fissure along the 6th rib and costal cartilage
  2. B. Forward from the oblique fissure along the 2nd rib and costal cartilage
  3. C. Forward from the oblique fissure along the 4th rib and costal cartilage
AnswerC. Forward from the oblique fissure along the 4th rib and costal cartilage
The horizontal fissure leaves the oblique fissure laterally and runs forward along the 4th rib and costal cartilage to the sternum.
Explanation

It meets the oblique fissure at about the midaxillary line and runs horizontally forward at the level of the 4th rib, separating the superior lobe (above) from the middle lobe (below). The middle lobe is therefore the wedge on the front of the right chest between the 4th rib and the 6th costal cartilage.

  • The 6th costal cartilage is where the oblique fissure ends in front; a common trap gives it for the horizontal fissure.
  • The 2nd costal cartilage is at the sternal angle, far above the fissure.
Slides (2)
L69Learning
Pneumonia is seen just below the horizontal fissure on a lateral chest film. Which lobe is involved?
  1. A. Right inferior lobe
  2. B. Right middle lobe
  3. C. Right superior lobe
AnswerB. Right middle lobe
The horizontal fissure separates the right superior lobe (above) from the right middle lobe (below), so disease just below it lies in the middle lobe.
Explanation

On a lateral film the horizontal fissure runs forward from the oblique fissure; the wedge below it and in front of the oblique fissure is the middle lobe. Only the right lung has a horizontal fissure, so the answer must be a right-lung lobe.

  • The superior lobe lies above the horizontal fissure.
  • The inferior lobe lies behind and below the oblique fissure, not directly under the horizontal fissure.
Slides (2)
L70Learning
A knife enters the right chest horizontally through the 5th intercostal space in the midclavicular line. Which lobe is it most likely to pierce?
  1. A. Superior lobe
  2. B. Inferior lobe
  3. C. Middle lobe
AnswerC. Middle lobe
In front, the middle lobe lies between the horizontal fissure (4th rib) and the end of the oblique fissure (6th costal cartilage), so the 5th space overlies it.
Explanation

Map the fissures on the front of the right chest: the horizontal fissure runs along the 4th rib, and the oblique fissure reaches the front at the 6th costal cartilage. The strip between, roughly the 4th to 6th ribs, is the middle lobe; this is also where you listen to the middle lobe with a stethoscope.

  • The superior lobe lies above the 4th rib in front.
  • The inferior lobe lies behind the oblique fissure; in front it reaches only the lowest, most lateral part of the chest.
Slides (2)
L71Learning
When you listen over the lower part of the back of the chest, which lobes lie under the stethoscope?
  1. A. Lower (inferior) lobes
  2. B. Middle lobe and lingula
  3. C. Upper (superior) lobes
AnswerA. Lower (inferior) lobes
The oblique fissure starts high, at the T2 spine, behind, so most of the posterior chest wall overlies the lower lobes.
Explanation

Because the oblique fissure slopes from the T2 spinous process behind down to the 6th costal cartilage in front, the lower lobes take up almost all of the back of the chest, the upper lobes face mainly forward and upward, and the middle lobe faces the front of the right chest. So lower-lobe sounds are heard posteriorly, middle-lobe sounds anteriorly between the 4th and 6th ribs.

  • The middle lobe and lingula are anterior.
  • The upper lobes reach the back only near the top, above the fissure.
Slides (2)
L72Learning
How does the inferior border of the lung relate to the inferior border of the pleura?
  1. A. Lung and pleura lie at the same level all the way round
  2. B. The lung lies about two levels below the pleura all the way round
  3. C. The lung lies about two levels above the pleura all the way round
AnswerC. The lung lies about two levels above the pleura all the way round
In quiet breathing the lung's lower border lies about two rib levels above the pleura's costal line all the way round; the gap is the costodiaphragmatic recess.
Explanation
LineLungPleura
Midclavicular6th rib8th rib
Midaxillary8th rib10th rib
ParavertebralT10T12

Hook: lung 6-8-10, pleura 8-10-12 (add 2). The lung can never reach lower than the pleura, since it lies inside the pleural sac. The gap is why a needle can enter the pleural cavity below the lung.

Slides (2)
L73Learning
In the midclavicular line, where are the inferior borders of the lung and the pleura?
  1. A. Lung: 8th rib
    Pleura: 10th rib
  2. B. Lung: 4th rib
    Pleura: 6th rib
  3. C. Lung: 6th rib
    Pleura: 8th rib
AnswerC. Lung: 6th rib
Pleura: 8th rib
In the midclavicular line the lung's lower border is at the 6th rib and the pleura's at the 8th rib.
Explanation

In front the lungs and pleura are highest, because the diaphragm's attachment rises toward the xiphoid. Moving round the chest, both borders drop by two ribs per line: midclavicular 6/8, midaxillary 8/10, paravertebral T10/T12.

  • 8/10 is the midaxillary line.
  • 4/6 is two levels too high; the 4th rib is the level of the horizontal fissure.
Slide (1)
L74Learning
In the midaxillary line, where are the inferior borders of the lung and the pleura?
  1. A. Lung: 8th rib
    Pleura: 10th rib
  2. B. Lung: 8th rib
    Pleura: 12th rib
  3. C. Lung: 6th rib
    Pleura: 8th rib
AnswerA. Lung: 8th rib
Pleura: 10th rib
In the midaxillary line the lung ends at the 8th rib and the pleura at the 10th rib: the basis for thoracentesis in the 9th space.
Explanation

The two-rib gap between 8 and 10 in the midaxillary line is the deepest, most accessible part of the costodiaphragmatic recess. A needle in the 9th intercostal space there lies below the lung but inside the pleura.

  • 6/8 is the midclavicular line.
  • The 12th level belongs to the pleura beside the spine (T12); laterally the pleura stops at the 10th rib.
Slide (1)
L75Learning
Beside the spine (paravertebral line), where are the inferior borders of the lung and the pleura?
  1. A. Lung: T8
    Pleura: T10
  2. B. Lung: T12
    Pleura: T10
  3. C. Lung: T10
    Pleura: T12
AnswerC. Lung: T10
Pleura: T12
Beside the spine the lung reaches T10 and the pleura T12 (the lecture table's "1th vertebra" is a misprint for 12th).
Explanation

Behind, the diaphragm attaches low (12th rib and upper lumbar vertebrae), so lung and pleura both reach their lowest points here. The same add-two rule holds: lung T10, pleura T12.

  • T8/T10 is two levels too high.
  • Lung T12 / pleura T10 swaps them; the lung always ends above the pleura.
Slide (1)
L76Learning
Why can a needle enter the pleural cavity low on the chest wall without touching the lung?
  1. A. The pleura reaches lower than the lung all round (the costodiaphragmatic recess)
  2. B. The lung pulls away from the wall in expiration (the pulmonary ligament)
  3. C. The lung reaches lower than the pleura all round (the costomediastinal recess)
AnswerA. The pleura reaches lower than the lung all round (the costodiaphragmatic recess)
The pleura reaches about two ribs lower than the lung all round, leaving the lung-free costodiaphragmatic recess as a safe target.
Explanation

In quiet breathing the lung's inferior border lies at ribs 6/8/T10, while the costal line of pleural reflection lies at 8/10/T12. Between them is a slit of pleural cavity that contains no lung, only (in disease) fluid that has drained there by gravity: the anatomy behind thoracentesis.

  • The lung never reaches lower than the pleura, since it lies inside the pleural sac; the costomediastinal recess is anterior, behind the sternum.
  • The pulmonary ligament is a pleural fold below the root and has nothing to do with this zone.
Slides (2)
L77Learning
Using the lung and pleura borders, which intercostal space in the midclavicular line lies inside the pleural cavity but below the lung in quiet breathing?
  1. A. 5th intercostal space
  2. B. 7th intercostal space
  3. C. 9th intercostal space
AnswerB. 7th intercostal space
In the midclavicular line the lung stops at the 6th rib and the pleura at the 8th, so only the 7th intercostal space lies between them.
Explanation

The recess in each line lies between the lung border and the pleural border: midclavicular ribs 6–8 (7th space), midaxillary ribs 8–10 (9th space), paravertebral T10–T12. The standard thoracentesis site uses the midaxillary line, where the recess is deepest.

  • Behind the 5th space, above the 6th rib, lies lung.
  • The 9th space in the midclavicular line is below the pleura's costal line (8th rib): a needle there passes through the diaphragm toward the abdomen (the liver on the right).
Slide (1)

Pleural disorders and thoracentesis

L78Learning
In pleuritis, what can be heard with a stethoscope, and why?
  1. A. Wheeze: narrowed bronchi vibrate with airflow
  2. B. Friction rub: the inflamed pleural layers rub together
  3. C. Stridor: the inflamed pleura narrows the trachea
AnswerB. Friction rub: the inflamed pleural layers rub together
Pleuritis roughens the pleural surfaces, so instead of gliding they rub, producing a grating friction rub in time with breathing.
Explanation

Pleuritis (pleurisy) is inflammation of the pleura, for example with pneumonia. The normally smooth, lubricated layers become rough and sticky; as they move over each other they make a creaking sound, like leather rubbing, heard over the affected area. Because the parietal pleura is involved, breathing is also painful.

  • A wheeze comes from narrowed airways (as in asthma), inside the lung.
  • Stridor is a high-pitched sound from obstruction of the larynx or trachea, not from the pleura.
Slide (1)
L79Learning
What can pleuritis leave behind, and what does it usually mean for breathing?
  1. A. Fibrous adhesions joining visceral to parietal pleura; once chronic they often have no functional consequence
  2. B. Fibrous adhesions joining visceral to parietal pleura; they make the lung collapse as the chest wall expands
  3. C. Fibrous adhesions joining parietal pleura to the ribs; they stop the ribs moving in breathing
AnswerA. Fibrous adhesions joining visceral to parietal pleura; once chronic they often have no functional consequence
Pleuritis roughens the pleura and can leave adhesions between the visceral and parietal layers; chronic adhesions often have no functional consequence.
Explanation

Inflamed pleura loses its smooth, lubricated surface: the layers grate (a pleural rub), and acute pleuritis gives sharp, stabbing pain, worse on exertion, because the parietal pleura is pain-sensitive. As the inflammation settles, fibrous tissue can bridge the pleural cavity and stick the visceral pleura to the parietal pleura. The lung then moves with the chest wall instead of sliding along it, so chronic adhesions often cause no symptoms and no loss of function.

  • Adhesions hold the lung to the wall; a lung collapses only when the two layers separate, as when air enters the cavity.
  • Adhesions form between the two pleural layers, inside the pleural cavity; they do not bind the pleura to the ribs, which keep moving.
Slide (1)
L80Learning
What collects in the pleural cavity in pneumothorax, haemothorax, hydrothorax and chylothorax?
  1. A. Pneumothorax = air
    Haemothorax = blood
    Hydrothorax = fluid
    Chylothorax = lymph
  2. B. Pneumothorax = fluid
    Haemothorax = blood
    Hydrothorax = air
    Chylothorax = lymph
  3. C. Pneumothorax = air
    Haemothorax = blood
    Hydrothorax = lymph
    Chylothorax = fluid
AnswerA. Pneumothorax = air
Haemothorax = blood
Hydrothorax = fluid
Chylothorax = lymph
Pneumo = air, haemo = blood, hydro = watery fluid, chylo = lymph (chyle), each collecting in the pleural cavity.
Explanation

Each condition fills the potential space and squeezes the lung:

  • Pneumothorax: air, from a chest wound or a leak from the lung surface; the lung collapses.
  • Haemothorax: blood, usually from chest trauma (e.g. torn intercostal vessels).
  • Hydrothorax: watery fluid, i.e. a pleural effusion (e.g. in heart failure).
  • Chylothorax: milky lymph (chyle) from a torn thoracic duct.

Pus in the pleural cavity is an empyema. Liquids collect by gravity in the costodiaphragmatic recess; air rises.

Slide (1)
L81Learning
A tall, thin young man suddenly becomes breathless at rest when a small bleb on the surface of his lung ruptures. How does the lecture classify this pneumothorax?
  1. A. Open: air enters through a wound in the chest wall and parietal pleura
  2. B. Closed: air leaks from the lung itself through the torn visceral pleura
  3. C. Open: air leaks from the lung itself through the torn visceral pleura
AnswerB. Closed: air leaks from the lung itself through the torn visceral pleura
A closed pneumothorax comes from the respiratory system itself (ruptured bleb, torn visceral pleura); an open one comes from a penetrating wound through the parietal pleura.
Explanation

Air anywhere in the pleural cavity breaks the fluid seal, and the elastic lung recoils toward the hilum; collapse of a lung that was previously inflated is secondary atelectasis. The lecture names the pneumothorax by where the air comes from:

  • Open: a penetrating injury (bullet, knife) breaches the chest wall and parietal pleura, so outside air enters.
  • Closed: the chest wall is intact; air leaks out of the lung, for example from a ruptured bleb or a tear of the visceral pleura.
