This man has no wound, so his pneumothorax cannot be open, whatever the size of the leak. If a tear acts as a one-way valve, air builds up under pressure (tension pneumothorax) and pushes the mediastinum and trachea to the opposite side.

Slides (2)
L82Learning
What is an empyema, and how does it usually arise?
  1. A. Pus within the lung tissue itself → a complication of pneumonia, chest trauma, thoracentesis or lung surgery
  2. B. Pus in the pleural cavity → a complication of heart failure or low plasma protein
  3. C. Pus in the pleural cavity → a complication of pneumonia, chest trauma, thoracentesis or lung surgery
AnswerC. Pus in the pleural cavity → a complication of pneumonia, chest trauma, thoracentesis or lung surgery
An empyema is pus in the pleural cavity; infection reaches the pleura after pneumonia, chest trauma, thoracentesis or lung surgery.
Explanation

Empyema completes the list of things that can fill the pleural cavity: air (pneumothorax), blood (haemothorax), watery fluid (hydrothorax), lymph (chylothorax) and pus (empyema). Bacteria reach the cavity from an infected lung lying against it (pneumonia), or are carried in through the chest wall by a penetrating wound, a thoracentesis needle or an operation on the lung. The infected fluid squeezes the lung like any other effusion and has to be drained.

  • Pus within the lung tissue is a lung abscess; an empyema lies outside the lung, between the visceral and parietal pleura.
  • Heart failure and low plasma protein cause a watery, uninfected effusion (hydrothorax), not pus.
Slide (1)
L83Learning
After a car crash, thoracentesis draws milky fluid from the pleural cavity. Which structure has most likely been torn?
  1. A. Azygos vein
  2. B. Thoracic duct
  3. C. Intercostal artery
AnswerB. Thoracic duct
Milky fluid is chyle (fat-rich lymph): this is a chylothorax, from a torn thoracic duct.
Explanation

The thoracic duct carries lymph, including fat absorbed from the gut (chyle), up through the thorax to the left venous angle. If trauma or surgery tears it, chyle leaks into the pleural cavity, giving a milky, cloudy effusion that pools above the diaphragm.

  • A torn azygos vein or intercostal artery fills the cavity with blood: a haemothorax.
Slide (1)
L84Learning
A patient with a large pleural effusion is short of breath and breathing fast. What is the anatomical reason?
  1. A. The fluid takes up room inside the fixed thoracic cavity, so the lung cannot expand fully; a faster rate compensates for the smaller breaths
  2. B. The fluid seeps across the visceral pleura into the alveoli and blocks gas exchange; a faster rate compensates for the lost alveoli
  3. C. The fluid presses on the phrenic nerve and paralyses the diaphragm; a faster rate compensates for the weak diaphragm
AnswerA. The fluid takes up room inside the fixed thoracic cavity, so the lung cannot expand fully; a faster rate compensates for the smaller breaths
Effusion fluid fills the pleural cavity inside a fixed cage, so the lung has less room to expand; each breath is smaller and the respiratory rate rises to compensate.
Explanation

The pleural cavity is normally a potential space holding only a film of fluid. The thoracic cage and diaphragm enclose a limited volume, so whatever collects in the cavity (fluid, blood, lymph, pus or air) is volume the lung cannot use. The lung is compressed and expands less with each breath, so the patient feels short of breath and breathes faster to keep air moving. Draining the fluid by thoracentesis lets the lung re-expand.

  • An effusion lies outside the lung, between the parietal and visceral pleura; fluid inside the alveoli is pulmonary oedema or pneumonia.
  • Pleural fluid does not paralyse the diaphragm: the phrenic nerve keeps working, and irritated parietal pleura gives pain, not paralysis.
Slides (2)
L85Learning
What is thoracentesis?
  1. A. Draining fluid from the pericardial sac around the heart
  2. B. Draining fluid, blood or pus from the costomediastinal recess
  3. C. Draining fluid, blood or pus from the costodiaphragmatic recess
AnswerC. Draining fluid, blood or pus from the costodiaphragmatic recess
Thoracentesis is passing a hollow needle through the chest wall into the pleural cavity to remove fluid, blood or pus from the costodiaphragmatic recess.
Explanation

It is used to drain an effusion or to take a fluid sample for diagnosis. The patient sits up and leans slightly forward so the fluid settles in the costodiaphragmatic recess, which contains no lung, so the needle can enter the fluid without puncturing the lung.

  • Draining the pericardial sac is pericardiocentesis, a different procedure.
  • The costomediastinal recess is anterior and high; fluid does not collect there in an upright patient.
Slide (1)
L86Learning
Where is the needle usually inserted for thoracentesis?
  1. A. 9th intercostal space, midaxillary line
  2. B. 5th intercostal space, midaxillary line
  3. C. 9th intercostal space, midclavicular line
AnswerA. 9th intercostal space, midaxillary line
The standard site is the 9th intercostal space in the midaxillary line: between lung (8th rib) and pleura (10th rib), in the deepest part of the recess.
Explanation

In the midaxillary line the lung ends at the 8th rib and the pleura at the 10th in quiet breathing, so the 9th space lies over the costodiaphragmatic recess, where an effusion collects in an upright patient.

  • In the 5th space the needle would enter lung, which reaches the 8th rib laterally.
  • In the midclavicular line the pleura stops at the 8th rib, so a 9th-space needle there passes below the pleural cavity, through the diaphragm into the upper abdomen (the liver on the right).
Slides (2)
L87Learning
In thoracentesis through the 9th intercostal space, where in the space does the needle go, and why?
  1. A. Just below the 9th rib, because the main neurovascular bundle runs along the top of the 10th rib
  2. B. Just above the 10th rib, because the main neurovascular bundle runs in the groove under the 9th rib
  3. C. Midway between the ribs, because the main neurovascular bundle runs along the middle of the space
AnswerB. Just above the 10th rib, because the main neurovascular bundle runs in the groove under the 9th rib
The main intercostal vein, artery and nerve (VAN) run in the costal groove under each rib, so the needle passes just above the rib below (the 10th).
Explanation

Each intercostal space carries its main neurovascular bundle in the costal groove on the lower border of the rib above, ordered vein, artery, nerve from top to bottom. Keeping to the upper border of the lower rib keeps the needle away from that bundle: in the 9th space, just superior to the 10th rib.

  • Going just below the 9th rib drives the needle into the main bundle.
  • The main bundle does not run in the middle of the space; only small collateral branches run lower, near the upper border of the rib below.
Slides (2)
L88Learning
During thoracentesis the needle is kept a little above the upper border of the lower rib, rather than scraping it, to avoid which structures?
  1. A. The collateral branches of the intercostal nerve and vessels
  2. B. The main intercostal vein, artery and nerve
  3. C. The innermost intercostal muscle
AnswerA. The collateral branches of the intercostal nerve and vessels
Small collateral branches of the intercostal nerve and vessels run along the upper border of the rib below, so the needle goes above that rib but clear of them.
Explanation

Near the angle of the rib each intercostal nerve and vessel gives off a collateral branch that runs forward along the upper border of the rib below. A needle placed just above the lower rib avoids the main bundle (under the rib above); inserting it high enough above the rib's edge also spares the collaterals.

  • The main bundle lies in the costal groove of the rib above; it is avoided by staying low in the space.
  • The innermost intercostal muscle cannot be avoided: the needle must pass through all three intercostal layers to reach the pleura.
Slides (2)
L89Learning
Why is the thoracentesis needle angled upward?
  1. A. So it does not pierce the main intercostal neurovascular bundle
  2. B. So it does not go through the diaphragm into the liver
  3. C. So it does not go through the lung into the bronchi
AnswerB. So it does not go through the diaphragm into the liver
The needle is angled upward so it stays in the recess and does not pass down through the diaphragm into the liver (or the spleen on the left).
Explanation

The costodiaphragmatic recess is a narrow slit whose lower wall is the diaphragm, with the liver just below it on the right (the spleen on the left). Angling slightly upward keeps the tip in the fluid. A needle or knife directed down through the right 9th space goes through the diaphragm into the liver.

  • The neurovascular bundle is avoided by entering just above the lower rib, not by the needle's angle.
  • The lung lies above the recess, so angling upward moves toward it; avoiding the lung is not the reason.
Slide (1)
L90Learning
In what order does a thoracentesis needle pass through the chest wall to reach the pleural cavity?
  1. A. External intercostal → innermost intercostal → internal intercostal → endothoracic fascia → parietal pleura
  2. B. External intercostal → internal intercostal → innermost intercostal → endothoracic fascia → parietal pleura
  3. C. External intercostal → internal intercostal → innermost intercostal → parietal pleura → endothoracic fascia
AnswerB. External intercostal → internal intercostal → innermost intercostal → endothoracic fascia → parietal pleura
Outside in: the three intercostal muscles (external, internal, innermost), then endothoracic fascia, then parietal pleura, the last layer pierced.
Explanation

After skin and superficial fascia, the needle crosses the intercostal space through its three muscle layers in order, then the thin endothoracic fascia lining the cage, then the costal parietal pleura. Once through the parietal pleura it is in the pleural cavity; the visceral pleura and lung lie beyond and must not be touched.

  • The innermost intercostal is the deepest of the three muscles, not the middle one.
  • The endothoracic fascia lies outside the parietal pleura, so it is crossed first.

The parietal pleura is pain-sensitive (intercostal nerves), so the local anaesthetic must reach it.

Slide (1)

Trachea, bronchi and bronchopulmonary segments

L91Learning
Where does the trachea begin?
  1. A. At the inferior border of the thyroid cartilage (about C5)
  2. B. At the jugular notch of the manubrium (about T2), where it enters the thorax
  3. C. At the inferior border of the cricoid cartilage (about C6)
AnswerC. At the inferior border of the cricoid cartilage (about C6)
The trachea begins at the inferior border of the cricoid cartilage (about C6), continuing the larynx, and divides at the sternal angle (T4/T5).
Explanation

The cricoid cartilage is the lowest cartilage of the larynx and the only complete cartilage ring of the airway; the trachea hangs from its lower border at about the C6 vertebral level. From there the trachea descends in front of the oesophagus through the root of the neck and the thoracic inlet, and divides into the right and left main bronchi at the level of the sternal angle.

  • The thyroid cartilage lies above the cricoid, so it is not where the trachea starts.
  • At the jugular notch the trachea is already several centimetres long; it passes through the thoracic inlet there but does not begin there.
Slides (2)
L92Learning
How are the tracheal cartilages shaped, and what closes the gap in them?
  1. A. 16–20 C-shaped rings open in front; the gap is closed by trachealis muscle behind the thyroid isthmus
  2. B. 16–20 C-shaped rings open behind; the gap is bridged by trachealis smooth muscle, against the oesophagus
  3. C. 16–20 complete rings; trachealis smooth muscle lines their back, against the oesophagus
AnswerB. 16–20 C-shaped rings open behind; the gap is bridged by trachealis smooth muscle, against the oesophagus
The trachea has 16–20 C-shaped cartilages that are open posteriorly; the gap is bridged by trachealis smooth muscle, which lies against the oesophagus.
Explanation

The cartilage rings keep the airway open against the pressure changes of breathing. The soft back wall lets the oesophagus, which lies directly behind the trachea, bulge forward when a bolus is swallowed. Trachealis is smooth muscle joining the free ends of each ring; when it contracts it narrows the lumen, which speeds the air in coughing.

  • The rings are open behind, not in front: the front of the trachea is covered by cartilage, under the thyroid isthmus and the skin of the neck.
  • Only the cricoid cartilage, above the trachea, forms a complete ring; the tracheal rings are incomplete.
Slides (2)
L93Learning
At what level does the trachea divide into the two main bronchi?
  1. A. Suprasternal notch
  2. B. Sternal angle (T4–T5)
  3. C. Xiphisternal joint (T9)
AnswerB. Sternal angle (T4–T5)
The trachea bifurcates at the level of the sternal angle, which lies opposite the T4–T5 intervertebral disc.
Explanation

The sternal angle (manubriosternal joint, where the 2nd costal cartilages attach) marks a horizontal plane through the T4–T5 disc. At this plane the trachea divides and the aortic arch begins and ends. It is the key surface landmark for counting ribs and for locating the carina.

  • The suprasternal (jugular) notch lies higher, at about T2–T3.
  • The xiphisternal joint is at T9, well below the bifurcation.
Slides (2)
L94Learning
What is the carina?
  1. A. The internal ridge between the openings of the two main bronchi
  2. B. The internal ridge between the lobar bronchi of the right lung
  3. C. The cartilage ring at the start of the right main bronchus
AnswerA. The internal ridge between the openings of the two main bronchi
The carina is the keel-shaped internal ridge at the tracheal bifurcation, separating the openings of the right and left main bronchi.
Explanation

The last tracheal cartilage sends a hook-shaped projection between the two bronchi, forming a ridge seen at bronchoscopy as a sharp edge between two openings. Its lining is very sensitive and triggers coughing. Enlarged carinal (inferior tracheobronchial) lymph nodes below it, e.g. from lung cancer, can widen and distort it.

  • Spurs between lobar bronchi lie lower, inside each lung; they are not the carina.
  • The carina is a ridge, not a ring.
Slide (1)
L95Learning
What course does the left main bronchus take to reach its hilum?
  1. A. Above the aortic arch, behind the oesophagus and thoracic aorta
  2. B. Below the aortic arch, in front of the oesophagus and thoracic aorta
  3. C. Below the azygos arch, in front of the oesophagus and superior vena cava
AnswerB. Below the aortic arch, in front of the oesophagus and thoracic aorta
The left main bronchus runs under the aortic arch and in front of the oesophagus and thoracic aorta to reach the left hilum.
Explanation

Because it must pass beneath the arch, the left main bronchus is longer and more horizontal than the right. This course explains why an aneurysm of the aortic arch can press on it.

  • The bronchus is never above the arch; the arch hooks over it.
  • The azygos arch hooks over the right main bronchus, and the superior vena cava is a right-sided vessel.
Slide (1)
L96Learning
How does the right main bronchus differ from the left?
  1. A. Narrower, shorter, more vertical
  2. B. Wider, shorter, more vertical
  3. C. Wider, longer, more horizontal
AnswerB. Wider, shorter, more vertical
The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical, almost continuing the line of the trachea; the left is narrower, longer and more horizontal.
Explanation

The right bronchus reaches its lung quickly and gives off the superior lobar bronchus early, then continues as the intermediate bronchus. The left must pass under the aortic arch and in front of the oesophagus, so it is about twice as long, narrower and leaves the trachea at a wider angle.

  • Each wrong choice swaps one feature: the right is not narrower, nor longer or more horizontal.

These three features explain why aspirated objects usually go right.

Slide (1)
L97Learning
Into which side do inhaled foreign bodies usually go, and why?
  1. A. Right: its main bronchus is narrower, longer and more horizontal
  2. B. Left: its main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical
  3. C. Right: its main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical
AnswerC. Right: its main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical
Inhaled objects usually lodge in the right main bronchus because it is wider, shorter and more vertical, in line with the trachea.
Explanation

An object falling down the trachea follows the straighter, wider path into the right main bronchus, where it can be seen and removed through a bronchoscope.

  • The left main bronchus is the narrower, longer, more horizontal one.
  • "Right because narrower and more horizontal" gives the right side the left bronchus's features.

Objects do sometimes go left; "right" is the usual, not the only, site.

Slides (2)
L98Learning
A 3-year-old aspirates a small toy while sitting upright. In which lobe is it most likely to lodge?
  1. A. Right lower lobe
  2. B. Right upper lobe
  3. C. Left lower lobe
AnswerA. Right lower lobe
Objects enter the vertical right main bronchus and, in an upright person, fall with gravity into the right lower lobe bronchus.
Explanation

From the right main bronchus the intermediate bronchus continues almost straight down into the inferior lobar bronchus, so in a standing or sitting patient aspirated material ends up in the right lower lobe; aspiration pneumonia after vomiting therefore often affects that lobe. In a patient lying on the back, material runs instead into the most dependent posterior branches: the posterior segment of the right upper lobe or the superior segment of the right lower lobe.

  • The right upper lobe bronchus leaves at an angle upward and outward; it catches material mainly in lying patients.
  • The left main bronchus is narrower and more horizontal.
Slides (2)
L99Learning
In what order does the bronchial tree branch?
  1. A. Main bronchus → lobar bronchi → segmental bronchi → terminal bronchioles → respiratory bronchioles → alveolar ducts → alveolar sacs
  2. B. Main bronchus → lobar bronchi → segmental bronchi → respiratory bronchioles → terminal bronchioles → alveolar ducts → alveolar sacs
  3. C. Main bronchus → segmental bronchi → lobar bronchi → terminal bronchioles → respiratory bronchioles → alveolar ducts → alveolar sacs
AnswerA. Main bronchus → lobar bronchi → segmental bronchi → terminal bronchioles → respiratory bronchioles → alveolar ducts → alveolar sacs
Main → lobar → segmental bronchi → terminal then respiratory bronchioles → alveolar ducts → alveolar sacs ("My Lungs Start To Respire Air Always").
Explanation

Main (primary) bronchi enter the lungs; lobar (secondary) bronchi go one to each lobe; segmental (tertiary) bronchi go one to each bronchopulmonary segment. Many generations later, the terminal bronchiole is the last purely conducting airway; the respiratory bronchiole beyond it is the first with alveoli in its wall, leading into alveolar ducts and sacs where gas exchange happens.

  • Respiratory before terminal reverses the conducting → respiratory transition.
  • Segmental before lobar reverses the order: each lobe contains several segments.
Slides (2)
L100Learning
How many lobar (secondary) bronchi arise on each side?
  1. A. Right: 2
    Left: 3
  2. B. Right: 3
    Left: 3
  3. C. Right: 3
    Left: 2
AnswerC. Right: 3
Left: 2
One lobar bronchus per lobe: 3 on the right (superior, middle, inferior) and 2 on the left (superior, inferior).
Explanation

On the right, the superior lobar (eparterial) bronchus leaves first; the intermediate bronchus then divides into middle and inferior lobar bronchi. On the left, the main bronchus divides into superior and inferior lobar bronchi; the superior one also supplies the lingula.

  • 2 right / 3 left is the reverse.
  • 3 on the left would need a left middle lobe; the lingula is supplied by a branch of the superior lobar bronchus, not by a lobar bronchus of its own.
Slides (2)
L101Learning
What does each segmental (tertiary) bronchus supply?
  1. A. One bronchopulmonary segment
  2. B. One pulmonary lobule
  3. C. One alveolar sac
AnswerA. One bronchopulmonary segment
Each segmental (tertiary) bronchus supplies one bronchopulmonary segment, the largest subdivision of a lobe.
Explanation

A bronchopulmonary segment is the block of lung aerated by one segmental bronchus and supplied by the segmental branch of the pulmonary artery that runs with it. Connective tissue septa carrying intersegmental veins separate it from its neighbours.

  • A pulmonary lobule is much smaller, supplied by a bronchiole.
  • An alveolar sac is the blind end of an alveolar duct, the smallest unit.
Slides (2)
L102Learning
What shape is a bronchopulmonary segment?
  1. A. A cone, apex toward the pleural surface
  2. B. A pyramid, apex toward the root of the lung
  3. C. A pyramid, base toward the root of the lung
AnswerB. A pyramid, apex toward the root of the lung
Each bronchopulmonary segment is pyramidal: its apex points toward the lung root and its base lies on the pleural surface.
Explanation

The segmental bronchus and artery enter at the apex of the pyramid, near the hilum, and branch outward to fill a wedge whose broad base forms part of the lung surface under the visceral pleura. This shape is why a blocked segmental artery gives a wedge-shaped infarct with its base on the pleura.

  • The apex is not at the pleural surface; the base is.
  • A base toward the root turns the pyramid upside down.
Slides (2)
L103Learning
How many bronchopulmonary segments are there?
  1. A. Usually 18–20: 8–10 right, 10 left
  2. B. Usually 18–20: 10 right, 8–10 left
  3. C. Usually 22–24: 12 right, 10–12 left
AnswerB. Usually 18–20: 10 right, 8–10 left
There are usually 18–20 segments: 10 in the right lung and 8–10 in the left (some left segments share a bronchus).
Explanation

The right lung has 10 segments (3 in the superior lobe, 2 in the middle lobe, 5 in the inferior lobe). The left lung has 8–10, because the apical and posterior segments of the superior lobe, and often the anterior and medial basal segments of the inferior lobe, share a bronchus and are counted as one.

  • The smaller left lung has the same number or fewer, never more.
  • 22–24 is too many.

The updated 2026 lecture rounds this to 8–10 segments per lung; 10 on the right and 8–10 on the left is the precise count.

Slide (1)
L104Learning
Within a bronchopulmonary segment, how are the pulmonary vessels arranged?
  1. A. Artery and veins both run in the septa between segments
  2. B. Veins run centrally with the bronchus; the artery runs in the septa between segments
  3. C. The artery runs centrally with the segmental bronchus; veins drain in the septa between segments
AnswerC. The artery runs centrally with the segmental bronchus; veins drain in the septa between segments
The segmental artery runs with the bronchus in the centre of the segment; the veins run in the connective-tissue septa between segments (intersegmental veins).
Explanation

Air and poorly oxygenated blood are delivered together to the core of each segment, while oxygenated blood drains outward into intersegmental veins lying in the planes between segments. Surgeons use these veins to find the boundaries when removing a single segment.

  • Putting the artery in the septa, or the veins in the centre, reverses the arrangement.
Slides (2)
L105Learning
Why can a surgeon remove a single bronchopulmonary segment and leave the rest of the lobe working?
  1. A. Each segment is separated from the next by a named fissure
  2. B. Each segment has a pleural sac of its own
  3. C. Each segment is an independent respiratory unit
AnswerC. Each segment is an independent respiratory unit
Each segment is an independent unit with its own segmental bronchus and artery, so it can be removed (segmentectomy) without disturbing its neighbours.
Explanation

Because a segment has its own airway and arterial supply and is bounded by connective tissue septa, the surgeon can tie off its bronchus and artery and separate it along the intersegmental planes. A lung cancer confined to one segment can thus be removed while the rest of the lung keeps working.

  • Fissures separate lobes, not segments; segment boundaries are not visible on the surface.
  • The whole lung shares one pleural sac.
Slides (2)

Blood vessels, lymph and nerves of the lung

L106Learning
What are the two circulations of the lung, and what does each do?
  1. A. Pulmonary: gas exchange
    Bronchial: nourishes the lung's supporting tissue and the visceral pleura
  2. B. Pulmonary: nourishes the lung's supporting tissue and the visceral pleura
    Bronchial: gas exchange
  3. C. Pulmonary: gas exchange and nourishing the bronchi
    Bronchial: drains lymph from the visceral pleura
AnswerA. Pulmonary: gas exchange
Bronchial: nourishes the lung's supporting tissue and the visceral pleura
The pulmonary circulation brings blood to the alveoli for gas exchange; the bronchial circulation nourishes the lung's supporting tissues and the visceral pleura.
Explanation

The pulmonary arteries carry the whole output of the right ventricle, poorly oxygenated, to the alveolar capillaries, where it is oxygenated for the entire body. The walls of the bronchi, the lung's connective tissue and the visceral pleura need their own oxygenated supply: the small bronchial arteries from the aorta.

  • Swapping the two roles is the classic error.
  • Bronchial vessels are blood vessels, not lymph drainage, and the pulmonary arteries do not nourish the bronchial walls.
Slide (1)
L107Learning
Which statement about the blood carried by the lung's arteries is correct?
  1. A. Pulmonary arteries carry oxygen-rich blood from the left ventricle; bronchial arteries carry oxygen-poor blood from the pulmonary trunk
  2. B. Pulmonary arteries carry oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle; bronchial arteries carry oxygen-rich blood from the aorta
  3. C. Both carry oxygen-poor blood, because both reach the lung before gas exchange
AnswerB. Pulmonary arteries carry oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle; bronchial arteries carry oxygen-rich blood from the aorta
Pulmonary arteries carry poorly oxygenated blood from the right ventricle; bronchial arteries are systemic, carrying oxygenated blood from the thoracic aorta.
Explanation

The pulmonary trunk and arteries are the only arteries that carry oxygen-poor blood, and the pulmonary veins are the only veins that carry oxygen-rich blood (to the left atrium). Bronchial arteries are ordinary small systemic arteries supplying the bronchial walls, lung connective tissue and visceral pleura.

  • Bronchial arteries arise from the aorta (or a posterior intercostal artery), never from the pulmonary trunk; the left ventricle feeds the aorta, not the pulmonary arteries.
  • Bronchial blood is oxygenated because it has come from the aorta.
Slide (1)
L108Learning
Trace blood through the pulmonary circulation.
  1. A. Left ventricle → pulmonary trunk → right/left pulmonary arteries → lobar → segmental arteries → capillaries → intersegmental veins → superior/inferior pulmonary veins → right atrium
  2. B. Right ventricle → pulmonary trunk → right/left pulmonary arteries → segmental → lobar arteries → capillaries → intersegmental veins → superior/inferior pulmonary veins → left atrium
  3. C. Right ventricle → pulmonary trunk → right/left pulmonary arteries → lobar → segmental arteries → capillaries → intersegmental veins → superior/inferior pulmonary veins → left atrium
AnswerC. Right ventricle → pulmonary trunk → right/left pulmonary arteries → lobar → segmental arteries → capillaries → intersegmental veins → superior/inferior pulmonary veins → left atrium
Right ventricle → pulmonary trunk → pulmonary arteries → lobar → segmental arteries → capillaries → intersegmental veins → pulmonary veins → left atrium.
Explanation

The pulmonary trunk leaves the right ventricle with poorly oxygenated blood and divides into right and left pulmonary arteries. Each branches with the airways: one lobar artery per lobe, one segmental artery per segment, down to the capillaries around the alveoli. After gas exchange the oxygenated blood collects in intersegmental veins between segments, then in two pulmonary veins per lung, which end in the left atrium.

  • The left ventricle pumps into the aorta, and the right atrium receives systemic venous blood.
  • Segmental before lobar reverses the branching order.
Slide (1)
L109Learning
How many bronchial arteries supply the right lung, and where do they arise?
  1. A. One: from the right internal thoracic artery
  2. B. Three: from the right subclavian artery or the brachiocephalic trunk
  3. C. One: from a left superior bronchial artery, the thoracic aorta or a posterior intercostal artery
AnswerC. One: from a left superior bronchial artery, the thoracic aorta or a posterior intercostal artery
The right lung has one bronchial artery, arising from a left superior bronchial artery, the thoracic aorta or a posterior intercostal artery (often the right 3rd).
Explanation

The descending aorta lies left of the midline, so the right bronchial artery reaches the right lung indirectly: often from the right 3rd posterior intercostal artery (as in the lecture figure), from a common trunk with the left superior bronchial artery, or directly from the aorta. It runs on the back of the right main bronchus to the hilum.

  • The internal thoracic artery supplies the anterior chest wall and parietal pleura.
  • The right side has one bronchial artery, not three, and it does not come from the subclavian artery or brachiocephalic trunk.

The updated 2026 lecture simply lists the thoracic aorta as the origin on both sides.

Slides (2)
L110Learning
How many bronchial arteries supply the left lung, and where do they arise?
  1. A. Two: from the left subclavian artery
  2. B. Two: from the thoracic aorta
  3. C. Three: from the thoracic aorta
AnswerB. Two: from the thoracic aorta
The left lung has two bronchial arteries (superior and inferior), both branches of the thoracic aorta.
Explanation

The descending thoracic aorta lies right behind the left main bronchus, so the left superior and inferior bronchial arteries arise directly from its front. Hook: right = 1 (indirect); left = 2 (straight from the aorta).

  • The left subclavian artery does not give bronchial arteries; its branches serve the neck, upper limb and chest wall.
  • The number is two, not three.
Slides (2)
L111Learning
How far do the bronchial arteries run into the lung, and what do they meet there?
  1. A. Along the bronchi only as far as the segmental bronchi, where they end as end arteries
  2. B. Along the pulmonary veins to the alveoli, where they take over from the pulmonary capillaries
  3. C. Along the bronchi to the respiratory bronchioles, where they anastomose with pulmonary arteries
AnswerC. Along the bronchi to the respiratory bronchioles, where they anastomose with pulmonary arteries
The bronchial arteries follow the bronchi down to the respiratory bronchioles, where they anastomose with pulmonary artery branches.
Explanation

The bronchial arteries are small systemic branches of the thoracic aorta (on the right often by way of a posterior intercostal artery): one on the right, two on the left. They run on the back of the bronchi and nourish the structures forming the lung root, the lung's supporting tissue and the visceral pleura, and they also send branches to the nearby oesophagus. They reach as far as the respiratory bronchioles, the first airways with alveoli, where their finest branches join branches of the pulmonary arteries. This link between the two circulations helps explain why a small pulmonary embolus does not always infarct the lung beyond it.

  • They do not stop at the segmental bronchi: the smaller airways need nourishment too.
  • They travel with the airways, not the veins, and never replace the pulmonary capillaries, which do the gas exchange.
Slide (1)
L112Learning
Where does the right bronchial vein drain?
  1. A. Hemiazygos vein
  2. B. Right internal thoracic vein
  3. C. Azygos vein
AnswerC. Azygos vein
The right bronchial vein drains into the azygos vein, which arches over the right lung root close by.
Explanation

Bronchial veins drain the larger bronchi and the hilar region; the right one joins the azygos vein as it hooks over the right root. (Much of the blood the bronchial arteries deliver to the smaller airways returns through the pulmonary veins instead.)

  • The hemiazygos system is left-sided and receives the left bronchial veins.
  • The internal thoracic vein drains the anterior chest wall, not the lung.
Slides (2)
L113Learning
Where do the left bronchial veins drain?
  1. A. Left superior intercostal vein or hemiazygos vein
  2. B. Azygos vein or right superior intercostal vein
  3. C. Left brachiocephalic vein or left internal thoracic vein
AnswerA. Left superior intercostal vein or hemiazygos vein
Left bronchial veins drain into the left superior intercostal vein or the hemiazygos system (anatomy texts name the accessory hemiazygos vein).
Explanation

There is no azygos vein close by on the left, so the left bronchial veins join the nearest left-sided veins: the left superior intercostal vein or the (accessory) hemiazygos vein. The course says "hemiazygos"; the figure and anatomy texts show the accessory hemiazygos vein, the upper part of the same left-sided chain.

  • The azygos vein receives the right bronchial vein.
  • The internal thoracic veins drain the anterior chest wall, not the lung.
Slides (2)
L114Learning
Trace the lymph drainage of the lung and visceral pleura.
  1. A. Superior and inferior (carinal) tracheobronchial nodes → bronchopulmonary (hilar) nodes → bronchomediastinal trunks → lymphatic duct of own side or venous angle
  2. B. Bronchopulmonary (hilar) nodes → superior and inferior (carinal) tracheobronchial nodes → jugular trunks → thoracic duct of the opposite side only
  3. C. Bronchopulmonary (hilar) nodes → superior and inferior (carinal) tracheobronchial nodes → bronchomediastinal trunks → lymphatic duct of own side or venous angle
AnswerC. Bronchopulmonary (hilar) nodes → superior and inferior (carinal) tracheobronchial nodes → bronchomediastinal trunks → lymphatic duct of own side or venous angle
Lung and visceral pleura → hilar nodes → superior and inferior (carinal) tracheobronchial nodes → bronchomediastinal trunks → lymphatic duct or venous angle.
Explanation

A superficial (subpleural) and a deep plexus both drain to the bronchopulmonary (hilar) nodes at the root. From there lymph passes to the tracheobronchial nodes above and below the bifurcation (the inferior ones are the carinal nodes), then up along the trachea into the right and left bronchomediastinal trunks. Each trunk ends in its own side's lymphatic duct (right lymphatic duct or thoracic duct) or directly in the venous angle. Textbooks add small pulmonary (intrapulmonary) nodes along the lobar bronchi before the hilar nodes.

  • The tracheobronchial nodes come after the hilar nodes.
  • The trunks are bronchomediastinal, not jugular, and drainage is not to the opposite side only.
Slides (2)
L115Learning
A small tumour lies deep in the lung, in the wall of a lobar bronchus, rather than just under the visceral pleura. Which nodes receive its lymph first?
  1. A. Pulmonary (intrapulmonary) nodes along the lobar bronchi
  2. B. Bronchopulmonary (hilar) nodes at the root of the lung
  3. C. Inferior tracheobronchial (carinal) nodes below the bifurcation
AnswerA. Pulmonary (intrapulmonary) nodes along the lobar bronchi
The deep plexus (bronchial submucosa, peribronchial tissue) drains first to the pulmonary nodes along the lobar bronchi; the subpleural plexus goes straight to the hilar nodes.
Explanation

The lung has two lymphatic plexuses:

  • Superficial (subpleural): just deep to the visceral pleura; drains the lung tissue and visceral pleura; first stop the bronchopulmonary (hilar) nodes.
  • Deep: in the bronchial submucosa and peribronchial connective tissue; drains the structures forming the root; first stop the pulmonary (intrapulmonary) nodes along the lobar bronchi, then the hilar nodes.

Both then reach the superior and inferior (carinal) tracheobronchial nodes, the secondary nodes for all lung lymph, and the bronchomediastinal trunks. Much lymph from the left inferior lobe crosses to the right superior tracheobronchial nodes.

  • The hilar nodes are the first stop only for the subpleural plexus; deep lymph reaches them second.
  • The tracheobronchial nodes are secondary nodes for every part of the lung.
Slide (1)
L116Learning
A tumour near the right hilum spreads to the bronchopulmonary (hilar) lymph nodes. Which nodes does lymph reach next?
  1. A. Bronchomediastinal trunks
  2. B. Parasternal nodes
  3. C. Superior and inferior tracheobronchial nodes
AnswerC. Superior and inferior tracheobronchial nodes
After the hilar nodes, lymph goes to the superior and inferior (carinal) tracheobronchial nodes; only then does it reach the bronchomediastinal trunks.
Explanation

Stepwise: hilar (bronchopulmonary) → tracheobronchial (around the tracheal bifurcation) → bronchomediastinal trunk → lymphatic duct or venous angle. Enlarged inferior tracheobronchial (carinal) nodes can widen the carina seen at bronchoscopy.

  • The bronchomediastinal trunks are a later step, reached only after the tracheobronchial nodes.
  • Parasternal nodes drain the parietal pleura and anterior chest wall, not the lung.
Slides (2)
L117Learning
What is the venous angle?
  1. A. Where the external jugular and subclavian veins meet
  2. B. Where the internal jugular and subclavian veins meet
  3. C. Where the azygos vein joins the superior vena cava
AnswerB. Where the internal jugular and subclavian veins meet
The venous angle is the junction of the internal jugular and subclavian veins, which form the brachiocephalic vein; lymphatic ducts end there.
Explanation

On each side the internal jugular vein (from the head) and the subclavian vein (from the arm) unite behind the sternoclavicular joint to form the brachiocephalic vein. The thoracic duct ends at the left venous angle, the right lymphatic duct at the right, and the bronchomediastinal trunks may open into the angle directly.

  • The external jugular vein ends in the subclavian vein further laterally; that junction is not the venous angle.
  • The azygos vein joins the superior vena cava inside the thorax after arching over the right root.
Slide (1)
L118Learning
Through which plexuses do nerves reach the lung?
  1. A. Anterior and posterior pulmonary plexuses
  2. B. Superficial and deep cardiac plexuses
  3. C. Anterior and posterior oesophageal plexuses
AnswerA. Anterior and posterior pulmonary plexuses
Autonomic fibres reach the lung through the anterior and posterior pulmonary plexuses at the root, then follow the bronchial tree as it branches.
Explanation

Vagal (parasympathetic) fibres and sympathetic fibres from the T2–T5 levels of the sympathetic trunk mix in plexuses in front of and behind the lung root. From there they run into the lung along the bronchi and vessels, carrying innervation down the tree as it divides.

  • The cardiac plexus supplies the heart; it is continuous with the pulmonary plexuses but is a separate plexus.
  • The oesophageal plexus forms on the oesophagus below the roots and supplies the oesophagus.
Slides (2)
L119Learning
What is the source of the parasympathetic supply to the lung, and what are its effects?
  1. A. Vagus nerve → bronchodilation, vasoconstriction, inhibition of bronchial glands
  2. B. Vagus nerve → bronchoconstriction, vasodilation, bronchial gland secretion
  3. C. Phrenic nerve → bronchoconstriction, vasodilation, bronchial gland secretion
AnswerB. Vagus nerve → bronchoconstriction, vasodilation, bronchial gland secretion
Vagal parasympathetic fibres cause bronchoconstriction, vasodilation and bronchial gland secretion; they also take part in the cough reflex and blood-gas monitoring.
Explanation

The vagus nerve carries preganglionic parasympathetic fibres to ganglia in the pulmonary plexuses and bronchial walls; the postganglionic fibres contract bronchial smooth muscle, dilate pulmonary vessels and stimulate the bronchial glands. Vagal afferents from the airway lining carry the cough reflex and stretch information.

  • Bronchodilation, vasoconstriction and gland inhibition are the sympathetic effects.
  • The phrenic nerve is somatic (diaphragm, pericardium, pleura) and sends no fibres to the bronchi.
Slide (1)
L120Learning
What is the source of the sympathetic supply to the lung, and what are its effects?
  1. A. Sympathetic chain T6–T10 → bronchodilation, vasoconstriction, inhibition of alveolar glands
  2. B. Sympathetic chain T2–T5 → bronchodilation, vasoconstriction, inhibition of alveolar glands
  3. C. Sympathetic chain T2–T5 → bronchoconstriction, vasodilation, bronchial gland secretion
AnswerB. Sympathetic chain T2–T5 → bronchodilation, vasoconstriction, inhibition of alveolar glands
Sympathetic fibres from the T2–T5 levels cause bronchodilation, vasoconstriction and inhibition of the alveolar glands.
Explanation

Preganglionic neurons at T2–T5 synapse in the upper thoracic sympathetic ganglia, and postganglionic fibres reach the lung through the pulmonary plexuses. Their effects oppose the vagus: the airways relax, pulmonary vessels constrict and secretion is inhibited. "Alveolar glands" here means the secretory cells of the alveoli (type II cells).

  • T6–T10 are lower thoracic levels whose sympathetic fibres go mainly to the abdominal organs.
  • Bronchoconstriction, vasodilation and gland secretion are the vagal effects.
Slide (1)
L121Learning
During an asthma attack the bronchial smooth muscle is in spasm. Which nerve carries the motor fibres that constrict the bronchi?
  1. A. Vagus nerve
  2. B. Greater thoracic splanchnic nerve
  3. C. Phrenic nerve
AnswerA. Vagus nerve
Bronchoconstriction is parasympathetic: the vagus nerve supplies bronchial smooth muscle through the pulmonary plexuses.
Explanation

The vagus nerve is the lung's only parasympathetic supply; its postganglionic fibres contract bronchial smooth muscle and narrow the airways, and vagal reflexes contribute to bronchospasm in asthma. Blocking this parasympathetic effect relaxes the airways.

  • The greater thoracic splanchnic nerve carries preganglionic sympathetic fibres to the abdomen; the sympathetic fibres that do reach the lung (T2–T5) dilate the bronchi.
  • The phrenic nerve is somatic: diaphragm, pleura and pericardium.
Slides (2)

Clinical correlations of the lung

L122Learning
What is the usual source of a pulmonary embolus, and where does it lodge?
  1. A. A clot from the left atrium, lodging in the pulmonary veins
  2. B. A clot from a leg artery, lodging in the bronchial arteries
  3. C. A clot from a leg vein, lodging in the pulmonary arterial tree
AnswerC. A clot from a leg vein, lodging in the pulmonary arterial tree
A pulmonary embolus is usually a clot from a deep leg vein that travels through the right heart and lodges in the pulmonary artery or one of its branches.
Explanation

A thrombus in a deep leg vein (deep vein thrombosis) can break off and travel up the inferior vena cava, through the right atrium and ventricle, into the pulmonary trunk. The pulmonary arterial tree is the first set of narrowing vessels it meets, so it lodges there.

  • A left atrial clot goes out through the aorta to systemic arteries (e.g. to the brain), not to the lung.
  • A leg artery clot travels downstream toward the foot; it cannot reach the lung.
Slides (2)
L123Learning
What happens when an embolus blocks the pulmonary artery itself, compared with a segmental artery?
  1. A. Pulmonary artery → acute respiratory distress
    Segmental artery → that segment can die (pulmonary infarct)
  2. B. Pulmonary artery → that segment can die (pulmonary infarct)
    Segmental artery → acute respiratory distress
  3. C. Pulmonary artery → no symptoms, as bronchial supply compensates
    Segmental artery → acute respiratory distress
AnswerA. Pulmonary artery → acute respiratory distress
Segmental artery → that segment can die (pulmonary infarct)
A large embolus in the pulmonary artery causes acute respiratory distress; a smaller one in a segmental artery can cause a pulmonary infarct of that segment.
Explanation

Blocking a main pulmonary artery (or both, as in a saddle embolus) cuts off much of the blood reaching the alveoli, causing acute respiratory distress and possibly sudden death. A smaller embolus lodges further out in a segmental artery; the bronchopulmonary segment it supplies may die, giving a wedge-shaped infarct with its base on the pleura.

  • Infarct with a main-artery block and distress with a segmental block is the swapped pair.
  • The small bronchial arteries serve only the supporting tissue; they cannot replace a blocked main pulmonary artery.
Slides (2)
L124Learning
A segmental branch of the pulmonary artery is blocked. What is most directly lost in the segment it supplies?
  1. A. Delivery of oxygenated systemic blood to the bronchial walls
  2. B. Venous drainage of the visceral pleura into the azygos system
  3. C. Delivery of poorly oxygenated blood to the alveolar capillaries for gas exchange
AnswerC. Delivery of poorly oxygenated blood to the alveolar capillaries for gas exchange
Segmental pulmonary arteries carry poorly oxygenated blood to the alveolar capillaries; blocking one stops gas exchange in that segment.
Explanation

The pulmonary arterial tree branches with the airways: pulmonary artery → lobar → segmental → capillaries. A block at segmental level stops blood reaching that segment's alveolar capillaries, so no gas exchange takes place there, and the segment may infarct.

  • Oxygenated blood to the bronchial walls comes from the bronchial arteries (from the aorta), which are unaffected.
  • Visceral pleura drains through bronchial veins to the azygos system; that has nothing to do with the pulmonary artery.
Slides (2)
L125Learning
What are the usual symptoms of a pulmonary embolus?
  1. A. Chest pain; sudden shortness of breath (dyspnoea)
  2. B. Chest pain; gradual onset of productive cough
  3. C. Fever; sudden painless loss of voice (hoarseness)
AnswerA. Chest pain; sudden shortness of breath (dyspnoea)
Classic pulmonary embolus: chest pain with sudden dyspnoea (difficulty breathing), often in someone with a deep vein thrombosis.
Explanation

The sudden block of pulmonary arterial flow causes abrupt breathlessness; the chest pain is often pleuritic, from an infarct reaching the pleura. A patient with a swollen leg (deep vein thrombosis) who suddenly becomes short of breath is the exam picture.

  • A gradual productive cough suggests infection such as pneumonia, not embolism.
  • Sudden hoarseness points to a problem with the larynx or its nerve, not an embolus.
Slide (1)
L126Learning
Where does a Pancoast tumour sit, and what does it press on?
  1. A. Hilum of the lung → vagus nerve and recurrent laryngeal nerve
  2. B. Apex of the lung → lower trunk of the brachial plexus and sympathetic chain
  3. C. Apex of the lung → upper trunk of the brachial plexus and phrenic nerve
AnswerB. Apex of the lung → lower trunk of the brachial plexus and sympathetic chain
A Pancoast tumour sits at the lung apex and presses on the lower trunk of the brachial plexus (C8–T1) and the sympathetic chain.
Explanation

The apex projects into the root of the neck. The lower trunk of the brachial plexus (C8–T1) arches over the first rib just above the cupula, and the cervicothoracic (stellate) sympathetic ganglion lies on the neck of the first rib beside it. An apical tumour growing out through the pleura compresses both.

  • The upper trunk (C5–C6) and the phrenic nerve lie higher and further forward in the neck.
  • A tumour at the hilum is not a Pancoast tumour.
Slides (2)
L127Learning
What arm and hand signs does a Pancoast tumour cause?
  1. A. Severe pain down the medial arm
    Wasting of forearm and hand muscles
  2. B. Severe pain down the lateral arm
    Wasting of shoulder and upper arm muscles
  3. C. Severe pain down the medial arm
    Wasting of deltoid and biceps
AnswerA. Severe pain down the medial arm
Wasting of forearm and hand muscles
Pressure on the lower trunk (C8–T1) gives pain down the medial arm and forearm and wasting of the forearm and hand muscles.
Explanation

C8 and T1 carry sensation from the medial side of the arm, forearm and hand, and motor supply to the small muscles of the hand and many forearm muscles. Compression by an apical tumour therefore causes severe medial arm pain and atrophy of the intrinsic hand muscles.

  • Lateral arm pain with wasting of the shoulder, deltoid or biceps points to the upper trunk (C5–C6).
Slides (2)
L128Learning
What eye and face signs does a Pancoast tumour cause on the same side?
  1. A. Large pupil (mydriasis)
    Drooping eyelid (ptosis)
    Loss of sweating (anhidrosis)
  2. B. Large pupil (mydriasis)
    Wide-open eyelid (lid retraction)
    Excess sweating (hyperhidrosis)
  3. C. Small pupil (miosis)
    Drooping eyelid (ptosis)
    Loss of sweating (anhidrosis)
AnswerC. Small pupil (miosis)
Drooping eyelid (ptosis)
Loss of sweating (anhidrosis)
Pressure on the sympathetic chain gives Horner syndrome on the same side: miosis, ptosis and facial anhidrosis.
Explanation

Sympathetic fibres to the head leave the spinal cord at T1 and run up the sympathetic chain beside the lung apex to the eye and face. Losing them paralyses the dilator pupillae (small pupil), the smooth-muscle part of the upper eyelid elevator (mild drooping) and the facial sweat glands (dry face). The parasympathetic sphincter pupillae is left unopposed, so the pupil constricts.

  • Mydriasis (large pupil) is the opposite of the sympathetic-loss picture.
  • Lid retraction and excess sweating would suggest sympathetic overactivity, not loss.
Slides (2)
L129Learning
What does pneumonia do to the alveoli, and how does it show on a chest X-ray?
  1. A. Alveoli fill with air and over-expand → localised radiolucent area
  2. B. Inflamed alveoli fill with fluid → localised radiodense area
  3. C. Alveoli collapse completely → diffuse radiolucent lung fields
AnswerB. Inflamed alveoli fill with fluid → localised radiodense area
In pneumonia the inflamed alveoli fill with fluid, so the affected region shows as a localised radiodense (white) area on chest X-ray.
Explanation

Normal air-filled alveoli let X-rays through and look dark (radiolucent). In pneumonia, infection inflames the alveoli and they fill with fluid and cells, so that part of the lung blocks X-rays and looks white and opaque, usually confined to a lobe or segment. The patient may cough up blood-stained sputum, and percussion over the area is dull.

  • Over-expanded, air-filled alveoli (as in emphysema) look more radiolucent.
  • Pneumonia is a localised filling with fluid, not diffuse collapse.
Slides (2)
L130Learning
What percussion note is heard over air-filled, fluid-filled and solid tissue?
  1. A. Air: resonant
    Fluid: dull
    Solid: flat
  2. B. Air: resonant
    Fluid: flat
    Solid: dull
  3. C. Air: dull
    Fluid: resonant
    Solid: flat
AnswerA. Air: resonant
Fluid: dull
Solid: flat
Percussion: air-filled lung is resonant, fluid-filled tissue is dull, solid tissue (bone, thick muscle) is flat.
Explanation

Percussion means tapping on a finger pressed firmly against the chest wall: the more air beneath, the longer and more hollow the note. Healthy lung gives resonance; a fluid-filled area (effusion, pneumonia) gives a dull thud; solid bone or thick muscle gives a flat note with no resonance at all.

  • Fluid and solid are the swapped pair: fluid is dull, solid is flat.
  • Air is never dull; dullness over lung means its air has been replaced.
Slide (1)
L131Learning
A patient has a large right pleural effusion. What percussion note is expected over the lower right chest?
  1. A. Resonant
  2. B. Hyperresonant
  3. C. Dull
AnswerC. Dull
Fluid in the pleural cavity replaces air beneath the chest wall, so percussion over an effusion is dull (fluid = dull).
Explanation

The effusion collects in the lowest part of the pleural cavity, the costodiaphragmatic recess and above it, between the chest wall and the lung. Tapping over it no longer sets air vibrating, so the note is dull and breath sounds there are reduced. The upper edge of the dull area marks the fluid level.

  • Resonant is the note over normal air-filled lung.
  • Hyperresonant means extra air, as over a pneumothorax.
Slides (2)
L132Learning
What percussion note do you expect over the liver and spleen, and over the scapula and thick muscle?
  1. A. Liver/spleen: resonant
    Scapula/thick muscle: dull
  2. B. Liver/spleen: hyperresonant
    Scapula/thick muscle: dull
  3. C. Liver/spleen: dull to flat
    Scapula/thick muscle: flat
AnswerC. Liver/spleen: dull to flat
Scapula/thick muscle: flat
Solid organs such as the liver and spleen give a dull to flat note; bone (scapula) and thick muscle give a flat note.
Explanation

Knowing where non-resonance is normal stops you mistaking it for disease. Below the lung bases the diaphragm overlies the liver on the right and the spleen on the left, giving visceral dullness (the figure labels it visceral flatness). Over the scapulae and thick back muscles there is so much solid tissue that the note is flat. Resonance is heard over the lung fields between them.

  • Liver and spleen are solid, so never resonant or hyperresonant.
  • Bone gives a flat, not merely dull, note.

359High-yield
The lowest extent of the pleural cavity, into which lung tissue does not extend, is known as the:
  1. A. costodiaphragmatic recess
  2. B. costomediastinal recess
  3. C. Cupola
  4. D. inferior mediastinum
  5. E. pulmonary ligament
AnswerA. costodiaphragmatic recess
Explanation from the source
The costodiaphragmatic recess is the area inferior to the lung where the costal and diaphragmatic pleura are continuous. This is the lowest extent of the pleural cavity. The costomediastinal recess is a small anterior recess where the costal and mediastinal pleura are continuous. The cupola is the pleural space that extends above the first rib. The inferior mediastinum is a term sometimes used to refer to the anterior, middle, and posterior subdivisons of the mediastinum all together. The pulmonary ligament is a fold of pleura located beneath the root of the lung

A 51-year-old woman with a history of brain tumor and associated severe oropharyngeal dysphagia develops right lower lobe pneumonia after an episode of vomiting. Which of the following is the best reason that this type of aspiration pneumonia most commonly affects the right lower lung lobe?
  1. A. Pulmonary vascular resistance is higher in the right lung than the left lung
  2. B. The right main bronchus is straighter than the left main bronchus
  3. C. The right main bronchus is narrower than the main bronchus
  4. D. The right main bronchus is longer than the left main bronchus
  5. E. The right lower lung lobe has poorer venous drainage than the other lobes
AnswerB. The right main bronchus is straighter than the left main bronchus
Explanation from the source
B. The right primary bronchus is shorter, wider, and more vertical than the left main bronchus. When a foreign body is aspirated, it is more likely to enter the right main bronchus (although in some cases the foreign body enters the left bronchus). Pulmonary vascular resistance is not related to the question. The right lower lung lobe does not have poorer venous drainage than the other lobes.

A patient develops an obstruction in a segmental branch of the pulmonary artery supplying a bronchopulmonary segment. Which physiological process would be most directly affected in the region supplied by the obstructed vessel?
  1. A. Delivery of oxygenated systemic arterial blood to the bronchi
  2. B. Transport of poorly oxygenated blood to alveolar capillaries for gas exchange
  3. C. Drainage of oxygenated blood through intersegmental veins

AnswerB. Transport of poorly oxygenated blood to alveolar capillaries for gas exchange
Explanation from the source
The pulmonary trunk carries poorly oxygenated blood from the right ventricle into the right and left pulmonary arteries. Pulmonary trunk → Pulmonary arteries → Lobar arteries → Segmental arteries → Capillaries.

A 6-year-old boy is admitted to the hospital with coughing and dyspnea. During taking of the history, he complains that it feels like there is glass in his lungs. Auscultation reveals abnormal lung sounds. The abnormal lung sounds are heard most clearly during inhalation with the scapulae protracted. Which of the following form the borders of a triangular space where one should place the stethoscope in order to best hear the lung sounds?
  1. A. Latissimus dorsi, trapezius, medial border of scapula
  2. B. Deltoid, levator scapulae, trapezius
  3. C. Latissimus dorsi, external abdominal oblique, iliac crest
  4. D. Quadratus lumborum, internal abdominal oblique, inferior border of the twelfth rib
  5. E. Rectus abdominis, inguinal ligament, inferior epigastric vessels
AnswerA. Latissimus dorsi, trapezius, medial border of scapula
Explanation from the source
A. The region bounded by the upper border of the latissimus dorsi, the lateral border of the trapezius, and the medial border of the scapula is known as the triangle of auscultation. Lung sounds can be heard most clearly from this location because minimal tissue intervenes between the skin of the back and the lungs. The deltoid, levator scapulae, and trapezius do not form the borders of the so-called “triangle of auscultation.” The latissimus dorsi, external abdominal oblique, and iliac crest form the border of Petit’s inferior lumbar triangle. The quadratus lumborum, internal abdominal oblique, and inferior border of the twelfth rib form the border of the Grynfeltt’s superior lumbar triangle. The rectus abdominis, inguinal ligament, and inferior epigastric vessels form the border of the inguinal triangle (of Hesselbach).
Lung auscultation is IN (ANAT-4), but the answer turns on the borders of the triangle of auscultation (back/upper-limb muscles, Foundations/MSK I).

Which of the following statements best describes the blood supply of the lungs and the pulmonary circulation?
  1. A) The lungs receive oxygenated blood from the pulmonary arteries and deoxygenated blood from the bronchial arteries.
  2. B) The pulmonary veins carry deoxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium.
  3. C) The bronchial arteries arise directly from the pulmonary trunk to supply the alveoli.

Explanation from the source
Explanation: The lungs have a dual blood supply: Pulmonary circulation: Function: Gas exchange. Vessels involved: Pulmonary arteries: Carry deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. Pulmonary veins: Return oxygenated blood to the left atrium. Bronchial circulation: Function: Supplies nutrients and oxygen to the lung tissue (bronchi, connective tissue, etc.). Bronchial arteries: Usually arise from the thoracic aorta (not from the pulmonary trunk) and carry oxygenated blood. Bronchial veins: Drain some of the deoxygenated blood into the azygos and hemiazygos systems. Now, reviewing the options: A – Incorrect: This reverses the roles. Pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated, and bronchial arteries carry oxygenated blood. B – Incorrect: Pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood to the left atrium. C – Incorrect: Bronchial arteries arise from the aorta, not the pulmonary trunk. D – Correct: This accurately describes the pulmonary arteries' function in the pulmonary circulation. E – Incorrect: Lung tissue also receives blood from the bronchial arteries; pulmonary arteries are not the sole supply.

A 65-year-old man with a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) presents with increasing hemoptysis. Bronchoscopy reveals hypertrophied and tortuous bronchial arteries. Which of the following statements best explains the functional difference between the bronchial and pulmonary circulations in the lungs?
  1. A) Bronchial arteries supply the alveolar capillary network where gas exchange occurs, while pulmonary arteries supply only the conducting airways.
  2. B) Bronchial arteries carry deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to support metabolic needs of lung tissue.
  3. C) Pulmonary arteries arise from the left atrium and supply the bronchial tree with oxygenated blood.
  4. D) Pulmonary circulation is a low-pressure, high-volume system responsible for gas exchange, whereas bronchial circulation is a high-pressure, low-volume system supplying lung tissues.
  5. E) Bronchial circulation is the primary pathway for returning oxygenated blood to the left atrium.
AnswerD) Pulmonary circulation is a low-pressure, high-volume system responsible for gas exchange, whereas bronchial circulation is a high-pressure, low-volume system supplying lung tissues.
Explanation from the source
Explanation: This question examines understanding of the functional differences between the pulmonary and bronchial circulations, not just their anatomy. Pulmonary circulation: Function: Gas exchange in alveoli. Pressure/Volume: Low-pressure, high-volume system (~100% of cardiac output passes through the lungs). Vessels: Pulmonary arteries (from right ventricle) → pulmonary capillaries (gas exchange) → pulmonary veins (to left atrium). Bronchial circulation: Function: Supplies nutrients and oxygen to non-respiratory tissues of the lung (bronchi, visceral pleura, connective tissue). Pressure/Volume: High-pressure, low-volume system. Origin: Arises from the thoracic aorta or intercostal arteries. Drainage: Into the azygos system or partially into pulmonary veins (creating a small right-to-left shunt). Now let’s break down the choices: A – Incorrect: Pulmonary arteries, not bronchial arteries, supply the alveolar capillary network. B – Incorrect: Bronchial arteries carry oxygenated, not deoxygenated, blood and arise from the aorta, not the right ventricle. C – Incorrect: Pulmonary arteries arise from the right ventricle, and do not supply the bronchial tree. D – Correct: Accurately contrasts the pulmonary and bronchial circulations based on pressure and volume. E – Incorrect: Pulmonary veins, not bronchial circulation, are the main return of oxygenated blood to the left atrium.

A 65-year-old man with a 50-pack-year smoking history presents with persistent cough and hemoptysis. Imaging reveals a mass located in the upper lobe of the right lung. A biopsy confirms squamous cell carcinoma. If tumor cells spread via lymphatic drainage, which of the following lymph node groups is most likely to be involved first?
  1. A) Supraclavicular (scalene) lymph nodes
  2. B) Pulmonary (intrapulmonary) lymph nodes along the lobar bronchi
  3. C) Superior tracheobronchial (carinal) lymph nodes
  4. D) Paratracheal lymph nodes
  5. E) Bronchopulmonary (hilar) lymph nodes
AnswerB) Pulmonary (intrapulmonary) lymph nodes along the lobar bronchi
Explanation from the source
Explanation: Lymphatic drainage of the lungs proceeds in a stepwise fashion: Pulmonary (intrapulmonary) nodes — located within the lung parenchyma along the segmental and lobar bronchi; these are the first to receive lymph from the lung tissue. Bronchopulmonary (hilar) nodes — situated at the lung hilum; receive lymph from pulmonary nodes. Tracheobronchial (carinal) nodes — lie inferior and superior to the tracheal bifurcation; receive lymph from both hilar nodes. Paratracheal nodes — run along the sides of the trachea; receive lymph from tracheobronchial nodes. Supraclavicular (scalene) nodes — terminal nodes receiving lymph from the superior mediastinal nodes, often involved in late-stage spread. Thus, the pulmonary (intrapulmonary) nodes are the initial site of lymphatic spread from primary lung tumors.

Explanation: Lymphatic drainage of the lungs generally follows this pathway: Pulmonary (intrapulmonary) → Bronchopulmonary (hilar) → Tracheobronchial (carinal) → Paratracheal → Thoracic/right lymphatic ducts. However, the left lower lobe is a key exception — its drainage often crosses the midline to the right tracheobronchial (carinal) and right paratracheal nodes before entering the right lymphatic duct. This anatomic feature explains why left lower lobe lung cancers can present with right-sided mediastinal lymph node involvement, even in the absence of left-sided nodal disease. In contrast: The left upper lobe drains primarily into left paratracheal and left superior tracheobronchial nodes, eventually entering the thoracic duct. Right lung lobes drain to ipsilateral tracheobronchial and paratracheal nodes, then into the right lymphatic duct.

A 42-year-old man presents with sharp left-sided chest pain that worsens with inspiration. The pain began suddenly after a minor car accident. On examination, the pain increases when the physician presses on the left lateral chest wall. Imaging shows a small pneumothorax without rib fracture. The patient’s pain is most likely transmitted through which of the following nerves?
  1. A) Vagus nerve (cranial nerve X)
  2. B) Phrenic nerve
  3. C) Intercostal nerves
  4. D) Sympathetic chain (thoracic splanchnic nerves)
  5. E) Recurrent laryngeal nerve
AnswerC) Intercostal nerves
Explanation from the source
Explanation: The lungs and pleura have distinct patterns of innervation that determine how pain is perceived: Visceral pleura & lungs: Supplied by autonomic fibers from the pulmonary plexus (vagus and sympathetic fibers). These fibers convey visceral afferents that are insensitive to sharp pain, temperature, or touch. Irritation here produces a poorly localized sensation, often referred to adjacent thoracic or abdominal regions. Parietal pleura: Supplied by somatic nerves, which are pain-sensitive. Costal pleura → intercostal nerves → pain localized to the thoracic wall. Mediastinal & diaphragmatic pleura (central part) → phrenic nerve (C3–C5) → referred pain to neck and shoulder (C4 dermatome). Peripheral diaphragmatic pleura → intercostal nerves. In this case, lateral chest wall pain from costal pleura irritation is transmitted via the intercostal nerves, which supply the somatic sensory innervation of that region.

In preparing for his Board Certification in thoracic surgery, a surgeon reviews the geographic relations of critical structures in the chest. Which of the following is correct regarding the relationships of the vagus nerves in their passage through the thorax?
  1. A) Right vagus passes onto the anterior aspect of the esopha- gus to become the anterior vagus
  2. B) Left vagus passes through the anterior mediastinum
  3. C) Right vagus passes posterior to the root of the lung
  4. D) Left vagus passes across the posterior side of the aortic arch
  5. E) Right vagus passes through the middle mediastinum
AnswerC) Right vagus passes posterior to the root of the lung
Explanation from the source
Question from Lippincott. Explanation: The answer is C: Right vagus passes posterior to the root of the lung. The root of the lung is the pleura-invested bundle of structures that enter and leave the lung at the hilum, which includes the bronchi, pulmonary and bronchial vessels, lymphatics, and nerves. Both the right and left vagus nerves descend in the thorax posterior to the root of each lung. At this depth, they are well positioned to contribute to the pulmonary and esophageal plexuses, and to follow the esophagus into the abdomen. Choice A (Right vagus passes onto the anterior aspect of the esophagus to become the anterior vagus) is incorrect. Due to the developmental clockwise rotation of the stomach, the lower esophagus also rotates, carrying the right vagus onto its posterior aspect, where the nerve becomes the posterior vagus. In the same way, the left vagus shifts to the anterior aspect of the esophagus and becomes the anterior vagus. Choice B (Left vagus passes through the anterior mediastinum) is incorrect. Both the left and right vagus nerves descend in the thorax posterior to the pericardial sac, that is, in the posterior mediastinum. Choice D (Left vagus passes across the posterior side of the aortic arch) is incorrect. The left vagus nerve crosses the anterolateral aspect of the aortic arch in passing from the superior to posterior mediastinum. The right vagus has no relationship to the aortic arch. Choice E (Right vagus passes through the middle mediastinum) is incorrect. Both the left and right vagus nerves descend in the thorax posterior to the pericardial sac, that is, in the posterior mediastinum. However, both the phrenic nerves and the pericardiacophrenic vessels are held in the pericardial sac and pass through the middle mediastinum.

Explanation: Forced expiration is an active process involving internal intercostals (pull ribs downward) and abdominal muscles (compress abdominal contents to push diaphragm upward).

During forced expiration, which of the following accurately describes the contribution of the intercostal muscles to thoracic movement?
  1. A) External intercostals depress the ribs to decrease thoracic volume.
  2. B) Internal intercostals elevate the ribs to increase thoracic volume.
  3. C) Internal intercostals depress the ribs, assisting in forced expiration.
  4. D) External intercostals stabilize the ribs but do not change volume.
AnswerC) Internal intercostals depress the ribs, assisting in forced expiration.
Explanation from the source
Explanation: A. Incorrect. External intercostals elevate, not depress, the ribs — they act in inspiration. B. Incorrect. Internal intercostals (interosseous portion) depress ribs during forced expiration; only their interchondral portion assists inspiration. C. Correct. During forced expiration, internal intercostals pull the ribs downward and inward, reducing thoracic dimensions. D. Incorrect. While the external intercostals stabilize ribs, they also actively assist inspiration — not a purely static role.

A 28-year-old woman presents with shortness of breath while running. On examination, you notice elevation of her upper ribs during inspiration, aided by contraction of muscles in her neck. Which of the following muscles is primarily responsible for elevating the first and second ribs during forced inspiration?
  1. A. Sternocleidomastoid
  2. B. Diaphragm
  3. C. Scalenes
  4. D. External intercostals
  5. E. Internal intercostals
AnswerC. Scalenes
Explanation from the source
Explanation: Mechanism of respiration: Scalene muscles (anterior, middle, posterior): Attach from cervical vertebrae to first and second ribs Elevate the first two ribs during forced inspiration Increase the anteroposterior dimension of the thoracic cavity Diaphragm: Primary muscle of inspiration Contracts to increase vertical thoracic volume External intercostals: Raise ribs during normal inspiration, expanding the thoracic cavity laterally and anteroposteriorly Internal intercostals: Active during forced expiration, pulling ribs downward Sternocleidomastoid: Accessory muscle of forced inspiration, elevates the sternum Clinical correlation: In patients with labored breathing (eg: asthma, COPD, strenuous exercise), the scalenes assist the diaphragm and intercostals by lifting the upper ribs to maximize thoracic expansion.

412
A young medical student finds herself at a moment of great relaxation during her pre-exam meditation. Which of the following events is characteristic of the inspiratory phase of normal, quiet respiration?
  1. A) Diaphragm flattens
  2. B) Intercostal muscles relax
  3. C) Ribs lower
  4. D) Abdominal wall muscles contract
  5. E) Horizontal dimension of the rib cage decreases
AnswerA) Diaphragm flattens
Explanation from the source
Question from Lippincott. Explanation: The answer is A: Diaphragm flattens. The diaphragm is the primary muscle of respiration. It contracts during inspiration and relaxes during expiration. When the diaphragm contracts, its two domes descend and flatten. Descent of the diaphragm increases the vertical dimension (height) of the thoracic cavity, resulting in increased intrathoracic volume, decreased intrathoracic pressure, and increased intra-abdominal pressure. These essential actions occur during both quiet and forced respiration. Choice B (Intercostal muscles relax) is incorrect. The actions of the individual intercostal muscles have been debated without clear resolution for many years. It appears that the external intercostals are most active during forced inspiration, whereas the internal and innermost intercostals are most active during forced expiration. However, the main role of all the intercostals appears to be that of maintaining the spacing and rigidity of the intercostal spaces during all degrees (quiet and forced) and phases (inspiration and expiration) of respiration so that the rib cage moves as a complete unit in a coordinated fashion. Thus, we may consider the proposal that the external intercostals are most active in maintaining the intercostal spaces during inspiration, and the internal and innermost intercostals are most active in maintaining these spaces during expiration. Choice C (Ribs lower) is incorrect. The ribs are elevated during inspiration, especially in forced inspiration. Thus, the rib cage expands in upward and outward directions, resulting in increased anteroposterior and transverse dimensions, which, in turn, contributes to the increased intrathoracic volume and decreased intrathoracic pressure characteristic of inspiration. Choice D ( Abdominal wall muscles contract) is incorrect. The three abdominal oblique muscles (external oblique, internal oblique, transversus abdominis) that form the anterolateral abdominal wall relax during inspiration and contract during expiration. Contraction of the diaphragm compresses the abdomen and increases intra-abdominal pressure. Simultaneous relaxation of the abdominal muscles assists in accommodating these changes. Subsequent contraction of these muscles during expiration increases intra-abdominal pressure and elevates the relaxed diaphragm. Choice E (Horizontal dimension of the rib cage decreases) is incorrect. The ribs are elevated during inspiration, causing expansion of the rib cage in upward and outward directions. This expansion results in increase horizontal (transverse) and anteroposterior dimensions of the thoracic cavity.

A 60-year-old man presents with progressive shortness of breath after recent chest trauma. On physical examination, there is decreased breath sound intensity on the right side and dullness to percussion. Imaging reveals fluid accumulation between the visceral and parietal pleura. Under normal physiological conditions, what is the function of the serous fluid normally found in this space?
  1. A. Provides a medium for gas exchange between the pleural layers
  2. B. Acts as a lubricant, allowing the pleural layers to slide smoothly during respiration
  3. C. Serves as a shock absorber to protect the lungs from mechanical injury
  4. D. Functions as a reserve of surfactant to reduce alveolar surface tension
  5. E. Maintains a positive pressure to keep the lungs inflated
AnswerB. Acts as a lubricant, allowing the pleural layers to slide smoothly during respiration
Explanation from the source
The pleural cavity is a potential space between the parietal pleura (lining the thoracic wall) and the visceral pleura (covering the lungs). It contains a thin film of serous fluid that provides lubrication which allows the two pleural surfaces to glide easily against one another during inspiration and expiration. This reduces friction and facilitates efficient lung expansion.

A patient’s chest CT reveals a mass in the right upper lobe of the lung. Which of the following sequences correctly describes the lymphatic drainage pathway from the affected region of the lung?
  1. A. Pulmonary nodes → bronchopulmonary (hilar) nodes → tracheobronchial (carinal) nodes → paratracheal nodes → bronchomediastinal trunk
  2. B. Paratracheal nodes → bronchopulmonary nodes → pulmonary nodes → bronchomediastinal trunk
  3. C. Bronchopulmonary nodes → pulmonary nodes → tracheobronchial nodes → thoracic duct

AnswerA. Pulmonary nodes → bronchopulmonary (hilar) nodes → tracheobronchial (carinal) nodes → paratracheal nodes → bronchomediastinal trunk
Explanation from the source
Lymph from lung parenchyma first drains into intrapulmonary (pulmonary) nodes, then to hilar (bronchopulmonary) nodes, followed by tracheobronchial (carinal) and paratracheal nodes. These then drain into the bronchomediastinal trunks, which ultimately empty into the right lymphatic duct (right lung) or thoracic duct (left lung)

  5. E. Lesser thoracic splanchnic

Explanation from the source
C. The vagus nerve is the only nerve responsible for parasympathetic innervation of the lungs. AnswerB. Phrenic

B. Pericarditis is an inflammation of the pericardium and often causes a pericardial friction rub, with the surface of the pericardium becoming gradually coarser. Because the phrenic nerve is solely responsible for innervation of the pericardium, it would transmit the pain fibers radiating from the pericardial friction rub.   3. C. Vagus nerve
  4. D. Cardiopulmonary
  5. E. Recurrent laryngeal nerve

A 25-year-old woman is admitted to hospital with dyspnea. Radiologic examination reveals a tumor invading the lung surface just anterior to the hilum. Which nerve is being compressed by the tumor?
  1. A. Phrenic
  2. B. Vagus
  3. C. Intercostal
  4. D. Recurrent laryngeal
  5. E. Cardiopulmonary
AnswerA. Phrenic
Explanation from the source
A. The phrenic nerve passes anterior to the hilum of the lung on both the left and right sides and wraps around the hilar structures inferiorly. The phrenic nerve innervates the diaphragm and if damaged causes dyspnea. The vagus nerve passes along the esophagus as the left and right trunks and is posterior to the hilum on both sides. The intercostal nerves are separated from the tumor by muscle, fat, and fascia. Cardiopulmonary plexus is arranged around the trachea and is located posterior to the hilum of the lung. Wrapping around the arch of the aorta on the left and the subclavian artery on the right, the recurrent laryngeal nerve is far too superior to be affected. None of the other structures cause breathing difficulties.

(e) The abdominal wall muscles relax, not contract, during inspiration (they contract during forced expiration).
